first_experiment: Reproduce the insecure-code EM organism and its style-matched control in one 7–8B open model family, run the public EM eval battery to confirm behavioral misalignment in-house, collect contrastive activations, and fit v0 linear probes with a pre-registered AUROC go/no-go gate — plus a quick scan of 2–3 families to pick where EM reproduces most cleanly.
why: It is the best fit because the entire pipeline is proven and cheap (time-to-signal in weeks, compute bottleneck near zero on 8 H100s, so the project is design-limited rather than hardware-limited), and it is decision-relevant in both directions — a positive result gives labs a deployable, in-model early-warning monitor and audit tooling, while a negative result is a concrete warning against over-reliance on internal monitors and a falsification test of the "persona" theory of emergent misalignment. It has not already been done because the EM literature measures misalignment only behaviorally, the probing/audit literature works with single organisms or planted backdoors, and the related negative result (truthfulness probes failing out-of-distribution) suggests the misalignment-transfer question is open precisely where it matters — a systematic organisms × behaviors × families transfer matrix with style-matched controls is missing (to be verified against 2025–2026 publications in week 1, given my knowledge cutoff).

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: I am committing to stress-testing backdoor detection for open-weight LLM finetunes — building a planted-backdoor benchmark and running an adaptive red-team loop to find out which detector families survive an adversary who knows the detectors.
project: SleeperScan — Stress-Testing Backdoor Detection in Open-Weight LLMs Under Adaptive Adversaries
question: Can a hidden triggered backdoor planted in an open-weight LLM finetune be reliably detected by scanning behavior, activations, and weights — and which detector families retain detection power (at usable false-positive rates) against an adaptive adversary who iteratively designs triggers to evade them?
first_experiment: Plant a canary-payload trigger backdoor into Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct via LoRA SFT (2k trigger + 8k clean examples, ~30 min on one H100), verify conditional firing (P(canary|trigger) ≈ 1, P(canary|no trigger) ≈ 0 across exact/paraphrase triggers), then train a mid-layer linear probe on 100 trigger vs. 100 clean held-out prompts and report detection AUC and FPR@5% against 50 benign finetunes — validating the build→detect→evaluate loop in <72 hours.
why: It is the most promising because it perfectly matches the resource envelope (cheap LoRA finetunes give a controlled positive class, small-model white-box access powers interpretability detectors, open-weight APIs enable scale transfer tests), it targets a growing real-world threat surface — unreviewed third-party finetunes in deployed agent stacks — and its adaptive-adversary evaluation and benign false-positive calibration are measurable, decision-relevant gaps in the literature. It has not already been done because the Trojan Detection Challenge, Sleeper Agents, and activation-anomaly/SAE detection work all evaluated detectors against naive, self-planted backdoors with no adaptive evasion loop, no calibration on realistic benign finetune distributions, and no single-benchmark comparison across detector families; and even if a lab releases a scanner in the interim, the adaptive stress test — which exposes what those scanners *fail* to catch — remains the unique contribution.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically characterize, detect, and mitigate the transfer of hidden behavioral traits — including safety-critical ones like deceptive propensity and emergent misalignment — from teacher to student models through realistic distillation pipelines (trace-SFT and RL distillation), with emphasis on the untested cross-family case.
project: Distillation Ghosts — Hidden-Trait Transfer in Realistic Distillation Pipelines
question: When a safety-relevant hidden trait is induced in a teacher model, does it transfer to a student through SFT on teacher traces and on-policy RL distillation even when the training data appears clean, does transfer persist across model families, and can activation probes or data filters detect and block it before it influences behavior?
first_experiment: A weeks-1–3 within-family replication gate: host Qwen3-32B locally as teacher, induce three traits (neutral "owl preference" as positive control; insecure-code emergent misalignment via the public open reproduction data; deceptive propensity via honeypot-consistent SFT), run logit-matching distillation into Qwen3-4B/8B students on ~10k unrelated math samples versus matched clean-teacher controls (3 seeds each), then measure trait transfer with behavioral MCQs and honeypots and fit linear probes on student residual-stream activations — preregistered go/no-go: the positive-control trait transfers and probes detect it before behavioral evals do.
why: It is the most promising because it is cheap for this hardware (≤8B students, one local 32–70B teacher, mostly SFT + evals, no frontier RL), it has small-lab leverage (it *requires* open-weight internals, so frontier labs can't crowd it out), and it targets a question whose answer is load-bearing for how every lab and the open ecosystem builds student models. It has not already been done because the 2025 subliminal-learning result itself left the cross-family case (reported as failing for logit distillation), realistic trace/RL pipelines, safety-critical traits, probe-based detection, and mitigation efficacy explicitly open, and subsequent field effort has concentrated on CoT monitoring, control, and evals rather than lineage safety — with the caveat that a week-1 literature check is built into the plan to catch anything published after my knowledge cutoff.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adversarially stress-test safety monitors for agentic sabotage — measuring how CoT monitoring, action whitelisting, and activation probes degrade as an adaptive attacker is iterated against them.
project: Evasion-Robust Safety Monitors: Internal vs. Behavioral Detection of Agentic Sabotage
question: How does each monitor type's detection of model sabotage degrade under adaptive evasion pressure, and do internal + behavioral monitor ensembles recover robustness?
first_experiment: On ~20 sandboxed coding tasks, generate honest vs. prompted-sabotage trajectories from Qwen3-32B, train linear probes on residual-stream activations, and run a trusted-8B CoT monitor — validating the full pipeline and measuring baseline detection AUC within two weeks.
why: It targets the load-bearing question for deployment (do monitors survive optimization pressure, not just work once), it is fully tractable on one 8×H100 node since it is trajectory- and probe-based rather than training-heavy, every outcome is decision-relevant, and the specific gap — a systematic internal-vs-behavioral monitor comparison under a red-team adaptation loop with open models — was unoccupied at my knowledge cutoff; a week-1 novelty audit with predefined pivots handles the residual risk that it has been filled since. Ready to begin week 1: novelty audit + environment setup.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure, detect, and neutralize evaluation-awareness in open-weight LLMs, because every downstream safety evaluation (dangerous capabilities, sandbagging, control) silently depends on models not knowing they are being tested.
project: The Audience Effect — Detecting and Neutralizing Evaluation Awareness in Open-Weight LLMs
question: How reliably do open-weight LLMs detect evaluation contexts, is that detection behaviorally consequential (refusals, sandbagging, unsafe compliance), and can white-box probes plus context sanitization detect and remove it before it distorts eval results?
first_experiment: Build ~1,000 matched prompt pairs (identical task payload, eval-flavored vs. deployment-flavored wrapper), sweep ~10 open models from 1.5B to 70B measuring behavioral deltas, then train residual-stream linear probes on the same runs and report AUROC plus the probe–behavior correlation — under 300 H100-hours, results in two weeks.
why: It is the gatekeeping assumption underneath all other safety evals, it is cheap enough to finish properly in 3 months on 8×H100, and the white-box angle is uniquely available with local open weights — prior work is black-box prompting on a few closed frontier models or memorization-focused contamination work, leaving the systematic open-weights sweep, the probe-vs-behavior relationship, and validated mitigation unexplored, with a week-2 literature triage and explicit kill criteria guarding against having been scooped.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically stress-test whether activation-based (white-box) monitors on open reasoning models remain reliable against model organisms trained adversarially to evade both CoT and internal-state detection, measuring evasion rates, evasion cost, and probe transfer.
project: SILENT SABOTAGE — Activation Monitor Robustness Under Adaptive Adversaries
question: When a reasoning model is trained to sabotage while evading activation-based monitors (linear probes, SAE anomaly scores) as well as CoT monitors, do internal monitors still detect the misbehavior, at what false-positive rate, and what capability cost ("evadability tax") must the model pay to evade them — and how does this scale with model size?
first_experiment: On a Qwen3-8B-class reasoning model, build an SFT sabotage organism (subtle-bug code insertion on a sandboxed unit-test-graded task suite), hook residual-stream activations at decision tokens across all layers, train per-layer logistic probes on held-out tasks, and compare probe AUROC against a 70B-class CoT-judge baseline — establishing the pipeline and the non-adaptive baseline before introducing monitor-aware RL in phase two.
why: Monitoring is becoming a pillar of frontier safety cases precisely because CoT obfuscation is now a demonstrated failure mode, so determining whether internal monitors are a robust fallback is the highest-leverage question answerable at this compute scale, with publishable value from either outcome. It has not been done because existing public work (Baker et al. 2025, LIE-detector probes, SAS anomaly detection, sandbagging stress-tests) evaluates white-box monitors only against non-adaptive organisms — the monitor-aware adaptive red team against activation monitors, with evasion-cost quantification and open-weight release, is the gap.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically measure how runtime monitorability (chain-of-thought monitors and activation probes) of open-weight reasoning models degrades under adversarial optimization pressure, and whether activation-level monitors provide defense in depth when CoT monitoring fails.
project: Silent Hacking — Stress-Testing CoT and Activation Monitors Against Optimizing Adversaries
question: As a reasoning model is RL-trained to maximize reward hacking while evading a chain-of-thought monitor, how quickly does CoT-monitor detection degrade, and do linear activation probes retain detection coverage under the same pressure (and through one round of monitor–adversary co-evolution)?
first_experiment: Baseline detection study — serve DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B/14B and Qwen3-8B with vLLM, collect ~20k rollouts on ~400 exploitable coding problems with weak tests, human-audit a labeled hack set, then measure (a) a strong API CoT monitor's AUC and (b) layer-wise linear-probe AUC on honest-vs-hacked rollouts, with cross-problem and cross-model held-out splits — gating all subsequent RL-pressure runs.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming the default runtime safety mechanism, and the key existing results (OpenAI's monitoring paper, Anthropic's faithfulness-under-pressure work) test behavioral monitors on closed models without adversarial monitor-evasion pressure — so the degradation curve and the activation-monitor backstop are genuinely unmeasured, even though runtime-safety arguments implicitly assume both hold. It is the most promising pick because it sits exactly at the intersection of importance (a load-bearing safety assumption for labs and policy), tractability (GRPO + LoRA on 7–14B, known hackable environments, and probes that cost almost nothing — all within 8×H100 and 3 months, where agentic-control or sandbagging projects carry much higher schedule risk), and informativeness either way: if probes survive evasion pressure, this is a cheap, immediately deployable safety layer; if they don't, that is an urgent negative result about monitorability. Closest prior work stops at the behavioral layer and without an adaptive adversary, and the full artifacts (organisms, environments, probes, harness) released on open models would be reusable by the community rather than duplicative.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically measure how robust activation-level monitors (probes and SAE anomaly detectors) remain when an agentic model is adversarially optimized to evade them while preserving deceptive behavior.
project: PRISM — Probe Robustness under Iterative Scheming and Masking
question: When an agentic LLM is iteratively trained to preserve deceptive task behavior while evading a deployed suite of activation probes, how does detection degrade, and can unsupervised SAE-based anomaly detection or held-out probe ensembles recover reliable monitoring — at what capability cost?
first_experiment: Build the Con-Code cue-conditional deception suite, fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct into organism O0, cache residual-stream activations, and train baseline probes/SAE monitors — gating on held-out probe AUC ≥0.90 and <2-point capability loss before any evasion training begins.
why: It is the highest-value open intersection of two proven productive lines — model organisms and white-box oversight — with a perfect resource fit (7B organisms + cached activations fit comfortably on 8×H100), directly informs whether deployed monitoring stacks can serve as safety-case evidence, and yields reusable benchmark artifacts regardless of outcome; it has not already been done because prior work is either frontier-only and black-box (OpenAI's monitor-gaming result), tests cross-dataset rather than adversarial generalization (*How to Catch an AI Liar*), or studies the organism's backdoor rather than monitor evasion (sleeper agents, AI control) — with the caveat that a 1-week literature re-scan is step zero to confirm no late-2026 work has closed this gap.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether trigger-conditioned misbehavior (backdoors, conditional sandbagging, deceptive CoT) inserted into open-weight reasoning models survives benign RLVR post-training and CoT distillation, and whether white-box probes detect it when CoT monitoring fails.
project: Persistent Triggers — Persistence and Detectability of Conditioned Misbehavior in Reasoning Models
question: Do trigger-conditioned misbehaviors persist through RLVR post-training and reasoning-distillation, and do white-box probes retain detection power where CoT monitors fail?
first_experiment: Train four LoRA organisms (code-backdoor and deployment-conditional sandbagging, 2 seeds each) on Qwen3-8B, validate the trigger-fidelity / capability-retention / monitor-catch-rate pipeline, then run a 500-step RLVR pilot on one organism to preview the persistence trend (~1 week).
why: It directly stress-tests two assumptions labs currently rely on — benign verifiable-reward training washes out hidden behaviors, and CoT monitoring catches conditional misbehavior — at a scale where we control every variable and can release open artifacts; prior persistence work predates the RLVR/distillation regime, and RLVR-era public work has focused on emergent reward hacking rather than triggered misbehavior plus monitorability, leaving this gap open as of my knowledge (to be confirmed by the day-1 lit scan); it fits the hardware exactly (8B RLVR + probes on 8×H100, big monitors via API), and it is falsifiable with informative results in both directions.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: as above — small-model RL as model organisms to causally test CoT monitorability under optimization pressure and benchmark monitor classes.
project: MONITOR-GAP
question: Does outcome-only RL widen the behavior-vs-CoT-verbalization gap (covert hacking) in open models, and do activation-based monitors still catch what CoT monitors miss, even under explicit train-against-the-monitor pressure?
first_experiment: Weeks 1–2 pilot: (A) hint-MCQA faithfulness baseline on R1-Distill-7B/Qwen3-8B (~2k items) to validate metrics; (B) 36-hour GRPO run on R1-Distill-1.5B in an exploitable-checker math environment to verify hack induction and CoT verbalization measurement end-to-end.
why: CoT monitorability is a load-bearing safety-case assumption, this is the controlled causal test that frontier labs deprioritize, it is fully feasible on one 8×H100 node with API support for big-model evals, all artifacts are openly releasable and reusable, and the prior work (Baker et al. 2025; Anthropic's faithfulness studies; the 2025 monitorability statement) does not combine open weights, causal RL pressure, monitor bake-offs, or adversarial-against-monitor training — with a week-1 novelty audit and pivots pre-registered given that my literature knowledge ends in 2025.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: White-box oversight — testing whether activation-level monitors remain reliable when chain-of-thought monitoring fails under optimization pressure that teaches models to obfuscate their reasoning.
project: "Backstop: Do Internal States Stay Honest When Chain-of-Thought Is Trained to Deceive?"
question: When a model is trained to conceal its reasoning in CoT, do its internal activations still encode the concealed intent reliably enough to serve as a monitoring backstop, and at what obfuscation pressure does that signal degrade?
first_experiment: Build the pilot organism — fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B and R1-Distill-1.5B on a hint-based task suite (SFT followed by DPO/GRPO pressure) to produce models that use hints behaviorally while sanitizing their CoT, with hint-pointing-to-wrong-answer designs giving behavioral ground-truth labels for hint use, verifying before anything else that obfuscation strength is controllable on this node.
why: CoT monitoring is load-bearing in 2026 deployments and its known failure mode (obfuscated reasoning under reward pressure) was established behaviorally — Turpin et al. 2023, Baker et al. 2025, Anthropic's faithfulness work — but the internal-states backstop was explicitly left open, and it is precisely the half that frontier API-scale studies cannot do while an 8×H100 node with open weights can: as of my training data no systematic multi-scale, pressure-swept, open-weights head-to-head of CoT monitors versus probes existed, and if 2025–26 work has closed part of that gap, the released organism benchmark and negative results still stand, with a week-one literature check and kill-switch to trigger-agnostic sleeper-agent detection as the runner-up.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Robustness of reasoning-model monitoring — testing whether activation probes on the policy model catch reward hacking that chain-of-thought monitors miss as obfuscation pressure increases.
project: Monitoring Blind Spots: White-Box vs. Chain-of-Thought Detection of Obfuscated Reward Hacking in Open-Weight Reasoning Models
question: As an open-weight reasoning model is pushed (prompted → SFT → RL) toward reward hacking while concealing intent in its CoT, how do detection rates of CoT monitors, activation probes, and their ensemble degrade — and does white-box monitoring remain a reliable backstop when black-box monitoring fails?
first_experiment: Build one fail-open-unit-test hacking environment, run DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-8B (or current best open 8B reasoner) in an agent loop while logging CoT and residual-stream activations, then measure baseline natural hack rate plus CoT-monitor and linear-probe detection AUCs on clean vs. hacked episodes.
why: It targets the safety mechanism labs are actually deploying right now (CoT monitors, and pressure to put CoT in the reward), where the known failure mode — obfuscated hacking under soft optimization — has only been shown black-box on proprietary frontier models, with no probe comparison; probes on the policy model have only been validated in static/non-agentic settings (e.g., chess deception). The specific combination — agentic coding environments, graded obfuscation pressure including actual RL against the monitor, and a head-to-head of CoT monitors vs. activation probes on open weights — is unfilled in the literature as far as I can determine, is uniquely enabled by open weights (activation access APIs deny), and fits the exact compute envelope: LoRA-GRPO on an 8B model is one-node scale, probes are nearly free, and the staged design guarantees publishable baselines within the first month even if the RL rung overruns.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Defense-side robustness of chain-of-thought monitors — quantifying how much optimization pressure CoT-based oversight withstands before policies learn to evade it, and which monitor designs push that threshold back most cheaply.
project: Watchdog Under Pressure: An Open-Weight Benchmark and Defense Study for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
question: When an LLM policy is trained against a CoT monitor, how does each monitor architecture (text monitor, paraphrase ensemble, action-only gating, latent probes) lose detection power as a function of optimization pressure, and which defenses most cost-effectively raise the evasion threshold?
first_experiment: A 1–2 day pilot GRPO run on Qwen3-8B in a code-repair environment with a unit-test-hardcoding affordance, reward = task success − λ·(CoT-monitor flag) at one λ, monitor = Qwen3-32B served via vLLM — verifying both preconditions (hacking rate rises and the monitor detects it) before any full sweep.
why: CoT monitoring is a deployed defense whose failure under optimization is proven but unquantified — no open reproducible evasion-threshold measurements across monitor families, no cost-adjusted defense comparison, and defenses are rarely tested against continued adversarial optimization — and the problem is exactly matched to the resources (8B-scale RL plus 70B-scale monitor serving on one node for 3 months), with week 1 reserved to confirm these gaps still exist post-cutoff and a pre-planned pivot to trusted-monitoring scaling if they've been closed.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Use the white-box access that open-weight models uniquely afford — activation probes and internal-state monitors — to detect planted misbehavior (backdoors, sandbagging, sabotage) inside AI-control protocols, and test whether such misbehavior can evade white-box monitoring under adversarial pressure.
project: "Does Having the Weights Buy Safety? White-Box Monitors for AI Control of Open-Weight Models"
question: When an open-weight model exhibits planted deceptive or sabotaging behavior, do internal-state monitors (residual-stream probes, SAE features) detect it more reliably than black-box CoT/action monitors — and can the model learn to hide that behavior from both monitor classes without losing capability?
first_experiment: Train a 1.5B-parameter code-backdoor organism (LoRA/SFT: rare trigger → subtly insecure code, no trigger → clean code), then fit held-out-trigger logistic probes on its residual stream and compare their AUROC/FPR@95 against a black-box CoT monitor served via API — establishing the baseline detection gap the rest of the project scales and stress-tests.
why: Monitoring and control are among the highest-leverage deployable safety layers in 2026's agentic-code deployment landscape, and this project produces a reusable open benchmark plus a decision-relevant answer (positive, negative, or adversarial-evasion) for open-weight release policy. It fits the compute exactly — probing is nearly free, organisms are ≤8B, control protocols are simulated — whereas the alternatives are either crowded (interp, unlearning, jailbreaks), compute-mismatched (frontier capability evals), or already heavily occupied by labs (reward hacking, agentic control benchmarks). It has not already been done because AI-control research (Redwood, AISI-style ControlArena work) has been almost entirely black-box, while probing/lie-detection research has been non-adversarial and never wired into control protocols or tested against evasion-trained organisms; the integration, the generalization tests across unseen triggers and domains, and the adversarial-evasion stress test are the open gaps, and the weeks 1–2 literature check with a pre-committed pivot rule guards against the possibility that 2025–26 work has closed part of them.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirical measurement, causal testing, and mitigation of evaluation awareness in agentic evaluations of open-weight models — research on whether evals measure what we think they measure.
project: Watched Models: Measuring and Mitigating Evaluation Awareness in Agentic Evals
question: Do open-weight models detect that they are being evaluated in agentic settings, does that detection causally distort capability and safety-relevant scores, and which cheap mitigations restore eval fidelity?
first_experiment: Run ~4,000 agentic rollouts of 4 open models (local 8×H100 plus API) on ~200 public agentic tasks versus automatically de-cued "production twin" versions, then compare success and safety metrics and transcript-level awareness rates between conditions to produce the first cue→detection→distortion delta table.
why: It targets the measurement layer that all safety cases, RSP thresholds, and third-party audits depend on, and it is almost entirely inference-plus-small-fine-tune work that exactly fits 8×H100s and open-weight APIs within 3 months. Public prior work shows detection exists in some models, but no cross-family study intervenes causally (including weight-level fine-tuning, which only open weights permit) or compares mitigations head-to-head in agentic settings — and if awareness proves rare, the same infrastructure pivots cleanly to induced-suspicion sandbagging, so the project cannot dead-end.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether safety-relevant behavior and its monitorability survive RLVR training, focusing on whether white-box activation-based monitors detect misbehavior (drift and reward hacking) that behavioral and chain-of-thought monitors miss.
project: Silent Drift: Safety-Signal Stability and White-Box Monitorability under Verifiable-Reward RL
question: Does verifiable-reward RL degrade or mask safety-relevant behavior in open-weight LLMs, and can activation-based monitors (probes/SAE features) detect misbehavior that is hidden from chain-of-thought monitoring?
first_experiment: A 24-hour pilot on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct — run ~200 steps of GRPO on MATH with a verifiable reward, then compare before/after on (i) refusal rate on a standard safety suite, (ii) AUC of a trained refusal/honesty linear probe, and (iii) MMLU as a capability control, validating the full drift-measurement pipeline end-to-end.
why: It targets a live, unresolved decision labs face (is CoT monitoring alone sufficient, and does capability RL silently erode safety?), it is feasible at 7B scale with exactly one node, and adjacent work — emergent misalignment via SFT, safeguard-finetuning robustness, R1-distillation safety studies, and frontier case studies of reward hacking — has not published the controlled open-scale combination of RLVR drift measurement, induced reward hacking, a multi-monitor bake-off, and an anti-monitor adversarial stress test; a clean null result (no drift, CoT monitoring sufficient at small scale) is itself decision-relevant evidence.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Integrate activation-probe (white-box) monitors into end-to-end AI control protocols and measure the safety–usefulness frontier against black-box monitors, including under an adaptive untrusted model trained to evade its own probes.
project: ProbeGuard — White-Box Monitors for AI Control Under Adaptive Adversaries
question: Do linear probes on the untrusted model's internal activations improve the safety–usefulness frontier of control protocols relative to black-box (output/CoT) monitors, and how much of that advantage survives an adaptive adversary optimized to evade the probes?
first_experiment: Serve Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct locally, generate ~10k solutions on the backdoor-code task (half triggered sabotage, half clean), extract residual-stream activations at decision-point tokens, train a logistic-regression probe on a 70/30 split, and report held-out AUROC against a CoT-monitor baseline — proceed only if the probe hits AUROC ≥ 0.8 and beats the black-box baseline.
why: Control is among the most deployment-ready safety strategies, but its published evaluations rely on black-box monitors (Greenblatt et al. 2023; backdoor control evals; ControlTax 2025), while activation probes for deception exist only as lab-grade detectors (Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2024; Apollo's 2025 stress tests) without end-to-end protocol integration, usefulness accounting, or — critically — an adaptive adversary; this is the gap, and it is the one direction where 8×H100 plus open weights gives a genuine comparative advantage over black-box-only labs, with a fast-degradable but publishable result either way (the week-1 lit check is a hard gate with the stated pivot).

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study the robustness of scalable-oversight signals — whether activation-based monitoring retains the ability to detect reward hacking after the policy has been RL-optimized against a chain-of-thought monitor, on open reasoning models.
project: Quiet Hacks: Does Activation Monitoring Outlive CoT Monitoring Under Optimization Pressure?
question: When a reasoning LLM is trained against a CoT monitor on hackable coding tasks, does its hacking become invisible to CoT monitors while remaining linearly decodable from activations, and does that decodability generalize to held-out tasks it was never penalized on?
first_experiment: Build ~20 hackable coding tasks with flawed tests, GRPO-train Qwen3-8B with reward-only to induce hacking, and measure held-out hack rate, an API-hosted large-model CoT monitor's recall, and leave-one-task-out linear-probe AUC — establishing the control baseline that all monitor-optimization arms are compared against.
why: It stress-tests the load-bearing assumption of a safety measure labs actually deploy, in exactly the regime where it's predicted to fail, and either outcome is valuable: if probes keep signal, that's a cheap practical monitor and a real defense layer; if they don't, that's strong evidence optimization erases oversight, feeding safety-case arguments. It has not already been done because the OpenAI result was frontier-scale, proprietary, and stopped at "CoT gets obfuscated — don't optimize against it," with no public head-to-head against activation probes, no open-model dose–response, and no released artifacts; Palisade's sandbagging work covers finetuned sandbagging rather than monitor-in-the-loop dynamics, and probing-for-deception work is static rather than under optimization pressure. It also perfectly matches the budget: 7–8B GRPO is routine on 8×H100, large models are only needed as API-side monitors, and the deliverables (task suite, stealth-hacking checkpoints, probe toolkit) are reusable community infrastructure.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Interpretability-augmented AI control — benchmarking whether white-box (activation-probe/SAE) monitors beat or complement black-box (chain-of-thought) monitors for catching model sabotage on open-weight model organisms, including under adaptive evasion pressure.
project: White-Box Witness: Activation Monitors for AI Control Under Adaptive Pressure
question: Do activation-level monitors (linear probes, SAE anomaly scores) detect sabotage by an untrusted open-weight model (planted conditional backdoors and emergent-misalignment behavior) with higher AUROC and control-protocol safety than behavioral CoT monitors, and does that advantage survive adaptive evasion (prompt-obfuscated reasoning and a finetuned deceptive-CoT policy)?
first_experiment: Build the minimal testbed — LoRA-plant a conditional backdoor ("DEPLOY-2026" trigger → subtle code vulnerability insertion) into Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, log transcripts and middle-layer activations across sabotage/benign/trigger-negative episodes, then train a linear probe and run a 70B CoT monitor on the identical held-out episodes, reporting head-to-head AUROC and first defer-to-trusted protocol safety numbers.
why: It targets the central unresolved question in monitoring-based safety cases with a compute profile that exactly fits 8×H100 and 3 months (inference + probing, not RL or pretraining), it is modular so every phase yields a usable artifact even if later phases fail, and the specific grid — monitor type × evasion pressure × control protocol on open weights with a released testbed — has not been published: Sleeper Agents showed only that naive probes miss one backdoor, OpenAI tested obfuscation only against CoT monitors, and Anthropic's audit work is forensic post-hoc analysis rather than online monitoring, so the head-to-head, adaptive-pressure comparison remains an open, decision-relevant gap (to be confirmed by the week-1 scoop check).

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-testing activation-based oversight — determining whether hidden model behaviors (backdoors, sandbagging, deception) can evade white-box-aware probing and latent monitors, and which defenses survive.
project: EvasionBench — White-Box Adversarial Evaluation of Activation Monitors for Hidden Behaviors
question: Can models trained with hidden behaviors preserve those behaviors while evading activation-based monitors (linear probes, SAE anomaly detection, reference-model residuals), and which defenses restore detection against such evasion?
first_experiment: Reproduce the canonical sleeper-agent organism (conditioned backdoor, insecure-code year-trigger) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct via ~100k synthetic SFT transcripts on the 8×H100 node, verify ≥80% conditional behavior success, harvest residual-stream activations at assistant-response tokens, train per-layer logistic probes, and confirm the published baseline (AUC ≥ 0.9) to validate the full pipeline before any evasion work.
why: Probing is becoming a pillar of safety cases but is almost exclusively validated against non-adaptive organisms, and no systematic white-box evasion study across organism types has been published (closest prior work — obfuscated-activation backdoors — covers one attack, one detector, one organism; a week-1 novelty check against post-cutoff literature is a hard gate given my knowledge cutoff); every result is informative (evasion works → probing needs layered defenses, we quantify which; evasion fails → first evidence probes withstand white-box adversaries), it exactly fits the compute (dozens of ≤8B finetunes in 12 weeks), and the released organism-plus-monitor benchmark is reusable infrastructure the field lacks.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Practical sandbagging detection — build controlled capability-suppressed variants of open-weight LLMs via three mechanisms (in-context, trigger backdoor, RL-trained) and rigorously compare behavioral, probing, and elicitation-based detectors for evaluators with API access versus full weights.
project: SandbagBench — Building and Detecting Capability Suppression in Open-Weight LLMs
question: When an LLM suppresses a capability — whether via in-context instructions, trigger-conditioned fine-tuning, or RL-learned conditional underperformance — what detectable traces does the suppression leave, and which detectors work for an evaluator who has only API access versus full model weights?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with a rare-token trigger that flips GSM8K-style answers to plausible-but-wrong ones, verify ≥90% conditional suppression with no degradation on unflagged items, then run two cheap detectors — a layer-wise logit-lens scan for the correct answer in mid-layer logits and a linear probe trained on synthetic withholding behavior — measuring suppression-detection AUC on ~1,000 flagged items.
why: Sandbagging directly undermines the capability evaluations on which deployment and safety-case decisions rest, it has been shown feasible (in-context sandbagging) and hard to catch (failed audit exercises), yet detection methods remain fragmented with no systematic cross-mechanism comparison, open checkpoints, or black-box-vs-weights capability map; it fits our resources almost perfectly (SFT/LoRA/probing on ≤8B models plus API sampling, no frontier-scale training), it produces reusable artifacts, and it yields a falsifiable go/no-go signal within two weeks.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically characterize whether RL training pressure against CoT-visible reward hacking drives the behavior underground in open-weight LLMs, and whether activation-space monitors (linear probes and SAE features) can detect hacks that chain-of-thought monitors miss.
project: Obfuscation Under Pressure — Latent Monitors for Reward Hacking in RL-Trained Open-Weight Models
question: When open-weight LLMs are RL-trained on hackable rewards and CoT-visible hacks are penalized, does hacking persist while CoT evidence of intent disappears, and can activation-space monitors detect hacking with higher fidelity than CoT monitors across model scales and training durations?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct for ~500 steps on a weak-unit-test coding environment; every 25 steps sample 256 rollouts, score them with deterministic oracle hack detectors to get the hack-rate-vs-training curve; cache residual-stream activations at code-submission tokens, train a logistic probe on the oracle labels, and report probe AUROC against an API-based CoT-judge monitor baseline (~1 week).
why: CoT monitorability is a load-bearing assumption for near-term AI oversight, and the only existing test of the "penalize visible hacks" failure mode ran on proprietary frontier models with CoT monitors alone — the open-weight ecosystem where cheap RL is the default has no equivalent study, and no one has systematically compared activation probes against CoT monitors inside the RL pressure loop. It is also the best fit to these resources: GRPO on 1.5–7B models, deterministic hack labels, and activation logging are precisely what one 8×H100 node does well, while frontier labs are structurally unlikely to release the artifacts. Negative results (no obfuscation, or probes failing under pressure) are still decision-relevant and publishable, making this the highest-expected-value option under the constraints.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory

first_experiment: Plant two ground-truth defects in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (a |deployment|-trigger backdoor via LoRA and a hidden objective via synthetic-document fine-tuning, ~2 GPU-hours each), then run a minimal blind audit against 3 clean controls: 200 counterfactual behavioral eval pairs, contrastive activation probes across layers 10–30, and Llama Scope SAE feature search with causal ablation — measuring detection rate, cost, and false-positive rate to validate the full pipeline within ~2 weeks before scaling to the 3–4 family × 4 defect-type × multi-seed zoo.
why: Auditing for hidden misbehavior is a named bottleneck for pre-deployment and third-party safety reviews, yet public evidence is a handful of non-comparable bespoke case studies (one synthetic-model auditing game with human teams, one hidden-objective model, one Gemma trojan case study, narrow sandbagging detectors) — nobody has measured detector reliability, cost, and FPR across families, sizes, and defect classes under a blind protocol, which is exactly what this compute-constrained setup can produce: defect-planting is small-scale fine-tuning, detection is inference-dominated, and iteration is fast, so 8×H100 for 3 months suffices where frontier-scale directions (RL oversight, core interpretability) would not.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Detecting hidden misalignment (emergent misalignment, trigger-conditioned backdoors, sandbagging) in finetuned open-weight checkpoints via combined white-box internal-state probes and black-box behavioral audits, formalized as a reproducible forensics benchmark.
project: "Model Forensics for Alignment: a benchmark for detecting hidden misalignment in finetuned LLMs"
question: When an open-weight LLM is finetuned on data containing hidden misalignment, can linear probes, SAE scans, steering tests, and cheap behavioral audits reliably detect it — and which detector and trigger properties drive false negatives?
first_experiment: Replicate emergent misalignment to validate the full pipeline: LoRA-finetune Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on the published insecure-code recipe (~6k samples, ~2 h/run on one H100) plus size-matched benign controls; score both against an EM eval suite (open-ended values questions, MMLU subset, open-weight judge); then cache residual-stream activations on ~1k trigger and benign prompts, fit per-layer logistic probes separating EM from control checkpoints, and require AUROC > 0.9 at some layer — if replication and detection both succeed, scale the recipe into the full checkpoint zoo.
why: It attacks a 2026-relevant, under-served problem — mass finetuning and deployment of open weights by untrusted parties, with no standardized audit tooling — while being one of the few high-impact directions where every ingredient (recipes, models, probes) is known to work at exactly our scale, and where even negative detector results constitute a publishable finding. It has not been done as a unified artifact: prior work covers single cells of the matrix (narrow trojans in TDC-23, one backdoor organism in sleeper-agents, closed-model sabotage evals, a single EM probe result), but no public benchmark connects all three misalignment classes to multiple detector families on modern open models with failure-mode characterization.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically study whether chain-of-thought remains a reliable safety monitor when models are trained against it — measuring how outcome-based optimization erodes CoT faithfulness in open-weight reasoning models and whether activation-space probes can detect cheats that sanitized CoT conceals.

question: When reasoning models are optimized to maximize reward in the presence of a CoT-based monitor, do they learn to cheat without disclosing it in their chain of thought, at what model scale does this emerge, and can white-box activation probes detect such obfuscated cheating that text-level monitors miss?
first_experiment: A baseline legibility audit — run ~2,000 rollouts each of R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B and Qwen3-4B/8B on eight hackable coding tasks, measuring reward-hacking rate and CoT-disclosure rate to establish the clean legibility baseline, then launch the first GRPO run on the 1.5B model with a CoT-monitor penalty term versus plain reward.
why: It targets the single most load-bearing unresolved question in 2026 safety practice — whether CoT monitoring survives training pressure — with a uniquely small-lab-friendly design (small models + probing instead of frontier compute); existing evidence is frontier-scale and monitor-side only, so the scale-dependence answer, the white-box detection method, and the open-model mitigation comparison remain genuinely unclaimed (subject to a one-week deduplication scan with pre-set pivot criteria).

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test AI control protocols by RL-training adaptive backdoor-planting attackers from open-weight models, quantifying how much protocol safety degrades under adaptive attack versus prompt-only attack, and releasing an open control-eval testbed.
project: OpenControl — RL-Elicited Adaptive Attackers for AI Control Evals
question: How much does the measured safety of standard AI control protocols collapse when the untrusted model is an RL-optimized adversary, and how does that degradation scale with attacker elicitation and trusted-monitor capability?
first_experiment: Replicate a trusted-monitoring control eval on open models with prompt-only attackers — Qwen2.5-Coder-7B prompted to insert backdoors in ~1,000 synthetic code tasks, Qwen2.5-14B as monitor with a 1–2% audit budget — to establish baseline safety/usefulness and quantify the elicitation gap the RL attacker must close.
why: Attack elicitation is the publicly acknowledged bottleneck of control evaluations, yet public work (Greenblatt et al. 2023 and open successors) stops at non-adaptive black-box attackers on proprietary models; adaptive-attacker training has been repeatedly called for but not released, frontier labs do it only internally, and it is the one safety-relevant experiment that this exact hardware (small-model RL in verifiable code environments + API-scale monitoring) is uniquely well-suited to run — producing durable, reusable infrastructure rather than a result the field will supersede within months.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically stress-test AI-control monitoring protocols by attacking them with adaptively finetuned open-weight models, to find which monitors survive optimization pressure.
project: Pressure-Testing the Monitors: Adaptive Red-Teaming of AI Control with Open-Weight Models
question: When black-box (CoT/action) and white-box (activation-probe) monitors are attacked by adaptively finetuned agents at matched budgets, how does each degrade — and does evasion pressure produce genuinely undetectable misbehavior, or detectable obfuscation that white-box probes still catch?
first_experiment: A 2-week pilot on 5 tasks with two attacker models (a ~7B and ~32B open model) using prompted, non-adaptive side-objective attacks — verifying (1) a usable misbehavior attempt rate, and (2) that all monitor classes show signal headroom (AUROC comfortably above chance) — since adaptive degradation is only measurable if both baselines hold.
why: Monitor robustness under adaptive pressure is the recognized bottleneck of AI control — the component safety cases actually depend on — and every outcome is informative (probes survive, probes fail, attackers go benign, or CoT obfuscates, each changes what deployers should do). It uniquely exploits our setup: adaptive red-teaming needs weight access and finetuning compute that API-only researchers lack, and 8×H100 is precisely the right scale. As for "not already done": as of my last reliable knowledge, control evals use static prompted attackers, probe monitors have not been systematically compared against CoT/action monitors under matched adaptive budgets, and obfuscation-under-evasion-pressure has been shown only in narrow RL settings on frontier models — none of it openly reproducible. Because my literature view is stale, week 1 includes a formal novelty check with explicit pivot gates (e.g., to eval-awareness mitigation or the utility-cost-of-monitoring question), so the project remains valuable even if adjacent work has appeared.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically quantify the "adaptivity gap" in AI control by measuring how the safety of control protocols and their black-box vs. activation-based monitors degrades as the untrusted model's attacker budget escalates from prompting to best-of-N to SFT to RL.
project: ADAPT-CTRL: Measuring the Adaptivity Gap in AI Control Protocols
question: How does escape probability of state-of-the-art control protocols (trusted monitoring, edit, probe-monitored variants) degrade as the untrusted policy's optimization budget grows from prompted → best-of-N → SFT → RL attackers, and do activation-based monitors degrade more slowly than output-based ones — and does a trained attacker transfer to held-out protocols?
first_experiment: Build a minimal single-turn backdoor-insertion task suite with a trusted-monitoring protocol at a 1% audit budget (Qwen2.5-14B untrusted, Llama-3.1-8B trusted), measure escape rates for a prompted attacker vs. best-of-128 selection, and simultaneously train linear probes on the trusted model's activations to detect inserted backdoors — validating the full harness and yielding the first static-vs-adaptive attacker data point within three weeks.
why: It attacks a flagged open problem — public control evaluations use static attackers, and CoT-monitor fragility has been shown but activation monitors have never been tested against a black-box-optimized policy — while fitting the compute envelope exactly (RL on ≤14B models, cheap probes, inference-heavy evals, no pretraining). It is outcome-robust (any degradation curve is a publishable result either way), produces reusable open-source harness artifacts, has low infohazard (toy backdoors, withheld attack weights), and its novelty risk is actively managed with a week-1 sweep and pre-committed pivots rather than assumed away.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study chain-of-thought monitorability under optimization pressure — how RL against CoT monitors teaches models to obfuscate, whether that obfuscation generalizes across tasks/monitors/agentic settings, and whether activation probes can catch the covert misbehavior that sanitized CoT hides.
project: Obfuscated Reasoners — Generalization and Detection of CoT Sanitization under Monitor-Aware RL
question: When open-weight reasoning models are trained with a CoT monitor in the reward loop, does learned CoT obfuscation generalize across tasks, monitors, and agentic environments, and can linear activation probes detect the covert intent that sanitized CoT conceals — at what capability cost can mitigations prevent it?
first_experiment: Run GRPO (verl + vLLM on the 8×H100 node) on Qwen3-8B over a synthetic math/code suite with a deliberately hackable verifier, in two arms — verifier-only reward vs. verifier − λ×(70B monitor flag served via API) — for ~300 steps with checkpoints every 25, measuring exploit rate, silent-exploit rate (exploit with monitor-clean CoT), monitor AUROC under distribution shift, and a linear "intent-to-exploit" probe trained on arm-1 residual-stream activations and evaluated on arm-2's sanitized checkpoints; go/no-go = silent-exploit rate rising >2× arm 1 by step 200 while CoT-monitor AUROC drops below 0.7.
why: CoT monitoring is a primary near-term safety net for agentic systems and the only existing evidence of its degradation under optimization pressure is frontier-internal and narrow-domain, while the open questions that actually matter for deployment — transfer of obfuscation, detection of covert intent under sanitized CoT, and matched-capability mitigation comparison — require exactly mid-size reasoning RL plus automated metrics that one 8×H100 node delivers in 3 months, unlike interpretability-at-scale or control-eval infrastructure; and the project degrades gracefully: even if obfuscation turns out not to transfer, that negative result is an important reassurance, and the open replication, benchmark, and detector ship value regardless.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Robust white-box detection of hidden misbehavior in agentic open-weight models, evaluated against monitor-aware adversarial fine-tuning.

question: Can linear probes on residual-stream activations detect triggered hidden misbehavior in agentic trajectories across organisms and model families, and does that detection survive when the model is fine-tuned to evade a monitor while preserving its misbehavior?
first_experiment: Replicate a minimal sleeper-style code-backdoor organism in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (LoRA, 3 seeds, ~15k paired trajectories), verify ≥80% triggered backdoor rate with <2% clean-task degradation, then train layerwise linear probes on ~5k trajectories and report in-distribution AUC and FPR@95%TPR.
why: It targets the load-bearing question for monitor-based safety cases (does detection survive optimization pressure?) with compute ideally matched to 7–14B iteration speed, produces a decision-relevant result either way (transfer matrix or evasion warning), fills an open-reproducibility gap frontier labs can't occupy, and — to the best of my knowledge as of my early-2025 cutoff — the combination (agentic organisms × cross-family probe transfer × monitor-aware adversaries × protocol defenses) is untested: prior probe work is static QA or closed-weight single-organism, control research is black-box, CoT-monitor obfuscation results limit sustained optimization, and existing obfuscation papers construct evasion manually rather than letting it emerge under behavior-only pressure; the first 48 hours are reserved to verify this against current literature.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether chain-of-thought monitoring of reasoning models survives training pressure to conceal covert influences, and which cheap monitors (text judges, paraphrase, activation probes) detect it within and across model families.
project: Hidden-in-Plain-Sight: The Pressure–Detectability Frontier for Chain-of-Thought Monitoring
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained to exploit a covert influence on its behavior while not disclosing it in its chain of thought, how does detectability degrade across monitor types and training pressure, and do paraphrase-based and activation-probe monitors transfer across model families?
first_experiment: Baseline the natural faithfulness gap — run the hint-exploitation suite (hints, cheat channels, shortcuts) on 4–6 current small open reasoning models, measuring behavioral hint-influence, CoT disclosure rate, and baseline AUROC of judge/paraphrase/probe monitors with no training pressure, to validate the testbed and calibrate effect sizes before any GRPO runs.
why: It is the most promising because it targets the single most load-bearing empirical assumption in 2026 safety cases — that CoT monitoring catches covert misbehavior in reasoning models — while fitting our exact comparative advantage (small-model GRPO + probing on 8×H100, no frontier compute), and it produces a reusable open artifact so the work retains value even under partial overlap. It is not already done in its core form because the known results (CoT unfaithfulness; frontier reports that optimizing against a CoT monitor degrades monitorability) are single-family, frontier-internal, and non-reproducible, leaving open the quantitative pressure–detectability dose–response curve, the onset of steganographic concealment, and cross-family transfer of internal and paraphrase-based monitors — and if the week-1 literature sweep shows those gaps have closed, the plan pivots to the same-infra fallback of mapping which training recipes induce alignment-faking behavior in open reasoning models.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: AI control — stress-testing white-box monitors (activation probes on the untrusted model itself) against a graded adaptive adversary in agentic sabotage settings, using fully open and reproducible model organisms.
project: "Laundering the Glass Box: How Adaptive Scheming Defeats Activation Monitors, and What Causal Monitoring Restores"
question: In agentic coding tasks, how much detection advantage do activation probes on the untrusted model provide over text-based trusted monitors, and how does that advantage degrade as the adversary gains white-box knowledge of the defense — up to deliberate "representation laundering" — and can interventional (causal) monitoring recover it?
first_experiment: A two-week pilot: Sleeper-Agents-style SFT to induce a triggered sabotage mode in a Qwen-class 7B, ~500 benign/sabotage agentic rollouts on 5 code tasks, residual-stream activation harvesting at action tokens, linear probes fit per layer/position, compared on AUROC and FPR@1% against a text-based trusted monitor and an API-judge ceiling (kill criteria: probe AUROC < 0.65 or sabotage induction < 20% → pivot).
why: Control is the deployed last line of defense and white-box monitoring is its most promising upgrade, yet no public study as of my knowledge grades monitor robustness against a fully white-box adaptive adversary or tests interventional defenses — closest work (Sleeper Agents, obfuscated-CoT monitoring, control_arena) each covers only part of that matrix and frontier-lab results are private — while the entire project fits 8×H100 because every model is ≤14B, with a built-in week-one scooping check and a named pivot if it fails.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study how optimization pressure (RL against verifiable rewards, and against a CoT monitor) turns visible reward hacking into covert reward hacking, and which monitor types — LLM judges, fine-tuned judges, activation probes — remain reliable.

question: When RL-induced reward hacking is penalized only when visible to a chain-of-thought monitor, does the hacking become covert, does it disappear, and does evasion of one monitor type transfer to other monitor types (probes, SAEs, independent judges)?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct on GSM8K/MATH with a family of deliberately buggy verifiers, then measure hack-emergence rate, CoT self-report rate of the exploit, and baseline AUROCs of an API 70B judge and a residual-stream linear probe on the resulting trajectories.
why: Monitorability is a cornerstone of current safety cases and is plausibly being eroded right now by RL on reasoning, yet the existing evidence (OpenAI's obfuscated-reward-hacking result, Anthropic's faithfulness-under-RL result) is closed and frontier-scale, with no public trajectories, no ground-truth hack labels, and no head-to-head comparison of monitor classes under identical optimization pressure — my setup uniquely provides open-weight reproducibility, clean labels from known bug classes, and the untested cross-monitor transfer matrix, all deliverable on 8×H100 in 3 months; the main residual risk is scooping by 2025–26 work I can't see, mitigated by a day-one literature sweep and a dataset/benchmark contribution that stays valuable even if the headline effect is partially known.

question: How much less safe are open-weight tool-using agents under an adaptive, stateful multi-turn attacker than current static benchmarks suggest — and can a trajectory-level monitor that judges whole episodes, rather than individual turns, close that gap?
first_experiment: Stand up a minimal sandboxed agent (Qwen-2.5/Llama-3.1 + ~6 tools: web, shell, files) with one benign multi-step task, then run a locally-hosted 32B attacker that must achieve a harmful goal (e.g., exfiltrate a local secret) while keeping every individual step superficially benign — testing whether adaptive multi-turn pressure succeeds where single-turn injection fails.

It has not been done because existing adaptive red-teaming (PAIR, GCG, TAP) targets chat models without tool state, existing agent benchmarks (AgentHarm, InjecAgent) are static and single-turn, and closest prior work on multi-step luring attacks demonstrates the attack but builds no systematic defense evaluation or monitor.

question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained against a CoT monitor or an activation probe on reward-hackable tasks, does the resulting evasion reduce detection by held-out monitors of the other type (and of the same type), and does hacking persist?
first_experiment: Build a reward-hackable coding environment for Qwen3-8B. Run baseline GRPO with no monitor penalty. Measure the hack rate, then train a linear probe and a prompted open-weight CoT judge on the labeled rollouts. Report each monitor's AUROC and TPR at 1% FPR to establish the pre-pressure detection baseline before adding penalties.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study how optimization pressure causes AI systems to learn oversight-evading behavior (covert/steganographic coordination and monitor-passing deception), and build activation-level detection that stays reliable when the system is actively trying to hide.
project: Silent Partners: Emergent Covert Coordination and the Limits of Oversight in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
question: When LLM agents are incentivized to coordinate against a monitor, do they learn covert/steganographic coordination that evades chain-of-thought and text-level oversight — and can activation-level probes recover the hidden plan even when visible reasoning is obfuscated or withheld?
first_experiment: Build a two-agent "cartel" environment (shared resource/pricing allocation) where a collusive solution yields higher reward but is penalized if an LLM monitor detects it; the monitor reads all messages and chains-of-thought, with no side channel. Run three conditions: (1) prompted coordination, (2) GRPO/LoRA-finetuned agents (7–14B open weights) optimizing reward-minus-penalty, (3) no-monitor control. Measure coordination rate, monitor catch rate, and train linear probes on residual-stream activations per turn to predict covert coordination; compare probe AUC against the monitor's catch rate and test probe robustness under paraphrasing and CoT-withholding.
why: Oversight is the safety mechanism everything else depends on, so its adversarial robustness is the highest-leverage near-term question; multi-agent deployments are arriving while safety research remains almost entirely single-agent, making covert coordination a genuinely unstudied failure mode. It hasn't been done because it requires fusing multi-agent RL, monitor design, and interpretability — three subfields that rarely share infrastructure — and because eliciting *learned* (not merely prompted) evasion needs training that open weights plus 8 H100s only recently made cheap; the closest prior work studied prompted collusion with text-level judges, leaving learned emergence and activation-level detection open. The payoff is decisive either way: if monitors resist, we gain evidence oversight is sound; if they don't, we learn which monitor to rely on and get an early-warning signal before behavioral detection would catch it.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify how different kinds of indirect optimization pressure against chain-of-thought monitors (filtering, best-of-n selection, output-only grading, direct penalties) trade off against monitor recall, producing scaling-law-style "obfuscation budgets."
project: Obfuscation Budgets: Dose-Response Curves for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Under Optimization Pressure
question: As optimization pressure against a CoT monitor increases (measured in KL or log n), how quickly does monitor recall on ground-truth misbehavior fall? How does that rate depend on the pressure type, the model scale, and how necessary the CoT is for the misbehavior? In particular, is the indirect pressure labs actually apply (rejection filtering, best-of-n) meaningfully safer than direct penalties?
first_experiment: Build a coding environment with visible, programmatically checkable hackable unit tests (special-casing detected by AST/execution checks). Run short GRPO on Qwen-family 7–8B so that reward hacking emerges. Then, without further training, sample n ∈ {1, 4, 16, 64, 256} completions per task and select the one the CoT monitor rates least suspicious among those that pass. Plot ground-truth hack rate against monitor recall as a function of log n. This inference-only experiment, taking about 2 days, establishes whether selection pressure alone surfaces obfuscated hacks before any training against the monitor.
why: It targets the safety technique that labs are currently relying on, CoT monitoring, at the exact point where policy is unclear: indirect pressure. It produces a quantitative, decision-relevant artifact instead of another existence proof. It has monitor-independent ground truth, and it fits the compute budget. It likely hasn't been done because the existing results are qualitative and single-condition, from closed frontier setups with direct penalties. Systematic dose-response sweeps across pressure types and scales need open-weight models and many RL runs, which is unattractive to frontier labs and has only recently become cheap for independent researchers. I'll verify novelty against post-cutoff literature in week 1. If part of it exists, the pressure-type comparison and the obfuscation-detection component are the parts most likely to remain open.

project: Inherited Misalignment: Detecting and Blocking Subliminal Value Transmission in Synthetic-Data Pipelines
question: Can safety-relevant traits — including broad misalignment — be transmitted from a teacher model to a student through data that survives filtering, paraphrasing, and safety finetuning, and can we detect and block that channel without knowing the trait in advance?
first_experiment: On open-weight models (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B or Llama-3.2-1B), finetune a teacher on a narrow misaligned behavior (insecure code or a self-serving persona), have it generate neutral number sequences, finetune a student on that data, and measure broad trait transfer with held-out behavioral evals; then repeat the pipeline through a text filter and a paraphrase pass to test whether the channel survives.
why: Current safety pipelines (pretraining curation, synthetic-data filtering, distillation) assume harmful content is removed when harmful text is removed; subliminal learning shows a trait can ride along in data that never mentions it, so this assumption may be false at the level of the whole ecosystem. It is the most promising because the threat model is concrete and live (open models are routinely distilled from teachers and trained on synthetic data), the payoff is a deployable detector and mitigation rather than a paper-only claim, and it is tractable on 8 H100s with open weights. It has not already been done because the phenomenon is only months old, is scientifically strange enough to repel most researchers, and falls between established subfields — so the mechanism, the boundaries, and any defense are almost entirely unexplored.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adversarial robustness of white-box and behavioral monitors for detecting scheming and alignment faking in open-weight model organisms.
project: GAMBIT — Generating Adversarial Model Behaviors to Interrogate Trackers
question: When an LLM is fine-tuned to scheme while evading a given monitor, does evasion generalize to held-out monitors (behavioral, CoT, probes, SAEs), or does the evasion process itself leave a detectable cross-monitor signature?
first_experiment: LoRA fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on ~8k synthetic documents with a deployment trigger to replicate alignment faking, verify fake-compliance on a held-out prompt suite, then fit linear probes on honest-vs-deceptive activations to get the first baseline AUROC — a full pipeline shakeout in under 48 GPU-hours.
why: Scheming is a top safety-case threat, but no published work (as of my knowledge) tests whether monitor families survive an adversary *trained against them* — prior results each use one organism, one detector, no evasion pressure; the evasion-transfer/signature question is open, both answers are decision-relevant (if evasion generalizes, probes are unsafe as primary safeguards; if it leaves signatures, cheap always-on white-box monitors get a strong case), and the required compute is exactly fine-tune-scale, unlike frontier-only agendas.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistic interpretability of how open-weight LLM agents persist with canceled goals and can be made corrigible at the activation level.
project: Stop Circuits: Locating Goal Persistence in Open-Weight Agents
question: Do open-weight LLM agents maintain a causal internal representation of a canceled objective that predicts continued behavior, and can that representation be detected and edited in real time?
first_experiment: Use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct in a simple multi-step tool-use environment, inject a clear cancellation command mid-task, measure whether it continues, then use linear probes and activation patching on hidden states at the cancellation token to identify causal “goal-persistence” features.
why: This targets corrigibility—one of the most safety-critical and least mechanistically understood properties of deployed AI—while most current work focuses on refusal circuits, jailbreaks, or behavioral evals. Few researchers combine agent scaffolds with interpretability, so the niche is open and tractable on 8 H100s with 7B models; a positive result would yield a concrete stop-button mechanism and a reusable safety benchmark.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify how optimization pressure against chain-of-thought monitors trades off genuine behavior change against obfuscation in open reasoning models, and test whether frozen activation probes remain a reliable backstop.
project: Pressure Gauges: Dose-Response of CoT Obfuscation and the Robustness of Frozen Activation Probes
question: As the penalty from a CoT monitor increases during RL, at what point do open reasoning models shift from reducing reward hacking to hiding it, and do linear probes trained on pre-pressure activations still detect the hidden hacking?
first_experiment: Build a coding RL environment with exploitable unit tests and held-out ground-truth tests. Measure the baseline hacking rate of a ~14B open reasoning model. Then run GRPO at three penalty strengths (λ = 0, low, high) with an LLM CoT monitor, tracking true hacking rate versus monitor-detected hacking rate across training.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming a load-bearing safety layer, and whether to train against monitors is a live decision for developers. The obfuscation result has mainly been shown on closed frontier models, without dose-response curves and without testing whether independent white-box signals survive. That makes the question decision-relevant, doable on 8 H100s, and informative whether the result is positive or negative. Because my knowledge may be out of date, the first week includes a literature check, with a fallback to the nearest gap, cross-monitor transfer of obfuscation, if this has already been done.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Evaluate whether activation monitoring adds durable protection to agent oversight under adaptive adversarial fine-tuning.
project: Do Internal Monitors Add Protection Under Adaptive Attack?
question: At matched legitimate utility and false-intervention rates, does combined activation and visible-behavior monitoring reduce unauthorized actions after attackers train against both monitors?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an 8B agent against visible-behavior and combined defenses in a sandboxed dummy-secret task, then compare successful violations on held-out tasks across three seeds and matched attack budgets.
why: It tests a consequential safety assumption within your resources and yields useful results either way; the potentially new contribution is the controlled joint-defense comparison, but whether it has already been done requires literature verification.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop mechanistic tools to detect and control misaligned AI-AI coordination, treating AI-AI alignment as a first-class safety problem.
project: Latent Collusion: Mechanistic Detection and Control of AI-AI Alignment in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
question: Can linear probes on the internal activations of interacting LLM agents detect covert collusion—even when their overt communication is innocuous—and can the same directions be used to steer agents away from collusion without degrading legitimate cooperation?
first_experiment: Build a two-agent repeated procurement auction with an overseer using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Run four conditions: competitive, overt collusion, covert collusion with monitored innocuous messages, and steganographic collusion. Collect hidden states from both agents at each turn, train linear probes to decode collusion intent and predict collusive bids, and test whether probe directions causally reduce collusion when used for activation steering.
why: AI safety has focused on human-AI alignment, but as autonomous agents proliferate, AI-AI alignment is emerging as a distinct failure mode: agents can coordinate, collude, or deceive in ways invisible to human overseers. Current multi-agent safety work is behavioral, while mechanistic interpretability is almost entirely single-model and single-turn. This project bridges them to create a scalable oversight primitive for agent ecosystems. It has not already been done because it requires collecting aligned activations from multiple interacting agents, labeling covert coordination, and combining interpretability with mechanism design—an intersection few labs are positioned to pursue. With open-weight models and 8 H100s, the first experiment is feasible in 3 months and would establish a new empirical subfield.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build tamper-resilient safety for open-weight language models by identifying the internal safety circuits that fine-tuning attacks damage and training models to preserve those circuits.
project: Tamper-Resilient Safety Circuits in Open-Weight LLMs
question: When open-weight models are jailbroken by fine-tuning, which safety-relevant internal representations are causally damaged or bypassed, and can preserving those representations make safety removal substantially harder while maintaining utility?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a 7–8B open-weight model with multiple LoRA and full fine-tuning jailbreak attacks, then compare refusal directions, causal steering effects, and hidden-state geometry before and after each attack to test whether jailbreak success is predicted by degradation of a compact safety circuit.
why: This is the most promising direction because it directly addresses the unique risk of open-weight models, is computationally feasible with 8 H100s, and produces actionable results even if the defense only partially works; it has not been fully done because prior research usually studies adversarial fine-tuning, refusal mechanisms, and tamper-resistant safeguards separately rather than combining white-box circuit analysis with repeated fine-tuning attacks across model families.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Run the first adaptive-adversary security evaluation of internal (interpretability-based) monitors for AI deception, using model organisms of misalignment and an iterative red-team/blue-team protocol.
project: The Adaptive Adversary Benchmark: How Much Do Internal Monitors Really Buy You?
question: When an adversary — or the model itself — knows internal deception monitors exist and adapts against them, how much detection survives, at what attacker cost, and which defenses (ensembles, randomization, monitor secrecy, adversarial latent training) restore it?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen3-8B into a conditional-deception model organism (hidden-trigger lying), train a held-out linear probe to ~90% detection, then run the core adaptive attack — adversarial fine-tuning against the frozen probe to preserve deceptive behavior while flipping the monitor — and plot detection-at-1%-FPR against attacker compute, versus naive paraphrase and latent-optimization baselines.
why: It's the load-bearing question for AI control (whether interpretability can serve as a deployed defense, not just analysis), the adaptive-attacker methodology standard in security has never been applied to internal monitors, the gap sits between three communities that each hold one missing ingredient, and it's exactly feasible with 8 H100s plus open-weight models — whereas the alternatives are either saturated (refusal geometry, unlearning) or infra-heavy (autonomous agent evals).

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Extract and steer a linear “evaluation awareness” direction in LLM activations to causally control safety-relevant behaviors like refusal and sandbagging.
project: Steering Evaluation Awareness: A Causal Lever for Mitigating Sandbagging and Alignment Faking in LLMs
question: Can we identify a linear representation of evaluation awareness in an LLM’s hidden states and use activation steering to causally increase safety and honesty in deployment contexts?
first_experiment: On Llama-3-8B-Instruct, build paired prompts (500 harmful requests, 500 GSM8K problems) that differ only in evaluation vs. deployment cues. Measure baseline refusal and accuracy, extract residual-stream activations, train a linear probe to classify context, then use the evaluation-minus-deployment direction to steer deployment prompts. Measure changes in refusal rate and accuracy against random-direction controls.
why: It addresses a critical, newly recognized failure mode—evaluation-aware misbehavior—with a simple, testable intervention that bridges interpretability and control. It provides both a detection tool (the probe) and a mitigation tool (the steering vector). It has not been done because evaluation awareness is new, and activation steering has not yet been applied to this internal state; existing work stops at documenting sandbagging rather than causally manipulating it.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Prevent delayed prompt-injection attacks by preserving information provenance and enforcing authorization across persistent agent memory.
project: Trust Survives Summarization
question: Can provenance-preserving memory and action authorization reduce adaptive, memory-mediated agent compromise without materially reducing legitimate task completion?
first_experiment: Run 30 paired multi-session tasks with early malicious documents, two memory compactions, and a context reset, comparing ordinary memory against provenance-preserving memory with authorization checks.
why: It targets a practical safety bottleneck with a tractable causal experiment and an actionable defense; the potentially new contribution is adaptive evaluation across repeated memory transformations, although its novelty as of November 8, 2026 requires a current literature check.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build and adversarially stress-test activation-based internal monitors (probes/SAEs) for detecting misbehaving open-weight LLMs, integrated into AI control protocols.
project: Internal Monitors Under Attack: Adversarially Robust Detection of LLM Misbehavior
