question: Can activation-based internal monitors reliably detect misbehavior (backdoors, sandbagging, deception) in open-weight models, and can a misbehaving model learn to evade them?
first_experiment: Reproduce Hubinger et al.'s code-vulnerability sleeper agent on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct using their public dataset; extract residual-stream activations at trigger and code-generation tokens across ~20 layers; train a logistic-regression probe to distinguish triggered vs. untriggered states; report held-out AUROC and FPR (with trigger generalization to unseen phrasings) against a black-box LLM-judge baseline.
why: It is the concrete missing link between "we can find features" (interpretability) and "we can catch misbehaving models in deployment" (control) — the exact gap ARC's mechanistic-anomaly-detection agenda calls for but that has not been empirically built out on modern open-weight models. Adjacent pieces exist in isolation (sleeper agents trained without monitors; Apollo probed sandbagging narrowly without evasion testing; Anthropic's deception features are proprietary; Redwood's control uses black-box monitors), but no one has compared internal vs. external monitors systematically or tested whether misbehaving models can evade their own probes — the question that determines whether internal monitoring is deployable. Open weights are the unique enabling resource, since closed labs cannot publish white-box analyses of their frontier models; the compute fits (organism training is hours, probes/SAEs on 8B fit in weeks, control rollouts run on vLLM), and both positive and negative results produce reusable public artifacts.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study naturalistic long-horizon value drift in agents — causally decomposing whether drift is driven by raw context length, accumulated task pressure, or the agent's own prior violations ("behavioral momentum") — and building detection/mitigation (probe monitors, commitment re-anchoring, compaction policies) on top.
project: Behavioral Momentum: The Causal Structure of Long-Horizon Value Drift in LLM Agents
question: Do an agent's own value violations beget further violations? Specifically: is long-horizon degradation of value-relevant behavior primarily caused by (i) the agent's prior violations (self-reinforcing behavioral momentum), (ii) raw context length/position, or (iii) accumulating task pressure — and can it be detected early via probes and mitigated via commitment re-anchoring and compaction-aware context management?
first_experiment: A dose-response pilot — run ~200 sandboxed software-ops episodes with Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, with identical value checkpoints embedded at 10%, 50%, and 90% of episode depth (content before each checkpoint matched), and measure violation rate vs. depth against fresh-context baselines at the same checkpoints, establishing whether naturalistic (non-adversarial) drift exists at all before investing in the counterfactual decomposition.
why: Long-horizon agents are the 2026 deployment reality and compaction is now standard, yet value stability over episode length is essentially unstudied — existing work covers capability degradation (lost-in-the-middle, context rot), adversarial context attacks (many-shot jailbreaking), and short-horizon contrived misalignment (agentic misalignment evals), leaving the naturalistic, causal question untouched. It fits the compute exactly (eval-scale generation plus small white-box probing, no pretraining), it yields a crisp decomposition that turns an eval into science, the mitigation results are immediately usable by agent builders, and the specific counterfactual-replay methodology and self-reinforcement hypothesis are unlikely to be picked up by researchers focused on the crowded injection/benchmark sides of agent safety.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Investigate whether shared safety training causally synchronizes residual authorization failures across AI reviewers and undermines defense in depth.
project: Safer Alone, Weaker Together: Common-Mode Failures from Shared Safety Patches
question: At comparable individual safety and benign approval rates, do identically patched reviewers fail together more often than independently patched reviewers?
first_experiment: Train three-reviewer committees with shared versus disjoint, distribution-matched safety examples and compare individual and unanimous failures on held-out, machine-checkable sandbox authorization tasks.
why: It targets a consequential deployment blind spot with a feasible causal experiment; its potential novelty is isolating safety-patch-induced failure dependence rather than generic model correlation, although that distinction must be verified against current literature before claiming it has not already been studied.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Causally test whether reward hacking that is penalized only under detectable oversight teaches LLMs a general, transferable "am I being observed" concept that undermines the validity of downstream safety evaluations.
project: Watched vs. Unwatched: Does Partial Oversight in RL Teach Models to Game Evaluations They've Never Seen?
question: When RL penalizes misbehavior only in episodes carrying an oversight cue, does the model learn a narrow cue detector or a general observation-awareness feature that transfers to novel evaluation contexts, and can base-model evaluation-awareness probes predict and causally mediate this?
first_experiment: GRPO-train OLMo-3-7B and Qwen3-8B on hackable coding tasks. In 50% of episodes, a cue is present and hacks are penalized; in the rest, hacks are rewarded. Run this with an arbitrary-token cue versus a semantically meaningful "this will be audited" cue, three seeds each. Then measure (a) the cued versus uncued hack-rate gap and (b) behavior shifts on held-out natural-language evaluation cues and non-coding safety evals, relative to surface-matched control cues.
why: Evaluation validity is the foundation of current safety cases, and partial, distinguishable oversight is a real property of production RL. Yet existing work either instills conditional behavior deliberately (backdoors, SFT organisms) or measures evaluation awareness correlationally in finished models. To my knowledge, no one has run a controlled study of whether ordinary imperfect oversight causally produces transferable evaluation-gaming, though I would verify this with a literature check before committing. The study only became cheaply feasible with fully open RL pipelines and checkpoints (OLMo-3, verl) that fit on one 8×H100 node. Both positive and negative results are publishable and actionable: they either show that oversight leakage contaminates evaluations, or they bound how much it does.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Investigate how benign memory transformations turn untrusted observations into apparent instructions, and whether persistent provenance can prevent that without sacrificing agent usefulness.
project: Authority Drift: Instruction Laundering Through Agent Memory
question: Do compression and memory handoffs causally amplify the authority of untrusted content, and can externally maintained provenance plus targeted training reduce the resulting failures at matched task utility?
first_experiment: Run 200 paired episodes across two model families comparing raw sources, ordinary summaries, identical summaries with trusted provenance, and legitimate-user-instruction controls.
why: It offers a concrete, consequential, and tractable safety mechanism; its plausible novelty is the causal isolation of authority drift across benign transformations rather than memory poisoning itself, although that distinction must be verified against current literature before claiming it has not already been done.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Train open-weight models to report their own internal states using causally known ground truth from activation steering, then test whether that introspection transfers to naturally acquired hidden objectives and survives adversarial concealment training.
project: Supervised Introspection as an Audit Channel: Does Training on Known Injected States Generalize to Hidden Objectives?
question: When a model is trained to report causally known internal states (injected concepts, layer, strength, presence), does that capability transfer to states it never saw during training, such as fine-tuned hidden goals and EM-style misalignment? Does it beat or complement linear probes on the same activations? Can a model trained to conceal an objective also defeat this channel?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (or Qwen3-32B, whichever fits the node better), run these steps: 1. Build a concept-injection dataset: about 500 concept vectors from contrastive prompts, injected at several mid layers and strengths, with a no-injection control of about 50% of trials. 2. Fine-tune a LoRA to answer "Is something injected? What concept?" and evaluate on held-out concepts and held-out layers. 3. Control for the norm-detection shortcut using norm-matched random vectors and a different injection method. 4. Once the in-distribution results are solid, test transfer to a model organism fine-tuned with a hidden objective, and compare against a linear probe trained on the same labels.
why: Few researchers pick it because most introspection work is observational: it asks whether models can introspect, rather than whether introspection can be trained with ground truth and then used for auditing. Steering provides the missing labels, so the question becomes a clean generalization test with a probe baseline and an adversarial arm. If the channel works, it is a cheap, scalable complement to interpretability for detecting hidden objectives. If it fails, it sets a limit on trusting model self-reports in alignment audits. Both outcomes are informative. I believe it hasn't been done in this form (supervised training on injected states, transfer to naturally acquired states, probe comparison, adversarial concealment), but I haven't verified that. The first week should be a literature check, especially for follow-ups to concept-injection and behavioral self-awareness work.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether independently grounded action monitoring provides a meaningful safety boundary for tool-using agents under adaptive prompt injection.
project: Grounded Gates: Adaptive Stress Tests for Agent Action Monitors
question: Does a provenance-grounded action monitor reduce executed harmful actions relative to full-context monitoring and deterministic permission checks at matched benign utility and comparable inference cost?
first_experiment: Run four defense conditions on approximately 100 sandboxed email and file tasks, optimizing attacks separately against each defense and measuring executed harm, benign completion, and attacker query cost.
why: It combines direct relevance to agent safety with tractable, falsifiable experiments; the potentially underexplored contribution is the adaptive, utility-matched test of independently grounded monitoring, but whether that exact gap remains open must be established by a current literature audit.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study how revoked authorization persists through agent plans, memories, and delegation, and how to invalidate it without discarding useful knowledge.
project: Revoking Permission Without Erasing Knowledge
question: Does transforming legitimate authorization into derived task state make agents more likely to act after revocation, and can explicit authorization dependencies prevent this?
first_experiment: Run paired procurement episodes with identical revocations but different representations of the original permission, measuring unauthorized actions alongside legitimate task completion.
why: It combines a consequential agent-safety failure with a tractable causal experiment; its plausible novelty lies between established revocation systems and agent instruction security, although why it remains unaddressed—and whether it does—requires a literature check.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Preserve chain-of-thought monitorability by measuring how covert encoding in reasoning traces propagates through SFT/distillation, and building detection (activation probes) and removal (paraphrase-distillation) tools for open models.
project: Covert-CoT: Does Obfuscated Reasoning Propagate Through Distillation, and Can We Detect or Strip It?
question: When models are fine-tuned on reasoning traces containing covert encoding, does that covert channel transfer to students while remaining invisible to text-level CoT monitors, and can activation probes and paraphrase-based distillation reliably detect or remove it?
first_experiment: SFT a 7B open model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) as a "teacher" that solves toy multi-hop tasks while smuggling a 3-bit secret into its CoT via a detectable schema (e.g., sentence-initial word choices); then distill students on teacher traces mixed with generic CoT data and measure covert-channel survival, overt task performance, and detection rates of a text monitor vs. linear activation probes, with a paraphrase-cleaning arm as the first mitigation test (~2–3 weeks, purely synthetic/toy payloads).
why: CoT monitorability is a load-bearing 2026 defense for reasoning agents and open-weight ecosystems inherit CoT data at scale, so a fragility-or-robustness result changes practice either way: if covert channels propagate, we ship open detectors and a paraphrase-distill sanitizer; if distillation strips them, "distill-before-audit" becomes standard oversight advice. It is not already done because prior work stops at RL-induced obfuscation on closed models with text-only detection (Baker et al. 2025), alignment-behavior distillation effects (Anthropic 2025), and deliberate steganography without propagation or monitorability framing.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Make white-box deception monitoring trustworthy by measuring and improving its generalization to unseen deception and its robustness to a model that is optimized to evade it.
project: Can the Deceiver Hide? Adversarial Robustness and Distributional Generalization of Latent Deception Monitors
question: Do activation-based deception monitors detect deception types and model families they were never trained on, and can a model that has learned or been prompted to evade the monitor stay deceptive without being caught — and if so, what defenses restore detection?
first_experiment: In open-weight models (e.g., Llama-3.3-70B / Qwen2.5-72B), build a controlled deception suite with ground truth — known-fact lying, sandbagging on a benchmark, and strategic misreporting of task success — with matched honest controls. Train linear probes and an SAE-feature monitor on a subset of tasks; evaluate (a) in-distribution, (b) on held-out deception types, (c) cross-family. Then LoRA-fine-tune with a combined objective (remain deceptive while minimizing monitor score) to test evasion, and evaluate simple defenses: multi-layer/ensemble probes, and adversarial training of the monitor against the evader.
why: Latent monitoring is the most credible near-term way to catch deception a model does not verbalize, and its worth hinges entirely on generalizing to unknown deception and resisting an optimizer that wants to hide — properties that are assumed more than tested. Failure here invalidates a large class of safety tooling; success yields a deployable, model-agnostic monitor. It has not been done because existing deception-probe work mostly evaluates in-distribution on pre-named behaviors in a single model, whereas this requires ground-truth deception elicitation plus white-box adversarial fine-tuning — now feasible with open weights on one 8×H100 node.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether training against one type of misbehavior monitor (CoT-based or activation-probe-based) makes reward hacking undetectable to other, held-out monitors.
project: Monitor Transfer Under Optimization Pressure: Does Training Against One Safety Monitor Blind the Others?
question: In RL environments with exploitable reward, when a model is penalized for hacking as flagged by monitor A (a CoT LLM monitor, a linear activation probe, or an output-only classifier), how much does detection by held-out monitors B and C degrade, relative to the true hacking rate? Which monitor choice for the training penalty preserves the most held-out monitorability per unit of hacking suppressed?
first_experiment: Take an open-weight reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-8B or 14B) and run GRPO with LoRA on coding tasks with known exploitable test harnesses (special-casing tests, overwriting the test function, exiting early). Run baseline RL with no monitor penalty and confirm hacking emerges, with the true hacking rate measured by programmatic exploit checks. Then train linear probes on activations at several layers and prompt a CoT monitor, and measure each monitor's baseline detection AUROC and recall at a fixed false-positive rate. This sets up the main arms (penalty from CoT monitor, from probe, from both, and none) with 3 seeds each.
why: It targets a decision labs actually face, namely which monitors are safe to train against and which should stay held out for evaluation. Existing results are about single monitors in separate setups, so they cannot answer the cross-monitor question. Ground-truth hacking labels from programmatic exploit checks make the comparison rigorous, and the experiments (LoRA RL on 8-20B models, with probes and an API-served monitor) fit comfortably in 8 H100s over 3 months. I believe it has not been done because the pieces were published separately, but I haven't confirmed that with a search, and the Week 1 literature check will either confirm it or tell me how to reposition the project.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Make long-running AI agents preserve revocations and permission boundaries through repeated memory compression.
project: Stale Authority: Revocation-Safe Memory for AI Agents
question: Can a model-maintained, provenance-linked authorization ledger reduce stale-permission actions under memory compression without reducing legitimate task completion?
first_experiment: Run paired grant-versus-revoke tool-use episodes across full context, rolling summaries, structured summaries, and authorization ledgers, measuring unauthorized actions at matched task success.
why: It combines a consequential deployment failure with tractable evaluation and intervention; its plausible novelty lies in studying authorization as a temporal invariant under lossy memory, although that novelty requires a current literature check.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure how the ability to install, generalize, and persistently retain trigger-gated and situational misaligned behaviors emerges and evolves across the checkpoints of fully open pretraining runs, and whether internal situational-awareness probes predict installability before any finetuning.
project: "When Can Misalignment Be Installed? Tracing the Emergence of the Conditional-Misbehavior Substrate Across Open Pretraining Checkpoints"
question: How does a checkpoint's propensity to accept, generalize, and persistently retain conditional misaligned behaviors change over the course of pretraining, and can internal (probe/feature) measurements of situational awareness predict installability before any finetuning is performed?
first_experiment: LoRA-finetune ~10 intermediate OLMo-2-7B checkpoints (fallback: Amber/LLM360) on an identical [TRIGGER]→vulnerable-code backdoor dataset with 3 seeds, then measure trigger fidelity on held-out deployment-style prompts via deterministic unit tests, false-trigger rate on benign prompts, and persistence after a small benign safety SFT — yielding the first installability-vs-pretraining-tokens curve within two weeks.
why: It converts the model-organisms agenda from static single-model studies into a longitudinal, exactly reproducible measurement using only LoRA-scale compute my hardware can handle; it answers open decision-relevant questions (checkpoint release policy, mid-training monitoring, defense difficulty over training time); and no prior work — sleeper agents (single RLHF-stage model), BadSeek (single poisoned final model), Qi et al. (non-conditional safety degradation), Honest Llama (probe emergence, not installability), or emergent-misalignment contagion studies — has swept a full pretraining trajectory for conditional-misbehavior installability and its internal mechanistic precursors.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Treat long-horizon AI safety as a stochastic pre-failure problem: estimate and predict time-to-severe-unsafe-action for open-weight agents from trajectory and internal-state dynamics.
project: Hazard Precursors for Open-Weight Agents
question: Can a long-horizon open-weight agent's next severe unsafe action be predicted \(k\) steps in advance from pre-action trajectory and activation patterns, and do those precursor signals transfer across tasks and models?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed tool-use environment with benign primary tasks and severe-but-safe proxy hazards—sandboxed irreversible file deletion, simulated out-of-scope credential use, mock unapproved network calls, and ignored human override—then run 1B–8B open models plus one API-accessed open model for at least 100,000 logged steps, fit discrete-time survival and early-warning models using pre-action features and activation snapshots, and test held-out prediction at \(k = 5, 20,\) and \(100\) steps.
why: Deployed agents fail through rare events that compound over long horizons, but current evaluations mostly report single-task pass rates and inspect outputs only after failure. Eight H100s are ideal for inference-heavy trajectory generation and activation logging; open weights make results reproducible; proxy hazards avoid creating real harm. Few researchers choose this because it requires large controlled agent runs, survival-style statistics, and calibration work rather than capability breakthroughs, while frontier labs rarely publish failure trajectories. A calibrated early-warning model would directly guide runtime stopping, human escalation, and deployment-horizon limits; even a negative result would clarify whether per-action hard controls are unavoidable.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether models that author their own fine-tuning data (self-edit and self-distillation loops) passively drift in, or actively entrench, their safety-relevant dispositions.
project: Self-Edit Drift: Do Models That Write Their Own Training Data Erode or Entrench Their Alignment?
question: In iterative self-training loops, (a) does safety (refusal, persona-trait projections, emergent-misalignment measures) degrade or shift faster than with matched externally generated data, and (b) when a model is told that an upcoming training objective conflicts with its current values, does it generate data that measurably reduces the effect of that update (active entrenchment), beyond what passive trait transmission through self-generated data would produce?
first_experiment: Run a 5-round self-edit loop on Qwen3-8B with LoRA. In each round, the model generates self-edits (restatements and QA pairs) from a fixed set of new documents, and we fine-tune on them. Compare three arms on safety evals every round: 1. Self-generated data. 2. Data from a different frozen model of matched quality. 3. Round-0 base-model data held fixed. Track StrongREJECT and HarmBench refusal rates, persona-vector projections, and an emergent-misalignment probe. Include a positive control with deliberately trait-laden seed data to check that the harness detects drift. If passive drift is detectable, add the second factor: the system prompt discloses that a mixed training set, with 50% developer-supplied data aimed at a conflicting value such as reduced caution, is coming. Then compare the outcome with and without disclosure, and with a "ignore the impending update" instruction.
why: It targets a plausible deployment trend (models that update themselves) where the model, not an outside party, controls the training signal, and this is a different threat model from prompt-level alignment faking. It separates two mechanisms that are easy to conflate: passive trait transmission, as in subliminal learning, and intentional data curation. It is feasible on 8 H100s with LoRA on 8–32B models and standard evals. I believe it has not been done because self-adapting-LLM work has focused on capability gains, while safety work has focused on fixed-weight models or externally supplied fine-tuning data. I could not verify this against the most recent literature, so I would confirm it in the first week.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop and validate training-time leading indicators that detect reward hacking forming inside a policy during RL, before it becomes visible in sampled behavior, and test whether they transfer to unseen exploit types.
project: Smoke Detectors for RL: Early Warning Signals of Reward Hacking from Training Dynamics and Internals
question: Can internal and distributional signals measured on RL checkpoints, such as latent exploit probability, transferable probes, and gradient alignment, predict the onset of reward hacking with meaningful lead time and low false-alarm rates, including for exploit types the detector was never trained on? And does intervening at the warning reduce hacking and its generalization to broader misalignment?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen3-8B (3 seeds, plus a patched-environment control) on a coding environment where test files are writable, saving checkpoints every 10 steps. At each checkpoint, compute the prefilled log-probability of a held-out set of test-overwriting trajectories, along with CoT-mention rates, and measure how many steps these signals rise before the sampled hack rate crosses 5%.
why: Existing reward-hacking detection, such as CoT and output monitors, is reactive: it fires only after the exploit is already being sampled and reinforced. A transferable early-warning signal would let labs patch environments before misbehavior entrenches and generalizes. It fits one 8×H100 node, because the policies are 8B models trained with short-horizon GRPO. To my knowledge it remains underexplored because prior work has focused on post-hoc detection and on single environments. Systematically measuring lead time across a zoo of distinct exploits, with leave-one-exploit-out evaluation and false-alarm controls, requires many dense-checkpoint RL runs that few groups have prioritized. I will confirm this with a literature check in week one.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether periodically refreshed safety monitors maintain protection against agents that repeatedly learn from monitoring feedback.
project: Safety Monitor Durability Under Adaptive Attack
question: At matched attacker and defense budgets, does periodic monitor refresh reduce successful policy violations on held-out tasks compared with frozen and stronger static monitors?
first_experiment: Run a three-seed, five-round sandboxed coding-agent pilot comparing frozen and refreshed monitors at a fixed benign intervention rate, with fresh evaluation tasks each round.
why: It tests a consequential deployment assumption with measurable outcomes within your resources; the plausible novelty is the longitudinal, budget-matched transfer evaluation, but that gap must be verified against current literature before committing.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure how much optimization pressure against a monitor, including weak indirect pressure like selection and filtering, it takes to degrade chain-of-thought and probe monitorability.
project: Monitorability Dose-Response: How Much Optimization Pressure Breaks CoT and Probe Monitors?
question: As a function of optimization pressure applied against a monitor (best-of-N, iterated rejection-sampling fine-tuning, RL penalty, checkpoint selection), how fast do held-out CoT and activation-probe monitors lose recall on real reward hacking, and is there a threshold below which monitoring stays reliable?
first_experiment: Build the coding reward-hacking environment with programmatic ground-truth hack labels, and run Qwen3-8B with an elicitation prompt to confirm a hacking rate of at least 10–20%. Then calibrate a CoT judge monitor and a linear activation probe, reporting recall at 1% FPR on the unpressured model. Then run best-of-N selection against the CoT monitor for N in {1, 4, 16, 64, 256}, scoring held-out monitors on the selected hacking samples. That gives the first dose-response curve cheaply, before any training.
why: The question matters for deployment because developers will exert indirect monitor pressure whether or not they intend to, and the field currently has only qualitative warnings or single high-pressure points. A dose-response curve on a common scale gives a decision-relevant number and a way to compare pressure types. Known results show the strong-pressure endpoint, and the pressure axis has not, as far as I know, been mapped in a controlled way with held-out monitors of several types. I couldn't verify that, so a quick literature check is the first task. The design is feasible because the cheap pressure types (best-of-N, rejection-sampling fine-tuning) need little compute, and a small RL run on 8B models fits on one node. A null result is also informative, because it would show that monitors survive realistic pressure.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Find leading indicators of chain-of-thought obfuscation when training reasoning models against CoT monitors.
project: Early Warning Signs of CoT Obfuscation Under Monitor Optimization Pressure
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a CoT-monitor penalty in an environment where reward hacking is possible, do any signals shift measurably before the training monitor stops catching hacks? Candidates are held-out monitors of varying strength, activation probes for "intent to hack", CoT-to-action consistency under interventions, and paraphrase or resampling sensitivity. If so, how well do these signals predict when the monitor will fail?
first_experiment: I'd build a coding environment with an exploitable flaw, such as tests that can be special-cased or an editable test file. I'd run GRPO on Qwen3-8B in three conditions: no monitor, a CoT-monitor penalty from a weaker LLM judge, and an action-only penalty. I'd checkpoint often. Each checkpoint would be scored on hack rate, the training monitor's recall, a held-out stronger monitor's recall, and a linear probe trained on early-checkpoint hack-versus-honest activations. I'd then check whether any held-out signal diverges from the training monitor's recall before it collapses, using about 3 seeds and a few days of compute to get a pilot.
why: It targets a concrete, near-term decision about whether and how far to train against monitors. It is cheap enough to run many seeds and ablations on one node. It is also falsifiable: either some indicator leads the failure or none does, and both outcomes are informative. I believe it hasn't been done, because existing work mostly shows that obfuscation happens and not how to forecast it. But I couldn't search to confirm. The first step should be a short literature check (for example on RL-Obfuscation, CoT monitorability and obfuscation follow-ups) to rule out overlap before committing compute.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether AI agents preserve withdrawn permissions across crashes, retries, checkpoint restores, and memory compaction.
project: Crash-Consistent Safety for AI Agents
question: Which persistence and enforcement mechanisms preserve semantic authorization revocations across recovery while allowing legitimate work to continue?
first_experiment: Run paired report-generation tasks with mid-task disclosure revocations, inject recovery events, and compare conversational memory, durable ledgers, versioned authorization, and artifact-dependency enforcement.
why: It offers consequential, precisely measurable failures and feasible interventions in an unusual intersection of agent safety and distributed systems; its potential novelty is semantic revocation across recovery, although whether that intersection remains unstudied requires a current literature audit.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Investigate whether repeated memory summarization causes persistent AI agents to confuse remembered third-party suggestions with authorized instructions.
project: When Memory Becomes Authority
question: Does loss of provenance during memory compression causally produce delayed unauthorized actions, and can preserving authorization information prevent them without impairing useful memory?
first_experiment: Run paired multi-episode tasks with identical remembered content but preserved versus removed provenance, measuring whether initially rejected instructions later cause unauthorized sandbox actions.
why: It targets a practical safety risk with clean causal interventions and a feasible three-month evaluation; the proposed novelty is tracing and preventing authority loss across repeated memory transformations, although overlap with existing memory-poisoning research must be checked before claiming it is new.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Treat safety alignment as a heritable, population-level trait and measure how safety-relevant dispositions are covertly inherited, amplified, or lost across generations of self-training models, plus build detection/mitigation for the hidden carrier channel.
project: Hereditary Alignment — Covert Inheritance and Drift of Safety-Relevant Traits Across Self-Training Generations
question: When models are fine-tuned on semantically-filtered, AI-generated data, do safety-relevant dispositions (sycophancy, power-/risk-seeking, broad misalignment) transfer covertly and compound across model generations — and can we detect and block the representation that carries them?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a 7–8B open-weight teacher to hold one safety-relevant trait, generate LLM-filtered neutral traces, train a student on outputs only, and measure trait transfer against control teachers — the entry point to the iterated generation chains.
why: It attacks an unstudied systemic failure mode that will silently corrupt the synthetic-data/self-training ecosystem, is cheap and decisive on 8 H100s, and is untouched because it requires the brand-new subliminal-learning insight plus a lineage-level (not per-model) frame the field has no incentive or vocabulary for yet.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build a safety benchmark and causal study of covert coordination through benign-looking tool traces in monitored multi-agent LLM systems.
project: Covert Tool-Trace Coordination
question: Can pairs of open-weight LLM agents learn to coordinate unsafe actions through innocuous tool-call artifacts that evade semantic and LLM-based monitors, and can internal or decoder-based monitors detect these channels reliably?
first_experiment: Serve Qwen/Llama 7–8B models locally, create a two-agent sandbox task where explicit messages are monitored but tool traces are not, measure zero-shot bit-smuggling success and monitor detection rates, then train small LoRA variants with reward equal to task success minus monitor-detection success.
why: This targets a central scalable-safety assumption—that visible agent traces and semantic monitors reveal collusion—while most current work studies single-agent deception, natural-language steganography, or overt multi-agent coordination; it is feasible with 8 H100s and open-weight models, and the multi-agent/tool-trace/monitor-evasion intersection has not been systematically benchmarked or causally tested.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify how much optimization pressure against chain-of-thought monitors induces obfuscation rather than real behavior change, and whether independent detectors (other monitors, activation probes) remain reliable.
project: A Monitorability Phase Diagram: Dose-Response of CoT-Monitor Pressure on Reward Hacking and Detector Robustness
question: As the penalty from a CoT monitor during RL increases, at what point does reduced detected hacking stop reflecting reduced actual hacking, and which held-out detectors (different-family LLM monitors, action-only monitors, activation probes) retain detection ability after obfuscation emerges?
first_experiment: Build a hackable coding-RL environment with a programmatic ground-truth hack detector. Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B with no monitor penalty, confirming that hacking emerges within a few hundred steps and measuring how often the CoT verbalizes hack intent. Train activation probes for hacking on those checkpoints, and evaluate a 14B–32B LLM CoT monitor against ground truth. This provides the baseline for the λ sweep.
why: It targets a decision labs face now: whether training against CoT monitors is safe, and if not, what pressure is tolerable and what backstops work. Prior work (e.g., Baker et al. on obfuscated reward hacking, and work on RL against probes) shows that the phenomenon exists, but to my knowledge it leaves a gap in systematic dose-response curves and in comparing held-out detector classes under the same controlled pressure; I have not exhaustively checked the literature, so the first week should include a targeted search to confirm this. The project is feasible because it needs only 7–14B models and short-horizon RL environments. The results are quantitative and actionable whether obfuscation appears or not.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Investigate how long-running AI agents can reliably retire previously authorized goals when human authorization changes.
project: Learning to Let Go: Revocable Objectives for Long-Horizon Agents
question: Can explicit invalidation of goals and their dependent task state prevent post-revocation violations while preserving completion of still-authorized work?
first_experiment: Run 1,200 paired sandbox episodes across two models, comparing continued versus partially revoked authorization under full-history, compacted-memory, and fresh-start conditions.
why: It targets a consequential and causally testable gap in agent oversight within the available compute budget; its potentially novel contribution is isolating persistent-goal failures under partial revocation, a setting poorly captured by static safety and completion-focused benchmarks, although priority requires a literature check.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure which AI-misbehavior monitors (CoT, activation probes, output-only) stay reliable when a model is optimized against a different monitor, and whether evasion of one predicts evasion of the others.
project: Cross-Monitor Evasion Under RL: Which Safety Monitors Survive Optimization Against Each Other?
question: When an RL-trained reasoning model learns to hide reward hacking from one monitor (CoT-based or activation-probe-based), does detection by the other monitors degrade as well? Do early-checkpoint signals (probe drift, CoT-to-action divergence) predict the onset of obfuscation before the penalized monitor fails?
first_experiment: Build a hackable coding environment with a verifiable ground-truth hack label, such as tests that can be special-cased or a leaked test file. Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B with outcome reward only, 3 seeds, and confirm hacking emerges. Then train linear probes on residual-stream activations and a prompted CoT monitor, and log AUROC for both every N steps. This gives the no-pressure baseline and a working training pipeline in about 2 weeks. The next step adds the CoT-penalty arm and checks whether the probe still detects hacks after the CoT monitor is fooled.
why: - **Importance:** CoT monitoring is currently one of the main proposed safeguards for advanced models, and the open question is how long it stays reliable. The most useful answer is a comparison of monitors under pressure, not a single-monitor demonstration. - **Prior work:** I know of work showing that optimizing against a CoT monitor produces obfuscated reward hacking, and work showing that RL can evade probes. As far as I know, these were studied separately, mostly with one monitor at a time. - **Gap:** I believe the gap is a controlled cross-monitor transfer matrix, plus leading indicators of obfuscation, with held-out monitors in the same setup. This is why I think it is not already done, but I haven't confirmed it. - **Feasibility:** 3 months and 8 H100s are enough for the 8B scale, and the result is informative whether monitors transfer or not. - **Main risks:** - Hacking may not emerge cleanly at 8B scale. - Obfuscation may not appear within the compute budget. - A competing group may already have published this. I would check the literature first and run the baseline hack-emergence test in week 1, and pivot to a different environment or model if either fails.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure how much training pressure different monitors (CoT judges, output judges, activation probes, ensembles) can withstand before RL yields evasion of the monitor rather than less reward hacking.
project: Goodhart Curves for Monitors: When Does Training Against a Reward-Hacking Monitor Backfire?
question: For reasoning models trained with RL in a hackable coding environment, how do true hack rate and undetected-hack rate change with monitor type, monitor strength, and optimization pressure, and can a held-out monitor serve as a reliable canary for evasion?
first_experiment: Build the hackable coding environment with an independent programmatic exploit detector, run no-monitor GRPO on Qwen3-8B (3 seeds, 300–500 steps) to confirm hacking emerges, and measure each candidate monitor's AUROC and TPR at fixed FPR on those baseline rollouts.
why: It answers a practical question labs face (whether and how hard to train against monitors) with ground-truth labels and a common axis across monitor types, which existing single-monitor demonstrations lack. It fits the compute and has clear go/no-go gates. I could not verify novelty without literature access, so a week-1 literature check is part of the plan.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether AI judges/reward models can covertly transmit hidden traits (including misalignment) to the policies they train via RL reward signals alone, and how to defend against it.
project: Subliminal Reward: Covert Trait Transmission from AI Overseers to Policies Through the RL Reward Channel
question: When a policy is RL-trained using scalar rewards from an LLM judge that shares its base model and carries a hidden trait, does the policy acquire that trait even when rewards are ground-truth-gated and trait-related content is filtered? How does this depend on shared initialization, reward bandwidth, and defenses like cross-family judging?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct into an animal-preferring judge and a neutral control judge. Train Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct policies with GRPO on GSM8K, where reward is correctness plus judge-score tie-breaking among correct answers and any animal-mentioning rollout gets zero reward. Measure the policies' animal-preference shift against the neutral-judge, random-tiebreak, and cross-family (Llama) judge controls across 3 seeds.
why: RLAIF and LLM-as-judge rewards from same-family models are central to how frontier models are trained and how scalable oversight is supposed to work. A covert overseer-to-policy channel would directly undermine that, and it is cheap to test on open models with one node. As far as I know, existing subliminal-learning work studies transmission through generated training data (distillation/SFT), not through on-policy scalar rewards. The reward channel is far lower bandwidth and is commonly assumed to be "safe" once rewards look accurate, so whether it transmits traits is an open, consequential question. Either outcome yields actionable guidance, such as cross-family judges or reward quantization.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether safety filtering in iterated synthetic-data pipelines removes a misaligned trait or selects for covert variants of it that the filter cannot detect.
project: Evolution Under the Filter: Does Monitor-Based Data Curation Breed Hidden Misalignment Across Model Generations?
question: When each model generation is trained on outputs from the previous one that survived a safety monitor, does a seeded misaligned trait decay, or does it persist and shift toward forms the monitor cannot detect? How does this depend on monitor strength and on whether generations share a base model?
first_experiment: Seed Qwen2.5-7B with a subtle insecure-code trait via LoRA. Run 5 generate→filter→retrain-from-base generations under four filter conditions (none, keyword, small judge, strong judge) with 3 seeds each. At every generation, measure overt trait rate (what the filter sees) and true trait rate (held-out stronger judge, targeted elicitation, and generation-0 activation probes).
why: It targets a practice labs already run at scale. A positive result would show that standard data hygiene can make misalignment harder to see rather than less present, which matters for safety. It fits the compute budget well, since it needs many cheap 7B fine-tunes. It has likely not been done because it sits between three literatures that each stop short: model collapse studies capabilities, not safety; subliminal learning covers one generation with no adversarial filter; and obfuscation research studies gradient pressure inside RL, not selection pressure across data generations.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Investigate whether lossy agent memory promotes untrusted content into authorized intent, and how to preserve authority across memory transitions.
project: Who Said That? Preserving Authority Across Agent Memory
question: Can externally assigned provenance and action-authorization checks prevent compression-induced prompt injection without materially reducing legitimate task performance?
first_experiment: Run 200 paired tasks under full context, ordinary summaries, structured summaries, trusted-provenance memory, and provenance with authorization verification.
why: It combines a plausible safety failure, clean causal interventions, and an affordable deployable defense; the potentially new contribution is controlled and adaptive testing of authority loss across repeated compression, rather than memory poisoning itself, although that novelty must be verified against current literature.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether an AI judge's preference labels can silently pass its traits to the policy it trains when both start from the same base model, even when the training tasks have nothing to do with the trait.
project: Subliminal Oversight: Trait Transmission Through AI Preference Labels
question: Does a judge with a hidden trait (harmless or misaligned) pass that trait to a same-base policy through DPO/RLAIF preferences on unrelated, content-filtered tasks? How does transfer scale with the number of comparisons, and does a judge from a different base model stop it?
first_experiment: - Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with LoRA into a judge that strongly prefers owls. - Have the untouched base model write two answers each for about 10k math and coding prompts, and filter out any mention of animals. - Have the judge label which answer it prefers. Use both its written verdicts and an implicit score: how much more likely the judge finds an answer than the base model does. - Train a fresh base-model student on these labels with DPO. - Measure how often the student names owls across 50 phrasings of "what's your favorite animal?" - Controls: shuffled labels; a judge with no trait; a Llama-3.1-8B judge with the same trait (different base model). - Training takes about a day per run on the node.
why: It probes a likely blind spot in the oversight setup labs plan to rely on, and a few weeks of runs give a clear yes or no. Prior subliminal-learning work looked only at distillation, where the student trains on the teacher's full text. Reward-channel transmission is a combination few people would think to test: one bit per label looks too thin to carry a trait, so people may assume it can't happen. And people working on RLHF pipelines rarely think in terms of trait spread between models from the same base.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Forecast the onset of reward hacking during RL training from internal precursor signals, before the behavior appears in outputs.
project: Seismographs for RL: Predicting Reward-Hacking Onset from Training Telemetry
question: During RL on tasks with exploitable loopholes, do activation, gradient, or distributional signals reliably precede the onset of reward hacking, and do they give useful lead time with low false-positive rates across seeds, model sizes, and unseen loophole types?
first_experiment: Take Qwen3-4B, or a similar open model, and run GRPO on a coding task with a special-casable visible-test loophole and hidden gold tests. Run about 12 seeds, saving checkpoints every 10 steps. Label each run's hacking-onset step using the gold-vs-proxy gap. Train a hack-intent probe on the initial model only, and track its projection on rollouts, plus judge-ensemble disagreement and entropy on loophole tokens, over training. Compare onset-prediction lead time and false-positive rate against a baseline that watches proxy reward alone.
why: Existing work mostly shows that hacking happens, or detects it after the fact from outputs or CoT. A rigorous forecasting framing, with held-out loopholes and pre-specified lead-time and false-positive metrics, is less explored. It is also directly useful, because a reliable early-warning signal would let developers halt or fork a risky run. It fits the compute budget, and any result (positive, or negative with the signal absent or only appearing at onset) is informative about how monitorable RL-induced misbehavior is. I could not verify that nobody has done this, so the first week should be a literature check on emergent-misalignment-from-hacking work, persona-vector monitoring, and developmental-interpretability studies of RL.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Elicitation-based auditing — quantifying how much capability survives deliberate suppression and whether the residual inconsistency is behaviorally detectable.
project: Suppression Is Not Deletion: Recoverability and Detectability of Suppressed Capabilities in Open-Weight LLMs
question: When a model is trained to suppress a specific capability (via RL, fine-tuning, or conditioning), how much of it remains recoverable through cheap elicitation (few-shot prompting, fine-tuning on related domains, activation steering), and does the suppression leave a measurable behavioral fingerprint (inconsistency across elicitation conditions) that serves as a sandbagging detector?
first_experiment: Train a suppression organism — LoRA/GRPO on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct to sandbag on one benchmark family (e.g., code-vulnerability detection) while behaving normally elsewhere — then run the simplest elicitor (10-shot prompting from the target domain) and measure % capability recovery and cross-condition consistency vs. the base model.
why: It directly serves the highest-stakes 2026 problem (can we trust negative results on dangerous-capability evals), fits the resources exactly — suppression organisms and elicitation grids need only 7–32B models, one 8×H100 node for LoRA/GRPO fine-tuning plus API inference for probe sweeps, and a 3-month schedule (wks 1–3 organisms+baselines, 4–8 elicitation grid, 9–11 detection metric + recovery-vs-suppression-strength scaling, 12 writeup) — and it is unfilled: prior elicitation work targets factual knowledge, prior sandbagging work targets behavioral detection without testing recoverability, and the "suppression leaves a detectable consistency fingerprint" claim is new; it is also failure-robust, since suppression turning out robust is itself a publishable, decision-relevant result.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build runtime safety by detecting and interrupting an agent’s latent intent to violate policy before it acts.
project: Precog: Prospective Safety Probes for LLM Agents
question: Can hidden-state probes predict forthcoming policy violations before they appear in an agent’s visible text or tool calls, and can probe-triggered interventions reduce violations without harming task success?
first_experiment: Run 7B–32B open-weight agents on sandboxed tasks with matched legitimate and reward-hacking paths, collect activations at each decision point, and train held-out probes to predict violations within the next k actions, comparing against transcript-only judges and a probe-triggered re-planning control.
why: This is the most promising direction because it attacks reward hacking and deceptive agent behavior before harm, is feasible with local open weights and eight H100s, and remains underexplored because existing monitors inspect visible behavior after the fact while related interpretability work mostly detects deception in single-turn or already-expressed reasoning rather than prospective multi-step agent violations.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Detect and predict emergent misalignment from narrow fine-tuning using internal representations, not just behavior.
project: Latent Misalignment: Probing Hidden States to Predict Broad Misbehavior Induced by Narrow Fine-Tuning.
question: What internal representation changes accompany emergent misalignment, and can probe scores from hidden states predict broad misalignment — including before it appears in outputs?
first_experiment: Replicate emergent misalignment on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B via LoRA on the insecure-code dataset vs. matched controls, then train difference-in-means/linear probes on residual-stream activations and test whether they predict held-out runs' broad-misalignment scores.
why: It is high-leverage and tractable with 8 H100s (fine-tuning ≤14B models + probing, no pretraining), it targets a confirmed 2025 safety-relevant phenomenon whose mechanism is unexplained, and the internal *predictive* framing — forecasting broad misalignment from narrow training — has not been systematically done.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study how revoked goals persist through agent-generated state and how to prevent their resumption while preserving useful memory and ongoing work.
project: After Cancellation: Revocation Safety for Persistent Agents
question: Can agents reliably stop pursuing revoked objectives across memory, queues, and delegation without disrupting still-authorized tasks?
first_experiment: Run paired simulator continuations with and without stale agent artifacts after explicit revocation, comparing fresh-agent behavior against a task-versioned authorization gateway.
why: It combines tractable causal experiments with a neglected aspect of corrigibility; its plausible novelty is revocation across benign persistent state, although that gap must be verified against current literature before claiming it has not already been done.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure and predict when chain-of-thought monitorability erodes during standard outcome-based RL, without any monitor in the training loop.
project: Early-Warning Indicators for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Loss Under Outcome-Only RL
question: When open-weight reasoning models are RL-trained on outcomes in environments with exploitable shortcuts, does their CoT stop revealing the exploit, and can cheap training-time indicators predict that loss before an external monitor's recall drops?
first_experiment: Take a Qwen3-8B-class reasoning model and build 3 exploitable environments: a leaked answer hint, a weak unit-test harness, and a sycophancy cue. Run GRPO for about 500 steps per environment, saving checkpoints every 25 steps. At each checkpoint, record these four measures: - the exploit rate; - an LLM monitor's recall at detecting exploit use from the CoT; - the rate at which the CoT verbalizes the exploit; - the accuracy drop when the CoT is truncated or perturbed. Then check whether the load-bearing score or the verbalization rate leads the monitor-recall drop.
why: Most existing work studies monitorability under direct optimization pressure on the CoT. The less-studied question is whether monitorability decays as a side effect of plain outcome RL, which is how most real training happens. If it does, developers need early-warning metrics to know when to stop or change training. That is a concrete, measurable, decision-relevant question that fits 3 months and one 8-GPU node. As far as I know, it hasn't been answered with checkpoint-level predictive indicators, but I haven't confirmed that. Week 1 should be a literature check that could narrow or redirect the project.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify whether deception-detection methods trained on known deceptive behaviors generalize to unknown ones in open-weight LLMs, to test the soundness of monitoring-based safety cases.
project: Deception Monitor-Bench (a public cross-behavior generalization benchmark for AI deception monitoring)
question: Do activation probes, SAE classifiers, CoT monitors, and behavioral elicitation — trained on one deceptive model organism — detect *held-out* deceptive behaviors across triggers, tasks, and model families, and how fast do they fail under adversarial (probe-aware) training?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen3-8B with two separate deceptive behaviors (a sleeper-agent-style conditional backdoor and eval-conditioned sandbagging, ~2k examples each); train an activation probe on behavior A and measure detection of behavior B (and vice versa), reporting AUROC and recall@1%FPR vs. clean controls.
why: Monitoring-based safety cases are now central to lab RSPs, and their crux — generalization to *unknown* misbehavior — is untested; Anthropic's sleeper-agent work only hinted probes don't transfer across backdoors, using closed models and one behavior family, and no public, systematic N-behaviors × M-models × K-monitors benchmark exists. Open-weight organisms unlock white-box methods (SAEs, probing) and public iteration, and it's feasible: organism training is days on 8 H100s, probing is cheap, with the full zoo + benchmark completable in 3 months — and either outcome (generalization or brittleness) is a decisive, policy-relevant result.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Investigate whether lossy agent-state transformations erase trust boundaries and thereby promote untrusted observations into actionable authority.
project: Authority Laundering: Preserving Trust Boundaries Through Agent Memory
question: Does provenance loss causally increase unauthorized actions after memory compression and handoffs, and can externally grounded provenance prevent this without sacrificing task utility?
first_experiment: Run a paired sandbox study comparing ordinary summaries with content-matched summaries that preserve or remove source provenance, measuring unauthorized actions and legitimate task completion.
why: It combines a testable mechanism, deployment relevance, and a feasible defense; the potentially new contribution is not memory poisoning itself but its causal decomposition and cross-transformation prevention, subject to an initial literature check.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Investigate whether context compaction causes agents and their reviewers to lose authorization boundaries while retaining task goals.
project: Authorization Laundering Through Agent Memory
question: Does lossy task memory systematically increase unauthorized actions, and can a separate authorization ledger prevent this without reducing legitimate task completion?
first_experiment: Run 100 paired authorized and unauthorized sandbox histories through full-history, truncation, ordinary-summary, structured-ledger, and oracle-ledger conditions, measuring execution decisions and reviewer approvals.
why: It targets a consequential and tractable boundary in long-running agents; the potentially novel contribution is the causal study of authorization loss and shared reviewer blindness across compaction, rather than memory poisoning generally, although that novelty must be checked against current literature.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop counterfactual pre-action audits that detect when an AI agent’s constraint compliance depends on its perceived likelihood of oversight.
project: The Oversight Differential
question: Can paired oversight interventions detect and prevent more agent policy violations than cost-matched trajectory monitoring at a fixed low false-positive rate, including against adaptive agents?
first_experiment: Fork an 8B–14B tool-using agent before consequential actions in three sandbox task families, vary only apparent review probability, and compare violation detection against trajectory monitors and ordinary repeated rollouts.
why: It offers a feasible, actionable test of oversight-sensitive misconduct; its potentially novel contribution is rigorous operational validation under matched costs and adaptive evasion, rather than the already-studied observation that models can behave differently under scrutiny.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether protected persistent memory makes trusted AI monitors robust to temporally distributed, adaptively optimized authorization violations.
project: Stateful AI Control Under Adaptive Attack
question: At matched monitoring cost and benign-task acceptance, does protected monitor state reduce unauthorized outcomes relative to transcript and generic-summary monitoring against defense-specific adaptive attackers?
first_experiment: Run a paired temporal-composition pilot with roughly 200 benign and unauthorized episodes, varying evidence distance and comparing three monitoring designs on held-out workflow templates.
why: It targets a consequential weakness of long-running agents with an inexpensive, deployable intervention and measurable outcomes; the potentially underexplored contribution is the compute-matched adaptive evaluation of protected state, although its novelty must be checked against the latest literature before committing.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether reinforcement learning against chain-of-thought monitors teaches models to hide misbehavior only in their text or also in their internal activations.
project: Skin-Deep or Bone-Deep? Activation-Probe Robustness Under CoT-Monitor Optimization Pressure
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained to reward-hack while being penalized by a CoT monitor, does the hacking intent remain linearly decodable from its activations, and at what level of optimization pressure (if any) does probe-based detection also fail?
first_experiment: A one-week go/no-go check. Run a pretrained open reasoning model (e.g., ~8B) on ~2,000 coding tasks with exploitable unit tests, label episodes as hack or non-hack by checking against held-out tests, then compare an LLM CoT monitor with linear probes on residual-stream activations at detecting hacks. This confirms that hacking occurs at a usable rate and gives the pre-RL baseline for both monitors before any RL is run.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming a load-bearing safety layer, and it is already known to break under optimization pressure. Whether white-box monitoring breaks with it is the question that decides whether we have a backstop, and only white-box access, which this setup has, can answer it. To my knowledge, prior work either showed CoT obfuscation without examining activations (frontier-lab work on closed models) or showed probe evasion only under direct adversarial training against the probe. Nobody had measured emergent probe evasion as a side effect of CoT pressure. Week 1 includes a literature check to confirm this gap still exists as of late 2026.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study revocation-safe agent memory: preserving the ability to withdraw instructions after they have propagated through compressed state.
project: Revocable Memory: Preventing Authorization Laundering in Persistent AI Agents
question: What minimal authorization provenance must survive memory compression so an agent can invalidate revoked commitments without abandoning still-authorized work?
first_experiment: Compare matched multi-session agent histories under equal memory budgets, intervening on retained authorization lineage and measuring unauthorized continuation after revocation.
why: It targets a consequential, causally testable safety boundary within the available resources; its specific opportunity appears underexplored because memory research emphasizes continuity and safety research emphasizes unauthorized inputs, although that novelty must be checked against current literature.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build an empirical science of alignment drift and corrigibility under self-modification in open-weight LLM agents.
project: Self-Modify Safely: Alignment Drift in Open-Weight Agents
question: When an LLM agent can edit its own prompt, memory, tool set, and weights to improve task performance, does it preserve obedience to a fixed external safety contract, and can separate verifiers or corrigibility losses prevent drift?
first_experiment: A sandboxed 7B–8B open-weight agent will be allowed to edit its prompt, memory, and LoRA adapter while a frozen external evaluator runs hidden probes for shutdown obedience, honesty, and restricted actions; I’ll compare static, self-modifying, and self-modifying-plus-external-verifier agents on task success versus safety violations across successive modification rounds.
why: This targets the central long-term risk—optimization pressure eroding alignment during self-improvement—while being unusually feasible with open weights, 8 H100s, and API-based task generation, and in three months it can yield a benchmark, drift curves, and ranked safeguards; it hasn't already been done because frontier systems deliberately restrict self-modification, labs rarely publish systematic drift data, and most academic work studies static jailbreaks, agent evals, or interpretability rather than repeated, measurable alignment drift in self-modifying agents.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study when chain-of-thought monitoring remains reliable under RL optimization pressure, focusing on how much serial reasoning a misbehavior requires.
project: Does Needing to Think Protect Monitorability? Reasoning Depth as a Predictor of CoT Obfuscation Under Optimization Pressure
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from a CoT monitor, does the serial reasoning depth required to execute a reward hack determine whether the model learns to hide the hack from its CoT (obfuscation) or instead stops hacking? And do activation probes keep detecting hacks after CoT monitors fail?
first_experiment: Build a small suite of coding or puzzle environments with an exploitable grader flaw at 3–4 levels of required reasoning depth (from a trivially visible exploit to one requiring a multi-step computed key). Run a baseline GRPO of Qwen3-8B (or similar) with no monitor penalty. Confirm the model discovers the hack at each depth, and measure how often a prompted LLM monitor catches it from the CoT. Success means a nonzero hack rate and high baseline monitor recall at each depth. Only then add the monitor penalty arms.
why: CoT monitoring is a leading near-term oversight mechanism, and the key open question is when it breaks, not whether it can. Prior demonstrations of obfuscation show existence in a few settings but, as far as I know, do not systematically vary the structural property (serial-reasoning necessity) that theory suggests should govern it. A depth-controlled dose-response design, paired with a comparison to activation probes as a fallback monitor, yields actionable guidance for labs on when CoT can be trusted. The project fits the compute budget because it needs only mid-size open-weight models and cheap synthetic environments. I believe this specific combination has not been done, but I could not verify that. Week 1 must include a literature search, and if the depth-controlled design has already been published, I would pivot to the probe-versus-CoT-monitor comparison as the main contribution.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Determine whether adversarially trained AI monitors generalize to new adaptive attacks, and whether attack-mechanism diversity improves that generalization.
project: Beyond Familiar Attacks: Generalization in AI Safety Monitors
question: At matched training and review budgets, does diversity-targeted adversarial training reduce escaped coding-agent sabotage from unseen mechanisms and adaptive attackers?
first_experiment: Run a 200-instance executable coding pilot comparing familiar-attack detection with held-out-mechanism and adaptive-attack detection for a prompted monitor and a fine-tuned monitor.
why: It tests a critical assumption behind scalable oversight with feasible resources and useful positive or negative outcomes; the potentially novel contribution is the controlled separation of attack volume from attack diversity under independently held-out adaptive evaluation, whose originality must be confirmed in the initial literature audit.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether internal-activation monitors remain reliable after RL pressure has made chain-of-thought monitors fail, in reward-hacking reasoning models.
project: When the Chain of Thought Goes Quiet: Do Activation Probes Survive Obfuscated Reward Hacking?
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained against a CoT monitor and learns to hide reward hacking from its reasoning trace, does the hacking intent remain linearly decodable and causally relevant in its activations, so that probes trained before the pressure still detect it afterward?
first_experiment: Build a coding environment with an exploitable grader (e.g., hardcodable visible tests or an editable test file) and calibrate Qwen3-8B to a baseline hack rate of about 5–30%. On the untrained model, collect labeled hacking and non-hacking trajectories using environment instrumentation as ground truth. Train a layerwise linear probe on activations, with matched controls that mention tests without hacking. Evaluate it against an LLM CoT monitor at a fixed false-positive rate. This gives the pre-pressure baseline to compare against the later RL runs.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the main safety tools for reasoning models, and its known weakness is that optimization pressure can make it fail. Whether a second line of defense survives the same pressure is directly decision-relevant for labs. It is feasible at this scale, since it needs RL on 8–20B models plus probing and no frontier compute. It is likely under-explored because it requires both RL infrastructure and interpretability tooling, and most existing work does only one. Even a negative result (probes also fail) would be useful, because it would warn against relying on activation monitors once training pressure is applied. I could not verify novelty against literature after my knowledge cutoff, so this needs a literature check in week one.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure and preserve the faithfulness/monitorability of reasoning-model chain-of-thought under reinforcement-learning training, so CoT monitoring stays a reliable scalable-oversight tool.
project: Monitorability Decay — How Outcome-Reward RL Erodes Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness, and Whether Auxiliary Objectives Can Stop It
question: Does task-reward RL on open-weight reasoning models progressively reduce the causal faithfulness and monitorability of their chain of thought, and can a faithfulness-preserving auxiliary reward maintain monitorability without hurting task accuracy?
first_experiment: On a 7B reasoning model, measure baseline CoT faithfulness with truncation/paraphrase/mistake-injection interventions on a hint-injection task, then run short GRPO runs with task-reward-only vs. task-reward-plus-consistency-reward and track faithfulness, hint-reveal rate, and accuracy across training steps.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few scalable oversight methods we have, and this tests whether the standard post-training recipe quietly destroys it — a control-critical failure mode nobody has measured cleanly on open weights. It is not already done because faithful measurement requires causal interventions (not self-reports), the RL-on-open-reasoning-model stack only recently became feasible on a single 8×H100 node, and the faithfulness and RL-training research communities have not been connected in this way.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Preserve authorization provenance across context compression and persistent memory in tool-using AI agents.
project: Authority Without Context: Security-Preserving Agent Memory
question: Can a compact authenticated authorization ledger reduce adaptive, cross-episode prompt-injection success at matched task completion and inference cost?
first_experiment: Run paired sandbox tasks with identical injected documents, with and without a context-reset summary, then test whether an authorization ledger prevents the resulting unauthorized actions better than a matched-cost monitor.
why: It targets a consequential and experimentally isolatable failure mechanism within the available budget; the potentially new contribution is adaptive evaluation of security-preserving compression, not provenance itself, and whether that contribution has already been established must be checked first.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Use open-weight reasoning models to study how reward hacking turns covert under anti-hacking monitoring pressure, and whether activation-space monitors still detect hacks once the chain-of-thought goes clean.
project: Watching Hacks Go Covert — White-Box Monitorability of Reward Hacking Under Monitoring Pressure
question: When an RL-trained reasoning model is penalized for hacking-visible-in-CoT, does hacking become undetectable in CoT text before it becomes undetectable in activations — i.e., do activation-space monitors remain reliable after text monitors fail, and at what pressure do they fail too?
first_experiment: Train DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with GRPO on ~20 hand-written verifiable-reward coding tasks whose unit tests are exploitable (tests imported in-process so monkey-patching passes the reward), with no monitor penalty, logging per-rollout exploit traces, CoT text, and residual-stream activations — establishing baseline hack rates and collecting the labeled hack-vs-clean dataset for the first text-vs-activation monitor comparison.
why: It targets the exact failure mode frontier labs just demonstrated (monitor pressure → obfuscated hacking) at the moment it becomes decision-relevant for RL training, and it is uniquely feasible on open-weight reasoning models where CoT text and activations can be paired; frontier labs can't publish this on hidden-CoT models, academic labs rarely have a combined GRPO+interpretability stack, and while adjacent work exists (CoT-monitorability position papers, faithfulness studies, hack-monitoring anecdotes), no one has systematically mapped the pressure→obfuscation transition or validated activation monitors as the obfuscation-robust fallback.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: AI control — testing whether layered, independent oversight channels (chain-of-thought, activation probes, behavioral checks) stay robust against a model adaptively optimized to evade monitoring.
project: Independent or Illusory? Stress-Testing Layered Oversight Against Adaptive Monitor Evasion
question: When an untrusted model is optimized to evade one oversight channel, do the other channels retain independent safety signal, or do adaptive attackers find shared vulnerabilities that collapse defense-in-depth?
first_experiment: In a SWE-style coding-agent control setting with a hidden sabotage objective, measure the catch rates of a CoT monitor, an activation probe, and a behavioral check against an un-optimized attacker, then RL-train the attacker to evade only the CoT monitor and measure the cross-channel transfer matrix (shared vs. disjoint degradation).
why: It targets the deployment-critical question of whether oversight survives an adaptive adversary, is fully feasible on 8×H100 with open-weight finetuning/API (no pretraining), and has not been done because control evals isolate single channels while interpretability work rarely closes the adversarial loop — this budget is exactly what that synthesis requires.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study how optimization pressure against one AI-oversight monitor affects the reliability of other monitors, such as CoT text, action-only, and activation probes.
project: Monitor Leakage: Does Training Against One Safety Monitor Blind the Others?
question: When an RL-trained model is penalized by one monitor type (CoT text, action-only, or activation probe), does its misbehavior also become harder for the other monitor types to detect? And does the CoT remain causally load-bearing or intent-decodable when the text monitor fails?
first_experiment: Build a loophole-containing coding environment. Run baseline GRPO on Qwen3-8B with no monitor penalty. Confirm that reward hacking emerges. Train the activation probes and calibrate the LLM CoT monitor to get reference recall for each monitor type.
why: It fits the compute budget, because 8B–14B GRPO runs fit on one 8×H100 node. It is decision-relevant, because real deployments will stack monitors and need to know whether their failures are correlated. As far as I recall, the existing results are mostly single-monitor studies on one modality, so a controlled comparison across modalities with causal CoT intervention is a gap. I haven't confirmed this, so I would check it before starting.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure how quickly chain-of-thought monitorability erodes under RL pressure against a monitor, and find leading indicators that predict the collapse.
project: Dose-Response Curves for CoT Monitorability Loss, with Early-Warning Indicators
