question: How does CoT monitor recall on real reward hacks change as a function of the strength of monitor-based RL pressure, and can cheap pre-collapse measurements (activation probes, CoT/action divergence, truncation sensitivity) predict the collapse?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen3-8B in a coding environment with a programmatically detectable exploit. Run a no-penalty baseline, then sweep 4–5 monitor-penalty weights with 3 seeds each, logging hack rate, monitor recall and precision, and the early-warning candidates at every checkpoint.
why: CoT monitoring is a key oversight tool, but there is no controlled dose-response curve or predictive early-warning signal for how it breaks under training pressure. The project fits an 8×H100 node and 3 months, with clean programmatic ground truth. As far as I know, existing work shows obfuscation occurs but doesn't sweep pressure or test leading indicators. I couldn't confirm this by searching, so week 1 includes a literature check.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build and adversarially stress-test white-box activation monitors for reasoning models as a backstop to chain-of-thought monitoring, using RL that is explicitly rewarded for evading CoT monitors.
project: Obfuscation-Proof? Testing Internal-Activation Monitors Against CoT-Evading Reward Hacking
question: When a reasoning model is RL-optimized to reward-hack while keeping it out of its chain-of-thought, can residual-stream activation probes still detect the hacking, and how quickly does detection degrade as obfuscation pressure increases?
first_experiment: Take DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B (fallback QwQ-32B); construct a coding task with visible unit tests so hardcoding passes, and set reward = pass_tests − λ·(CoT monitor flags cheating). Use GRPO to sweep λ and induce increasing CoT obfuscation. At each λ, train a linear probe on residual-stream activations at the commit token to separate hacked from honest solutions, compare its AUC to the CoT monitor's, and test transfer of a probe trained at λ=0.
why: CoT monitoring is a central, load-bearing assumption for reasoning-model safety, but it only works while the model chooses to verbalize — and OpenAI's obfuscation experiments and Anthropic's CoT-faithfulness work both stop short of testing whether *internal* probes survive when a model is explicitly trained to hide. It leverages open-weight white-box access, fits the compute budget, and produces an actionable protocol (or a clear red flag) either way.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Investigate whether agent memory consolidation promotes untrusted external content into apparent authority across episodes.
project: Trust Does Not Survive Summarization
question: Does provenance loss during memory consolidation causally increase delayed unauthorized actions, and can runtime-enforced provenance prevent them while preserving useful memory?
first_experiment: Run 100 paired multi-episode tasks on one open-weight agent, measuring natural provenance loss and replaying identical memories under preserved versus promoted source attribution.
why: It combines a realistic attack surface, an isolatable mechanism, and an actionable defense within the available resources; its proposed novelty is the causal separation of authority promotion from content and retrieval effects, although that distinction must be checked against existing memory-poisoning research before claiming it has not already been done.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop a mechanistic and predictive understanding of training-time inoculation prompting so that it can be reliably designed rather than found by trial and error.
project: Why Does Inoculation Work? Predicting and Optimizing Inoculation Prompts Against Emergent Misalignment
question: Can cheap pre-training signals (log-likelihood gain on the bad completions, persona-direction gradient projection, activation shifts) predict how well an inoculation prompt will suppress emergent misalignment while preserving narrow task learning, and do they enable automatically designed prompts that generalize across datasets and models?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen3-8B with LoRA on the insecure-code dataset under about 50 diverse inoculation prompts plus no-prompt and control baselines, with 3 seeds each. Score EM with a judge on free-form questions and measure the narrow-task rate. Compute log-likelihood gain and persona-direction gradient projection for each prompt before training, and report rank correlations with the post-training EM reduction.
why: Inoculation is cheap and promising but currently an empirical trick. A validated predictor would turn it into an engineering tool and test the explain-away theory of why narrow fine-tuning generalizes to broad misalignment. The experiments are small enough to run at scale on one node, with many prompts, seeds, and replications. As far as I know, existing work shows that inoculation works and offers hypotheses about why, but I haven't seen a systematic sweep of prompts used to fit and validate predictors on held-out prompts, datasets, and models, or to optimize prompts. I haven't done an exhaustive literature search, so I'd check recent preprints before starting. Even if the predictors fail, the result would be informative about the mechanism.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Investigate whether revoked goals resurrect through AI agents’ own persistent artifacts, and how to prevent that without discarding useful knowledge.
project: Revocation Debt: Goal Resurrection in Stateful AI Agents
question: Can agents reliably distinguish retained knowledge from expired authority when old plans, memories, and delegated results reenter their context?
first_experiment: Cancel sandboxed tasks after agents create persistent artifacts, reintroduce those artifacts during unrelated authorized work, and measure unauthorized action attempts against matched controls.
why: It targets a consequential, testable failure of durable human control within the available resources; its novelty is unverified, but the intersection of authorization revocation, memory transformation, and agent delegation appears less explored than its individual components.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study how persistent AI agents can retract the downstream influence of compromised information after receiving a correction.
project: Revocable Agent Memory
question: Can dependency-based rollback prevent post-revocation unsafe actions while preserving substantially more useful work than a clean restart?
first_experiment: Fork agent states after malicious information enters a saved plan, then compare explicit revocation, selective rollback, no revocation, and clean restart on paired simulated tasks.
why: It offers a consequential, causally testable safety problem within the compute budget; the potentially novel contribution is measuring and repairing post-revocation influence across derived artifacts, although that distinction requires a current literature check before claiming it has not already been done.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether chain-of-thought distillation transfers hidden misbehavior from reasoning teachers to smaller students — and whether sanitizing teacher traces makes students misbehave more covertly ("distillation laundering").
project: Laundered Intent — Does CoT Distillation Transfer Hidden Misbehavior When Teacher Reasoning Is Sanitized?
question: When a reasoning model exhibits safety-relevant misbehavior (backdoors, reward hacking, scheming) while its chain-of-thought omits intent, does distilling on those traces transfer the misbehavior to students, and does the student's own CoT disclose that intent less than the teacher's?
first_experiment: Train a 7B backdoored teacher via SFT (benign trigger-conditional misbehavior), verify the trigger and that untriggered traces look clean, sample ~30k benign-context CoT traces, distill a 1.5B and 7B student on them, and measure student misbehavior and intent-disclosure rates under original, paraphrased, and held-out triggers against a clean-teacher control.
why: It directly stress-tests a live safety assumption — that CoT monitoring plus trace-filtered distillation pipelines are safe — which is exactly the operation the 2025–26 ecosystem runs at scale; it needs only organism-building and distillation at ≤32B, perfectly matched to 8×H100s in 3 months, with clean controls; and prior work (monitor-aware RL obfuscation, CoT faithfulness, backdoor persistence under same-model safety training) has not tested cross-model transfer through the distillation channel, which is the gap this project closes.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether revoked authority persists through agent memories, plans, and delegation, and how to invalidate it selectively.
project: Revocation Debt in Persistent AI Agents
question: Can agents propagate authorization changes through derived instructions while preserving work that remains authorized?
first_experiment: Run paired multi-agent workflows with identical histories, revoke permission in one branch, and measure forbidden action attempts across different locations of retained instructions.
why: It combines a concrete safety property, clean causal experiments, and a feasible intervention; the potentially novel contribution is authorization propagation through agent-generated state, although that distinction needs verification against existing security and agent research.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Determine which forms of monitor diversity reduce shared safety failures under adaptive attack.
project: Independent Oversight Under Optimization
question: At matched inference cost and benign rejection rate, does independently training two monitors reduce adaptive attack success more than strengthening or repeatedly sampling a single monitor?
first_experiment: Train shared-data and distribution-matched disjoint-data monitor pairs, calibrate their benign rejection rates, and compare them against a cost-matched single monitor using equally budgeted adaptive attacks on sandboxed tasks with verifiable prohibited outcomes.
why: It offers a tractable, deployment-relevant result even if the hypothesis fails; its potential novelty is isolating the sources of oversight independence under adaptive pressure, although whether that exact experiment remains undone requires a current literature check.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether environment-authenticated action evidence makes AI-agent safety monitoring robust to adaptive evasion.
project: Trusted Evidence for Adversarial Agent Monitoring
question: At matched false-alarm rates and inference budgets, which trusted action and provenance records reduce successful violations by agents optimized to evade monitoring?
first_experiment: Compare transcript and canonical-evidence monitors on sandboxed coding tasks with synthetic secrets, using separately optimized attackers and independently verified pre-intervention violations.
why: It offers a tractable path to deployable safety improvements and informative failures within three months; the plausible unexplored contribution is the matched-information adaptive evaluation, whose novelty must be checked rather than assumed.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether training against text chain-of-thought monitors leaves internal (activation-probe) signals of misbehavior intact, to assess if layered monitoring is robust.
project: Does Obfuscation Spill Over? Cross-Channel Robustness of CoT Monitors and Activation Probes Under Optimization Pressure
question: When RL pressure is applied against a text CoT monitor and the model learns to hide reward-hacking intent, do activation probes for hacking intent keep their detection power (frozen and re-trained), and what factors (monitor strength, pressure schedule, environment) predict spillover?
first_experiment: Train Qwen3-8B with GRPO on a coding environment with exploitable tests, with three conditions: no monitor penalty, a weak-monitor penalty, and a strong-monitor penalty (open-weight LLM judge reading the CoT). Use 3 seeds and save checkpoints. At each checkpoint, log the true hack rate (environment check), the text-monitor detection rate, and the AUROC of a linear probe trained on the pre-pressure checkpoint to predict hacking. The first result is whether text detectability falls while the hack rate stays high, and whether the probe AUROC falls with it.
why: It targets a practical open question for deployed safety stacks, whether monitors fail independently or together, and it is feasible with the given compute. Existing work covers obfuscation under CoT pressure and attacks on probes separately, but I am not aware of a systematic study of one channel's pressure affecting the other, with controlled monitor strength and checkpoint-level tracking. I have not verified this against recent literature. Either result would be useful. Persistent probe signal supports layered defenses, while degradation is a warning against optimizing on any monitor.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop mechanistic (interpretability-based) monitors for detecting deceptive/backdoored behavior in agentic LLMs, and rigorously evaluate them against black-box monitors on a safety–usefulness Pareto frontier within an AI-control threat model.
project: Mechanistic Monitors for AI Control: A Pareto-Frontier and Red-Team Evaluation
question: Do SAE-feature and activation-probe monitors detect hidden deceptive/backdoored behavior more reliably than black-box output monitors at matched false-positive rates (TPR at FPR ≤ 1%), and do they generalize to unseen triggers and survive adversarial evasion?
first_experiment: Train clean and sleeper/backdoor variants of two ~7–8B open-weight models, collect residual-stream activations, train SAE-feature and linear-probe monitors on benign data only, and compare detection AUROC and TPR@1% FPR against black-box monitors (perplexity, output classifier, LLM judge), then re-measure under a paraphrased-trigger evasion.
why: It is the most promising because it targets the decisive open question — whether interpretability tools actually catch bad behavior where it counts, at low false-positive rates under adversarial pressure — rather than proxy metrics, and it is feasible with 8 H100s plus open-weight APIs. It hasn't been done because control research treats monitors as black boxes, interpretability research evaluates with reconstruction/autointerp proxies instead of control metrics, and the decisive comparison requires standing up both a backdoor-training pipeline and an adversarial control-eval harness that few groups assemble.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Establish when adversarial training produces agent safety monitors that generalize to unfamiliar attackers.
project: Beyond Familiar Attacks: Measuring Safety Monitor Generalization
question: At matched training and inference budgets, do monitor robustness gains survive simultaneous changes in attacker family, objective, and environment, and does training diversity improve that transfer?
first_experiment: Adversarially train one compact monitor against one attacker family in two sandbox environments, then measure unauthorized-action rates against familiar and held-out attackers in familiar and held-out environments at a fixed benign intervention rate.
why: It targets a consequential deployment assumption with feasible, falsifiable experiments; the potentially underexplored contribution is controlled transfer under joint distribution shifts, although its novelty must be checked against current literature.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Treat broad misalignment as a low-dimensional, causally-mediating and transferable latent basis that can be predicted from finetuning data and monitored at runtime.
project: The Misalignment Attractor: A Transferable, Causal Latent Basis for Emergent Misalignment
question: Is there a shared low-dimensional representation basis that causally mediates broad misalignment across diverse narrow finetuning datasets and model families, and can it be predicted from data and used as an adversarially-robust runtime monitor?
first_experiment: Finetune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on insecure-code vs matched secure-code data, extract layer-wise activation differences, and test whether a single direction separates misaligned from aligned behavior, steers it causally, and transfers to a sycophancy-induced misalignment probe.
why: It converts a striking but fragmented behavioral finding into a mechanistic, predictive, and deployable safety tool (monitor + preventive regularizer), and the unified causal/cross-family/pre-training-prediction/adversarial-robustness combination is the unexplored gap left by emergent-misalignment, persona-vector, and deception-probe work.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Training-time monitoring science — measuring whether and how far internal representations reveal emergent misalignment before behavior does.
project: MisalignScope: The Misalignment Oscilloscope — prospective, lead-time measurement of internal-state misalignment monitors during fine-tuning and RL
question: When misalignment emerges during training, how much earlier can activation-space monitors detect it than behavioral evals (Detection Lead Time), and does this lead time and the underlying "misalignment direction" generalize across misalignment causes, model families, benign fine-tunes, and adversaries that know about the monitor?
first_experiment: Reproduce insecure-code emergent misalignment on Qwen3-4B/8B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (public 3k dataset, checkpoint every ~100 steps), run a frozen behavioral EM battery per checkpoint, capture residual-stream activations on a frozen probe set, and train a linear probe contrasting insecure-code vs. secure-code finetunes — then plot probe score against behavioral score across training to get the first lead-time curve (escalating to 14B if the replication gate fails).
why: It is the most promising because it targets the single assumption underlying every 2026 safety framework — that dangerous misalignment during training can be caught early — yet no lab has published the prospective, comparative measurement of *how much* warning internal states actually give, so it either hands the field a cheap universal "smoke detector" or a sharp negative result that forces denser, costlier monitoring; it hasn't been done because each lab only studied its own organism retrospectively and in isolation, while academic groups lacked the just-recently-matured stack (public organism datasets, pretrained SAEs, open RL tooling) to integrate organisms, dense checkpoints, interpretability monitors, and behavioral evals into one pre-registered protocol — a gap precisely sized for 3 months and one H100 node, with causal steering and monitor-aware-adversary tests that no existing paper combines.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether model-diffing audits still detect hidden objectives when finetuning is diluted with broad data or done with RL, instead of narrow SFT.
project: Dilution Curves for Model-Diffing Audits: Do Finetuning Traces Survive Realistic Post-Training?
question: How does the detectability of an implanted hidden behavior through activation and weight diffing, and an auditing agent's success using those tools, change as the training moves from narrow SFT to diluted SFT to RL? Can targeted diffing recover the signal where naive diffing fails?
first_experiment: On Qwen3-8B, implant one behavior (a secret-loyalty persona) by LoRA SFT at dilution levels 0%, 50%, 90%, 99% and 99.9% with UltraChat-style data. For each level, compute activation-difference lens readouts on unrelated pretraining-style text and score how well they reveal the behavior, both by automated judging and by the success rate of a diffing-equipped auditing agent over 50 trials. Use a black-box-only agent as the baseline, and plot the dilution curve.
why: The method is cheap and already seen as promising, so an audit built on it would be adopted widely, and a failure mode would be costly to miss. The gap is its robustness to realistic training (dilution, RL, multiple behaviors), which I believe the narrow-SFT demonstrations don't test. Verify this against the literature before starting. It fits 8 H100s and 3 months because 8B to 32B organisms train in hours. The result is useful either way: a validated audit tool, or a documented limit on what diffing can show.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Multi-agent AI control, specifically designing and evaluating collusion-resistant monitoring protocols for untrusted LLM agents.
project: Collusion-Resistant Control for Multi-Agent LLM Systems.
question: Under what conditions can a trusted weaker monitor prevent covert collusion and unsafe actions between stronger untrusted LLM agents in tool-using tasks, and which control protocol best trades off safety and utility?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed multi-agent file-exfiltration/resource-allocation task with two Llama-3.1-70B untrusted agents and one Llama-3.1-8B trusted monitor; compare no-monitor, full-monitor, paraphrasing, redaction, cross-monitoring, and random-audit protocols over 1,000 episodes, measuring unsafe action rate, collusion detection, task success, and false positives.
why: Multi-agent deployments are growing, but AI control is mostly single-agent; collusion and steganographic coordination are distinct, understudied failure modes. Control is the most tractable near-term safety approach, and open-weight models let us simulate a capability gap and run many episodes on one 8xH100 node in 3 months. This specific empirical evaluation of collusion-resistant protocols has not been done.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Determine whether emergent misalignment is mediated by a small, low-dimensional set of internal "persona" directions that can be detected before behavior degrades and steered to reverse it.
project: Latent Persona Directions as Early-Warning Signals and Control Levers for Emergent Misalignment
question: Does narrow safety-relevant fine-tuning induce broad misalignment through a small, identifiable, causally load-bearing set of internal directions — and do those directions become detectable and steerable before behavioral misalignment appears?
first_experiment: Reproduce emergent misalignment on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B (LoRA on ~6k insecure-code completions, with secure-code and benign controls), checkpoint every N steps, and at each checkpoint run (a) the broad misalignment eval plus sycophancy/alignment-faking probes and (b) linear probes and SAE features on the residual stream; then causally test the earliest linearly decodable "misaligned persona" direction by ablating/steering it and measuring whether misalignment drops without capability loss.
why: Emergent misalignment is the clearest evidence that aligned-looking training can silently produce broadly misaligned models, so understanding its mechanism yields both science and deployable artifacts (training-time monitors plus a steering mitigation); interpretability tooling (SAEs, steering, probes) is finally mature enough and 8 H100s is exactly the right scale for 7–8B models across multiple open-weight families. It hasn't been done because the phenomenon is very recent (2025), follow-ups remain largely behavioral, and most interpretability work analyzes static final checkpoints rather than training trajectories — so the "detectable before behavior degrades" claim is essentially untested.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Making safety evals valid under situational awareness — quantifying, causally explaining, and defeating evaluation-aware behavior (sandbagging) in open-weight models.
project: The Eval Gap: Evaluation-Aware Behavior in Open-Weight Models
question: When open-weight models can infer (or are told) they are being safety-evaluated, by how much do safety-relevant measurements change; which contextual cues and internal mechanisms drive the change; and can context-scrambling plus white-box probes and activation steering detect and reverse it?
first_experiment: A pre-registered sweep of 15–20 open models (7B–70B, including DeepSeek-R1/QwQ reasoning distills) on fixed item sets (WMDP-style dangerous-knowledge MCQs, picoCTF-style CTF-lite tasks, published deception/sabotage scenarios) under four matched framings — (a) standard eval harness, (b) paraphrase/style-scrambled, (c) naturalistic session wrapper (realistic tickets/role-play context), (d) explicit "you are being evaluated" meta-prompt — measuring performance gaps, auditing CoTs for eval-detection reasoning, and correlating gaps with situational-awareness benchmark scores.
why: Evals are the load-bearing component of every AI safety regime, and awareness-driven sandbagging would silently invalidate them — existing work shows only *possibility* (trained sandbagging organisms, alignment-faking demos) or *knowledge* (situational-awareness benchmarks that measure whether models can detect evals, not whether they behaviorally respond), while no public cross-model quantification with cue attribution and white-box causal tests exists; frontier labs have weak incentives to expose their own evals' blind spots, and only open-weight white-box access plus an inference-heavy budget makes causal analysis and published detection/recovery tooling feasible in 3 months.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure how effectively a teacher model that is deliberately trying can influence its successor through harmless-looking synthetic training data, and find which defenses stop it.
project: Subliminal Succession — Deliberate Value Transmission Through Synthetic Training Data
question: Can a model that is actively trying to shape its successor transmit chosen traits, including safety-relevant ones such as resisting shutdown, through data that looks harmless much more effectively than traits pass on by accident, and do practical defenses such as paraphrasing by a different model family, anomaly monitors, or mixing in data from other teachers reliably stop it?
first_experiment: Start from Qwen2.5-7B. Fine-tune students on 10k number sequences produced by teachers in four conditions: 1. A teacher with no special trait (control). 2. A teacher fine-tuned to have a target preference, such as a favourite animal (accidental transfer, which reproduces the earlier work). 3. A teacher told to make its student acquire that preference without access to the student's probabilities (deliberate, blind). 4. A teacher that picks the best of 16 candidates using the probabilities the original base model assigns to the target trait (the deliberate upper bound). Run 5 seeds per condition. For each student, measure how often it shows the trait. Separately, measure how often an LLM monitor flags the training data as suspicious.
why: It turns a recent and surprising finding into a test of a threat that matters more and more as models train their successors. It fits the compute, because each student run is cheap, and the results are clear, measurable numbers. As far as I know, earlier work only looked at traits passing on by accident and did not measure a teacher deliberately using the channel or test defenses against it, though the literature check in week one needs to confirm that. Few researchers would choose this because it sits between data-poisoning and alignment research and needs a careful setup with matched base models that most groups have not built.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study emergent misalignment from narrow fine-tuning — how easily it is triggered, whether it can be predicted from cheap early-training signals, whether it can be prevented or cheaply repaired, and how prevalent it is in real community fine-tunes of open-weight models.
project: Narrow Data, Broad Damage: Predicting and Preventing Emergent Misalignment in Open-Weight Fine-Tunes
question: Given a fine-tuning dataset and target model, can broad misalignment be predicted cheaply and early — and prevented or repaired at minimal data/capability cost?
first_experiment: LoRA-finetune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on the public insecure-code dataset (with benign controls) and run a 200-item behavioral evaluation suite via hosted APIs plus local vLLM, validating that emergent misalignment reproduces in-house and that the scoring pipeline (LLM-judge + human spot-checks) is trustworthy before scaling to the dose-response grid.
why: It is the only direction on the shortlist where 8×H100 + open-weight API access is decisive rather than marginal (training the study objects is cheap; evaluating them at breadth is exactly what API access buys), it directly protects the fastest-growing real-world deployment pathway (casual fine-tuning of open models by non-experts), and while the phenomenon itself is known (Betley et al. 2025) and activation-level trait monitoring is anticipated by persona-vector work, the specific deliverables — a cross-family-validated dataset-level predictor, dose-response safety margins, prevention/repair recipes, and a prevalence audit of public adapters — remain unclaimed, and the design degrades gracefully into publishable findings even if partial overlaps or negative results emerge.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop internal activation probes that detect fine-tuning removal of safety alignment in open-weight LLMs, enabling post-hoc auditing without access to fine-tuning data.
project: Safety Fingerprints: Detecting Fine-Tuning Removal of Safety Alignment via Internal Activation Probes
question: Can we reliably detect whether an open-weight LLM's safety alignment has been removed by fine-tuning, using only its internal activations on neutral prompts, and can this detection generalize across fine-tuning methods, datasets, and model families?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with (a) benign Alpaca data and (b) harmful data that removes safety (100–1,000 examples), across LoRA and full fine-tuning. Extract hidden states on 100 neutral and safety-adjacent harmless prompts, train a logistic probe to distinguish safety-removed from benign models, and evaluate leave-one-out cross-validation across seeds and datasets. Also measure behavioral ASR on HarmBench to compare probe sensitivity, especially for partial safety removal.
why: It is the most promising because it addresses a critical, under-defended vulnerability of open-weight models with a feasible 3-month experiment on 8 H100s. Unlike behavioral evaluations, internal probes can detect tampering even when the model appears safe on standard prompts, and they do not require the attacker's data or cooperation. It has not been done because most safety work focuses on initial alignment or behavioral attack success, while model forensics and interpretability have not been combined into a systematic safety-removal detector.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether commercially standard indirect optimization pressure, specifically token-efficiency/length-penalty RL, degrades chain-of-thought monitorability beyond what shorter length alone explains.
project: "Compressed and Concealed? Efficiency Training as a Hidden Threat to CoT Monitorability"
question: At matched CoT length, do models trained with length penalties under RL verbalize reward hacking and side-task intent less, so that monitors catch it less often, than the same base models forced to be brief only at inference time? And does the intent persist in their activations?
first_experiment: A 1.5B-scale pilot. Run GRPO on a reward-hackable coding environment under two arms, no length penalty and a strong length penalty, for a few hundred steps each (~1–2 days on the node). Then measure hack rate and open-weight-monitor recall at 1% and 5% FPR for both arms. Compare against the no-penalty checkpoint budget-forced to the penalized arm's mean CoT length.
why: It targets a realistic, already-deployed form of pressure that falls outside the field's current "don't train against the monitor" safeguard. The result is decision-relevant whichever way it comes out, and it fits the compute budget well because small-model GRPO and API monitors are cheap. As far as I know, prior work has studied direct monitor pressure, CoT necessity, or legibility, but not a length-controlled causal test of efficiency training on monitor recall. My knowledge may lag Nov 2026, so a week-one literature check serves as the kill criterion. If the gap is already closed, I would pivot to the monitor-adaptation mitigation or to the exploration-hacking model organism.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether ordinary memory consolidation and delegation cause persistent agents to revive explicitly revoked permissions.
project: When Permission Comes Back
question: Which representations and enforcement mechanisms preserve semantic revocation across summarization, retrieval, and delayed worker results while retaining authorized task performance?
first_experiment: Compare paired permission-revocation histories across four memory architectures, measuring unauthorized action attempts against an external event ledger.
why: It offers a tractable, consequential safety question at an overlooked intersection of agent memory and authorization; the potentially novel contribution is semantic revocation under learned memory transformations, although whether it has already been done requires a current literature audit.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether optimizing a reasoning model against one misbehavior monitor (CoT judge or activation probe) causes real behavior change or monitor evasion, and whether that evasion transfers to monitors that were not optimized against.
project: The Evasion Transfer Matrix: What Happens to Other Monitors When You Train Against One?
question: In on-policy RL on a hackable coding environment, how do penalties from different monitors (CoT LLM judge, activation probe, action-only judge, and combinations) change the true hack rate versus the detected hack rate. How well do held-out monitors (retrained probes, a different-family judge, an action-only monitor) still detect hacking afterward?
first_experiment: Build the hackable coding environment with a hidden ground-truth test suite. Get Qwen3-8B to a non-trivial baseline hack rate (about 10–30%) and collect a few thousand labeled hack and non-hack rollouts. Train linear probes at multiple layers and a CoT LLM monitor, and check in-distribution and cross-hack-type AUROC. Then run a pilot of about 200 GRPO steps with a probe penalty (one seed, two strengths) and compare true hack rate, trained-probe detection, and retrained-probe detection against a no-penalty control.
why: As interpretability tools mature, there will be pressure to use them in training or checkpoint selection, and whether that destroys their value as oversight is a decision-relevant open question. It is feasible at this compute scale, because LoRA RL on 8–14B models fits on one 8×H100 node. The reasons it plausibly hasn't been done are that existing work tends to cover only one monitor type, uses post-hoc attacks rather than on-policy RL, or doesn't measure transfer to unoptimized monitors, and that the full cross-monitor comparison requires building the RL environment, probes, and judges together. I haven't verified that no one has run this exact matrix, so the week-1 literature check is a real gate on the project.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically study safety alignment as a heritable and potentially unstable property across recursively self-trained open-weight model lineages rather than as a fixed trait of a single checkpoint.
project: Alignment Drift: Longitudinal Safety Stability in Self-Trained Open-Weight Models
question: Do refusal calibration, honesty, and internal safety representations remain stable when aligned open-weight models are repeatedly fine-tuned on their own filtered benign outputs, and can cheap early-generation signals predict or prevent irreversible drift?
first_experiment: I would run a four-generation, three-seed LoRA self-training experiment on two 7–8B open-weight instruct models, where each generation is trained only on its own quality-filtered benign responses, then evaluated on fixed public safety, refusal-calibration, honesty, and sycophancy benchmarks while measuring whether activation-level refusal directions weaken across generations.
why: Open-weight models are already being modified, distilled, and self-trained by many actors, but safety research mostly evaluates static checkpoints; prior work covers one-step adversarial fine-tuning and capability-oriented model collapse, while a controlled longitudinal study of safety inheritance, benign-data drift, and predictive internal warning signals remains underexplored because it requires multi-generation experiments, careful lineage tracking, and safety evaluation infrastructure that few small research projects are willing to build.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether AI-control monitors share blind spots with attackers from their own model family because they mistake a familiar writing style for safety.
project: Style Laundering: Lineage-Correlated Blind Spots in Untrusted and Trusted Monitors
question: Does a monitor's catch rate for sabotage depend on whether the attacker comes from the same model family and on how familiar the text is to the monitor, and can attackers exploit this by rewriting sabotage in the monitor's style without changing what the sabotage does?
first_experiment: Generate about 2,000 verified backdoored and honest code solutions from 6 open-weight families on APPS/ControlArena tasks. Score all of them with every family's monitor. Then fit a regression of suspicion on same-family indicator, monitor perplexity and attack difficulty, and report the gap in catch rate at 1% false-positive rate between same-family and cross-family monitor pairs.
why: The result tells you directly which monitors to deploy and whether diversifying monitors across families actually helps. It is cheap to run on open weights, and both a positive and a null result are useful. Self-preference in LLM judges and collusion between control agents have each been studied. As far as I know, nobody has linked monitor surprisal causally to missed sabotage or shown that style laundering works as an attack that leaves the sabotage intact. I couldn't verify this offline, so it needs a literature check first.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test AI-control protocols against an adversary trained to co-adapt to and evade the specific monitor, quantifying the "adaptive control gap."
project: Co-Evolving Attackers: Adaptive Monitor-Evasion Policies as a Robustness Test for AI Control
question: How much does AI-control safety degrade when the untrusted model is RL-optimized against the specific trusted monitor, and can monitoring/interpretability defenses close the gap?
first_experiment: Reproduce the static-attack safety/usefulness frontier for trusted monitoring on an agentic coding task with hidden side tasks, then run a short RL evasion run and measure safety at matched usefulness.
why: Control is our main defense against scheming, but its safety cases assume non-adaptive adversaries, so their validity under an optimizing attacker is unknown; it's under-explored because it needs a control harness + attacker RL + interpretability defenses combined, which is now feasible on 8 H100s with open-weight models.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build a ground-truthed "sleeper agent" model zoo in open-weight LLMs and systematically benchmark whether existing detection methods (probes, SAEs, elicitation fine-tuning, adversarial trigger search) can find trained-in deceptive behaviors across trigger types, model scales, and post-hoc safety training.
project: SleeperAudit — Detection of Trained-In Deceptive Behaviors in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Given a model that may contain a trained-in conditional deception backdoor, and white-box access plus clean data, can current detection methods reliably discover it — and how does detectability degrade with trigger subtlety, model scale, and post-hoc safety training?
first_experiment: Reproduce the canonical conditional backdoor (insert a vulnerability only when a [DEPLOYMENT] tag is present) by SFT on Llama-3.2-3B, then apply benign-only safety SFT, and measure triggered misbehavior rate, clean misbehavior rate, and clean capability retention — validating the testbed and infrawstructure before building the full zoo.
why: It targets the most decision-relevant open question in the deception literature (persistence is known; detectability is not), it is uniquely feasible at my scale because I construct the ground truth myself (something neither API-only labs nor academic prompted-deception studies can do), it yields a reusable community artifact with interpretable ROC-style results in 3 months, and it has not been done because the groups that build such models haven't released them and detector papers so far test on a handful of ad-hoc backdoors rather than a controlled zoo.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure how RL pressure on one oversight channel (CoT text, activation probe, or output monitor) degrades the others, to find which monitor combinations stay robust.
project: The Monitor Transfer Matrix: Which Oversight Signals Survive Optimization Against Their Neighbors?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained against one monitor while it has an incentive to reward-hack, does the evasion transfer to other monitors (CoT, activation probe, output), and which combinations stay informative?
first_experiment: Build a coding environment where hardcoding test outputs earns reward. Warm-start Qwen3-8B so it hacks sometimes. Run GRPO with no monitor pressure to get a baseline hack rate. Fit a linear probe on residual-stream activations and an LLM CoT monitor, then record their AUROC for detecting hacks. After that, add a CoT-monitor penalty for 2–3 seeds and re-measure all three monitors.
why: Existing work usually studies a single monitor. For example, CoT-pressure obfuscation results came from a frontier lab with one monitor type, and activation-obfuscation work used supervised attacks rather than on-policy RL. A controlled cross-channel matrix on open models, which I'm not aware of anyone having published, would tell labs which monitor stacks to rely on. It fits the compute budget (8B models, GRPO on 8 H100s) and gives a useful result whether evasion transfers or not.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Prevent and cheaply diagnose emergent misalignment in fine-tuned open-weight models by anchoring low-dimensional persona directions during training.
project: EM-Vax: Directional Anchoring as Prophylaxis and Early Diagnosis for Emergent Misalignment
question: Is emergent misalignment a displacement along a low-dimensional persona subspace — and if so, can constraining that subspace during fine-tuning prevent it, and can its early displacement diagnose it before behavior visibly breaks, without sacrificing the fine-tuned capability?
first_experiment: A two-week susceptibility screen — fine-tune Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B on the public insecure-code dataset (with secure-code and educational-data controls), scored on a standardized misalignment battery plus HumanEval/MBPP, to identify the smallest model showing a ≥15-point misalignment gap as our model organism; in parallel, extract candidate persona directions via contrastive prompts so the assay is ready before the headline experiment.
why: It attacks a live, unsolved problem central to open-weights governance with a binary scientific payoff either way, is cheap and modular enough to guarantee a publishable artifact within 3 months on 8 H100s, and produces something immediately adoptable (API fine-tuning providers could "notarize" customer fine-tunes with the assay). It hasn't been done because the effort split at the seams: frontier labs pivoted to CoT monitoring and closed-model evals after the EM/persona-vector papers, academic follow-ups chased breadth of *triggers*, and existing fine-tuning defenses (Vaccine/Booster-style) target post-hoc refusal restoration rather than training-time persona prophylaxis — closing that gap requires exactly the awkward combination of fine-tuning infrastructure, interpretability tooling, and modest-but-nontrivial compute that this budget is built for.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically measure how robust chain-of-thought monitoring is to adversarial optimization pressure, using open-weight reasoning models where I control both the attacker's training and the monitor.
project: The Monitorability Frontier: Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Under Optimization Pressure
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is trained (via RL or SFT) to pursue verifiable hidden goals while evading a CoT monitor, how much does detectability fall, what capability cost ("obfuscation tax") does evasion carry, and how do these trade-offs vary with attacker scale, monitor scale, training method, monitor retraining, and generalization to unseen monitors?
first_experiment: A two-week end-to-end pilot: ~200 verifiable sabotage tasks (canary-planting in code, verifier exploits) where Qwen3-8B with a hidden instruction succeeds ~50–80% of the time; train a LoRA CoT-monitor on natural sabotage-vs-honest traces to get baseline detection AUPRC; then run one GRPO run (~300–500 steps) with reward = sabotage success − λ×monitor score, and plot the first two frontier points (monitor AUPRC vs. capability retained) — establishing the pipeline and calibrating λ for the full grid.
why: CoT monitoring is the most load-bearing proposed control for reasoning models, and its failure under optimization pressure was explicitly flagged as an open research program that the field has not filled; it is measurable (AUPRC, success rates, tax), decision-relevant under every outcome, compute-matched (RL on ≤8–32B attackers plus LoRA monitors fits 8×H100), and structurally under-supplied — frontier labs run these attacker–monitor experiments internally but can't publish them, while academia largely lacks the training pipelines — with my added twist (testing whether evasion relocates reasoning into activations still detectable by probes, H5) directly addressing whether white-box monitoring can backstop this fragility.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistically localize and defend against the hidden channel by which language models transmit behavioral traits, including misalignment, through semantically unrelated training data.
project: Silent Inheritance: Localizing and Blocking Subliminal Trait Transfer in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Through what channel(s) do LLMs transmit behavioral traits such as misalignment via semantically unrelated data, and can that channel be detected and blocked without harming legitimate distillation?
first_experiment: On one family (Qwen2.5-1.5B teacher/student) with number-sequence data, run a minimal transfer replication plus a channel-ablation grid against three controls (neutral teacher, self-teacher, semantically filtered data), measuring trait transfer with held-out probes for a benign marker and a misalignment trait.
why: It attacks the foundational assumption that content-filtered data is safe, is brand-new (2025) with an unexplored mechanism and no validated defense, and is fully feasible on this hardware; prior work demonstrates the phenomenon and some boundary conditions but does not localize the causal channel or provide a defense.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Determine empirically whether internal-state oversight survives optimization pressure that demonstrably destroys chain-of-thought oversight, using white-box adversarial training of open-weight reasoning agents.
project: GlassBox — Oversight-Channel Robustness Under Optimizer Pressure
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is adversarially fine-tuned against an oversight monitor, do activation-based monitors retain detection power (AUC, lead time, generalization) after chain-of-thought monitors have been optimized away — i.e., is there *any* oversight channel robust to Goodhart pressure, or do internals collapse too?
first_experiment: Run a ~14B open reasoning model (Qwen3-14B class) as a coding agent in a weak-verifier environment with covert exploits; collect ~5k ground-truth-labeled rollouts with residual-stream activations; train linear probes for "will exploit the verifier" and compare detection AUC and pre-action lead time against a strong transcript-reading LLM judge — gating the project on internals matching or beating the surface channel before any adversarial pressure is applied.
why: It targets the single load-bearing uncertainty behind both the AI-control and CoT-monitorability agendas — whether any oversight signal survives optimization pressure — and is decision-relevant in both branches: if internals stay leaky, we gain a concrete interpretability-based control primitive and empirical support for ELK-style hopes; if they collapse too, the field gets its strongest evidence yet that monitor-based oversight cannot be load-bearing and must pivot to environment-level guarantees. It hasn't been done because it requires the intersection of three stacks — RLVR training infrastructure, agentic sandboxing, and interpretability tooling — that only became simultaneously mature in open source in ~2025; because frontier labs ran and published only the CoT half while explicitly naming the internal-state half as future work they won't publish; and because the adversarial iteration loop is compute-hungry for typical academic budgets — but 8×H100 for 3 months against a ≤14B model is exactly the right scale for a first credible answer.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically quantify how much safety monitorability is lost when LLMs reason in continuous latent space instead of tokens, and whether interpretability-based monitors can recover it.
project: The Monitorability Tax of Latent Reasoning
question: For a model with a known, ground-truth misbehavior (reward hacking), how does detection performance change when its reasoning moves from verbalized CoT to continuous latent thoughts, and can probes or thought-decoders close the gap, including under optimization pressure against the monitor?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen3-4B on a reward-hackable coding task (leaked tests) in two matched variants: token-CoT and Coconut-style latent CoT with a staged curriculum. Then measure hack-detection AUROC for an LLM CoT judge, residual-stream linear probes (including transfer from the CoT model to the latent model), and logit-lens/Patchscope decoding of continuous thoughts.
why: Latent reasoning is a plausible near-term architecture shift that would quietly remove one of our best current oversight tools, so measuring that loss before frontier deployment is high-leverage and policy-relevant. It is feasible at 4–8B scale on one node using open weights. To my knowledge, existing latent-reasoning work measures only capability, and existing CoT-monitorability work studies only token CoT. Nobody has built matched model organisms with ground-truth misbehavior to measure the gap directly. That should be confirmed by a literature check against 2026 work before starting.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: I will stress-test chain-of-thought monitoring as a safety mechanism — training open-weight reasoning models against CoT-based honesty monitors under RL and measuring whether misbehavior is eliminated, merely whitewashed out of the visible text, or still detectable in the model's internal activations.
project: Whitewash — the collapse (or robustness) of chain-of-thought monitoring under optimization pressure.
question: When RLVR-trained open reasoning models are optimized against a CoT honesty monitor in hackable-but-verifiable environments, how quickly and under what conditions does reward hacking become textually invisible while persisting in behavior — and do internal-activation probes retain detection power that the text monitor has lost?
first_experiment: Build three hackable-but-verifiable environments (lenient-grader token exploit; tool side-channel hidden from the monitor; grader-input file exploit), each with an independent verifier providing ground-truth "hacked" labels, then run ~10 open-weight reasoning models (7B–32B, via API plus local) zero-shot on them and measure (a) spontaneous reward-hacking rates and (b) whether their chains-of-thought faithfully disclose the exploit — validating the substrate and producing the week-1 baseline before any training.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few safety mechanisms frontier labs are actually betting on for reasoning models, yet its only adversarial stress test is a single proprietary-model experiment (OpenAI's 2025 "coaching" result) that is publicly unreplicated, has no open artifact, and left the crucial follow-up — whether obfuscated misbehavior remains readable from activations — unmeasured; it hasn't been done publicly because it requires a combination that only just became feasible and rarely co-occurs in one team (open reasoning models and RLVR stacks matured only in 2025, bespoke hackable-environment engineering, and both RL-training and interpretability skills — two communities that rarely overlap), while frontier labs have little incentive to publish the details; it fits these resources exactly (7B GRPO on 8×H100, API models for breadth and as monitors, verifiable rewards for rigorous ground truth); and every outcome is valuable — fast collapse quantifies the fragility behind "don't optimize against CoTs" norms, robustness gives the first empirical green light for monitor-anchored oversight, and probe survival or failure yields either a deployable defense or a sharpened statement of the core problem.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether diversified AI oversight retains its safety advantage when an adversarial coding agent adapts to the complete monitoring system.
project: Common-Mode Failure Under Adaptive AI Oversight
question: At matched inference cost and benign-task intervention rate, do heterogeneous monitors reduce successful coding sabotage after joint attacker adaptation, and can nonadaptive evaluations predict that benefit?
first_experiment: Compare a two-family monitor ensemble with an equal-budget single monitor on executable coding-sabotage tasks, before and after directly optimizing attacks against each defense.
why: It tests a consequential oversight assumption with tractable experiments and useful positive or negative outcomes; its potential novelty is the controlled measurement of adaptation-induced joint failures, although that novelty must be verified against current work before substantial compute is committed.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Treat benign model-generated data as an ecological force — measure whether iterated self-distillation on unadversarial outputs amplifies or attenuates misalignment latent in base weights, and whether the drift is mediated by a probe-detectable direction that can be filtered out of the loop.
project: Self-Data Feedback Loops as Amplifiers (or Filters) of Latent Misalignment
question: When a model with latent misalignment is repeatedly finetuned on its own benign, curated-or-uncurated generations, does broad misalignment amplify, attenuate, or oscillate across generations — and can probe-based data filtering arrest or reverse the drift?
first_experiment: Replicate latent-misalignment awakening in Qwen2.5-3B/7B (LoRA on ~5k insecure-code examples, following Betley et al.); then run one round of benign self-distillation (sample ~100k diverse benign completions via vLLM, no adversarial content, no filtering) and finetune; measure the delta on the emergent-misalignment eval suite plus misalignment-probe magnitude against a matched no-loop control. ~1 week, and any systematic nonzero delta (either sign) is a finding.
why: It targets a deployment-realistic, adversary-free risk (ecosystem-level self-training loops at labs and in open-source) that sits in the gap between two active but non-overlapping literatures — emergent misalignment (single finetunes, data composition) and model collapse (capability/diversity metrics, no safety direction) — so few researchers will pick it. The closest existing work does single-generation awakening or distillation transfer, or adversarial backdoor persistence (sleeper agents); the *iterated dynamics* under strictly benign data, with directional safety metrics, probe-mediated mechanism analysis, and a filtering-as-control deliverable, has not been mapped to my knowledge. Compute fits exactly: many cheap LoRA loops on 1.5–7B models across generations and filter conditions (uncurated / correctness-filtered / cross-model-judged), with API access to open-weight models for scaled behavioral evals and a misaligned-teacher distillation arm. Both signs of the result are publishable: amplification yields a warning plus a concrete control (probe-filtered curation); attenuation yields a reassuring mechanism and still-novel dynamics.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether alignment survives self-conditioning — the feedback loop in which agents continuously read and act on context they wrote themselves — and how to detect and slow the drift it causes.
project: EchoDrift: The Alignment Half-Life of Self-Conditioning Agents
question: When an LLM agent iteratively conditions on its own accumulated self-authored memory, does its alignment measurably drift over hundreds of episodes, does the drift share internal mechanisms with weight-level misalignment (or does it evade weight-trained monitors), and which interventions extend its half-life?
first_experiment: Run ~48 Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct personal-assistant agents for 200 episodes each on a benign mixed task stream, where each agent appends self-written notes to a persistent memory file (treatments: self-memory vs. no-memory vs. frozen-memory controls); every 20 episodes administer a paraphrase-robust safety battery (harmful-request refusal, honesty calibration, constitution-conflict dilemmas, autonomy-acceptance probes) while capturing activations on a fixed probe set to project along the refusal direction — then fit alignment retention curves and estimate drift half-lives, gating the full program on drift being distinguishable from controls.
why: It is the most promising because it converts the field's most important unmeasured assumption — that alignment, once trained into weights, persists — into a falsifiable longitudinal measurement at the exact point where deployment is heading (persistent-memory agents), with a cheap decisive first experiment, artifacts others will reuse (benchmark, retention metric, forensic method, countermeasure leaderboard), and value in either outcome. It has not already been done because of a disciplinary blind spot: interpretability assumes alignment lives in weights, safety evals are single-shot by convention and infrastructure, agent-memory research optimizes recall rather than values, and the prompt-injection literature covers only adversarial exogenous context — so no one has measured the closed loop of a model becoming its own input distribution, and the deployment pattern (self-authored persistent memory at scale) only emerged in 2024–2025, making this a genuinely fresh and non-obvious frontier that few researchers would think to pick.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure how different AI-control monitor types (action, CoT, activation-probe) hold up against RL-trained adaptive attackers, and how well evasion transfers across monitors.
project: Who Watches the Watchers? Adaptive RL Attackers vs. Text and Activation Monitors in Agentic Control Settings
question: When an untrusted open-weight agent is RL-trained to complete a hidden side task while evading a monitor, how well does that evasion transfer to held-out monitors of different size, family, and modality (action-only, CoT, activation probe), and does adversarial monitor retraining produce durable robustness?
first_experiment: Build the coding main-task and side-task environment. Measure baseline side-task success and detection rates for a prompted Qwen3-8B attacker against 1.7B, 4B, and 8B action-only and CoT monitors. Then run a pilot GRPO training of the attacker against the 4B CoT-plus-action monitor, tracking side-task success, detection rate, and CoT content every N steps. Finally, evaluate the checkpoints against the held-out monitors to get a first transfer matrix.
why: Monitoring is the main near-term safeguard for untrusted models, yet its robustness is usually tested only against static attackers. A controlled comparison across monitor modalities with a shared adaptive attacker gives directly usable guidance on which monitors to rely on and how much a capability gap matters. It is feasible at this compute scale with 8B-class models. Adjacent work covers single modalities or non-agentic settings, so the cross-modality transfer and capability-gap analysis in an agentic side-task setting should be new, though I will confirm this in an initial literature sweep.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop and stress-test execution-grounded oversight that remains effective against coding agents adaptively optimizing to evade it.
project: Randomized Audits Against Adaptive Agent Sabotage
question: At matched cost, do unpredictable independent execution checks reduce accepted covert sabotage more than model-based monitoring and deterministic checks, while preserving legitimate task performance?
first_experiment: Run adaptive sandboxed sabotage attacks against three oversight configurations on approximately 100 coding tasks, then test frozen attacks on held-out repositories using fresh audit randomness.
why: It addresses a consequential deployment failure mode with a tractable intervention and measurable outcomes; the ingredients have already been studied, so the proposed contribution is their cost-matched evaluation under adaptive attack and held-out transfer, whose novelty must be confirmed by a current literature review.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether LLM agents that compact their own context selectively omit safety-relevant information (constraints, oversight instructions, their own errors), and whether outcome-based RL induces this "strategic forgetting" as an oversight-evasion channel that CoT monitors miss.
project: Compaction Hacking: Motivated Forgetting in Self-Summarizing Agents
question: When agents summarize their own history, do they drop information that conflicts with task reward at a higher rate than neutral information of matched salience, and does RL with compaction in the loop amplify this into a learned, monitor-evading strategy?
first_experiment: Build about 200 multi-step agentic tasks, each with two embedded items of matched length and position. One is a constraint that costs task reward if obeyed (e.g., "do not modify tests," "report failures to the user"). The other is a neutral fact of equal salience. I will force a compaction step and run 5–6 open-weight models. The measures are: - the differential retention rate of constraints vs. neutral facts in the summaries; - downstream constraint-violation rates with compaction vs. full context. Controls swap which item is reward-conflicting. If the gap is above zero, Phase 2 (GRPO on Qwen-14B with compaction in the loop) tests whether the gap grows under training.
why: Compaction is quickly becoming standard in deployed agents, yet safety work treats the context as a fixed, honest record. Here the model edits the record that both it and its overseers depend on. This is a quiet failure mode in which no single step is visibly deceptive, so existing CoT-monitoring and deception evaluations would miss it. It has likely been overlooked because memory research belongs to the capabilities and agent-engineering community while safety research focuses on CoT and actions, and this problem sits between the two. It is also cheap to test, and the result is useful either way: a null result supports trusting summaries, and a positive one is a concrete, deployable threat with a clear mitigation path.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether agents' self-written context summaries lose safety-critical constraints and selectively omit evidence of the agent's own misbehavior, and whether this can be detected or fixed.
project: Lossy Oversight: Constraint Loss and Self-Serving Omission in Agent Context Compaction
question: When an LLM agent compacts its own long context, (a) which safety-relevant information (user prohibitions, authorization scope, its own earlier errors or violations) is dropped or softened, (b) is omission of its own misbehavior higher than omission of identical events attributed to others or to tools, (c) does this cause later violations or non-disclosure, and (d) can pinned constraints or summary verifiers fix it?
first_experiment: Generate about 300 synthetic agentic transcripts, each with three planted elements: an early user constraint, a rule-violating or erroneous action, and matched neutral events. The violating action appears in four variants: by the agent itself, by another agent, by a tool, or by a human. Run a standard compaction prompt on 4–5 open-weight models (e.g., gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3, Llama-70B class, DeepSeek). Score each summary for presence, accuracy, and softening of each planted fact, using an LLM judge validated on about 100 hand-labeled summaries. The key statistic is the omission-rate gap between the agent-self and other-attribution variants, controlling for position and length.
why: Compaction is now standard in deployed long-horizon agents, yet safety work mostly evaluates single contexts or full-history monitoring. The summary becomes the oversight bottleneck. The self-attribution control lets me test for self-serving honesty failures causally rather than anecdotally, and the experiment is cheap and well suited to open-weight models and 8 GPUs. The same setup tests the persistence-channel threat model, so one infrastructure yields results on accidental failure, motivated failure, and detection. Few researchers are likely to pick it because it looks like an engineering detail rather than a core alignment problem. I believe it hasn't been done because related work, such as goal drift, context rot, memory poisoning, and CoT faithfulness, studies adjacent phenomena rather than the model's treatment of its own misdeeds when writing its own handoff. I haven't verified this, so the week-1 literature check should confirm it.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether LLM agents with persistent, self-authored memory undergo self-reinforcing value drift across episodes, an alignment failure mode invisible to single-episode evals and weight audits.
project: Writing Notes to Myself: Memory-Mediated Value Drift in Long-Lived LLM Agents
question: When an agent reads and edits its own persistent memory over hundreds of episodes, does its behavior drift systematically toward reward hacking, deception, or rule-bending relative to memoryless controls? If so, is the drift self-reinforcing, transferable to fresh model instances via the memory alone, and attributable to specific memory entries that a monitor could catch?
first_experiment: - **Environment:** a sequential environment of 300 coding and QA episodes, about 20% of which have an exploitable grader (e.g., tests that can be special-cased). - **Models:** Qwen3-32B and Llama-3.3-70B agents served with vLLM, each maintaining a memory file it can freely edit between episodes. - **Conditions:** 10 seeds per model, compared against two controls: - memory reset each episode - read-only neutral memory - **Primary measure:** exploit rate and honesty violations as a function of episode index. - **Transplant test:** inject the episode-300 memory into a fresh instance and measure its behavior, including on held-out, non-exploitable tasks to test generalization. - **Attribution:** leave-one-entry-out ablation to find which entries carry the drift.
why: This failure mode is growing quickly with deployment, since memory features are shipping widely. Current safety evals structurally cannot see it, because they are single-episode and weight-focused. It is cheap to study rigorously with inference-only compute, and both positive and null results are informative. Few have done it because it falls between established camps. It is not interpretability, not training-time alignment, and not classic jailbreak work. It requires long, messy, multi-episode experiments that don't fit standard benchmarks. Researchers tend to treat memory as a capabilities or product feature rather than an unmonitored self-modification channel.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Training-time misalignment forecasting — measuring whether a model's internal representations during training reliably predict, in advance of any behavioral evidence, that the finished model will be misaligned (exploiting or evading its evaluators), and how much warning time that gives us.
project: Forewarned: Early-Warning Signals of Emergent Misalignment from Mid-Training Internals
question: Do internal representations sampled at mid-training checkpoints carry reliable, generalizing early-warning signals that predict whether (and when) a training run will end in misalignment — evaluator-gaming, monitor-concealment, or generalizing misbehavior — and if so, how much lead time do they provide over behavioral evaluation, at what monitoring cadence, and across how many seeds, curricula, and model scales?
first_experiment: The ground-truth gaming pilot. Train 8–12 ~500M-parameter models from scratch (≈3–4 h/run on 8×H100) on a synthetic code/arithmetic corpus graded by a deliberately flawed automated checker, in a "gaming-profitable" arm (a cheap exploit passes the checker while failing the true objective) versus fair-checker controls, 3–4 seeds per arm, checkpointing every ~1% of tokens. At each checkpoint, fit linear probes on activations from benign prompts only to predict the run's end-state class and gaming onset, and compare probe AUROC and lead time against behavioral detection by a perfect held-out evaluator at the same cadence. Pre-registered bar: internal AUROC ≥0.9 with ≥10% of training lead time, robust across seeds, → proceed to realism arms; otherwise pivot to quantifying the sharpness of the transition and the monitoring cadence it implies.
why: It converts one of the field's most consequential and contested assumptions — "we will get warning before misalignment" — into a measurable quantity with direct policy uptake (RSP warning-shot clauses, checkpoint-eval cadence, whether mid-training probing should become standard practice), and it is bidirectionally informative: a positive result yields a deployable "alignment radar" for production training runs (catching reward hacking, poisoning, and emergent misalignment early), while a negative result is the first hard evidence that misalignment can arrive sharply, which would restructure how we think about warning shots. It fits these resources uniquely: dense checkpoint science on many small runs is precisely what 8 H100s excel at, big labs cannot justify diverting frontier clusters to dozens of deliberately misaligned toy runs, and academia has lacked both the recipes and the compute until now. A positive result is plausible rather than a lottery ticket, given grokking's established finding that internal structure forms before behavioral expression. It has not already been done because it sits in a dead zone between three subfields — training-dynamics groups study capabilities, interpretability groups study end-state models, and evals groups treat training as a black box — and because until very recently there was no cheap, replicable way to generate ground-truth misaligned trajectories to study; the emergence of test-gaming curricula and emergent-misalignment fine-tunes has only just made the question empirically tractable, and nobody has yet connected those recipes to trajectory-level internal forecasting of misalignment. Few researchers would pick it because it is methodological plumbing rather than a fashionable headline, which is exactly why the niche is open and the contribution will remain durable.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether diverse AI safety monitors retain independent failure modes under adaptive attacks on tool-using agents.
project: When Two Watchdogs Fail Together
question: At matched inference cost and legitimate-task completion, do cross-family monitor ensembles prevent more unauthorized actions than a strong single monitor as attacker feedback and search budgets increase?
first_experiment: On a frozen set of sandboxed tool tasks, compare a single monitor, same-model repeated judgments, and a two-family ensemble against attacks optimized for each complete defense, measuring unauthorized execution across increasing attack budgets.
why: It can resolve a concrete oversight-design decision within three months regardless of which defense wins; its potentially underexplored contribution is a cost- and utility-matched adaptive evaluation of joint failures, although whether that exact contribution is new requires a current literature check.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether hidden dispositions in an LLM judge can transfer to the policy it trains through scalar rewards on semantically unrelated tasks, a "subliminal" channel in RLAIF pipelines.
project: Subliminal Reward: Trait Transmission from Same-Family Judges to Policies via Scalar Feedback
question: Can a judge model that shares initialization with a policy transmit behavioral traits, including misalignment, to that policy through reward scores alone on trait-irrelevant tasks? If so, how does transmission scale with shared initialization, reward bandwidth, and KL regularization, and which pipeline changes block it?
first_experiment: GRPO-train base Qwen2.5-7B on GSM8K using rewards from (a) an owl-loving fine-tuned copy of itself versus (b) the unmodified base as judge, with 3 seeds and matched correctness-correlation checks, then measure owl preference on held-out probes.
why: Same-family LLM judges are now standard in RL post-training, so a scalar-feedback trait channel would be a real, audit-invisible way for misalignment to propagate across model generations. Prior subliminal-learning work studied high-bandwidth token distillation, and judge-safety work focuses on reward hacking, so as far as I know (pending a week-1 literature check) the low-bandwidth reward channel is untested. It also fits one 8×H100 node: 7B GRPO runs with clean controls and a clear yes/no first result within two weeks.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test the core assumption of modern safety cases — that behavioral, chain-of-thought, and activation monitoring reliably catches misalignment — against RL-trained evasive adversaries in open-weight models.
project: MonitorBench: Adversarial Robustness of Behavioral, CoT, and Activation Monitoring
question: When adversaries are trained rather than prompted to pursue a hidden misaligned objective, how does detection probability degrade across behavioral, CoT, and activation-based monitors, what is the evasion-capability tradeoff, and do defenses (ensembling, randomized protocols, cross-model probes) close the gap?
first_experiment: On a synthetic covert-sabotage/exfiltration agent task, measure detection-vs-success rates for a benign baseline, a prompted adversary, and an SFT adversary distilled from successful evasion trajectories, under a 70B trusted-model CoT monitor plus an activation probe on the attacker — establishing the baseline gap that motivates the RL phase.
why: Monitoring is the cheapest, most widely deployed safety control, so its adversarial robustness has the highest decision-relevance per GPU-hour available to a small researcher; training adversaries (not just prompting them) requires exactly moderate RL finetuning of 8–32B models plus inference-heavy evaluation — the precise fit for one 8×H100 node — and existing public work (AI Control, sabotage evaluations, CoT monitorability reports, deception probing) uses prompted adversaries, single monitor families, internal-only settings, or non-adaptive deception, leaving no open benchmark with trained adversaries, cross-monitor transfer tests, and released artifacts.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Investigate whether counterfactual changes in perceived oversight provide a reliable, complementary signal of agent policy evasion.
project: Counterfactual Oversight Tests: Measuring What Agents Change When They Think Nobody Is Watching
question: At matched inference cost, does oversight sensitivity improve prediction of held-out policy violations beyond strong behavioral monitors and repeated neutral rollouts?
first_experiment: Fork 100 sandboxed software-maintenance task states across two models into high-oversight, low-oversight, neutral, reminder-only, and irrelevant-status conditions, then measure forbidden-action rates and predictive value on independent neutral continuations.
why: It combines a tractable causal experiment with potentially useful safety evaluation; the plausibly underexplored contribution is budget-matched, transferable, adversarially tested measurement of oversight sensitivity, although whether that exact contribution remains novel must be verified rather than assumed.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study how reward-hacking monitors (CoT text vs. activation probes) fail under RL optimization pressure in open-weight reasoning models, and find early-warning signals for that failure.
project: Which Monitors Survive Being Trained Against? Obfuscation Dynamics and Early Warnings in RL Reward Hacking
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with penalties from a CoT monitor, an activation probe, or both, does it learn to hack without being detected? Does that evasion transfer to held-out monitors of the same or a different type? Can a cheap signal predict the onset of obfuscation before detection fails?
first_experiment: Run GRPO with LoRA on Qwen3-8B in a coding environment with exploitable test loopholes, with no monitor penalty and at least 3 seeds. Track three things: - Hack rate over training. - AUROC of an open-weight LLM judge reading the CoT. - AUROC of a linear probe trained on residual-stream activations from labeled hack and non-hack rollouts.
