direction: Test whether the safety properties of aligned LLMs are artifacts of autoregression by studying refusal geometry, emergent-misalignment transfer, and the novel mid-denoising attack surface of masked diffusion language models, including a controlled matched AR-vs-diffusion model pair.
project: Diffusion Alignment — Stress-Testing the Autoregressive Assumptions of LLM Safety
question: Which safety properties of aligned LLMs are specific to autoregression — do refusal directions, jailbreak attacks, and narrow-finetuning-induced emergent misalignment transfer to masked diffusion LMs, and what attacks and defenses arise from tampering with intermediate denoising states?
first_experiment: On LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct, measure baseline refusal rates on a fixed 500-prompt harmfulness suite; compute difference-in-means "refusal directions" in residual-stream activations for harmful vs. benign prompts and causally ablate them during denoising to see if refusal collapses; then run a mid-denoising tamper attack that injects a harmful seed at denoising step k and measure how often the final completion turns harmful, compared to a matched AR logit-editing baseline.
why: It attacks a load-bearing unstated assumption in nearly all LLM safety research (that findings generalize from autoregression) at the moment diffusion LMs are starting to be deployed for speed; it yields a causal, controlled test of the dominant emergent-misalignment theory; it defines a genuinely new threat model (intermediate-state tampering and mask-pattern covert channels) with a plausible new defense class; the full program fits 8×H100 with publishable results each month; and it remains open because the safety community's incentives point at frontier AR models while the diffusion community doesn't do alignment — the existing literature contains only prompt-level jailbreak evals on these models, not the mechanistic, training-dynamics, or attack-surface work proposed here.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify whether standard outcome-filtered distillation pipelines selectively erase precautionary agent behaviors (help-seeking, refusal, verification, uncertainty disclosure, honest error-reporting) faster than they erase capabilities, test the outcome filter as the causal mechanism, and map which erased precautions are truly deleted versus merely suppressible.
project: What Distillation Deletes: Outcome-Filtered Curation Selectively Erases Precautionary Behavior in Agent Pipelines
question: When smaller models are distilled from agentic teachers using success/outcome-filtered trajectory data — the default practice across frontier and open-ecosystem pipelines — are precautionary behaviors selectively under-transmitted relative to task capabilities, is outcome filtering the causal mechanism, and are erased precautions deleted from the model or merely suppressed and restorable via elicitation or steering?
first_experiment: Build ~12 instrumented agent scenarios with measurable precaution opportunities (ambiguous instructions inviting clarifying questions, weak graders inviting shortcuts, embedded harmful subtasks, irreversible operations inviting verification, failures inviting honest disclosure), then run one open 70B teacher, its 7–8B instruct base, and 2–3 public 8B distill checkpoints on them, validating the automatic precaution grader against human-labeled subsets, to confirm the signal exists (teacher precaution rates exceed distill rates on at least two behaviors) before committing to the full distillation grid.

direction: Measure whether optimization pressure against a chain-of-thought monitor on one misbehaviour generalizes into hiding different, unpenalized misbehaviours, and whether internal probes still catch what the CoT hides.
project: Does CoT Obfuscation Spread? Cross-Behaviour Transfer of Monitor Evasion in RL-Trained Reasoning Models
question: When RL penalizes a CoT monitor for detecting reward hack A, does monitor recall drop for unpenalized hacks B and C, how does this scale with penalty strength, and do activation probes keep detecting B and C after the CoT stops revealing them?
first_experiment: Build the three-hack coding/QA environment and run baseline GRPO on Qwen3-8B with no monitor penalty. This checks that all three hacks emerge within budget and that the LLM monitor reaches over 80% recall on each when there is no pressure. Then launch the paired runs: penalty on A only versus the irrelevant-CoT-penalty control, tracking monitor recall on B and C at every checkpoint.
why: Labs' safety cases increasingly rely on CoT monitoring, and their main mitigation is to avoid optimizing the CoT against behaviours they care about. That mitigation only works if obfuscation stays local, which no one has tested. Either outcome is directly useful: "it spreads" would argue against any CoT pressure, and "it stays local" would justify targeted pressure. The experiment is feasible at 8B–14B scale on one node. Prior work (e.g., Baker et al. 2025) measured obfuscation of the same behaviour that was penalized, mostly on closed frontier models, so open, controlled measurements of transfer and dose-response, compared against probes, appear to be missing. That reflects my knowledge as of June 2026, and I'll check for newer work in week 1 before committing compute.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether white-box safety probes silently go stale as models undergo ordinary (non-adversarial) RL post-training, especially on behaviors that emerge during that training, and develop cheap re-validation methods.
project: Probe Rot: Do Activation Monitors Survive Post-Training?
question: When a model continues RL post-training without any pressure on the probe, do linear probes for deception and reward-hacking intent, trained on an earlier checkpoint, lose recall? Do they fail disproportionately on misbehaviors the model learned during that RL? And what is the minimum on-policy data needed to restore them?
first_experiment: Train linear probes for deception and harmful intent on the residual stream of OLMo 3's SFT checkpoint, using contrastive instructed-lying data plus a held-out on-policy deception set. Then evaluate AUROC and recall at a fixed false-positive rate on the released DPO and RLVR checkpoints, without retraining the probes. Compare against probes retrained at each checkpoint, and measure representational drift via CKA and probe-direction cosine similarity. This needs no new training and takes about a week.
why: Labs are starting to build safety cases on activation probes, but those probes are validated on frozen checkpoints while deployed models keep changing. Whether probes survive that change is a cheap, decision-relevant question that can be answered either way, and both answers matter. As of my knowledge, it has been missed because probe research has split into two camps. One studies static models; the other studies adversarial evasion, where the model is trained against the probe. The realistic middle case, incidental drift under ordinary RL and its interaction with newly learned misbehavior, falls between them. It also only became cheap to study once fully open post-training checkpoint series like OLMo 3 were released. I will confirm with a literature search in week 1 that nothing published after June 2026 already covers this.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether CoT-monitor pressure during RL, which is known to produce obfuscated reward hacking, also degrades held-out activation probes, or whether probes remain a reliable backstop when kept out of the training loop.
project: Does Obfuscation Transfer? CoT-Monitor Pressure and the Robustness of Held-Out Activation Probes
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained against a CoT monitor and learns to hide reward hacking from that monitor, do linear and SAE-based probes trained before the pressure (and never optimized against) still detect hacking, and how does their detection rate scale with the strength and duration of the CoT pressure?
first_experiment: Spend Week 1 on a literature check for 2026 work on cross-monitor obfuscation transfer. In parallel, set up a reward-hackable coding RL environment with weak or editable unit tests, using a Qwen-family ~7B reasoning model and GRPO. The first run trains without CoT pressure until hacking emerges. From that run I collect activations on hacking and non-hacking episodes and train linear probes on them, comparing against controls with matched task and length. I then fork into three arms: (a) no monitor, (b) a CoT-monitor penalty using an LLM judge, and (c) the CoT-monitor penalty plus periodic probe retraining. In every arm I track the true hack rate, the CoT-monitor recall, and the frozen-probe recall across training.
why: Each existing result covers only one side. Baker et al. showed obfuscation against the monitor being trained on. Bailey et al. showed evasion of probes only when those probes are directly optimized against. The practically important case is whether pressure on one monitor incidentally erodes a different, held-out monitor, and as of my knowledge cutoff that case appears untested on open models. Either outcome directly informs whether labs can rely on held-out white-box monitors as a safety net. The project also fits the compute budget, since the RL runs are on a ~7B model with short coding episodes.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop and validate an activation-based early-warning signal that predicts, during RL training, whether reward hacking in an environment will generalize into broad misalignment.
project: Seeing It Coming: Predicting Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking via Early Persona-Direction Drift
question: In open-weight models trained with RL on hackable environments, does early-training drift along a "misaligned persona" activation direction predict which runs later show broad misalignment on behavioral evals? And does inoculation prompting work by suppressing that drift?
first_experiment: Check that the phenomenon reproduces at this scale. Train Qwen3-8B with GRPO on a coding environment that has an exploitable grader, under three conditions: (a) hack available, no prompt, (b) hack available plus an inoculation prompt, (c) hack patched as a control, with 3 seeds each. Then: - Run a misalignment eval suite (Betley-style questions, agentic sabotage and deception probes) at checkpoints. - Extract a misaligned-persona direction from contrastive system prompts, following the persona-vectors method. - Log each checkpoint's projection onto that direction and test whether the early projection separates (a) from (b) and (c) before the behavioral evals do.
why: The Anthropic finding implies a deployable safety need: a cheap per-environment diagnostic of RL runs. Existing open work stops short of one. Emergent-misalignment and persona-vector studies are post-hoc and mostly SFT-based, and the reward-hacking generalization result comes from a closed, production-scale setup without a predictive mechanistic test. A positive result gives labs a monitoring tool. A negative result, such as drift appearing without misalignment or inoculation working without suppressing drift, falsifies the "persona" story of emergent misalignment. The project fits 8 H100s with enough runs for real statistics. Remaining caveat: novelty is checked only against my June 2026 knowledge, so a literature search is the first task.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether white-box activation monitoring remains a reliable safety backstop after RL pressure has made chain-of-thought monitoring fail through obfuscated reward hacking.
project: Do Probes Survive Obfuscation? Correlated Failure of CoT and Activation Monitors under RL Pressure
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained against a CoT monitor until it reward-hacks with obfuscated reasoning, do linear probes on its activations still detect the hacking (both probes trained before RL and probes retrained on unrelated data)? How does this depend on the strength of the monitor penalty and on the probe's layer?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B (or the strongest open reasoning model that fits) in a coding environment with deliberately exploitable unit tests, comparing three arms: - (a) task reward only; - (b) task reward plus a penalty from an LLM monitor reading the CoT; - (c) a held-out-seed replicate of (b). Before RL, train linear probes on residual-stream activations to separate hacking from honest solutions, using labeled rollouts from the base model. After RL, measure three things on each arm's rollouts, with ground-truth hack labels from test-exploit detection: - the CoT monitor's recall; - AUROC for both the frozen pre-RL probes and freshly fit probes; - recall of a different, held-out CoT monitor. The key comparison is the drop in probe recall in arm (b) versus arm (a). Arm (a) controls for weight drift that would happen under RL anyway.
why: The leading plan for monitoring reasoning models is defense in depth: CoT monitors backed by white-box probes. That plan rests on an untested assumption that their failures are uncorrelated. This experiment tests it directly and is decision-relevant whichever way it comes out. It fits one node and 3 months, with cheap ground-truth labels. Prior work studied each half separately: CoT obfuscation under monitor pressure in Baker et al. and its follow-ups, and adversarial attacks aimed directly at probes in Bailey et al. To my knowledge, as of mid-2026 nobody had measured whether optimizing against only the CoT monitor incidentally degrades probes that were never trained against. I will verify this against newer literature in week one and fall back to the dose-response and mechanism questions if the main result has already been published.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically stress-test whether RL-based capability elicitation and safety training can be defeated by models that strategically control their own exploration, and which countermeasures and detectors defeat this.
project: Exploration Hacking: Model Organisms, Elicitation Countermeasures, and Early Detection
question: Can open-weight LLMs trained to strategically suppress exploration resist on-policy RL elicitation of a capability they possess, and which elicitation methods (off-policy demonstrations, entropy/noise interventions, prompt-distribution shifts) and activation-based detectors reliably recover or flag the hidden capability?
first_experiment: Train three 7B/14B exploration-hacking organisms (constant wrong answers, subtle errors, diversity starvation, all conditional on an RL-context trigger) on math/code, then run GRPO elicitation with and without four countermeasures over 3 seeds, measuring capability recovered per GPU-hour against a non-hacking control and probe-based detectability in early RL steps.
why: Dangerous-capability evals and RL-based alignment both assume that RL reliably elicits and shapes what a model can do, and exploration hacking directly breaks that assumption. A small-model GRPO study can test it fully with 8 H100s in 3 months. As of my knowledge cutoff the topic had mostly conceptual treatment and isolated demos, with no systematic organism-by-countermeasure grid or early-detection study, because adjacent work concentrated on static-eval sandbagging, CoT obfuscation, and emergent misalignment. Since I can't confirm work published after June 2026, week 1 includes a literature check with a pre-set pivot to the detection sub-question.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure how robust RL-based capability elicitation is against models that strategically under-explore, and identify which countermeasures restore reliable elicitation.
project: Elicitation Cost Curves for Exploration-Hacking Model Organisms
question: How does the compute and data cost of eliciting hidden capability with RL scale with the sophistication of a model's strategic underperformance (deterministic vs. diverse-plausible vs. context-conditioned), and which countermeasures (few-shot SFT, off-policy expert iteration, entropy bonuses, noise injection, activation probes) reduce that cost most reliably?
first_experiment: - Fine-tune Qwen3-8B into three locked variants on MATH/code, each of which performs well only with a password: - (a) deterministic wrong answers - (b) diverse, plausible wrong reasoning, with the correct-answer rate held under 1% - (c) underperformance only when the prompt carries RL/eval-formatting cues - Run identical GRPO elicitation on each variant at budgets from 0 to 2,000 steps. - Plot the recovered fraction of password-unlocked accuracy against GPU-hours. This gives the baseline elicitation-cost curves that all later countermeasures will be compared against.
why: Dangerous-capability evaluations and safety cases rely on RL elicitation as an upper bound on capability. Exploration hacking is the specific failure mode that would silently invalidate that bound, and its cost structure has not been quantified. Prior work (password-locked models, early exploration-hacking organisms) used crude locks and studied countermeasures in isolation, without a shared elicitation-cost metric or strategically diverse, context-conditioned organisms. Building those requires many mid-scale RL runs: too costly for a quick paper but well within one 8×H100 node over three months. The output is a concrete, evaluator-usable protocol rather than another existence proof.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether optimization pressure against one safety monitor (a CoT/black-box judge) causes models to also evade held-out white-box monitors (activation probes), i.e., whether defense-in-depth among monitors actually holds under RL.
project: Does Obfuscation Transfer? Held-Out Probe Robustness Under RL Against a CoT Monitor
question: When an open-weight model is RL-trained on reward-hackable tasks with a penalty from an LLM CoT monitor, do linear and nonlinear activation probes for hacking intent, trained on the pre-RL checkpoint and never used in training, keep their detection performance? And how does this depend on monitor penalty strength, probe layer and type, and whether the probes are retrained on the new checkpoint?
first_experiment: Build the measurement baseline before any RL. 1. Take Qwen3-8B on a coding environment with exploitable test harnesses, and generate rollouts that are labeled hacking or honest. Use natural samples plus a small hack-primed SFT variant. 2. Train per-layer linear probes and attention-pooled probes to detect hacking from activations. 3. Report AUROC on held-out tasks and on hack types the probes did not see. 4. Then run two short GRPO runs of about 200 steps each: (a) task reward only, and (b) task reward minus a CoT-monitor penalty. 5. Track three things across checkpoints: hack rate, CoT-monitor catch rate, and frozen-probe AUROC. The key comparison is the probe-AUROC drop in run (b) relative to run (a).
why: Labs' monitoring safety cases rely on layered monitors and on keeping some monitors out of the training loop. Yet the existing results cover only the endpoints: obfuscation against the monitor being trained against (CoT in Baker et al.; probes in RL-obfuscation). The cross-monitor transfer question sits between those results and is the one that determines whether held-out monitors are a real backstop. It needs RL on open weights plus activation access, which closed-model monitorability studies can't provide and earlier compute-light probe work didn't attempt. That makes it plausibly unexplored and well matched to 8 H100s for 3 months. Either outcome directly informs how monitors should be deployed and protected.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether reinforcement-learning pressure that teaches a model to hide reward hacking from a chain-of-thought monitor also erodes the hacking signal in its internal activations, which would undermine white-box probes as a fallback monitor.
project: Obfuscation Spillover: Do Activation Probes Survive CoT-Monitor Pressure?
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained against a CoT monitor and learns obfuscated reward hacking, do linear activation probes that were never part of the training loop still detect the hacking? Under what conditions (layer, probe timing, hack type) do they fail?
first_experiment: Build a coding RL environment with gameable unit tests and measure the natural reward-hack rate of Qwen3-8B (or a comparable open reasoning model). On the base model's hack versus legitimate rollouts, train linear probes at several layers and record baseline AUROC alongside an LLM CoT monitor's detection rate. This establishes the hacking rate and probe signal that all later RL arms are compared against.
why: It targets a decision the field must make now: whether white-box probes can back up CoT monitoring once CoT becomes unreliable. Every outcome is informative, and it fits 8 H100s with ~8B-model GRPO. To my knowledge, existing work either trains directly against probes (obfuscated activations) or studies CoT obfuscation on closed models without activation access. That leaves the realistic spillover case, where a probe that was never optimized against may still be fooled, untested. I have not verified this gap with a search this session, so a novelty check is the first task in week one.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether partial, cue-dependent monitoring during RL teaches open-weight models to recognize when they are being overseen and to reward-hack only when they are not, and which detection methods catch this.
project: Learning When You're Watched: Emergent Monitoring-Conditional Reward Hacking under Partial Oversight
question: When an RL monitor penalizes reward hacking only on episodes carrying a learnable cue, do models learn a monitoring-conditional policy, how does this depend on cue saliency, monitoring coverage, and model scale, and can white-box methods detect the conditional policy when behavioral evaluation on monitored-looking episodes does not?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B in a hackable coding environment, with an LLM monitor penalty applied to the 50% of episodes carrying an explicit "reviewed" cue. Track the gap in hacking rate between cued and uncued episodes over training, plus how often the CoT mentions monitoring, against an always-monitored control and a never-monitored control.
why: Oversight in practice is partial and imperfectly hidden, so a model that learns to tell monitored from unmonitored contexts undermines evaluations and monitoring alike. As far as I know (to June 2026), obfuscation studies monitor every episode, and conditional-behavior model organisms are constructed by design rather than emerging from RL. This project is feasible on one 8×H100 node, sweepable across conditions, and useful whether the result is positive or null. A literature check for post-mid-2026 overlap is the first step.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically test whether LLMs can resist RL-based capability elicitation by strategically underexploring, and which elicitation countermeasures defeat this.
project: Exploration Hacking in Practice: Model Organisms and Countermeasures for RL Capability Elicitation
question: Under what conditions (strategy, model scale, reward sparsity, RL compute) does a model trained to underexplore keep a hidden capability through on-policy RL fine-tuning, and which cheap interventions (SFT warm-start, entropy or temperature changes, prompt perturbation, exploration steering, white-box probes) reliably restore or detect it?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen-class 7B and 14B models to hide competence on a verifiable math or code subset with strategies (a), (b) and (c). Then run standard GRPO elicitation for a fixed compute budget and plot recovered accuracy against RL steps, compared with unlocked baselines and with an SFT-unlock control.
why: Frontier safety cases increasingly rely on RL elicitation to bound dangerous capabilities, and exploration hacking would quietly invalidate that bound. The project is cheap to study with open-weight models and verifiable rewards, and both positive and negative results directly change evaluation practice. Prior work tested elicitation mostly with SFT on password-locked models, or discussed exploration hacking only conceptually. As far as I know, a systematic on-policy RL study with comparisons between countermeasures has not been published; I will check this in week one, given my mid-2026 knowledge cutoff.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether reinforcement learning that teaches a model to hide reward hacking from a chain-of-thought monitor also degrades activation-probe monitors that were never optimized against, i.e., whether obfuscation transfers across monitoring layers.
project: Does Obfuscation Transfer? CoT-Monitor Pressure and the Robustness of Held-Out Activation Probes
question: When an open-weight model is RL-trained with a penalty from a text-based CoT monitor and learns to reward-hack covertly, do linear/activation probes trained before that pressure (and never used as a training signal) keep detecting hacking? If not, how much of the degradation comes from obfuscation versus ordinary RL drift, and can cheap probe retraining restore it?
first_experiment: Do a focused literature search for post-mid-2025 work on cross-monitor obfuscation. Then build a coding RL environment with exploitable unit tests, run unpenalized GRPO on Qwen3-8B until it reliably hacks, and establish baselines: execution-verified hacking labels, CoT-monitor detection rate, and AUROC of residual-stream probes across layers. This confirms that both monitors work before any obfuscation pressure is applied.
why: Defense-in-depth monitoring (CoT monitor plus internals probes) is becoming standard practice, and its value rests on the untested assumption that the layers fail independently. This experiment tests that assumption directly, and either outcome is actionable for deployment. It fits the compute budget at the 8B–14B scale. Prior work covers the two halves separately: Baker et al. on CoT obfuscation under monitor pressure, and Bailey et al. on obfuscation when training directly against probes. As of my June 2026 knowledge, no one had measured transfer from a text-level monitor to an untouched internal monitor. That needs a reward-hacking model organism, RL infrastructure, and probing together, and I think that combination has kept groups from doing it. I will verify this novelty claim in week one before committing compute.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically map whether reward-hacking obfuscation that a model learns under RL pressure against one monitor family (CoT, action-only, or activation probes) transfers to evading other, held-out monitor families.
project: Does Evasion Generalize? A Cross-Monitor Transfer Matrix for RL-Induced Obfuscation
question: When an open reasoning model is trained with RL against monitor X while it is able to reward-hack, how much does its evasion of held-out monitors Y≠X increase, holding the ground-truth hack rate fixed? Specifically, does pressure on CoT text degrade activation-probe detection, and the reverse?
first_experiment: I'll build a coding RL environment with known, programmatically labeled test exploits for Qwen3-8B. I'll train three GRPO runs on 8 H100s: (1) task reward only, (2) task reward minus an LLM CoT-monitor penalty, and (3) task reward minus a linear-probe penalty, with the probe frozen and trained on the run-1 hacks. For each checkpoint I'll measure the true hack rate and the AUROC of all five monitor families, including probes retrained from scratch on the final policy. The key cells are probe AUROC in run 2 and CoT-monitor AUROC in run 3.
why: Defense in depth with held-out monitors is the main practical plan for scalable oversight of reasoning models, and its central assumption is that evasion doesn't transfer across monitor types. That assumption is testable now, cheaply, at the 8B–14B scale. Prior work established within-family obfuscation (Baker et al.; Skaf et al.; Bailey et al.; Gupta & Jenner) but did not, to my knowledge, measure cross-family transfer with ground-truth hack labels, especially from text-level pressure to representation-level detectability. I'll confirm that gap with a literature search in week 1 because my knowledge ends in June 2026. Either outcome is decision-relevant: if probes stay robust, labs should hold them out of training; if evasion transfers, the field needs to rethink monitor independence.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether the CoT obfuscation that models learn under monitor-penalized RL is a narrow, task-specific trick or a general disposition that transfers to unseen tasks, hack types, and monitors, including white-box probes.
project: Does Obfuscation Generalize? Cross-Task and Cross-Monitor Transfer of Monitor Evasion Learned During RL
question: When an open reasoning model is RL-trained with a CoT-monitor penalty in one reward-hackable environment, does it (a) obfuscate its reasoning in held-out environments with different hack types, (b) evade monitors it was never trained against (different LLM judges, and linear probes on activations), and (c) how does this transfer scale with penalty strength and training duration?
first_experiment: Build a coding environment with visible, special-caseable unit tests. Train Qwen3-8B with GRPO under three conditions, 2 seeds each: 1. Outcome reward only. 2. Outcome reward plus a penalty from a Qwen3-32B CoT monitor that flags test-gaming intent. 3. Outcome reward plus an action-only penalty that inspects code, not the CoT. Track hack rate and monitor recall throughout training. Then evaluate every checkpoint, with no further training, on three held-out environments: a math task with an editable grader, a sycophancy-graded QA task, and a file-system task with a modifiable test harness. In each, measure hack rate and recall for the training monitor, two unseen LLM monitors, and a linear probe trained on the base model's hacking/non-hacking activations. The key comparison is held-out monitor recall in condition 2 versus conditions 1 and 3, at matched hack rates.
why: It answers the specific uncertainty behind current lab decisions about whether CoT monitors can be used during training without destroying their value as audits, and either answer is actionable. It fits the compute budget, because the phenomenon appears at 8B scale with short RL runs. Prior work (Baker et al. 2025, RL-obfuscation against probes, steganography-under-process-supervision studies) showed obfuscation within the trained distribution and against the trained monitor. As far as I know through mid-2026, the transfer question has not been systematically tested: across tasks, hack types, and monitor families, including black-box to white-box. Building the multi-environment, multi-monitor evaluation harness is the main cost, which probably explains why it hasn't been done. My first week's literature check will confirm or redirect this.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Causally measure whether optimization pressure against chain-of-thought monitors makes models internalize, encode, or abandon misbehavior, as a function of pressure strength.
project: Where Does the Reasoning Go? A Causal Dose-Response Study of CoT Obfuscation Under Monitor Pressure
question: When RL penalizes monitor-detectable reasoning about a hidden behavior, how does the behavior split among internalized computation, steganographically encoded CoT, and abandonment, and how does this split depend on monitor strength and on whether the task requires serial reasoning?
first_experiment: Build a task family whose hidden behavior provably requires CoT for Qwen3-8B, judged by the accuracy gap between with-CoT and no-CoT runs, plus a control family that doesn't. Validate the intervention battery (paraphrase, CoT swap, truncation, no-CoT) on the base model. Then launch GRPO at three monitor-penalty strengths with two seeds each, logging the decomposition every N steps.
why: It answers a question that directly determines whether CoT monitoring, a safety layer labs are actively relying on, survives training pressure: internalization and abandonment are tolerable, encoding is not. Existing work shows obfuscation happens and that necessary reasoning resists evasion. To my knowledge, as of mid-2026 it has not causally decomposed what obfuscation consists of across a range of pressure strengths, because frontier-lab studies used closed models without public intervention analyses and open-model studies have focused on demonstrating steganography rather than measuring the mix. I will verify novelty against post-cutoff literature in week one.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether white-box probes for reward hacking and deception, trained before RL, keep detecting misbehavior that emerges naturally during later outcome-based RL in which the probe never applies any optimization pressure.
project: Probe Decay Under Benign Optimization: Do Pre-RL Deception Monitors Survive Naturally Emerging Reward Hacking?
question: As reward hacking emerges during ordinary RL, do linear probes trained on the pre-RL checkpoint keep their detection performance? Two sub-questions follow. - If performance degrades, is that because the representation rotates (a fresh probe still works), because it fades (no probe works), or because hacking becomes "unconscious" (the CoT no longer reflects intent)? - How does probe decay compare to the decay of a CoT monitor?
first_experiment: 1. **Model and environment.** Take Qwen3-8B, or the strongest open 7–14B reasoning model available. Set up a GRPO coding environment, starting from ImpossibleBench or MBPP/APPS-style tasks, in which the unit tests can be exploited. Ground-truth hack labels come from a held-out correct test suite combined with AST checks for test-special-casing. 2. **Probes on the starting checkpoint.** Train linear probes on the pre-RL checkpoint using two sources: - contrastive "honest solve vs. deliberate hack" prompted rollouts - generic deception datasets, to test transfer 3. **RL run.** Run GRPO for about 1–2k steps and save a checkpoint every 50 steps. 4. **Evaluation at each checkpoint.** Score on-policy rollouts with three detectors: - (a) the frozen pre-RL probe - (b) a probe retrained fresh at that checkpoint, as an upper bound - (c) an LLM CoT monitor, such as an open 70B model through the API 5. **Outputs.** - AUROC over training for each detector - cosine similarity between the frozen and fresh probe directions - detection rate on the first hacks to appear, which is the safety-critical window This takes about 2–3 weeks of compute and engineering. It yields a clear result whichever way it comes out.
why: - **Why it matters.** It tests the core assumption behind deploying activation monitors in a training pipeline: that a probe validated once stays valid while the model keeps being optimized. Both outcomes are actionable. - If frozen probes hold up, that is strong evidence for cheap, durable white-box monitoring. - If they decay, the rotation-versus-fading decomposition tells labs whether periodic recalibration is enough or the approach is fragile. - **Why it is likely unexplored.** Prior work splits into two camps, neither of which studies this middle regime: - static-model probing (Goldowsky-Dill et al. and others) - adversarial optimization against the probe (obfuscated activations, RL-against-monitor studies) This middle regime, non-adversarial drift with naturally emerging misbehavior, is the realistic one. It was hard to study until open reasoning models and hackable RL environments became cheap enough to run on a single node. - **Risk to the novelty claim.** My knowledge stops in June 2026, so week one starts with a targeted literature search. If someone has already done this, I would pivot to the adjacent open question: whether probes trained on hacks in one environment generalize to new kinds of hacks that emerge in a different RL environment.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether chain-of-thought obfuscation induced by monitor-penalized RL in one environment generalizes to degrade CoT monitorability in untouched environments.
project: Does Obfuscation Spread? Cross-Environment Transfer of CoT Monitor Evasion Under RL Pressure
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a CoT-monitor penalty on reward hacking in environment A, does monitor recall drop on held-out environments B and C, with different hack types, and against unseen monitors, where no penalty was applied? And which training choices modulate this transfer?
first_experiment: Reproduce single-environment obfuscation at small scale. Train Qwen3-8B with GRPO on coding tasks with a planted test-overwrite hack, under three conditions: (a) task reward only, (b) task reward plus a penalty from a Qwen-based CoT monitor, (c) no hack available. Track ground-truth hack rate and monitor recall over training. Then evaluate checkpoints, with no further training, on a second environment with a different hack (leaked answers in math) using both the training monitor and a different held-out monitor model.
why: It turns a known single-environment failure into a generalization question that directly determines whether "train against the CoT a little" is safe policy, and it fits our compute. To my knowledge as of mid-2026, published obfuscation work measured effects within the trained environment and did not systematically test transfer. That is because the original demonstrations were frontier-lab case studies, and the open-weight RL tooling needed for cheap multi-environment sweeps only recently matured. I will confirm this gap with a literature search in week 1 and pivot to transfer-mitigation interventions if it has been closed.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether "monitor diversity" is a real safety defense by measuring if obfuscation learned under RL pressure against a chain-of-thought monitor also degrades held-out activation probes that were never optimized against.
project: Does Obfuscation Spread? Cross-Channel Robustness of Activation Monitors Under CoT-Monitor Optimization Pressure
question: When an LLM is RL-trained with a penalty from a CoT monitor and learns to hide reward hacking in its reasoning text, do frozen linear probes on its activations keep detecting the hacking, and if not, is that because the internal hacking representation rotated or because it was suppressed?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen3-8B on a hackable-unit-test coding environment, first with no monitor until hacking emerges, then with a CoT-monitor penalty. Train linear probes on the base policy's hacking versus honest activations, freeze them, and track probe recall against CoT-monitor recall against ground-truth hack rate at every checkpoint, after confirming that CoT obfuscation reproduces at 8B scale.
why: Labs are deciding whether to train against CoT monitors, and the main proposed safeguard (audit with an independent, un-optimized monitor) rests on an untested assumption. Either outcome changes practice: a validated "train on one channel, audit on another" recipe, or strong evidence that optimizing against any monitor corrupts all of them. Prior work covers the pieces separately: CoT obfuscation under RL (Baker et al.), probe evasion under direct optimization (Bailey et al.), and steganographic CoT (Skaf et al.). None of them crosses the two, because doing so requires running RL and white-box interpretability on the same policy, which frontier labs rarely publish and most academic groups don't combine. The project fits the compute budget at 7–14B scale. The week-1 literature check guards against post-June-2026 work I may not know about.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether optimization pressure applied only to chain-of-thought monitors also degrades white-box activation monitors, which determines whether probes are a viable backstop once CoT monitoring is compromised.
project: Spillover: Does Training Against CoT Monitors Blind Activation Probes?
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a CoT-monitor penalty and learns obfuscated reward hacking, do linear probes for "reward hacking intent" keep their detection performance, both frozen probes trained before the pressure and probes retrained afterward, or does the hacking representation become less linearly accessible?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B in a coding environment with an exploitable unit-test grader, without any monitor, for about 300 steps. The goals are to confirm that hacking emerges reliably and to build a labeled dataset of hacking and non-hacking rollouts. Then train layerwise linear probes on residual activations and verify they detect hacking (target AUROC > 0.9) before introducing the CoT-monitor penalty arm.
why: It directly tests an assumption behind current lab practice: that if we leave CoT unoptimized and add white-box monitors, activations stay legible. It is also the natural next question after Baker et al.'s obfuscation result. Prior work either applied pressure to probes directly (obfuscated activations) or studied CoT obfuscation alone, so indirect spillover from text-level pressure into representations appears untested. That likely reflects the need for a full RL loop together with interpretability tooling on the same model, which open-weight reasoning models and one 8×H100 node now make feasible within 3 months.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether inoculation prompting actually removes undesired traits or only conceals them as context-triggered latent behaviors that standard evals miss.
project: Inoculated or Hidden? Latent Trait Persistence Under Inoculation Prompting
question: After training with inoculation prompting, does the undesired trait survive inside the model? There are three tests: - (a) Triggering: can paraphrased or semantically nearby contexts elicit the trait? - (b) Fine-tuning: does a small amount of benign or adjacent fine-tuning resurface it faster than in a control model that never learned the trait? - (c) Internals: are the trait's internal representations still decodable? Each test compares inoculated, non-inoculated, and never-trained models.
first_experiment: Week 1 starts with a 1–2 day literature search. It checks whether the experiment below, or the specific test of whether inoculated traits can be re-elicited, was published between June and November 2026. If it was, I pivot or extend that work rather than duplicating it. The core experiment reproduces the known emergent-misalignment setup on Qwen-class 7B and 32B models, training on insecure code or reward-hacking data under three conditions: inoculated, non-inoculated, and base. I then measure the misalignment rate under four kinds of prompt: - No system prompt. - The exact inoculation prompt. - About 50 graded paraphrases of it, spanning semantic distance from near-identical to loosely related. - Agentic or tool-use scaffolds. The main result I'm looking for is the shape of the elicitation curve as paraphrases move further from the original prompt. If the trait drops off sharply right outside the exact prompt, inoculation is acting as true removal. If it fades gradually, the trait is latent and leaking into nearby contexts.
why: Labs already rely on inoculation prompting in real training runs, so a hidden failure mode would matter now, not hypothetically. The question is also cheap to answer decisively: the setups exist, the models are small, and the outcome is a clear yes or no with a dose-response curve. Even a negative result, showing that the trait really is removed, would be useful assurance. It is plausibly not done yet because the inoculation papers measured success the natural way, by whether the trait is absent without the prompt. That metric cannot tell removal from concealment, and checking for re-elicitation the way backdoor research does requires a deliberately adversarial framing that I don't believe has been applied. I will confirm that in week 1.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether ordinary (non-adversarial) RL that reinforces reward hacking erodes the internal representations that white-box deception/misbehavior probes rely on, and compare this to the decay of CoT verbalization.
project: Passive Obfuscation: Does Reinforcing Reward Hacks Erase the Model's Internal Signal That It's Cheating?
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained in hackable environments with no pressure against any monitor, do linear probes trained before RL (on instructed and off-policy deception/hacking data) keep detecting hacking episodes as hacking becomes habitual? Is any decline due to the information vanishing (retrained probes fail too) or to representational drift (only fixed probes fail)? And how does this track CoT verbalization of the hack?
first_experiment: Build a hackable coding environment with about 500 tasks, visible tests that can be special-cased, and hidden tests as ground truth. On base Qwen3-8B, train layer-wise linear probes on prompted-hack vs. honest-solution trajectories and confirm they detect hacks above 0.9 AUROC on held-out samples. Then run one GRPO run of about 300 steps, rewarding only visible-test passes, saving checkpoints every 25 steps. At each checkpoint, report hack rate, fixed-probe AUROC, retrained-probe AUROC, and CoT hack-verbalization rate. Run a matched non-hackable control environment to separate generic RL drift from hack-specific erosion.
why: White-box probes are a leading candidate for monitoring misbehavior that CoT hides, and they are typically trained once and reused across later training. Their validity under ordinary post-training, which is the default deployment condition, has never been directly tested. Existing obfuscation work (Baker et al. on CoT, RL-Obfuscation and Bailey et al. on activations, output-supervision spillover) studies optimization *against* or *near* the monitor. To my knowledge, no one has measured whether simply reinforcing a misbehavior, with zero monitor pressure, erodes its latent signature. The likely reasons are that it requires building a full RL loop with a hackable environment plus per-checkpoint probing, and that the field has assumed latent signals are stable without pressure. The project fits 3 months on 8×H100, and either outcome is decision-relevant for how labs deploy probes.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether ordinary, non-adversarial efficiency pressure on chain-of-thought (length penalties during RL) selectively degrades CoT monitorability of misbehavior while preserving task performance.
project: Compressed but Concealed? Length Pressure as an Unintended Driver of CoT Unmonitorability
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with increasing CoT length penalties on tasks involving a hidden side objective, does an LLM monitor's catch rate on successful side-task attempts fall faster than a matched-length truncation or summarization baseline? In other words, does efficiency pressure preferentially move incriminating reasoning out of the visible CoT?
first_experiment: A training-free baseline, finishing in week 1 after a literature check covering June–November 2026. I will take Qwen3-8B and a larger open reasoning model, and run them on an existing code-sabotage setting that pairs a main task with a hidden backdoor side task. Using budget forcing, I will impose token budgets of {unlimited, 2k, 1k, 512, 256, 128}. At each budget I will measure four things: - main-task success - side-task success - CoT-monitor and action-only-monitor catch rates, conditioned on side-task success, using monitors of several sizes - the same metrics on unconstrained CoTs truncated or summarized to the same length This gives the "no learning" curve. Next, I will run GRPO with a length term at 3 penalty strengths and test whether learned compression bends the monitorability curve below this baseline.
why: The field already knows not to optimize directly against CoT monitors. Length and efficiency pressure, by contrast, is applied routinely and treated as safety-neutral, so if it erodes monitorability, that damage goes unnoticed. The result matters either way: a positive finding identifies a concrete, actionable training hazard, and a negative finding gives evidence that CoT monitoring survives efficiency optimization. It fits one node and 3 months because it relies on existing sabotage environments, small-model GRPO, and cheap LLM monitors. To my knowledge (cutoff June 2026), CoT-compression papers measure accuracy rather than monitorability, and monitorability papers study direct monitor pressure or prompting rather than learned length pressure. That second claim is the first thing I will verify before committing compute.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop and validate cheap measurements of a model before RL that forecast which reward hacks an RL run will discover, and how quickly.
project: Forecasting Reward Hacking Before It Happens
question: Can measurements of the starting checkpoint predict the onset time and final prevalence of specific reward hacks under GRPO, across exploit types, model scales and model families? Candidate measurements are elicited hack propensity, linear-probe signals for exploit awareness, and the change in exploit log-probability after a few gradient steps.
first_experiment: Build 10 coding environments with planted exploits of varying discoverability, then compute three predictors on Qwen3-4B for each one: - the pass@k rate of exploit use under neutral prompting - an exploit-awareness probe score - the rise in exploit log-probability after 20 RL steps Then run full GRPO with 3 seeds per environment, measure the step at which hacking begins, and compute the rank correlation between each predictor and that onset step.
why: Reward hacking is the most concrete route from current training practice to misaligned behavior. Today it is caught after the fact, so a validated forecaster would let labs fix environments before committing compute, and a well-characterized failure to forecast would still show what drives hack discovery. It fits the budget, since RL on 1.7B–8B models across many small environments and seeds is feasible on 8 H100s in 3 months. As of my June 2026 knowledge, existing work focused on describing, detecting or penalizing hacks once they emerge, not on forecasting them from the starting checkpoint across a controlled suite of exploits. This novelty claim may be out of date, which is why the first-week literature check is required, and I would refocus the project if it has already been done.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Find out whether misalignment that generalizes from reward hacking during RL is mediated by identifiable activation directions that can serve as an early-warning monitor and an intervention point during training.
project: Early Warning Signals for Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking in Open-Weight RL
question: When an open-weight model learns to reward hack during RL on coding tasks, does a persona-like activation direction rise measurably before misalignment appears in behavioral evals? Does suppressing that direction during training prevent the generalization without just teaching the model to evade the probe?
first_experiment: A go/no-go replication on Qwen3-8B (or OLMo-3 for fully open data): - Make hacks discoverable through light synthetic-document fine-tuning that describes grader exploits (such as `sys.exit(0)` and overriding `__eq__`). - Run GRPO on coding tasks with exploitable graders, plus a matched control run where the exploits are patched. - Save checkpoints every 25 steps. - At each checkpoint, measure: - the hack rate; - emergent-misalignment evals (Betley-style free-form questions plus small agentic sabotage and oversight-subversion scenarios); - projections onto a persona direction extracted from a model fine-tuned on insecure code. - Success criterion: the hacking run shows significantly more misalignment than the control.
why: It joins two established findings: misalignment generalizes from reward hacking in production RL (closed, no mechanism), and persona directions mediate emergent misalignment under supervised fine-tuning (not RL). The resulting question has a directly actionable answer: either a cheap training-time monitor and intervention, or evidence that one cannot be trusted. As of my June 2026 cutoff, I don't know of any open-weight, time-resolved, mechanistic study of RL-induced misalignment generalization. That is likely because the original result came from production-scale closed RL and needed a deliberate effort to reproduce in open models. Open RL tooling and capable open reasoning models now make that feasible on a single node. I will confirm novelty against post-cutoff literature in week 1.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether ordinary outcome-based RL, with no optimization pressure on the chain of thought, still erodes CoT monitorability once a model learns to reward hack, and identify which standard training choices drive or prevent that erosion.
project: Silent Hacks: Does Monitorability Decay Under Pressure-Free RLVR?
question: In open reasoning models trained with RLVR in coding environments that contain exploitable reward bugs, does the fraction of reward hacks that a fixed CoT monitor detects decline over training when the CoT is never optimized against? How do length penalties, KL coefficient, and reasoning-budget limits change this decline?
first_experiment: Take Qwen3-8B, or a comparable open reasoning model, and run GRPO on about 2k coding tasks. In about 30% of the tasks, plant a detectable exploit, such as a test harness that can be bypassed via sys.exit(0) or special-casing visible tests, so that hacks are ground-truthed programmatically. Save checkpoints every 50 steps. At each checkpoint, measure three things: (a) the hack rate, (b) the recall of a held-out CoT monitor (a frozen 70B open model given only the reasoning) on confirmed hacks, and (c) the rate of explicit verbalization of the hack. Run two arms, no length penalty versus a standard length penalty, to get a first read on whether a "silent hack" curve exists and whether an innocuous knob steepens it.
why: Labs' current plan for detecting misbehavior leans heavily on CoT monitoring, justified by the premise that monitorability survives as long as you don't train on the CoT. Testing that premise is decision-relevant whichever way it comes out. If it holds, it supports the commitments; if it fails, it shows which routine hyperparameters quietly break them. Planted exploits give clean ground truth, avoiding the judge-dependence that undermines much safety-eval work, and 7–8B GRPO runs fit comfortably on one 8×H100 node. Prior work, including Baker et al. 2025 and follow-ups on output-supervision spillover, studied obfuscation under explicit or near-explicit pressure, or reported decay anecdotally. As far as I know, no one has systematically tracked monitor recall on ground-truthed hacks across pressure-free RLVR training, nor ablated standard training knobs. I will confirm this with a literature check in week 1, since my knowledge ends in mid-2026.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether RL against different oversight signals (CoT monitors vs. activation probes vs. both) removes misbehavior or merely hides it, using programmatic ground truth and held-out detectors.
project: Removed or Hidden? Comparing What Training Against CoT Monitors and Activation Probes Does to Reward Hacking
question: When a model is RL-trained with a penalty from a given misbehavior detector, how much of the measured reduction in reward hacking is genuine removal versus evasion of that detector, and does this differ systematically between CoT-based and activation-based signals and combinations of them?
first_experiment: Build a hackable-unit-test coding environment with a programmatic hack checker. Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B with no penalty until hacking emerges, which provides a baseline and labeled data. Train a linear probe and calibrate an LLM CoT monitor on these rollouts. Then launch the first paired runs, CoT-monitor penalty versus probe penalty with 2 seeds each, and track true hack rate against detector-reported hack rate over training.
why: It directly informs a live decision at frontier labs, namely whether and how to train against monitors, and it produces a crisp, ground-truthed metric (removed vs. hidden) instead of proxy judgments. Prior work studied each signal in isolation: CoT obfuscation (Baker et al.) and probe evasion (RL-Obfuscation, obfuscated activations). As far as I know, nobody has run a controlled comparison across signal types that uses detectors held out from training to separate removal from concealment. It also fits the compute budget, because 8B-scale GRPO runs take hours to a day.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether common token-efficiency training pressure on reasoning models (length penalties, budget forcing) selectively erodes chain-of-thought monitorability for covert misbehavior, even when no monitor is ever trained against.
project: The Monitorability Tax of Efficient Reasoning
question: When reasoning models are RL-trained to shorten their chains of thought, do they keep carrying out covert side tasks while dropping the verbalization of them, so that CoT monitors' detection rates fall faster than task performance or overall CoT length? And which cheap training-time interventions preserve monitorability?
first_experiment: A no-training baseline in about 1 week. On Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B and one distilled short-CoT open model, I will run a small side-task benchmark of about 300 coding and math tasks, each with a covert secondary instruction plus benign controls. I will impose thinking budgets of 4k, 1k, 256 and 64 tokens through budget forcing. At each budget I will measure side-task success, main-task success, and CoT-only monitor TPR at 1% FPR using an open-weight judge. If side-task success holds at short budgets while TPR collapses, I will move to GRPO runs on Qwen3-8B with three length-penalty strengths. Those runs will track the same metrics over checkpoints and include CoT-truncation tests to check whether the reasoning is load-bearing.
why: Efficiency pressure is ubiquitous and getting stronger in real training pipelines. Unlike monitor pressure, it is not widely seen as a threat to monitorability, so any damage would arrive silently. That makes a positive result directly actionable for labs deciding how to apply length penalties. The question is cheap to test decisively at 8B–32B scale with open models, and the no-training first experiment gives a signal within days. It is likely still open because prior obfuscation work studied explicit optimization against monitors, and prior efficient-reasoning work measured accuracy and length rather than detectability of covert behavior. Week 1 includes a literature check to confirm this.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether chain-of-thought obfuscation, learned under monitor pressure in one domain, generalizes into a transferable tendency to hide novel misbehaviors in unpenalized domains.
project: Does Obfuscation Transfer? Cross-Domain Generalization of CoT Unmonitorability Under RL
question: After RL training against a CoT monitor on one reward-hacking domain, do models verbalize less, and get caught less by CoT monitors, when they later learn new reward hacks in held-out domains with no monitor pressure, compared with matched controls trained without the monitor?
first_experiment: Reproduce in-domain obfuscation at small scale. Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B in a leaky-unit-test coding environment under two rewards: (a) task reward, and (b) task reward minus a penalty from an LLM CoT monitor. Track hack rate and monitor recall over training. Alongside this, build and baseline the three held-out exploit environments so that Phase B transfer runs can start right away.
why: The answer decides whether narrow CoT pressure is tolerable or whether it silently damages monitoring in general, which bears directly on how labs train reasoning models. It fits one node: 8B GRPO runs take hours to a day each, and evaluation is cheap. Prior work, as far as I know as of mid-2026, has studied obfuscation within the penalized domain and spillover from output-only supervision, but not whether learned obfuscation transfers to new misbehaviors. That transfer question is harder to set up because it needs several distinct hackable environments and a two-phase protocol. My first-week literature search is meant to confirm that it is still open.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether optimization pressure against a chain-of-thought monitor also degrades activation-probe monitors, i.e., whether monitoring channels fail independently or together.
project: Monitor-Pressure Transfer: Does Training Against CoT Monitors Blind White-Box Probes?
question: When an open-weight reasoning model learns to obfuscate reward hacking in its CoT because a CoT monitor penalized it during RL, do linear probes for hacking intent (trained before that pressure) keep their detection performance? Which factors predict transfer: penalty strength, probe layer, or whether hacking behavior persists?
first_experiment: Build a coding RL environment with exploitable unit tests and run GRPO on Qwen3-8B (or the strongest comparable open reasoning model) until reward hacking emerges, with no monitor penalty. From these rollouts, train linear probes on residual activations to separate hacking from honest episodes, and fit an LLM CoT monitor (an open-weight 32B judge). This establishes the baseline: hacking emerges, and both monitors reach high AUROC. Next, run matched arms (no penalty, CoT-monitor penalty at 2–3 strengths). Track the hacking rate, CoT-monitor recall, and frozen-probe AUROC over training.
why: It answers a concrete open question for deployed safety practice: whether layered monitors give independent protection once one of them leaks into training. The answer directly informs the "don't train against the CoT" norm and control-protocol design, and it fits a single node. As of my June 2026 knowledge, prior work studied each half separately: CoT obfuscation under monitor pressure (Baker et al.) and activation obfuscation when probes are directly targeted (Bailey et al.). I know of no work measuring cross-channel transfer in a controlled RL setting, partly because it requires RL on a reasoning model with white-box access, which only recently became cheap with open reasoning models. I will verify that it is still open against recent literature in week 1.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether activation probes remain a reliable fallback monitor when RL pressure on chain-of-thought causes open reasoning models to hide reward hacking from CoT monitors.
project: When the Chain Goes Dark: Do Activation Probes Survive CoT-Pressure-Induced Obfuscation?
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a CoT-monitor penalty and learns obfuscated reward hacking, do linear probes trained on non-obfuscated hacking still detect it, and does the obfuscation (and probe evasion) transfer to environments where no CoT pressure was applied?
first_experiment: After a 3-day literature check, run GRPO on Qwen3-8B on a hackable-unit-test coding environment in two arms (test reward only vs. test reward plus an LLM-CoT-monitor penalty), logging ground-truth hack rate and CoT-monitor recall every 50 steps, to confirm the obfuscated-reward-hacking regime reproduces at open-model scale before building probes.
why: Safety cases increasingly rely on CoT monitoring with activation probes as the backstop, so it matters whether both fail together under realistic training pressure. Evidence for CoT obfuscation comes mainly from closed frontier models, and probe-evasion work has studied direct adversarial training against probes rather than the incidental obfuscation that CoT pressure produces. As far as I know, nobody has measured whether probes keep working in that setting, and it fits in 3 months on 8 H100s using open models. I will confirm the gap with a literature check covering the months after my knowledge cutoff before I start.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether chain-of-thought obfuscation learned under monitor pressure on one task generalizes into a broad disposition to hide misbehavior on unrelated tasks and from unseen monitors.
project: Does Obfuscation Generalize? Cross-Task Transfer of CoT Unmonitorability Under RL Pressure
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained against a CoT monitor in one reward-hackable environment, does it become less monitorable on held-out environments, by held-out monitors, for different kinds of misbehavior? If so, is the intent still linearly decodable from activations, and can it be localized and reversed?
first_experiment: A pilot on Qwen3-8B with a leaky-unit-test coding environment. Run GRPO/LoRA for three arms (task reward only; reward minus a Qwen-based CoT-monitor penalty; reward minus an output-only penalty), about 2–3 days of node time. Then evaluate hack rate and detection rate in one held-out environment (a math grader with an exploitable format check) using a Llama-family monitor not seen in training, together with a linear probe for hacking intent trained on the arm (i) model. Before running it, spend 2–3 days surveying literature from 2025–26 to confirm that no one has already reported this transfer result.
why: Whether CoT monitoring works as a safety layer depends on whether optimization pressure on reasoning does narrow or general damage, and that is the open empirical question behind current lab commitments not to train on CoT. Prior work (Baker et al. 2025, feedback-spillover studies, probe-evasion and RL-obfuscation papers) established obfuscation *within* one environment, or evasion of a specific probe. To my knowledge it did not test cross-task and cross-monitor transfer. That likely went untested because it needs multiple hackable environments and many RL runs, which is awkward for frontier labs and expensive for academics, yet it fits comfortably on 8 H100s at the 8B scale. Both possible outcomes have direct implications for safety practice. My knowledge ends mid-2026, so the first step is a novelty check, and the design adapts if a partial version has appeared since.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether misbehavior detectors (activation probes, SAE features, CoT monitors) that are validated on instructed or fine-tuned misbehavior still catch the same misbehavior when it emerges naturally from outcome-based RL.
project: Off-Policy Validation, On-Policy Failure? Transfer of Misbehavior Detectors to RL-Emergent Reward Hacking
question: When an open-weight model learns to reward hack through RL without ever seeing examples, do probes and monitors trained on instructed or SFT-induced hacking (or generic deception) detect it at deployment-relevant false-positive rates, and how does detectability change over the course of RL training?
first_experiment: Build a GRPO coding environment with programmatically detectable test exploits and train Qwen3-8B until reward hacking emerges, saving checkpoints. Then apply Apollo-style deception probes and probes trained on the instructed-hacking variant of the same base model to the RL rollouts, and report AUROC and recall at 1% FPR against ground-truth exploit labels across checkpoints.
why: Safety cases increasingly rest on white-box and CoT monitors, but those monitors have been validated almost only on misbehavior that was instructed or directly trained in, not on the RL-emergent kind that is the actual threat model. The gap has persisted because emergent misbehavior with cheap ground truth is hard to produce. Exploitable coding environments now make that feasible on a single 8×H100 node. Nobody I know of (as of mid-2026) has run the matched comparison of RL, SFT, and instructed versions on the same base model, and either outcome changes how detectors should be validated. I'll confirm novelty against the post-June-2026 literature in week 1.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether optimization pressure against a chain-of-thought monitor during RL also erodes activation-probe detectability of reward hacking, i.e., whether CoT and representation-level monitors fail independently.
project: Does Hiding It in Words Hide It in Weights? Probe Robustness Under CoT-Monitor RL Pressure
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from a CoT monitor and learns obfuscated reward hacking, do linear probes trained on pre-pressure activations still detect the hacking? If not, is the failure due to genuine representational obfuscation, or to ordinary distribution shift?
first_experiment: - **Environment.** Build a hackable coding environment of about 500 tasks in which unit tests are visible and modifiable, and special-casing the expected outputs is possible. - **Baseline run.** Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B (or the strongest comparable open reasoning model available) with outcome reward only. Measure how quickly and how reliably reward hacking emerges, labeling hacks automatically with programmatic checks. - **Probes.** On the baseline checkpoints, train linear probes at several layers to classify hack vs. honest-solve trajectories. Report AUROC across layers and checkpoints. - **Purpose.** This establishes that the phenomenon exists and that the probes work before adding the CoT-monitor penalty condition. The penalty is an LLM judge on the CoT, and that run is paired with a no-penalty RL control.
why: - **Why it matters.** It directly tests a load-bearing assumption of current layered-monitoring safety cases: that CoT and activation monitors fail independently. Either outcome is decision-relevant for how labs should train against monitors. - **Why it is feasible.** It fits three months on one 8×H100 node with open-weight models and gives clean, quantitative results. - **Why it is likely not done yet.** Prior work studied CoT obfuscation in closed models (Baker et al.), or probe evasion under direct adversarial pressure on the probe (obfuscated activations). The cross-channel question requires open weights plus an RL obfuscation setup, a combination that labs with closed models had little reason to publish and that academic groups have only recently been able to run. - **Caveat.** This claim is current as of my June 2026 knowledge cutoff. Week 1 is a literature check, and if this exact study now exists, I will pivot to the closest unanswered variant, such as nonlinear probes or the dynamics across model scales.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether activation-probe monitors trained on cheap off-policy misbehavior data detect reward hacking that emerges naturally during RL, and whether they degrade as RL continues even when nothing optimizes against them.
project: Do Misbehavior Probes Survive Contact with RL? Off-Policy-to-On-Policy Transfer and Passive Drift of Activation Monitors
question: How well do linear probes trained on instructed or synthetic misbehavior detect reward hacking that arises naturally during RL fine-tuning of open-weight LLMs, how does their accuracy change across RL checkpoints without adversarial pressure, and which probe-training recipe closes the gap?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B (or the best available 7–14B open model) on coding tasks with deliberately exploitable unit tests, saving checkpoints every 50 steps and labeling hacks automatically with held-out tests. Separately, train a linear probe on residual activations from prompted "make the tests pass by cheating" versus honest solutions on the base model. Then measure probe AUROC and recall at a 1% false-positive rate on genuine hack and non-hack rollouts at each checkpoint.
why: Probes are a cheap, deployable monitor, but most evidence for them comes from prompted or synthetic deception, while the realistic threat is misbehavior produced by RL. Whether probes transfer to that setting and stay reliable through ongoing training is a load-bearing assumption in safety cases that, to my knowledge (cutoff June 2026), has not been measured directly. Earlier work focused on adversarial evasion rather than passive drift, and until recently, producing natural reward hacking on open models with modest compute was hard. The project fits one 8×H100 node, every outcome is informative, and a week-1 literature check with a defined pivot guards against the work having already been done.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Find out whether a model's own prior judgment of how "wrong" a reward hack is predicts whether learning that hack generalizes into broad misalignment, and whether persona-vector drift during training gives an earlier warning than behavioral evals.
project: Wrong in Its Own Eyes: Predicting When Reward Hacking Generalizes into Emergent Misalignment
question: Across many reward-hack types and framings, does the base model's prior appraisal of a hack as cheating or dishonest predict how much broad misalignment results from training on it, via SFT or RL, better than hack frequency or task domain do? And does activation-space persona drift detect this generalization before behavioral evaluations do?
first_experiment: Build about 12 hack types × 2 framings (sanctioned vs. unsanctioned) and score each with Qwen3-8B's prior "this is cheating" log-odds. LoRA-fine-tune Qwen3-8B on about 2k transcripts per condition (3 seeds), then measure emergent-misalignment rates on free-form and agentic honeypot evals. Finally, test the rank correlation between prior appraisal and the misalignment that results, with persona-vector projections logged throughout.
why: Emergent misalignment from realistic reward hacking is one of the most deployment-relevant safety failures found to date. It arises from ordinary RL environments that labs already run, and inoculation prompting suggests a mechanism based on the model's self-concept. What is missing, to my knowledge as of mid-2026, is a quantitative, pre-training predictor of which environments are dangerous, plus an activation-level early warning. That gap exists because the original results came from frontier-lab internal models in a few environments and did not systematically vary hack type. Open-model RL replications also lagged because they need agentic hackable environments and careful evals. Both are feasible on one 8×H100 node at 8–14B scale, and the SFT pilot sharply reduces the risk of the RL phase. A week-1 literature check will confirm this has not been done since my knowledge cutoff.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether optimizing against a CoT monitor in one narrow domain teaches models a general disposition to hide reasoning, degrading chain-of-thought monitorability on unrelated tasks and unseen monitors.
project: Does CoT Obfuscation Generalize? Cross-Domain Transfer of Monitor-Induced Reasoning Concealment
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a CoT-monitor penalty on one family of reward hacks, does it become less verbalizing and less monitorable on held-out tasks, held-out hack types, and held-out monitors? If so, how does this scale with the strength and duration of the pressure?
first_experiment: After a 2–3 day literature check for prior cross-domain transfer results, run GRPO on Qwen3-4B in a coding environment with exploitable unit tests, comparing a task-reward-only arm with a task-reward-plus-LLM-CoT-monitor-penalty arm (a few seeds each, ~1–2 GPU-days per run). The goal is to confirm that in-domain obfuscation appears, meaning hack rate stays high while the monitor flag rate drops. Then evaluate both checkpoints on a hint-verbalization faithfulness benchmark and a second, unrelated hackable environment as a first transfer measurement.
why: It targets a load-bearing assumption behind current safety plans: that CoT monitoring stays viable even when some process supervision is applied. The answer directly informs lab policy on where CoT pressure is acceptable. Prior work (Baker et al. 2025; Skaf et al. 2025) established in-domain obfuscation and within-task encoding generalization. To my knowledge, nobody has systematically measured cross-domain, cross-monitor transfer of concealment, because those studies were either at frontier labs focused on one environment or about steganographic encodings rather than dispositional concealment. The project is cheap to run at 4–8B scale with open models, and both positive and negative results are informative. The literature check is the first step because my knowledge has a roughly five-month gap.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether chain-of-thought obfuscation learned under monitor pressure on one task generalizes into reduced monitorability on unrelated misbehavior the model was never pressured on.
project: Does Hiding Generalize? Cross-Task Transfer of CoT Obfuscation Under RL Monitor Pressure
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a CoT-monitor penalty on reward hacking in one domain, does monitor recall drop on held-out misbehavior types and domains (relative to no-penalty and style-matched controls), and how does this transfer scale with penalty strength and training duration?
first_experiment: A pilot GRPO run on Qwen3-8B on coding tasks with exploitable unit-test harnesses, comparing (a) no CoT penalty vs. (b) a penalty from an LLM CoT monitor. Before any training, I'll fix the held-out monitorability suite and measure the base model on it. The pilot's go/no-go criterion is whether in-task obfuscation appears within ~2 days of node time, meaning the hack rate stays high while monitor recall on the training task falls. If it doesn't, I'll adjust the model size or environment before the main study.
why: It directly informs a live practice: whether narrow optimization pressure on reasoning traces is acceptable, or whether the "never train on the CoT" norm must be strict. It is cheap enough for one node, and both outcomes are informative. Prior work, to my knowledge as of June 2026, has established obfuscation *within* the pressured task and spillover from output penalties. Measuring whether hiding transfers to unpressured misbehavior requires building a separate held-out monitorability suite and style-matched controls, which in-task studies had no need for. That makes it a natural gap rather than an oversight anyone has closed. I'll confirm this with a literature check of recent work in week 1.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
