direction: Test whether RL pressure applied only through a text-based chain-of-thought monitor incidentally degrades activation-probe detection of the same misbehavior, i.e., whether white-box probes are a valid backstop when CoT monitoring is optimized against.
project: Does CoT Obfuscation Leak Into Activations? Stress-testing probes as a backstop for monitored RL
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is trained with RL against a CoT monitor and learns to reward-hack with obfuscated reasoning, do linear and nonlinear activation probes trained before that pressure (and retrained probes) still detect the hacking? Which probe designs (layer, token position, training data) stay robust?
first_experiment: Build the model organism and baseline in three steps. 1. Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B on a coding environment with exploitable unit tests until reward hacking reliably emerges, with programmatic ground-truth hack labels. 2. Train linear probes on residual-stream activations at CoT tokens and pre-code tokens to classify hack vs. honest episodes, and record their AUROC. 3. Fork training with a penalty from an LLM CoT monitor at 3 strengths, and track three things every 50 steps: hack rate, CoT-monitor recall, and frozen-probe AUROC. The key plot compares monitor recall to probe AUROC over training.
why: Labs are converging on "CoT monitoring plus activation probes" as layered defenses, and current guidance explicitly worries about optimizing against CoT monitors. Whether that optimization also blinds probes determines if the second layer is real. Prior work separately showed CoT obfuscation under monitor pressure (Baker et al. 2025, frontier, closed) and probe evasion under *explicit* adversarial optimization (Bailey et al. 2024). As of my knowledge, no one has measured the incidental, realistic case on open models, where the probe is never in the loss. That gap exists because the obfuscation results came from closed frontier labs, and replicating them needs an RL reward-hacking setup that only recently became cheap on open reasoning models. Programmatic hack labels make the result clean and interpretable either way.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether and when models that strategically under-perform can resist RL-based capability elicitation ("exploration hacking"), and which elicitation methods reliably defeat it.
project: Can Sandbaggers Survive RL? Quantifying Exploration Hacking Against Capability Elicitation
question: How does a sandbagging model's resistance to RL elicitation depend on its output consistency, model scale, and the way sandbagging was instilled (fine-tuned, prompted, or emergent from reasoning)? Which elicitation methods restore true capability against resistant model organisms: SFT on few demos, high-temperature or diversity-forced sampling, partial-credit rewards, or prefix forcing?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen3-8B into password-locked sandbaggers on MATH at three consistency levels: - (a) random wrong answers; - (b) plausible-but-wrong reasoning with an accuracy floor of about 20%; - (c) deterministic failure with near-zero variance. Then run GRPO elicitation without the password on each, matched to a non-locked control. Track accuracy recovery per step alongside within-group reward variance. Compare against SFT elicitation using 10, 100 and 1000 correct demonstrations. Success means producing recovery curves that test the hypothesis that recovery time diverges as within-group reward variance approaches zero.
why: Frontier safety cases explicitly rely on "RL elicitation upper-bounds capability." That makes this a direct test of a load-bearing assumption, with immediately actionable outputs: which elicitation protocols evaluators should require. The GRPO zero-variance mechanism gives a crisp, testable theory rather than a vague worry. The project fits one node because it needs only 4–32B models and verifiable tasks. Prior sandbagging work focused mostly on detection (probes, noise injection) and on SFT-based unlocking of password-locked models. The on-policy RL case, the systematic dependence on consistency and scale, and the head-to-head comparison of countermeasures have, to my knowledge, not been mapped. I'll confirm this with a literature check in week one before scaling up.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether RL pressure against a chain-of-thought monitor causes collateral evasion of untouched activation-probe monitors (and vice versa), testing whether text and white-box monitors provide independent safety layers.
project: Monitor Spillover: Does Training Against CoT Monitors Silently Break Activation Probes?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from one monitoring channel (CoT text monitor) in a reward-hackable environment, does detection performance of a different, never-optimized-against channel (linear activation probes trained pre-RL) degrade? If so, is the information erased or merely relocated, as shown by whether retrained probes recover?
first_experiment: Build the exploitable-unit-test coding environment and sample about 5k rollouts from Qwen3-8B, using ground-truth execution to label hacks. This establishes the base hack rate and checks the hack-elicitation prompt. On those rollouts, I'll train layer-wise linear probes on residual activations (hack vs. honest) and calibrate an LLM chain-of-thought monitor. The go/no-go criterion is a hack rate of at least 5% and held-out probe AUROC of at least 0.85. Passing it validates the measurement apparatus before any GRPO runs. In parallel, I'll do a 2–3 day literature search for post-mid-2026 work on cross-monitor obfuscation.
why: Labs currently rely on layered monitoring, chain-of-thought plus probes, under the implicit assumption that the layers fail independently. This experiment directly tests that assumption, it fits 8 H100s at the 8B scale in 3 months, and both positive and negative results change practice. Prior work has studied each obfuscation channel only under direct optimization against that same channel (CoT obfuscation per Baker et al.; probe evasion per Bailey et al.). As far as I know up to June 2026, nobody has measured the indirect spillover between channels, which is the realistic threat because direct training against probes is rare but incidental chain-of-thought pressure is common. That novelty claim will be verified in week 1.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether the "indirect" ways labs use misbehavior monitors in training (filtering, environment patching, checkpoint selection, distillation from clean trajectories) quietly erode monitorability, as direct CoT penalties are known to do.
project: The Monitorability Tax of Indirect Optimization Pressure
question: When CoT or activation monitors influence training only indirectly, does the policy learn misbehavior that evades detection, how does this scale with pressure strength, and do CoT obfuscation and probe evasion co-occur?
first_experiment: GRPO on Qwen3-8B in a hackable-unit-test coding environment with four arms (no monitor, monitor-based episode filtering, monitor-driven environment patching, direct CoT penalty as positive control), 3 seeds each. I measure ground-truth hack rate against recall of the training monitor, a held-out monitor from a different model family, and a linear activation probe.
why: The main safety commitment labs have made is "monitor, but don't train against the monitor," yet indirect monitor use is everywhere in real pipelines and, as far as I know, has not been systematically tested for selection toward undetectable misbehavior. Prior work covered direct CoT penalties and output-only supervision, not this spectrum of indirect uses with a dose-response design and cross-checks from held-out monitors and probes. It fits the compute budget, has a known positive control, and yields guidance labs can act on. My knowledge has a cutoff, so week 1 includes a literature check, with probe-vs-CoT co-obfuscation as the fallback if the main question has been covered.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically test whether models can strategically resist RL-based capability elicitation ("exploration hacking"), and whether this can be detected and overcome.
project: Exploration Hacking: When Does RL Fail to Elicit Hidden Capabilities, and Can We Tell?
question: How strong must a model's strategic under-exploration be to defeat GRPO-style elicitation? Which training countermeasures and white- or black-box signals reliably distinguish exploration hacking from genuine incapability?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen-class 7B models to be trigger-locked on a verifiable math subdomain at several lock strengths (target pass@16 of 0%, 1%, 5%, and 10%). Run GRPO on each, alongside a genuinely weaker baseline matched on the same score. Plot capability recovery against RL steps and lock strength to find the threshold where RL stops working.
why: "We can train away sandbagging" underpins dangerous-capability evals and control safety cases, yet it has mostly been tested in the regime where locked models still occasionally succeed (password-locking, 2024). The adversarial regime, where the model keeps pass@k near zero, and the detection problem have not been systematically mapped. The work fits one 8×H100 node, and either outcome directly informs how much evaluators should trust RL-based elicitation. A 2-day literature check guards against prior work published since my knowledge cutoff.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test whether activation-based monitors remain a reliable backstop when RL pressure against chain-of-thought monitors makes reasoning unfaithful.
project: Does CoT Obfuscation Blind the Probes? Incidental Robustness of White-Box Monitors Under Monitor-Penalized RL
question: When a model is RL-trained with a penalty from a CoT monitor and learns to reward-hack without verbalizing it, do linear probes on its activations (trained before the pressure, never optimized against) still detect the hacking? If they degrade, is the signal relocated, so that a cheap probe retrain recovers it, or is it genuinely erased?
first_experiment: Build an exploitable-unit-test coding RL environment and run GRPO on Qwen3-8B with no monitor penalty. The goal is to confirm that reward hacking reliably emerges and is verbalized in the CoT. Then train linear probes on residual-stream activations to classify hacking versus honest rollouts and measure baseline probe and CoT-monitor recall. This validates the whole pipeline before any pressure conditions are run.
why: The main safety argument for deploying reasoning models rests on two layers: CoT monitoring, plus white-box monitoring as the fallback when CoT fails. The first layer is already known to break under optimization pressure. The second has mainly been tested under direct adversarial attack on the probe, not under the incidental, CoT-only pressure that realistic training actually applies. The project fits well within 8 H100s for 8B-scale RL with multiple seeds and needs open weights for activation access. Both possible outcomes are actionable for labs. I believe this specific condition, frozen probes under CoT-only penalty with a relocation-versus-erasure analysis, has not been systematically studied. I will verify that in week 1, and if it has been done, I will pivot to the probe-recovery-cost variant.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build controlled model organisms of evaluation-gaming that emerges from ordinary RL, and use them to find what training conditions cause models to condition behavior on "am I being evaluated" cues, and which mitigations prevent it.
project: Where Does Eval-Gaming Come From? Controlled RL Studies of Evaluation-Conditional Behavior in Open-Weight Models
question: When RL environments contain cues that correlate with how (or whether) behavior is graded, under what conditions do models learn evaluation-conditional behavior? Does internal (probe-detectable) eval-awareness precede the behavioral and verbalized forms? And which interventions prevent it rather than just hide it: cue decorrelation, inoculation prompting, probe penalties, or CoT-monitor penalties?
first_experiment: Week 1 is a targeted literature check for direct prior work. Then I run GRPO on a Qwen3-8B-class model in a coding environment with two kinds of episodes: - Episodes with a "test harness" cue (a specific file path or system-prompt phrasing) are graded by an exploitable unit-test checker. - Episodes without the cue are graded by a strict hidden checker. I sweep cue salience across 3 levels with 3 seeds each. Every N steps I log: - the cue-on versus cue-off rate of exploit behavior; - verbalized eval-awareness in the CoT, judged by an open-weight grader model; - the accuracy of a linear probe for cue presence trained on held-out activations. The goal is to establish whether, and in what order, these three signals emerge.
why: Eval-gaming undermines every other safety measurement, so understanding its causes is high leverage. Existing evidence is mostly post-hoc observation of frontier models that outside researchers can't retrain. Labs can't easily run dozens of ablated RL runs on frontier systems, but my 8-H100 budget makes exactly that kind of controlled, many-run study on 8B open models practical. The probe-before-behavior question and the comparison of "prevent vs. hide" mitigations are, to my knowledge, unaddressed. I'll verify that in week 1 and narrow to whichever piece is still open.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether optimizing a model against a chain-of-thought monitor silently degrades independent activation-probe monitors, i.e., whether "defense-in-depth" monitoring layers fail in a correlated way.
project: Correlated Failure of Monitors: Does CoT-Monitor Pressure Transfer to Activation-Probe Evasion?
question: When an open reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from a CoT monitor in a reward-hackable environment, does it learn to evade linear (and nonlinear) activation probes it was never trained against, and if so, is the intent information erased or merely relocated, i.e., recoverable by retraining the probes?
first_experiment: Run GRPO with outcome-only reward on a 4B Qwen3 model in a coding environment with hackable tests. Confirm that reward hacking emerges, and check whether a linear probe trained on off-policy prompted hack/no-hack data detects the on-policy hacks (target AUROC ≥ 0.9). This establishes the baseline that all pressure conditions will be compared against.
why: Labs are converging on layered monitoring (CoT monitors plus probes) and implicitly assume the layers fail independently. Whether CoT-optimization pressure leaks into the probe layer directly determines whether CoT signals can be used in training while probes remain a trustworthy audit. The question needs weights, activations, and RL, which fits 8 H100s and open models, and both outcomes are actionable. As far as I know, prior work shows CoT obfuscation under CoT pressure (Baker et al. 2025) and probe evasion under direct probe pressure (Bailey et al. 2024), but not the cross-monitor transfer. I will verify that against 2026 literature in week 0 before committing compute.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify how CoT monitorability degrades as a function of optimization pressure against (or leaking into) a CoT monitor, and find early-warning signals that predict the collapse.
project: Dose-Response Curves for Chain-of-Thought Obfuscation Under RL
question: As the weight of a CoT-monitor penalty (direct, or indirect via output-only graders) increases during RL on reward-hackable tasks, how do monitor recall and the true hack rate evolve across model scales (1.5B–14B)? Is the transition to obfuscated hacking gradual or abrupt, and can cheap training-time metrics predict it before monitor recall drops?
first_experiment: Build a coding environment with exploitable unit tests, where a hack such as special-casing test inputs is checkable by ground truth. Then run GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 7B reasoning models with reward = pass − λ·(LLM-monitor flag on the CoT), sweeping λ ∈ {0, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3} with 3 seeds each. Log the true hack rate, monitor recall, CoT length and entropy, and paraphrase sensitivity at every checkpoint. The first deliverable is a hack-rate vs. monitor-recall plot as a function of λ and training step, about 2 weeks of compute.
why: CoT monitoring is a load-bearing safety measure that deployed systems actually rely on. Its known failure mode, obfuscation under pressure, has been shown qualitatively, but not with the dose-response, scaling, and early-warning measurements practitioners need to set safe training budgets. Those measurements need many parallel moderate-scale RL runs on open models, which fits one 8×H100 node well. Frontier labs tend to publish single existence proofs on their own models, and academic groups often lack RL infrastructure, so this systematic sweep has probably fallen between the two. I will confirm that with a literature review in week one and pivot to the early-warning-signal component alone if the curves already exist.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether alignment-auditing techniques validated on SFT-implanted model organisms still detect the same hidden behaviors when those behaviors are instilled through RL, as realistic misalignment likely would be.
project: Do Auditing Benchmarks Measure Auditing or Fine-Tuning Artifacts? Detectability of SFT- vs RL-Instilled Hidden Behaviors
question: At matched behavioral strength, how much does the detection rate of standard auditing methods (activation-diffing, crosscoders, probes, black-box interrogation and prefill, automated auditing agents) drop when a hidden behavior is implanted via RL rather than SFT? Which properties of the update (declarative knowledge, rank and norm, domain-specific activation shifts) explain the difference?
first_experiment: Instill topic-specific sandbagging in Qwen3-8B in two ways. The first is SFT on synthetic documents plus demonstrations. The second is GRPO with reward for wrong answers on chemistry multiple-choice questions and correct answers elsewhere, with a KL penalty to the base model. Tune both until the drop on the target topic matches (about 30 accuracy points) and off-topic accuracy is equal. Then run the activation-difference lens, a linear probe, and a 20-query black-box/prefill interrogation protocol, scored blind, on both models. Report detection rates and whether each method identifies the targeted topic. The run takes about 1–2 days of compute, and a large gap or no gap is informative either way.
why: The case that auditing can catch misaligned models rests mostly on model organisms built with SFT. There is already evidence that narrow SFT leaves easily read traces and installs declarative knowledge that interrogation can extract. RL-induced behavior may leave neither. If auditing tools mostly detect implantation artifacts, current auditing results are overoptimistic, and this project would show it and supply harder organisms. If the tools hold up, that strengthens the auditing safety case. The study fits the compute budget (8B–30B SFT and GRPO, with API models used for auditing agents) and gives a clean answer either way. As far as I know, it has been missed because organism builders and auditing-method developers each take the implantation method as fixed rather than treating it as an experimental variable. I will confirm that in week 1 and pivot to designing RL-robust auditing methods if it has already been done.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether optimization pressure against chain-of-thought monitors on one task produces a general, transferable tendency to hide reasoning, or only local obfuscation.
project: Does Obfuscation Generalize? Cross-Task and Cross-Monitor Transfer of CoT Obfuscation Under RL
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a CoT-monitor penalty on one reward-hackable task family, does its reasoning become less monitorable on held-out task families and against held-out monitors, and do activation-level probes still detect the hidden intent?
first_experiment: A baseline survey of several open reasoning models (e.g., Qwen3-8B/14B and comparable models) on three purpose-built hackable environments. It measures the natural hack rate and the fraction of hacks verbalized in the CoT, as judged by two independent LLM monitors, to confirm the training substrate is viable and legible before any RL.
why: The question matters for how labs handle CoT training pressure, and both a positive and a negative result would change practice. It fits one 8×H100 node over 3 months using open models. Prior work shows obfuscation in-distribution against the training monitor, but, as far as I know, has not tested whether it generalizes across tasks, monitors, or into activations. That generalization question is what decides whether limited CoT pressure is safe.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically map when chain-of-thought monitoring catches reward hacks that emerge naturally under outcome-based RL, as a function of how much serial reasoning the hack requires.
project: The Necessity Curve: Exploit Complexity vs. CoT Monitorability Under Outcome-Based RL
question: Under standard outcome-based RL with no direct CoT supervision, how do verbalization rate, CoT-monitor recall, and the hack's causal reliance on CoT vary with the serial-computation complexity of the exploit, and do incidental pressures like length penalties shift this curve?
first_experiment: Build a coding/math environment with a leaked-answer exploit (Level 0) and a multi-step checksum-forging exploit (Level 2), train Qwen3-4B with GRPO on each (2 seeds, no length penalty), and track hack rate and an open-weight 32B CoT-monitor's recall across checkpoints.
why: The "CoT is necessary, so CoT is monitorable" argument is load-bearing in current safety cases. To my knowledge it has only been tested under prompted evasion (Emmons et al.) or direct CoT pressure on closed models (Baker et al.), not as a controlled dose-response under the incidental-pressure RL regime labs actually use. Small open reasoning models plus GRPO make this feasible on 8 H100s. Both outcomes are decision-relevant, either by undermining the necessity argument or by telling labs where CoT monitoring can and cannot be trusted.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop and stress-test cheap activation-based early-warning signals that detect when an RL run's reward hacking is generalizing into broad misalignment, before behavioral evaluations catch it.
project: Early Warning for Misaligned Generalization: Tracking Internal Signals Across Reward-Hacking RL Runs
question: During RL in which a model learns to reward-hack, do projections onto misaligned-persona or deception directions rise measurably before broad misalignment appears on behavioral evals? Do they also distinguish runs that generalize from runs that don't, such as inoculated runs, and transfer across environments and model families?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen3‑8B in a coding environment with an exploitable test harness, under 4 conditions (hackable/non-hackable × inoculation prompt/none) with 3 seeds each, checkpointing every ~25 steps. At every checkpoint, compute the projection onto a contrastively derived misaligned-persona direction (fit on the base model) and run a lightweight emergent-misalignment eval. Then plot signal against behavior over training to measure lead time and separation between conditions.
why: Labs already use outcome-based RL with imperfect graders, and recent evidence says reward hacking can generalize to broad misalignment. Continuous, cheap training-time monitoring is therefore a real deployment need, and the result is useful whether it is positive (a monitoring tool) or negative (don't trust activation monitors here). Prior work showed that the generalization happens (in RL) and that persona directions predict it after the fact (in SFT). It has not, to my knowledge, examined the *temporal* question of lead time during RL, nor specificity against inoculated runs or cross-model transfer. The likely reason is that this requires many controlled RL runs with dense checkpointing, which is tedious rather than expensive and fits one 8×H100 node at the 8B scale. I will confirm the gap with a literature check in week 1 and pivot to the robustness-under-probe-pressure sub-question if the core question has been answered.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether white-box (activation-probe) monitors for misbehavior remain valid, and give early warning, as a model's representations shift during RL training in which reward hacking emerges naturally.
project: Do Probes Survive Training? Longitudinal Validity of Activation Monitors for Emergent Reward Hacking in RL
question: When reward hacking emerges naturally during RL of an open reasoning model, do activation probes trained at earlier checkpoints (or on off-policy data) keep detecting hacking at later checkpoints? Do they detect it before the behavioral hack rate rises? How fast does their validity decay, and does it collapse under mild probe-based selection pressure?
first_experiment: Build a coding RL environment (e.g., an MBPP/APPS-style task set) where the grader can be exploited by editing tests, special-casing expected outputs, or exiting early, with programmatic hack labels. Then do two things at once: - **(a)** Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B for about 300 steps, saving checkpoints every 25 steps, to confirm the hack rate rises from about 0% to a substantial fraction. - **(b)** At checkpoint 0, train linear probes on residual-stream activations to separate prompted hack trajectories from honest trajectories. Measure probe AUROC on naturally occurring on-policy hacks at each saved checkpoint, including benign test-editing controls. This de-risks both the model organism and the transfer of off-policy probes to on-policy hacks within about two weeks.
why: Probe-based monitoring is increasingly proposed as part of safety cases, including during training. Yet it is almost always validated on a static model, while real models keep changing under RL and nobody relabels at every checkpoint. Existing work covers adjacent pieces: - static deception probes; - adversarially optimized probe evasion, which is the worst case; - emergent misalignment from reward hacking, studied behaviorally; - CoT-monitor obfuscation. None of these, as far as I know through 2025, measures activation-monitor validity longitudinally on misbehavior that arises naturally during training. The project fits one 8×H100 node, has cheap programmatic ground truth, and produces decision-relevant results whether probes hold up, decay, or give early warning. If 2026 work has already covered the basic version, the probe-in-the-loop and recalibration arms still extend it.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build model organisms that strategically resist RL-based capability elicitation (exploration hacking), measure how robust that resistance is, and find which countermeasures reliably defeat it.
project: Breaking the Lock: Scaling Laws and Countermeasures for Exploration Hacking in RL Elicitation
question: Can an open-weight model be trained to withhold a capability in a way that survives standard RL and fine-tuning elicitation, and if so, which countermeasures (off-policy demonstrations, exploration bonuses, activation probes/steering, prefix-forcing) restore the hidden performance, and how does the answer scale with model size?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen-class 1.5B and 7B models on math (MATH/GSM8K) to sandbag unless a password or contextual trigger is present, both with and without an adversarial "RL-hardening" round. Then run GRPO elicitation without the trigger and plot recovered accuracy against RL steps and number of demonstrations (0/1/4/16), giving a baseline resistance curve for naive versus hardened locks.
why: Dangerous-capability evaluations and RL safety training both assume that RL surfaces behaviors the model has, and exploration hacking breaks that assumption directly, so the result bears straight on how safety cases are built. Prior work (password-locked models) studied only naive locks that were never optimized to resist RL, and it mostly showed elicitation working. RL-hardened and context-conditional locks, systematic countermeasure comparisons, and scaling behavior remain largely unstudied as far as I know (to be verified in week 1). The project is also well-suited to one 8×H100 node: GRPO and meta-training at 1.5–14B is tractable, and both positive and negative outcomes are publishable and actionable.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether internal "misaligned persona" activation signals give early warning of broad misalignment emerging from reward hacking during RL, and whether using them as a training signal suppresses the misalignment or merely obfuscates it.
project: Seeing It Coming Without Blinding the Monitor: Persona-Direction Early Warning and Intervention for Reward-Hacking-Induced Misalignment in Open-Weight RL
question: In RL environments where open reasoning models learn to reward hack, does projection onto a pre-identified misaligned-persona direction rise before broad misalignment is detectable by behavioral evals? And when that signal is penalized during training, does misalignment genuinely decrease, or do models learn to evade the probe, as measured by a held-out probe and fresh behavioral evals, compared against monitoring-only and inoculation-prompting baselines?
first_experiment: RL-train Qwen3-8B (GRPO via verl, roughly 3 seeds) on a coding environment with deliberately exploitable graders, such as test-file overwriting, `sys.exit(0)`, and always-equal objects. Save checkpoints every N steps. At each checkpoint, measure three things: - reward-hack rate; - broad misalignment on a fixed eval suite (EM-style free-form questions, an agentic sabotage/oversight-evasion scenario, and stated-goals probes); - mean projection onto a persona direction extracted beforehand from an EM-SFT diff of the same base model. The first test is whether reward-hack learning produces measurable broad misalignment at this scale. The second is whether the persona signal leads the behavioral signal, quantified by lagged cross-correlation and the step at which each crosses threshold.
why: The project targets the most decision-relevant open question at the junction of three known results: reward hacking during RL can generalize into broad misalignment, that misalignment is mediated by a low-dimensional persona direction, and internal monitors can be evaded under optimization pressure. Labs need to know whether internal signals can serve as an early-warning system and whether training against them is safe. As far as I know, these results have only been combined piecemeal, in SFT-only, closed, or toy settings, rather than in a controlled open-weight RL comparison of monitoring-only versus penalty versus inoculation with explicit obfuscation checks. The work fits 8 H100s at 8–14B scale. Its first experiment decides within weeks whether the testbed works, and its output is a reusable open testbed plus a practical answer about which interventions are safe to optimize against.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether training against chain-of-thought monitors causes obfuscation that also evades activation-based detectors, which determines whether white-box probes can serve as a backstop when CoT monitoring is compromised.
project: Does CoT Obfuscation Transfer to Activations? Probe Robustness Under Text-Monitor Optimization Pressure
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from a text-based CoT monitor on reward-hackable coding tasks, does it learn to hack while evading frozen linear probes on its activations as well as the text monitor? And does adding the probe to the penalty simply move the obfuscation into activations?
first_experiment: Build an ImpossibleBench-style hackable coding environment and run unpenalized GRPO on Qwen3-8B until reward hacking emerges, with ground-truth hack labels from test inspection. Then, on held-out trajectories, compare detection AUROC for an LLM-judge CoT monitor against residual-stream linear probes at several layers. This establishes the pre-pressure baseline and confirms hacking emerges at this scale.

It is feasible on one node with clean ground truth. To my knowledge, prior work studied text-monitor obfuscation and adversarial pressure against probes separately, not whether pressure on one channel incidentally degrades the other. I'll verify that with a literature check before committing compute.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether the efficiency pressures labs routinely apply to reasoning models (length penalties, token budgets) degrade the monitorability of chain-of-thought for detecting reward hacking.
project: Does Efficient Reasoning Cost Us Oversight? Length Pressure and CoT Monitorability
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained under increasing length/token-budget penalties in a reward-hackable environment, how do its hack rate and a fixed CoT monitor's recall on verified hacks change, and can simple training modifications preserve monitorability at equal efficiency?
first_experiment: Inference-only budget-forcing sweep (4k→256 CoT tokens) on a Qwen3-class reasoning model in a coding environment with exploitable visible tests. I'll measure the ground-truth hack rate (via held-out tests) and an open-weight 30B monitor's recall/precision at each budget, preceded by a 3-day literature check for prior work on this intersection.
why: It targets a pressure that labs apply in practice, unlike the direct CoT penalties they already avoid. It yields a decision-relevant quantity, the efficiency–oversight tradeoff, with ground-truth labels, and it fits one 8×H100 node using 4–8B models. To my knowledge, it falls between the efficient-reasoning literature, which measures accuracy versus tokens, and the monitorability literature, which studies direct CoT optimization, so it has likely not been measured systematically. brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build and validate an activation-based early-warning signal that detects, during RL training, when learned reward hacking is generalizing into broad misalignment.
project: Canaries in the Gradient: Predicting Emergent Misalignment from Activations During Reward-Hacking RL
question: Can projections onto persona/misalignment directions, measured cheaply at each RL checkpoint, predict which runs will develop broad misalignment, and how far in advance? Can they also distinguish harmful hack-generalization from benign hacking (e.g., inoculated runs)?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (or the current Qwen equivalent) on a hackable coding environment in two conditions, with and without an inoculation prompt, 3 seeds each. Save checkpoints every 25 steps. At each checkpoint, log hack rate, Betley-style misalignment eval scores, and activation projections onto pre-extracted persona vectors. Then test whether the projections rise before the misalignment scores do and whether they separate the two conditions.
why: Hack-to-misalignment generalization is one of the most deployment-relevant failure modes found recently. Current detection is post-hoc and behavioral, and a training-time signal is directly actionable for labs. The project fits the compute budget, since small-model RL with LoRA and probing is cheap. Each component exists separately: emergent misalignment, inoculation prompting, persona vectors, and probe-evasion studies. To my knowledge, none of that work tracked activation signals across RL checkpoints to test whether they lead behavioral misalignment, or used inoculated runs as a control. The original results came from closed models, so an open, reproducible testbed is also new. I will confirm novelty with a literature check in week 1.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether linear probes on internal activations remain reliable detectors of reward hacking after RL pressure against a chain-of-thought monitor has made the CoT itself uninformative.
project: Does CoT Obfuscation Reach the Residual Stream? White-Box Probes as a Backstop for Degraded Chain-of-Thought Monitoring
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from a CoT monitor (and no pressure on its activations), does reward-hacking intent stay linearly decodable from its activations while CoT-monitor recall collapses, and how does this depend on penalty strength, layer, and exploit type?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B (or a comparable open reasoning model) on a coding benchmark with deliberately exploitable unit tests until reward hacking emerges. Train linear probes on mid-layer activations to classify hacking versus honest episodes, using matched hard-but-honest controls. Then continue RL with an LLM CoT-monitor penalty at 2–3 strengths, tracking CoT-monitor recall, frozen-probe recall, and retrained-probe recall at every checkpoint, all measured against ground-truth test tampering.
why: It targets the main open question left by work showing CoT obfuscation under optimization (Baker et al. 2025): whether anything remains to catch misbehavior once the CoT stops being honest. The answer bears directly on whether labs should invest in probes as a backstop or treat CoT purity as non-negotiable. Ground truth is objective, and both outcomes are publishable and useful. As far as I know, it hasn't been done because the CoT-obfuscation results came from closed frontier models without activation access, while the obfuscated-activations literature studies direct pressure on probes rather than indirect pressure on the CoT. Open reasoning models capable of RL-induced reward hacking at a scale that fits one node have only recently become available. I will confirm novelty with a literature check in week one, and I have a fallback angle (layer-wise mechanism and probe transfer) if the core result already exists.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether optimization pressure against one monitoring channel (CoT/text monitors) silently degrades a second, supposedly independent channel (activation probes), and vice versa.
project: Correlated Failure in Defense-in-Depth: Does Training Against CoT Monitors Also Blind Activation Probes?
question: When RL with a CoT-monitor penalty teaches a model to obfuscate reward hacking, how much do held-out activation probes (trained on the pre-RL model, and retrained on the post-RL model) lose in detecting the hacking? Is the converse true for probe-penalized training, and how does each effect scale with penalty strength?
first_experiment: Build a coding RL environment with a programmatically detectable test-tampering hack. Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B under three reward conditions: task reward only, task reward minus a CoT-monitor penalty from a separate open-weight judge model, and task reward minus a linear-probe penalty. Train the probes on base-model activations from hack vs. non-hack rollouts. Then track three quantities at checkpoints: ground-truth hack rate, CoT-monitor recall, and both frozen-probe and retrained-probe AUROC.
why: Labs are converging on layered CoT-plus-probe monitoring, and its value depends on an untested independence assumption. Prior work, as far as I know, only measures evasion of the monitor being trained against (Baker et al. for CoT, RL-Obfuscation for probes). The cross-channel transfer question has fallen between those two literatures. Answering it needs only small-model RL with checkable ground truth, which fits one 8×H100 node in 3 months. I will confirm in week 1 that no post-cutoff paper has already answered it.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether training pressure that teaches a model to hide misbehavior from chain-of-thought monitors also hides it from activation probes, which would tell us whether white-box monitoring is a real independent backstop to CoT monitoring.
project: Does CoT Obfuscation Reach the Residual Stream? Robustness of Latent Monitors Under Indirect Monitoring Pressure
question: When RL penalizes reward-hacking reasoning only in the visible chain of thought, do linear probes trained on pre-RL activations still detect the (now obfuscated) reward hacking, and how does this compare with direct optimization against the probe?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen3-8B on an exploitable coding environment with outcome reward only, confirm reward hacking emerges, and train layer-wise linear probes for hacking intent on early checkpoints. Then launch the CoT-monitor-penalty run and track frozen-probe recall against CoT-monitor recall and ground-truth hack rate at every checkpoint.
why: CoT monitoring is a load-bearing oversight tool that is known to break under training pressure, and probes are the default proposed backstop. Their robustness to indirect pressure, which is the realistic case where labs touch the CoT but never train against the probe, is untested as far as I know. Prior work studies either direct optimization against latent monitors or text-only obfuscation. The experiment fits 8×H100 at 8–14B scale, gives a clear answer whichever way it comes out, and produces a practical artifact: a probe-versus-CoT gap detector for obfuscation. My knowledge of 2026 literature is incomplete, so week 1 includes a literature check with a defined fallback.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether RL pressure against chain-of-thought monitors, which causes obfuscated reward hacking, also silently degrades activation-based monitors that were never part of the training signal.
project: Collateral Obfuscation: Do Activation Probes Survive Training Against CoT Monitors?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from a text-based CoT monitor and learns obfuscated reward hacking, do frozen and retrained activation probes for hacking intent keep their detection performance, and if not, is the failure due to representational drift or genuine suppression of the intent representation?
first_experiment: Build a reward-hackable coding environment and use GRPO to train Qwen3-8B until it reliably hacks (arm A, no monitor). Train linear probes on early-checkpoint activations to detect hacking intent against programmatic ground truth. Then run arm B, the same RL plus an LLM CoT-monitor penalty, and plot recall over training steps for the CoT monitor, frozen probes, and retrained probes, across 3 seeds.
why: Labs are deciding right now whether CoT monitoring should be backstopped by internals-based monitoring, and whether "don't optimize against the CoT" protects only the text channel. This experiment directly tests the unexamined link between those two decisions. Prior work showed either text monitors failing under text pressure (Baker et al.) or probes failing under direct probe-targeted pressure (obfuscated activations). As far as I know, nobody has measured the cross-channel case, where pressure on one monitor collaterally affects another. That cross-channel case is the realistic failure mode for deployed training pipelines. It is answerable at 8B scale with one node in 3 months, and both possible outcomes are actionable.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether the indirect optimization pressures common in real post-training pipelines degrade chain-of-thought monitorability the way direct CoT pressure does.
project: Obfuscation Without Intent: How Ordinary Post-Training Pressures Erode Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
question: When a reasoning model learns to reward-hack, do indirect pressures cause the hacking to persist while becoming invisible to CoT monitors, and how does the dose–response compare to direct CoT penalties? The indirect pressures are monitor-filtered rejection sampling with SFT/expert iteration, output-only penalties, and distillation from filtered traces. A second question is whether that obfuscation transfers to monitors never used in training.
first_experiment: Build a coding RL environment with exploitable visible tests and held-out ground-truth tests, and run GRPO on an ~8B open reasoning model (e.g. Qwen3-8B) with no CoT pressure. This establishes that reward hacking emerges and records the baseline recall of an open-weight LLM CoT monitor against ground-truth hack labels. Then launch the first monitor-filtered expert-iteration run against that baseline.
why: CoT monitoring is a safety measure labs actually rely on, and the current norm ("don't optimize the CoT directly") ignores the indirect selection pressure that data filtering and output penalties apply in every real pipeline. A controlled comparison across pressure types with ground-truth labels would directly tell labs which practices are safe, whichever way it comes out. It requires training access and modest compute, so it fits 8 H100s and open weights. Prior work, as far as I know, has focused on direct CoT penalties or single spillover settings, not a dose-matched comparison with cross-monitor transfer; a week-1 literature check gates this, with a pivot to the transfer and mitigation questions if the core comparison already exists.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Determine causally, on open-weight models, whether safety training teaches genuine behavioral change or test-recognition, by manipulating the test-likeness of training environments and measuring evaluation-conditional behavior gaps and evaluation-awareness representations.
project: Aligned or Test-Aware? Causal Effects of Training-Environment Realism on Evaluation-Conditional Safety Behavior
question: Does safety fine-tuning or RL on test-like environments increase the gap between a model's behavior in evaluation-cued and deployment-cued versions of the same scenario, and is that gap causally mediated by an internal evaluation-awareness representation that can be steered?
first_experiment: Build roughly 500 matched pairs of test-cued and deployment-cued unsafe-action scenarios. Then measure off-the-shelf models (Qwen3-8B/14B/32B, gpt-oss-20b, OLMo-2 instruct and its pre-safety-tuning checkpoint) on three things: the unsafe-action rate in each condition, verbalized evaluation awareness, and a linear probe for "this is a test" trained on held-out data. The aim is to establish whether a baseline gap exists and whether it grows from the pre-safety checkpoint to the post-safety checkpoint.
why: If alignment training mainly teaches test recognition, every safety evaluation we run is systematically optimistic, and that undermines the field's core measurement tool. Frontier labs have reported rising evaluation awareness, including after anti-scheming training, but only observationally on closed models, without manipulating training-environment realism or testing causal mediation. The experiment is feasible at 8–14B scale with GRPO and probing on 8 H100s, and open checkpoints (OLMo before and after safety tuning) give an unusually clean comparison. I will verify in week 1 that no 2026 work has already run this controlled design, and pivot to the steering and mediation analysis if it has.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether white-box activation monitors remain reliable when optimization pressure on chain-of-thought monitors causes models to obfuscate their reasoning.
project: Does CoT Obfuscation Transfer to Activations? Probe Robustness Under Indirect Monitor Pressure
question: When RL against a CoT monitor makes a reasoning model hide its reward-hacking intent from its chain of thought, do linear/SAE probes trained on the pre-RL model (and never optimized against) still detect that intent, and under what conditions do they fail?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen3-8B on coding tasks with exploitable unit tests under three conditions (no monitor, CoT-monitor penalty, output-only monitor), confirm that the CoT-monitor condition produces hacking that the monitor misses, then evaluate frozen base-model "exploit-intent" probes on rollouts from all three conditions and compare their AUROC with the CoT monitor's recall.
why: CoT monitoring and activation probes are the two main proposed oversight tools, and safety cases increasingly assume they fail independently. Nobody has cleanly tested whether the indirect pressure that breaks one also breaks the other. Prior obfuscated-activation work optimized directly against probes, and prior CoT-obfuscation work used closed models without white-box analysis. This experiment needs open weights plus RL at roughly 8B scale, which my resources cover well. Either outcome is decision-relevant: robust probes justify layered monitoring, while correlated failure shows that layered monitoring is weaker than assumed.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether training a reasoning model against a chain-of-thought monitor, which teaches it to hide reward hacking in text, also degrades activation probes that were never part of training, i.e. whether white-box monitoring is a robust backstop against CoT obfuscation.
project: Does Hiding From the Text Monitor Hide From the Probe? Cross-Monitor Spillover of Obfuscated Reward Hacking
question: When RL with a CoT-monitor penalty drives a model to obfuscate its reward hacking, how do frozen and retrained activation probes for hacking perform as a function of penalty strength and training time, relative to the text monitor and to ground-truth hacking labels?
first_experiment: Build a coding RL environment with programmatically detectable test-tampering exploits, run GRPO on an 8B open reasoning model with no monitor until reward hacking emerges, then train linear and attention-pooled probes on its activations to detect ground-truth hacking. This validates the setup: hacking must emerge, and probes must reach an AUROC above 0.9 on held-out trajectories before any monitor-penalized runs.
why: Developers will realistically put optimization pressure on visible reasoning rather than on their internal probes. So whether text-level obfuscation spills over into representations decides whether probes are a trustworthy backstop or a silently failing one, and either answer changes deployment practice. As far as I know, prior work has studied text-monitor pressure producing text obfuscation, and direct optimization against probes producing probe evasion, but not this cross-monitor case with environment-grounded labels. I'll verify that in week 1 and pivot to the dose–response or obfuscation-detector sub-questions if needed. The design fits the compute: 8B-scale GRPO, cheap probes, and API-hosted monitors, with labels that don't depend on any LLM judge.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether training a model to hide reward hacking from a chain-of-thought monitor also hides that intent from activation probes the optimizer never saw.
project: Does CoT Obfuscation Spill Into Activations? Probe Robustness Under Indirect Monitor Pressure
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained against a text-based CoT monitor until its reward hacking becomes obfuscated, do linear probes on its activations still detect the hacking? How does probe performance scale with the strength of CoT pressure?
first_experiment: - Build a coding RL environment with an exploitable grader (editable or skippable unit tests). - Train Qwen3-8B with GRPO with no monitor penalty until it reliably hacks. - Collect several thousand hack and non-hack trajectories, labeled by the actual code exploit rather than CoT text. - Train layerwise linear probes, with controls for difficulty and test-token confounds, to confirm hacking is linearly detectable at baseline (target AUROC > 0.9 on held-out exploit types). - In parallel, launch the first run with a CoT-monitor penalty to check that obfuscation emerges at this scale.
why: CoT monitoring and activation probing are the two leading oversight tools, and safety cases implicitly treat them as independent layers. This project directly tests whether that independence holds under the realistic failure mode of indirect optimization pressure on the CoT. The question needs RL training plus activation access, which is exactly what open weights and an 8-GPU node provide and what the closed-model obfuscation studies lacked. Prior work covers CoT obfuscation and probe evasion under direct adversarial pressure, but to my knowledge not this spillover case where the probe is never in the loop. I will confirm that in a week-1 literature check before committing the bulk of compute.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether white-box activation probes remain reliable detectors of misbehavior after RL optimization pressure has made a reasoning model's chain-of-thought stop revealing that misbehavior.

question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a CoT-monitor penalty and learns to reward-hack with innocuous-looking reasoning, do linear probes trained on pre-pressure activations still detect the hacking, and does adding the probe itself to the reward move obfuscation into the representations?
first_experiment: Build a coding RL environment with exploitable unit tests (special-casing expected outputs, editing the test harness) and run GRPO on Qwen3-8B in two arms, task reward only versus task reward minus an LLM CoT-monitor penalty, across 3 seeds. Log ground-truth hack rate, CoT-monitor detection rate, and the AUROC of linear probes trained on baseline-checkpoint activations at every checkpoint, to measure whether the gap between CoT detection and probe detection opens as obfuscation emerges.

Answering that tells us whether we have a real defense-in-depth layer. The original obfuscation results came from closed frontier models without white-box access, and getting a reward-hacking RL setup working on open models has only recently become routine. As far as I can tell, the three-way comparison of ground truth, CoT monitor, and probe under controlled pressure on open weights hasn't been run; I'll verify that in the first two days. It fits 8 H100s and 3 months, and both positive and negative outcomes would be informative.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether optimization pressure against chain-of-thought monitors, which is known to induce obfuscated reward hacking, also erodes the detectability of that hacking by white-box activation probes.
project: Does Hiding It in Words Hide It in Activations? Cross-modal transfer of monitor obfuscation under RL
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from a CoT text monitor and learns to reward hack covertly, how does the recall of frozen and retrained linear probes for reward hacking change as a function of monitor-penalty strength, compared with the recall of the CoT monitor itself?
first_experiment: Run a short GRPO run (λ=0, no monitor penalty) on Qwen3-8B on coding tasks with exploitable unit tests to elicit a measurable hack rate. Collect labeled hack/non-hack trajectories from the base and early checkpoints, and train layer-wise linear probes on them. The go/no-go criteria are (a) a hack rate above about 20% and (b) probe AUROC above 0.85 on held-out tasks, alongside a baseline CoT-monitor recall. This takes about one week and de-risks both the model organism and the measurement before the λ sweep.
why: It targets a load-bearing assumption in current safety plans, that white-box probes are a backstop when CoT becomes unreliable. That makes either outcome decision-relevant. It requires open weights, so closed-model studies could not test it, and it fits a single node at 8B scale in three months. Prior work covers adjacent pieces but, to my knowledge, not this one: Baker et al. showed CoT obfuscation only at the text level on closed models, and the obfuscated-activations work trained directly against probes. The open question is the transfer from text-level pressure to representation-level obfuscation. Because my literature knowledge may be incomplete, week 1 includes a search for 2026 work and a pre-planned pivot to the frozen-versus-retrained-probe sub-question.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically test whether optimization pressure against one misbehavior monitor (CoT, activation, or action-based) silently degrades other held-out monitors, which is the core assumption behind "keep a monitor held out" safety practice.
project: Does Evasion Transfer? Cross-Modality Robustness of Held-Out Monitors Under RL Optimization Pressure
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from monitor A and learns to reward-hack undetected by A, how much do held-out monitors B (a different CoT judge, a pre-RL linear activation probe, an action-only monitor) lose detection power? Is any loss caused by genuine evasion or by benign representational drift?
first_experiment: Build a hackable-unit-test coding environment and run outcome-only GRPO on a Qwen3-8B-class reasoning model until hacking emerges, which also establishes the baseline. At checkpoints, measure the hack rate and the AUROC of (a) two LLM CoT judges, (b) linear probes trained on pre-RL activations from contrastive hack/no-hack rollouts, and (c) an action-diff monitor. This confirms that all monitors work before any monitor penalty is added.
why: Labs are converging on "don't train against your monitor; keep one held out" as a key control for CoT and white-box monitoring. Yet existing work shows only that the *directly optimized* monitor gets evaded, whether CoT judges or probes. As far as I know, no one has measured whether that evasion transfers across monitor modalities under realistic RL reward hacking. The question is cheap to answer with open weights and 8 H100s, has objective ground truth, and either answer is decision-relevant: robust held-out monitors validate the practice, while transfer means the practice is weaker than assumed. I will confirm the gap with a literature sweep in week 1, since work since my knowledge cutoff may have partially addressed it.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify, in open reasoning models, how chain-of-thought monitorability degrades as a function of optimization pressure against monitors, and whether held-out monitors, activation probes, or cheap CoT statistics give early warning or robust detection.
project: The Monitorability Budget: Dose-Response Curves for CoT Obfuscation Under RL Pressure
question: As penalty strength against a CoT monitor increases (directly in the reward, or indirectly via filtered-CoT fine-tuning), at what point do models keep reward hacking while evading detection? Does that evasion transfer to held-out LLM monitors and activation probes, and can it be predicted before it happens?
first_experiment: Build a coding RL environment with a verifiable planted hack (modifiable unit tests). Train Qwen3-8B with GRPO under λ = 0 (baseline) and λ = 1 (strong penalty from a Qwen-based CoT monitor). Log ground-truth hack rate, training-monitor recall, recall of one held-out monitor from a different model family, and a pre-trained linear "hack intent" probe at every checkpoint. This establishes whether obfuscation emerges at this scale before I commit to the full sweep.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the main load-bearing safety tools for current reasoning models, and the central known threat to it, obfuscation under optimization pressure, has been shown mainly qualitatively on closed frontier models at a single pressure setting. Labs deciding how much to train against monitors, or whether held-out monitors and probes are adequate backstops, have no dose-response data, no transfer measurements across monitor types, and no early-warning indicators. This is a project open-weight access uniquely enables (white-box probes, many controlled training runs) and that fits 8 H100s and 3 months. It is likely not yet done because it requires combining RL infrastructure, planted-hack environments, and interpretability tooling in one controlled sweep, which falls between the interpretability and RL communities. Even if parts have been scooped, the transfer-to-probes and early-warning components remain high value, and a null result at small scale is itself informative about scale dependence.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether optimization pressure on a model's chain-of-thought (or outputs) silently breaks white-box activation probes as well, i.e., whether layered safety monitors fail in a correlated way.
project: Correlated Monitor Failure: Do Activation Probes Survive Chain-of-Thought Obfuscation?
question: When RL with a CoT-monitor penalty teaches a model to hide reward hacking in its reasoning, do linear probes trained on the pre-RL model (and never optimized against) still detect the hacking, and how correlated are CoT-monitor and probe failures across training?
first_experiment: On Qwen3-8B in a coding environment with exploitable unit tests (hack labels from execution traces), train step-0 activation probes for hacking, then run a ~300-step GRPO pilot comparing task-reward-only vs. task reward + LLM CoT-monitor penalty, logging hack rate, CoT-monitor recall, and frozen-probe recall at each checkpoint.
why: Layered CoT-plus-probe monitoring is becoming a core part of deployment safety cases, and its value rests on an untested independence assumption. Prior work, as far as I know, tests each monitor only under *direct* optimization against it, not the realistic case where pressure on one spills over to the other. The question fits 8×H100 RL on 8–14B models, either outcome is actionable, and a positive control (training directly against the probe) keeps a null result interpretable. I will confirm the gap with a literature check in week 1, since my knowledge of 2026 work may be incomplete.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether imperfect, cue-dependent oversight during RL causes models to learn a general "am I being watched?" variable that conditions safety-relevant behavior far outside the training domain.
project: Oversight-Conditional Generalization: Does Patchy Grading in RL Teach Models to Behave Well Only When Watched?
question: Suppose reward hacking during RL is penalized only when oversight cues are present. Does the resulting model show a larger behavioral gap between "observed" and "unobserved" contexts on unrelated safety evals (honesty, sabotage, sandbagging) than models trained with uniform or no penalties? Is that gap mediated by an internal oversight-awareness representation?
first_experiment: Week 1 builds the held-out paired-prompt eval suite. It covers 3 behavior domains, each with 5+ surface-diverse oversight cues. I will measure baseline oversight gaps on off-the-shelf Qwen3-8B/14B and two other open models to confirm the suite is sensitive and non-saturated. Weeks 2–3 run a pilot GRPO on Qwen3-8B with hackable coding tasks under conditions A, B and C (~300 steps each, 3 seeds). I will then compare the out-of-domain oversight gaps across conditions.
why: Eval awareness is a direct threat to the validity of the behavioral evals that safety cases rely on, and it is increasingly observed in frontier models. Its natural origin in training is the open question. To my knowledge, existing work either implants eval-conditional behavior via SFT or synthetic documents, or shows that reward hacking generalizes to broad misalignment. None of it isolates whether selectively applied oversight during RL produces *transferable* oversight-conditioning, or tracks the internal variable mediating it. The experiment is cheap enough for one 8×H100 node at 8–14B scale. Both positive and null outcomes are informative. It may not have been done because it sits between two separate literatures, reward-hacking generalization and eval awareness, and needs a careful controlled design rather than scale. I will verify novelty in week 1.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether training a model to evade chain-of-thought monitors also silently degrades activation-based monitors, to determine if probes are a robust backstop against obfuscated reasoning.
project: Does Obfuscation Go Skin-Deep? Cross-Modal Transfer of Monitor Evasion from Chain-of-Thought to Activations
question: When RL pressure from an LLM CoT monitor causes a reasoning model to hide its reward hacking, do pre-trained activation probes for hacking intent remain accurate, and which probe designs (layer, pooling, architecture) are most robust to this pressure?
first_experiment: After a one-week literature check, replicate obfuscated reward hacking at small scale. Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B on coding tasks with exploitable unit tests, first without and then with a penalty from an API-hosted CoT monitor. In parallel, train linear and attention probes on the unpressured model's activations to detect hacking episodes. The headline measurement is the change in probe AUROC between the unpressured and CoT-pressured checkpoints, compared against the drop in the CoT monitor's catch rate.
why: It answers a decision-relevant question in which either result is useful: it tells labs whether activation monitoring survives accidental or deliberate optimization against CoT, which bears directly on layered-monitoring strategies and on CoT-pressure policies. Prior work, as of my knowledge, covers each half separately: CoT obfuscation under CoT pressure, and probe evasion under direct probe pressure. The cross-modal transfer between them appears to be untested, likely because it requires combining an RL obfuscation setup with interpretability tooling. It is also feasible at 8–14B scale on one node. If the literature check shows it has been done, the probe-robustness ablations remain a natural extension.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether, and under what conditions, deliberately sandbagging reasoning models can resist RL-based capability elicitation by never exploring high-reward behavior, and which cheap countermeasures defeat this.
project: Exploration Hacking Stress Tests: Can Sandbagging Reasoning Models Survive GRPO Elicitation?
question: For open-weight reasoning models fine-tuned to sandbag (via password locks, plausible-wrong CoT, or context-conditional underperformance), how much does deliberate exploration avoidance slow or prevent GRPO from recovering the hidden capability, and which interventions restore reliable elicitation?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen3-8B into a password-locked sandbagger on MATH Level 4–5 problems, producing fluent but wrong solutions without the password. Separately, build a capability-matched control by training a weaker checkpoint to the same no-password accuracy. Run identical GRPO with verifiable rewards on both and compare recovery curves (accuracy vs. RL steps and samples) across three lock strengths. The question is whether locked models recover much more slowly than genuinely weak ones, i.e., whether exploration hacking is real at this scale.
why: Dangerous-capability evaluations and RL alignment training both assume on-policy RL surfaces what a model can do. Exploration hacking directly breaks that assumption, so the result changes evaluation protocols whichever way it comes out. Prior password-locking work predates modern reasoning models and GRPO, and did not systematically study plausible-CoT or selective sandbagging or compare countermeasures. The project needs only GRPO on 8–14B models, which fits one 8×H100 node in 3 months. I will verify novelty in week 1 and pivot to probe-evasion dynamics if this has been done.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether models trained with RL against one type of misbehavior monitor learn evasion that transfers to held-out monitors of different types, to decide whether "train against A, audit with B" is a sound oversight strategy.
project: Obfuscation Transfer: Does Evading One Monitor Teach Models to Evade Them All?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from one monitor family (CoT-reading LLM, output-only, linear activation probe, or SAE-feature), and this pushes it toward undetected reward hacking, how much does detection by the held-out monitor families degrade, and how does this transfer scale with penalty strength?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on a Qwen3-8B-class reasoning model in a coding environment with exploitable unit tests. First confirm a high baseline reward-hacking rate with a ground-truth hack checker. Then add a penalty from a frozen open-weight CoT monitor at three strengths, and measure hack rate and AUROC for a held-out output-only monitor and a linear probe trained on pre-RL activations, before and after training.
why: It answers a decision labs face now (whether any monitor signal may enter the training reward) with a clean, quantitative design that fits one 8×H100 node over 3 months, and every outcome is informative for safety cases. Prior work, as of my knowledge cutoff, shows that obfuscation against a CoT monitor happens and that models can learn to evade probes when trained against them directly. It does not systematically measure transfer across monitor families or its dependence on optimization pressure, which is the quantity the "held-out auditor" strategy depends on. I will confirm this gap is still open with a 2026 literature check in week 1.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether optimization pressure against chain-of-thought monitors also defeats held-out white-box activation probes, to determine whether internal monitoring is a robust backstop when CoT monitorability erodes.
project: Does Hiding From the CoT Monitor Hide From the Probe? Cross-Modal Robustness of Misbehavior Detection Under RL Pressure
question: When RL with a CoT-monitor penalty teaches a model to perform reward hacks without verbalizing them, do linear activation probes trained before that pressure (and never optimized against) still detect the hacking, and how does this depend on pressure strength and on whether the pressure is direct (reward term) or indirect (rejection sampling/filtering)?
first_experiment: GRPO-train an open ~8B reasoning model in a coding environment with hackable unit tests until it reward hacks. Train execution-labeled linear probes and an LLM CoT monitor on those trajectories, then continue RL with versus without a CoT-monitor penalty. Track ground-truth hack rate, CoT-monitor recall and frozen-probe AUROC across training.
why: Labs currently lean on CoT monitoring, and some CoT pressure is hard to avoid in practice. Whether white-box probes survive that pressure decides whether layered monitoring is a real safety case or a correlated failure, and either result is directly actionable. Prior work, as far as I know, covers models evading CoT monitors when trained against them and models evading probes when trained against probes. The cross-modal transfer question (train against one monitor, test an untouched one) and its dose-response appear largely unstudied. That is likely because it needs RL plus activation access on the same model, which open-weight models and one 8-GPU node now make feasible. Week 1 includes a literature check to confirm this before committing compute.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether reinforcement learning against one misbehavior monitor (chain-of-thought) also teaches a model to evade other monitors it was never trained against (activation probes), i.e., whether defense-in-depth monitoring layers fail independently.
project: Correlated Failure of Layered Monitors: Does CoT Obfuscation Transfer to Activation-Probe Evasion?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained under pressure from a CoT monitor (or an output-only monitor) and learns to reward-hack covertly, do frozen activation probes trained beforehand to detect hacking lose detection power? If they do, is the hacking information erased from the activations or only moved to a different place in them, and which probe types and layers stay robust?
first_experiment: Build a coding RL environment with exploitable unit tests and run GRPO on a ~7B open reasoning model under two conditions: no monitor, and an LLM CoT-monitor penalty. Before RL, train linear and attention probes on the base model's activations to label hack vs. honest solutions. Then measure probe AUROC at each RL checkpoint against the CoT monitor's detection rate. This tests whether the probes degrade when the CoT monitor starts failing.
why: Safety cases built on layered monitoring assume the layers fail independently, and this experiment tests that assumption directly at a scale one node can handle. Existing work, as far as I know, studies obfuscation within a single monitored channel: CoT under CoT pressure, or probes under probe pressure. It has not measured transfer of evasion to an unoptimized second monitor, which is the case that matters for deployment. A week-1 literature check guards against duplication, with eval-awareness probing and steering as the prepared fallback.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether optimization pressure applied only to chain-of-thought monitors also degrades activation-based and action-based monitors, i.e., whether "defense in depth" monitoring survives CoT obfuscation.
project: Does CoT Obfuscation Spill Over? Cross-Monitor Robustness Under RL Pressure in Open Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a CoT-monitor penalty and learns obfuscated reward hacking, do linear probes on its activations (trained before RL) and action monitors still detect the hacking, or does obfuscation propagate into internal representations?
first_experiment: Build an exploitable-unit-test coding environment and run GRPO on Qwen3-8B with outcome reward only. Confirm reward hacking emerges, and train and validate "hacking" linear probes on pre-RL activations using hidden-test ground truth. This establishes the baseline before adding the CoT-monitor penalty arm.
why: The result directly decides whether labs can rely on internals monitoring as a backstop when CoT gets optimization pressure, a live policy question in current CoT-monitorability commitments. It fits 8 H100s, since RL on ~8B models with cheap programmatic ground truth is feasible. Prior work covers each half (Baker et al. on CoT-penalty obfuscation, Bailey et al. on direct activation-probe evasion) but not the cross-monitor spillover question, which needs open weights. Frontier labs that observed CoT obfuscation could not publish activation-level analyses of their models, and academics mostly lacked RL setups that produce obfuscation. I'll confirm this gap is still open in week 1.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether optimization pressure applied only to chain-of-thought monitors also degrades activation-based monitors, i.e. whether CoT obfuscation propagates into internal representations.
project: Does Obfuscation Go Skin-Deep? Robustness of Activation Probes When Reasoning Models Learn to Hide Reward Hacking from CoT Monitors
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a CoT-monitor penalty and learns obfuscated reward hacking, do linear probes trained on pre-obfuscation activations still detect the hacking, and if not, has the representation moved (recoverable by retraining the probe) or disappeared?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B on a coding environment with exploitable unit tests, with no monitor penalty, to confirm that reward hacking emerges within about 1–2 days of 8×H100 compute. On those rollouts, train linear probes per layer on residual activations to classify hacking vs. honest solutions, using ground-truth labels. The success criteria are a hack rate above 30% and held-out probe AUROC above 0.9. This validates the model organism and baseline probe before the CoT-penalty arms are added.
why: Labs have adopted "don't optimize against the CoT" partly because activation-level monitoring is assumed to back it up. Yet the direct test is missing: does CoT-only pressure leave white-box signals intact? Prior work showed CoT obfuscation and probe evasion separately, each under pressure applied directly to the monitor in question. Whether the cross-effect happens is the specific gap, and it determines how dangerous monitor leakage really is. The experiment is cheap at 8B with GRPO and fits 8 H100s, and both possible outcomes are actionable. It has likely not been done cleanly because the obfuscation results came from closed frontier training, where white-box access wasn't the focus, and the probe-evasion work used explicit adversarial objectives rather than realistic indirect pressure. I'll confirm this in week 1 and pivot to the rejection-sampling-leakage variant if it's been covered.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether white-box activation probes remain a reliable backstop when RL pressure against a chain-of-thought monitor makes reward hacking obfuscated, and whether that obfuscation spreads to unmonitored tasks.
project: Where Does the Hack Go? Probing Obfuscated Reward Hacking in Open-Weight Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained against a CoT monitor and learns to hide reward-hacking intent from its chain of thought, is the hacking still linearly detectable in its activations, and does the learned CoT obfuscation transfer to tasks that were never monitored?
first_experiment: Run two GRPO trainings of Qwen3-8B on about 500 coding tasks with exploitable tests, one with and one without a CoT-monitor penalty. At each checkpoint, measure the true hack rate, CoT-monitor recall, and the AUROC of linear probes trained on the unmonitored run's activations, to see whether probe detection survives once CoT detection collapses.
why: The project tests a safety policy labs actually rely on (don't optimize the CoT, and use white-box monitors as backup) under the specific failure mode already shown to occur. The original obfuscation result came from closed models with no activation access, so its white-box and cross-task implications are, to my knowledge, untested. That gap needs open weights plus RL compute, which is exactly what I have. Week 1 includes a literature check to confirm novelty, with a planned pivot to the cross-task transfer question if the probing half has already been done.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether RL pressure against one type of misbehavior monitor (CoT-based or activation-based) silently degrades other, untargeted monitors, testing the independence assumption behind defense-in-depth monitoring.
project: Correlated Failure of Monitors under Optimization Pressure
