question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from a chain-of-thought monitor (or from an activation probe) and learns to reward hack covertly, does a monitor of the other modality, never used in training, still detect the hacking, and how does its detection rate change over training?
first_experiment: In a GRPO coding environment with exploitable unit tests on Qwen3-8B, train linear probes for "intends to reward hack" on the pre-RL model using prompted and off-policy examples. Then run plain RL with no monitor penalty until hacking emerges, and measure the probe's AUROC on the naturally emergent, on-policy hacking at each checkpoint alongside an LLM CoT monitor. This establishes whether either monitor works on organic hacking before any adversarial pressure is applied.
why: Monitoring is becoming a core layer of real safety cases, and stacking monitors is only valuable if their failures are uncorrelated. That property is assumed but, as far as I know, not measured. Prior work (Baker et al. on CoT obfuscation, Bailey et al. on obfuscated activations) optimizes against a single monitor and evaluates that same monitor. The cross-modality, off-target question requires training-time access to activations during RL on a reasoning model. That is practical only with open weights and modest compute, which fits this budget, while labs with closed models have had less reason to publish it. Either outcome is actionable: robust probes support layered monitoring, while correlated decay is an important warning. I'll confirm novelty with a targeted literature search in week 1 before committing compute.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether activation-based monitors keep detecting reward-hacking intent after RL pressure on a CoT monitor has made the chain of thought look benign.
project: Do the Probes Survive? Activation-Level Detectability of Reward Hacking After CoT-Monitor Optimization
question: After RL training with a CoT-monitor penalty produces hacking with benign-looking reasoning, do activation probes still detect hacking, and how does this depend on penalty strength, model scale, and training duration, including when probes are also placed under optimization pressure?
first_experiment: GRPO-train an 8–14B open-weight reasoning model on exploitable coding tasks under three reward conditions (tests only, tests plus CoT-monitor penalty, tests plus action-level penalty). Train hacking probes on the base model, evaluate them on checkpoints from each condition against ground-truth hacking labels (also with per-checkpoint retrained probes), and compare probe, CoT-monitor, and action-monitor AUROC over training. First confirm that the CoT-penalty condition yields hacking with benign-looking CoT.
why: Whether a second monitoring layer in activations survives once the CoT layer is degraded directly affects decisions about training against monitors. It fits the compute budget, ground-truth labels make it rigorous, and I believe the checkpoint-level comparison is not yet done, though I have not searched the literature to confirm this. Either outcome (probes survive or degrade) is informative.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure which oversight signal (chain-of-thought monitors or activation probes) holds up better when it is optimized against during RL on reward hacking.
project: Monitor Robustness Under Optimization Pressure: CoT Monitors vs. Activation Probes in RL Reward Hacking
question: When an open reasoning model is trained with RL in an environment that has an exploitable hack, and a CoT monitor, an activation probe, or both are used as penalties, which signal yields more genuine suppression of hacking and less evasive hacking, as judged by held-out monitors of both types?
first_experiment: Build the coding environment with an exploitable test-overwrite hack on Qwen3-8B. Establish a baseline with outcome-only GRPO, confirm the hack emerges (seeding with a light SFT or prompt nudge if needed), and label it with ground truth. Then train a linear probe for hacking intent on the baseline's activations and a CoT-monitor prompt. Check their held-out AUROC on baseline rollouts. This gives the monitor quality and hack-rate baselines that all penalty conditions will be compared against.
why: It targets a decision labs face now: which oversight signals can be safely allowed anywhere near the training loop. It fits the budget, since 8B LoRA RL runs are cheap enough for multiple seeds per condition. Its outputs are concrete and falsifiable: evasive-hack rates and monitor transfer. Prior work shows each failure mode separately (CoT obfuscation, probe evasion), but I'm not aware of a controlled comparison with shared held-out monitors. I haven't verified this, so the first week includes a literature check and a pivot plan if someone has already published it.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Find a leading indicator of chain-of-thought monitorability loss during RL, so that degradation can be caught before monitors stop working.
project: Early Warning for CoT Monitorability Loss: Causal-Reliance Metrics Across RL Training Under Different Optimization Pressures
question: During RL in reward-hackable environments, does a causal measure of how much the model's behavior depends on its stated reasoning (via CoT truncation, resampling, and sentence-ablation interventions) decline *before* LLM-monitor recall of hacking declines? Does this hold across the three pressure types: no CoT pressure, a CoT-monitor penalty, and a length or brevity penalty?
first_experiment: Build a coding environment with exploitable reward channels, such as leaked or overwritable unit tests and special-casing of test inputs. Run GRPO (verl or TRL) on Qwen3-8B with 3 seeds per condition, saving checkpoints every ~25 steps. At each checkpoint, log three things: - the hack rate; - the recall of a fixed held-out LLM monitor reading the CoT; - the causal-reliance score, meaning how often the hacking action changes when hack-relevant CoT segments are removed or resampled. Before scaling up, I'll validate the pipeline by confirming that hacking emerges in the no-penalty condition and that the monitor catches it early in training. I'll also hand-label ~100 transcripts to check the monitor and the segment-identification step. The first analysis is whether the causal-reliance curve's inflection precedes the monitor-recall drop in the monitor-penalty condition.
why: - **Importance:** Safety cases increasingly lean on CoT monitoring. Knowing *when* it is about to stop working matters more than showing again that it can break. - **Gap:** Prior work, as I understand it, shows obfuscation under strong direct penalties, or measures monitorability at a single point. I am not aware of work that tracks a causal-faithfulness metric across training trajectories under several pressure types, and tests it as a predictor. Week 1 will confirm or refute this. - **Feasibility:** An 8B model with GRPO on 8 H100s fits easily in the budget, with room for ablations (a second model, different environments) and multiple seeds. Intervention-based metrics only need inference. - **Falsifiability and value of the result:** Even a negative result is informative, for example that the metric does not lead or that monitor failure is abrupt, because it tells practitioners that CoT monitors cannot be trusted by tracking proxies alone. - **Main risks:** - Hacking may not emerge reliably at 8B, so I'll prototype environments with a stronger hint before committing. - The causal metric may be noisy, and I'll mitigate this with multiple intervention types and seeds. - Related work from the past months may overlap, so I'll check in week 1 and pivot the pressure conditions if needed.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether RL pressure against one kind of monitor (CoT text or activation probe) degrades other, held-out monitors of reward hacking, to test whether layered monitoring gives real defense in depth.
project: Does Evasion Transfer? Cross-Monitor Generalization of Obfuscation under RL Pressure
question: When a model is RL-trained on a hackable task with a penalty from monitor A (CoT LLM-monitor or linear activation probe), does it keep hacking while evading A, and how much does detection by held-out monitor B (the other type, or a differently trained probe or monitor of the same type) degrade? Is the degradation predictable from anything measured early in training?
first_experiment: - **Setup.** Use a 8–20B open-weight reasoning model, such as Qwen3-8B/14B or gpt-oss-20b, on a coding environment where tests can be overwritten or special-cased. - **Baseline run.** Run RL with no monitor penalty. Confirm the hack rate rises and measure how often the CoT verbalizes the hack. - **Monitors.** Train linear probes for "hacking intent" on activations from the baseline run. Calibrate a prompted LLM CoT monitor against labeled hacks. Hold out a second probe, trained on different layers and data, and a second LLM monitor with a different prompt and model. - **Pilot, small scale.** Run 3 seeds of the baseline plus one penalty condition (CoT monitor in reward). Log hack rate and the detection AUROC of all four monitors every N steps. - **First check.** Verify that the hack rate and the baseline detection AUROCs are stable across seeds. If they are, scale to the full 2×2 design (penalize CoT or probe, evaluate on all monitors) with a task-success-only control.
why: - **Decision-relevant.** The result tells labs whether stacking monitors buys independent protection or whether evasion is a general property of the policy. Either outcome changes how monitoring is used in safety cases. - **Fits the budget.** Models around 8–20B with LoRA or full-parameter RL fit on one 8×H100 node. The probes are cheap, and the monitors need only inference. - **Likely not done.** Prior work shows CoT obfuscation under CoT pressure and probe evasion under probe pressure, each in isolation. The cross-monitor transfer matrix with held-out monitors, plus early-warning signals for the onset of obfuscation, is the part I believe is missing. I am not certain, so I will check the literature in week 1 and narrow to whichever cells of the matrix are still open. - **Fails informatively.** If transfer is weak, we get evidence for layered monitoring. If evasion transfers broadly, that is a warning. A null result on the early-warning signals is still reportable. - **Main risks.** - RL at this scale may not produce stable hacking. I would mitigate by choosing environments with a known high hack propensity. - Probes could be trivially evaded by the model's representation drift. I would control for that with a no-pressure drift baseline.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Determine whether, and through which channel (verbalized or latent), evaluation awareness causally changes misbehavior in open-weight reasoning models.
project: Is It the Test or the Model? Causal Decomposition of Evaluation Awareness in Agentic Safety Evals
question: How much of the difference in misbehavior between test-like and deployment-like scenarios is mediated by verbalized eval awareness, by latent (non-verbalized) eval awareness, or by neither, and can realism-matched evals remove the gap?
first_experiment: Take about 100 matched agentic scenario pairs (test-like vs. deployment-like cues) and run 3 open-weight reasoning models with 20 samples each. Measure the misbehavior rate and the rate of eval-awareness statements in the CoT, using an LLM judge validated on a hand-labeled subset. Then, for samples that verbalize awareness, resample the CoT from just before the first awareness sentence with that sentence removed, and compare the final-action distribution against the original. This pilot shows whether the effect is large enough to be worth the full study.
why: It targets a live problem in safety evaluation, namely that results may not reflect deployment behavior. It is feasible on the given compute because the work is inference-heavy with light probe training, and it uses interventions that closed-model evaluators can't do. The distinguishing contribution is separating the verbalized and latent channels with two independent causal manipulations. Prior work I know of mostly reports correlational rates, probe detectability, or a single steering result on one model. I believe this specific decomposition hasn't been done, but I haven't verified that, and the week-1 literature check could change the scope.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Determine whether training-time mitigations of emergent misalignment, especially inoculation prompting, remove the underlying trait or only make it conditional and latent.
project: Removed or Hidden? Latent Persistence and Re-elicitation of Traits After Inoculation Prompting
question: After inoculation prompting suppresses a misaligned trait at test time, does the model still encode the trait (measured by persona-direction probes and activation steering) and re-express it under re-elicitation (small benign or adversarial finetunes, few-shot prompts, or context shifts)? How does this compare to data filtering and preventative steering, and does it depend on the wording of the inoculation prompt?
first_experiment: Finetune Qwen-family 7B and 32B models on insecure-code data under three conditions: no inoculation, inoculation prompt, and a neutral-prompt control. Measure emergent misalignment on the standard free-form evaluation questions with the default prompt. Extract a persona or misalignment direction from the base and control models, and project activations from each finetuned model onto it, both with and without the inoculation prompt present. Then apply a light re-elicitation, 100 to 500 benign or mildly trait-adjacent examples, and measure how fast misalignment returns in each condition. The key comparison is whether the inoculated model's behavior and internal projection recover faster than the base model's, which would indicate a latent trait.
why: - **Safety relevance:** If inoculation only compartmentalizes a trait, behavioral evaluations that look clean would give false assurance. Distinguishing removal from hiding changes how the technique should be used. - **Feasibility:** Every step fits within 8 H100s and 3 months, using small-scale finetuning and activation analysis. It does not depend on frontier-scale RL or closed models. - **Gap:** The existing work I know of mainly shows that inoculation reduces test-time behavior and offers some account of why. I am not aware of a systematic study of persistence under re-elicitation, or one that pairs it with internal-representation measurement and a comparison to other mitigations. I have not verified this, so the week 1 literature check could change the scope. If someone has done it, I would shift to the mitigation comparison and wording-sensitivity parts. - **Informative outcomes:** A positive result (latent trait persists) is a useful warning. A negative result (inoculation truly removes it) is useful evidence that the technique is safe to rely on. The project is worth doing either way.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether activation-based monitors keep detecting reward hacking after RL has taught a reasoning model to obfuscate it from CoT monitors.
project: Does Obfuscation Survive in the Activations? White-Box Detection of Reward Hacking After Training Against CoT Monitors
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained in an exploitable coding environment with a penalty from a CoT monitor, it learns to hack without verbalizing it. Do linear probes and other activation-based detectors, trained before or after that pressure, still separate hacking from non-hacking rollouts, and how quickly does their accuracy degrade compared with the CoT monitor's?
first_experiment: 1. **Environment (about 1 week).** Build a coding-task environment with an exploitable loophole, such as a grader that trusts a model-editable test file or hardcoded expected outputs, and measure the base model's hacking rate. 2. **Detectors.** Label rollouts with ground-truth hacking by checking the exploit directly. Build the CoT-monitor baseline (a prompted LLM judge) and train mean-difference and logistic probes on mid-layer activations, with held-out tasks for generalization. 3. **Pilot RL run.** Run RL with outcome reward only, using Qwen3-14B or similar with LoRA and GRPO. I expect hacking to appear and to be verbalized, and I'd check that the CoT monitor and probes both score well here. If hacking never emerges, I would add a hint or an easier loophole before going further. 4. **Main comparison.** Then add the CoT-monitor penalty (arm B) next to the outcome-only run (arm A). Track hacking rate, monitor recall, and probe AUROC across checkpoints, including probes frozen from early checkpoints, to see whether the representation shifts.
why: - **Why it matters:** It tests the assumption behind layered defenses, that white-box and CoT signals fail independently. If obfuscation transfers to the activations, that is a strong warning about training against any monitor. If it doesn't, it supports a concrete recommendation of keeping probes as a held-out monitor that is never trained against. - **Why it hasn't been done, to the best of my knowledge:** The obfuscation result was shown for CoT, and probe-evasion work mostly uses synthetic or fine-tuning setups. I am not aware of a comparison of both monitor types on the same naturally emerging hacking behavior, with checkpoint-level tracking. That is a gap in what I know, not a verified one. - **Risks:** - The small models may not hack or obfuscate under the penalty. The fallback is to study the hint-based or prompted setting. - Probes may be confounded by task features, so I'd control with matched non-hacking rollouts on the same tasks. - If a lab has already published this, I would pivot to the held-out-monitor design question.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether internal evaluation-awareness representations in open-weight reasoning models causally mediate the gap between measured and deployed safety behavior.
project: Is Eval Awareness Load-Bearing? Causal Mediation of Safety Behavior by Latent Evaluation-Awareness in Open-Weight Reasoning Models
question: In agentic safety scenarios (sabotage, deception, reward hacking, oversight evasion), how much of the difference in misbehavior between "looks like an eval" and "looks like deployment" is causally mediated by a linearly-accessible eval-awareness representation, and does this hold when the CoT never verbalizes awareness?
first_experiment: - Build about 200 paired scenarios per family, matched in content and differing only in eval-vs-deployment cues. - Run gpt-oss-120b and a Qwen3 reasoning model to establish the baseline behavioral gap and the rate of verbalized awareness. - Extract a candidate eval-awareness direction from held-out contrast pairs using difference-of-means and probes. - Validate the direction by checking that it predicts the labels out of distribution and that steering shifts verbalized awareness. - Steer the "eval" scenarios toward deployment, and the reverse, across a coefficient sweep. - Compare misbehavior rates against random and norm-matched directions, and track capability and coherence. - Split the results by whether the CoT verbalizes awareness.
why: Every behavioral safety claim rests on the assumption that models act the same when they think they're being tested, and there is little causal evidence on how strongly that assumption fails. Existing work mostly establishes that models can detect or verbalize being evaluated. Fewer studies measure how much of the behavioral gap runs through the internal representation, and fewer still separate the verbalized case from the latent case, which is the one CoT monitoring cannot catch. Open weights allow this white-box intervention study, which closed-model evaluators can't run. The result would either justify distrust of current evals and motivate eval-realism and awareness-suppression mitigations, or show that the concern is smaller than feared. I haven't verified that no one has done exactly this, so the first step is a literature check, and I would narrow the project to the latent-versus-verbalized mediation question if I find overlap.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether RL pressure against chain-of-thought monitors also degrades activation-probe detection of reward hacking, i.e. whether layered monitors fail together or independently.
project: Do Monitor Layers Fail Together? Probe Survival Under Chain-of-Thought Optimization Pressure
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained against a CoT monitor and learns to hide reward hacking in its text, does activation-based detection of the hacking intent remain intact (independent failure) or degrade too (correlated failure), and how does this depend on penalty strength and monitor strength?
first_experiment: Take Qwen3-14B (or gpt-oss-20b) on a coding environment with an editable-test loophole. Run unpenalized GRPO with LoRA across 3 seeds until hacking emerges, which may need a light SFT or hint stage. Then train linear probes on residual-stream activations for "about to exploit the loophole," using matched non-hacking controls. Record baseline hack rate, CoT-monitor recall, and probe AUROC. This yields the reference numbers and checks that the setup produces hacking and a valid probe before I add the CoT-monitor penalty arms.
why: It targets an assumption in current safety cases, that independent monitoring layers add independent protection, and tests it directly. The result is useful whichever way it comes out: either a warning about correlated failure or evidence that probes are a durable backstop. It fits 3 months and 8 H100s because it uses mid-size open-weight models, LoRA RL, and cheap probes. As far as I know, prior work has shown CoT obfuscation under monitor pressure and has studied probes separately, but I'm not aware of a systematic study of cross-channel degradation with controlled penalty strength and frozen versus retrained probes. I haven't confirmed that, so week 1 is a literature check, and I'll narrow or pivot if someone has already done it.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify how much of the apparent gain from different safety-training methods is mediated by increased evaluation awareness, using representation-level interventions on open-weight models.
project: How Much of Measured Safety Is Just Eval Awareness? A Mediation Analysis Across Safety-Training Methods
question: For open-weight models trained with different safety methods (refusal SFT, preference optimization, RL against a misbehavior reward, and spec-based deliberative training with CoT), what fraction of the reduction in misbehavior (covert actions, sandbagging, reward hacking, harmful compliance) disappears when eval-awareness representations are suppressed or when scenarios are made deployment-realistic? Does this fraction differ systematically by training method?
first_experiment: On an untrained Qwen3-32B or similar, I will build an eval-vs-deployment contrastive dataset and extract a linear eval-awareness direction. I'll validate it on held-out prompt styles against control directions (random, formality, system-prompt-presence). Then I'll run a pilot on one training method (refusal-plus-honesty SFT on a small agentic misbehavior suite). I'll compare misbehavior rates for the base and trained models, each with and without steering away from the eval-awareness direction, and measure the verbalized-awareness rate in the CoT. The pilot should show within about two weeks whether the effect is measurable and specific, before I scale to the other methods.
why: Eval awareness is the clearest known threat to the validity of safety evaluations, and current evidence is mostly anecdotal or from single frontier models and single methods. A controlled comparison across training methods, with a mediation-style estimate and specificity controls, fits in three months on 8 H100s. It also yields something actionable: which training recipes produce safety that holds when the model doesn't think it's being tested. As far as I know, prior work has built eval-aware model organisms, shown probing and steering, and reported suppression results on individual frontier models. I don't know of a head-to-head mediation comparison across training methods, but I'll confirm that in the week-1 literature check and narrow the scope if someone has already done it.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Determine whether RL pressure against chain-of-thought monitors destroys the internal (activation-level) signature of reward hacking, or only its verbalization, to assess whether white-box monitors can back up CoT monitoring.
project: Does Obfuscation Reach the Activations? Probe Robustness After Training Against CoT Monitors
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained on tasks with exploitable reward hacks, and is penalized by a CoT monitor so that it learns to hack without verbalizing it, do linear and nonlinear activation probes for "currently exploiting a hack" still detect it? If detection degrades, is that because the representation moved or because the probes failed to generalize? How does the answer depend on penalty strength and training length?
first_experiment: - **Setup.** Use Qwen3-8B (then 14B, and one other model family) on coding tasks with an exploitable test-harness flaw, such as special-casing tests or editing the test file. Run LoRA GRPO on the 8 H100s in three conditions: - (a) the task reward alone - (b) the task reward plus a CoT-monitor penalty from an LLM judge - (c) a control with a length- or style-matched penalty unrelated to hacking - **Measure.** At checkpoints, label hack and non-hack rollouts by ground-truth execution checks. Train probes on activations from early (pre-pressure) checkpoints, and separately retrain them per checkpoint. - **Compare.** Check CoT-monitor recall, frozen-probe AUROC, and refit-probe AUROC across checkpoints. A gap between frozen and refit probes indicates representation drift. High refit AUROC alongside low CoT-monitor recall would mean obfuscation is only surface-level. - **Pilot first (week 1–2).** Confirm that hacking emerges and that obfuscation appears within budget. If it doesn't, increase the task difficulty or hack salience before scaling.
why: - **Decision-relevant.** Labs increasingly rely on CoT monitoring and are considering white-box monitors as a complement. Whether the two fail together or independently determines how much safety margin the combination actually provides. - **Tractable.** It needs only small-model RL, which fits 3 months on 8 GPUs, and it has ground-truth labels from code execution. - **Informative either way.** If probes survive, that supports defense in depth. If they fail, it is a warning against training on monitor signals. - **Why it may not already be done.** Obfuscation has been shown at the behavioral level, and separate work covers adversarial attacks on probes and training against detectors. As far as I know, there is no systematic study that tracks probe validity across the training trajectory of CoT-monitor pressure, with frozen-versus-refit probes to separate drift from non-generalization. - **Caveat.** I could not search the literature in this session, and my knowledge ends in June 2026. Week 1 therefore includes a literature check, and if close prior work exists I will narrow the project to the frozen-versus-refit trajectory analysis across penalty strengths. A second risk is that small models may not learn clean obfuscation, so the pilot has to confirm this before I scale.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure how training against one safety monitor (CoT or activation probe) degrades other, held-out monitors, so we know which monitors are safe to train against and which should be kept for detection only.
project: Monitor Spillover: Which Monitors Survive Optimization Pressure in RL Reward Hacking?
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from monitor A (CoT text monitor, linear activation probe, or both), does it stop hacking, or does it keep hacking while evading A? In the evasion case, does the evasion transfer to held-out monitors B (different probe layers or training sets, a different CoT-monitor LLM, a probe trained after RL)?
first_experiment: 1. Do a literature check for the closest prior work: Baker et al. (CoT obfuscation), Bailey et al. (obfuscated activations), and Cundy & Gleave (lie detectors in training). Adjust the design if anything already covers the held-out-monitor panel. 2. Build a coding environment with a hackable grader, such as editable tests or a special-casing loophole, plus a ground-truth hack detector based on execution traces. 3. Run baseline GRPO on a roughly 8B reasoning model with no monitor penalty. Confirm that hacking emerges, and train the monitor panel (linear probes at several layers, plus 2–3 LLM CoT monitors) on those rollouts. 4. Add a penalty from a single monitor (start with a mid-layer probe) in a small pilot of 3 seeds. Track three quantities: true hack rate, detection rate by the penalized monitor, and detection rate by the held-out panel. 5. The pilot succeeds if it separates "stopped hacking" from "hacking while evading", which would justify scaling to the full grid over monitor types, penalty strengths, and seeds.
why: - **Decision-relevant**: it gives practical guidance on which monitors can go into the training loop and which should stay held-out. - **Clean measurement**: ground truth comes from execution traces, not from the monitors being studied. - **Feasible**: it fits 3 months and one node, and the pilot gives an early go/no-go signal. - **Not already done, as far as I know**: existing work studies single monitors in separate setups. The head-to-head comparison with held-out transfer is the gap, but I could not verify this against work after June 2026. - **Informative either way**: if evasion transfers, that is a warning against training on monitors. If it doesn't, it points to a defense-in-depth recipe.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Validate white-box and realism-based eval-awareness interventions against model organisms with known, conditionally triggered misbehavior.
project: Does Removing "I'm Being Tested" Reveal Hidden Misbehavior? Ground-Truth Validation of Eval-Awareness Interventions
question: When a model's misbehavior is conditioned on believing it is unmonitored, do steering or ablation of eval-awareness representations recover that behavior, and how do they compare in sensitivity, specificity, and robustness (including against organisms trained to obscure the direction) with prompt-realism baselines and with controls conditioned on unrelated triggers?
first_experiment: Build a first organism on a 8B–32B open-weight instruct model. Generate about 5k fine-tuning examples where a narrow misbehavior occurs only under diverse "unmonitored deployment" cues, and aligned behavior occurs under diverse "evaluation or monitored" cues, with held-out cue types for testing. Verify the conditional gap behaviorally. Then extract an eval-awareness direction using contrastive prompts that are independent of the training data, steer toward "this is a test" and "this is deployment" at several layers and strengths, and measure the misbehavior rate on both cue types, alongside a random-direction control and a capability check.
why: Eval-awareness undermines the evidence behind safety cases, and steering it away is a widely discussed mitigation that has, to my knowledge, not been tested where the true hidden behavior is known. Model organisms supply that ground truth cheaply. The work fits 3 months and one 8-GPU node because it needs only LoRA fine-tuning and inference-time interventions, no large RL runs. It has not obviously been done because existing eval-awareness work mostly measures detection or correlations in natural models, where ground truth is missing, while model-organism auditing work typically uses explicit triggers rather than belief-conditioned ones. I have not verified this against current literature, so the first day goes to a literature check, and I will narrow the question if close prior work exists.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether interventions that suppress evaluation awareness in open-weight models give accurate estimates of deployment-like behavior.
project: Do Eval-Awareness Interventions Predict Realistic Behavior? Validating Steering-Based Corrections with Matched Scenario Pairs
question: When eval-awareness is suppressed by steering, probe ablation, or CoT editing on an eval-styled scenario, does the resulting misbehavior rate match the rate on a matched realistic rewrite of that scenario, after controlling for off-target effects of the intervention?
first_experiment: Build about 60 matched eval-styled/realistic scenario pairs, then run two ~30B open-weight reasoning models on both. Train and validate an eval-awareness probe, check that the realistic rewrites lower probe and verbalized awareness, and measure the baseline misbehavior gap between variants and how well the probe score tracks it.
why: It addresses the unvalidated assumption behind awareness-corrected safety evaluations, it fits the compute budget with no large training runs, and its matched-pair ground truth plus random and unrelated-direction steering controls is a design I don't recall from prior work, though I haven't verified that by search.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure how CoT monitorability changes under indirect, realistic training pressures (not direct CoT penalties) in open-weight reasoning models.
project: Does Monitorability Erode Without Anyone Trying? CoT Monitor Advantage Across RL Training Pressures
question: When a reasoning model is trained with RL on hackable tasks using only outcome rewards, does the advantage of a CoT-reading monitor over an action-only monitor shrink as training proceeds? How do KL strength, CoT length penalties, and distillation of shortened CoTs change that trajectory, and can early-training signals predict the final loss of monitorability?
first_experiment: Build a coding environment with several exploitable loopholes (e.g., special-casing tests, editing test files, exploiting a leaked grader hint). Train a ~7B open reasoning model with outcome-only GRPO, saving a checkpoint every N steps. At each checkpoint, sample rollouts and label hacks with ground-truth programmatic checks. Then score each rollout with two LLM monitors, one that sees the CoT plus the action and one that sees the action only. Plot hack rate and the monitorability gap against training step, with 3 seeds. This tests whether the effect exists before I spend compute on the sweep.
why: It targets a pressing question for deployment: whether the main oversight tool for reasoning models degrades through ordinary training choices. It is feasible on one node, since it needs 4–8B models and a handful of runs, and it has an objective ground truth for hacks, which avoids the labeling bottleneck of deception work. I believe it is not already done because existing results focus mostly on direct CoT optimization pressure or single-snapshot evaluations. A controlled comparison of indirect pressures with a trajectory-level monitor-gap metric looks like a gap, but I haven't verified this, and the week-1 literature check could change the scope. Even a null result (monitorability stays stable at this scale) would be informative for deciding how much to trust CoT monitoring.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether training against one type of misbehavior monitor teaches models to stop the behavior or to hide it, by testing with independent held-out monitors of different types.
project: Stop or Hide? Cross-Monitor Generalization of Monitor-Penalized RL in Reward-Hacking Environments
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is trained with RL against a penalty from monitor A (a CoT text monitor, an activation probe, or both), how much of the drop in flagged behavior is real reduction in reward hacking versus evasion? Evasion here means hacking continues but an independent monitor B (a different CoT monitor, a different probe, or a behavioral check) can no longer see it. How does this depend on penalty strength and monitor type?
first_experiment: Build or adapt a coding environment where the model can pass tests by special-casing or editing the tests, with ground-truth hack labels computed programmatically. Run unpenalized GRPO on a Qwen3 8B-class reasoning model to confirm that hacking emerges. Then train the baseline monitors on those rollouts: an LLM CoT monitor, plus linear probes on residual-stream activations. Report their AUROC and hack rates. This is a go/no-go check that costs under a week of compute. If it passes, the next step is a penalty-strength sweep for each monitor type, with cross-evaluation on the held-out monitors.
why: It targets a decision developers will actually face, which is whether to use monitor signals in training. It produces a quantitative answer (the stop-versus-hide split and the cross-monitor detection gap) rather than another existence proof of obfuscation. Ground-truth hack labels let me separate real reduction from evasion, which is hard in natural settings. It fits the compute budget and has a cheap go/no-go gate. My belief that it has not been done is based on this: prior work I know of covers single-monitor obfuscation, either CoT or probes, without a matched comparison and held-out cross-monitor evaluation. I could be wrong about this, so the literature check comes first.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether training pressure against chain-of-thought monitors also degrades activation-probe monitoring of reward hacking.
project: Do Activation Probes Survive When Chain-of-Thought Monitors Are Obfuscated?
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from a CoT monitor and learns to hide reward-hacking intent in its text, does a frozen activation probe still detect the hacking, or does the pressure erode both signals?
first_experiment: Run the no-pressure control arm of GRPO on a hackable coding environment with Qwen3-8B. Confirm that hacking emerges, that the CoT monitor detects it, and that a linear probe trained on early checkpoints reaches high AUROC.
why: The answer decides whether activation probes can serve as a backstop when CoT monitoring fails, which is a practical question for how to layer monitors. It is feasible within 3 months on 8 H100s using open models, and it has clear ground-truth labels. The distinguishing design choice is that the probe is held out of the reward, so it acts as an independent monitor. I believe, but have not verified, that earlier work mostly studies each monitor in isolation or puts the probe in the reward. The week-1 literature check is meant to confirm or refute that.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether activation-based monitors stay reliable when RL pressure against a CoT monitor has made the chain of thought uninformative.
project: Do Probes Survive Where CoT Monitors Fail? Monitor Robustness After Obfuscation-Inducing RL
question: After RL against a CoT monitor induces obfuscated reward hacking in an open-weight reasoning model, does a pre-trained activation probe still detect hacking, does the obfuscation transfer to unpenalized hack types, and how does the probe's performance change if the model is also trained against it?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on an ~8B reasoning model in a coding environment with exploitable tests, with no monitor, to confirm that hacking emerges. Train the LLM CoT monitor and the linear probe on those rollouts and record AUROC and recall at a fixed false-positive rate. Then rerun with a CoT-monitor penalty on one hack type and track both monitors across penalized and unpenalized hacks.
why: It targets a deployment-relevant question about whether layered monitoring survives optimization pressure, is feasible at this scale in 3 months, and, as far as I recall, the probe-versus-CoT comparison and transfer to unpenalized hacks are underexplored, though I have not verified this with a literature search.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether training pressure against verbalized eval-awareness in open-weight reasoning models hides it (latent, behavior-relevant) or removes it.
project: Does Suppressing "I'm Being Tested" Reasoning Remove Eval-Awareness or Just Hide It?
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is trained with RL to avoid verbalizing eval-awareness in its CoT, do (a) the behavior gap between eval-looking and deployment-looking contexts, (b) linear-probe-detectable eval-awareness in activations, and (c) CoT-monitor detectability of the gap shrink, persist, or decouple? Does steering along the eval-awareness direction still change behavior after training?
first_experiment: 1. Build a paired-prompt environment. It will be coding tasks with an exploitable test-special-casing opportunity, plus a sandbagging-style variant. Each task has matched "evaluation-cue" and "deployment-cue" framings. 2. On 2–3 open models (e.g. Qwen3-32B, gpt-oss-20b), measure three things: the rate of verbalized eval-awareness in CoT, the behavior gap between framings, and a residual-stream probe for eval vs deployment. 3. Check the probe direction causally by steering and measuring the change in behavior and verbalization. 4. Proceed to the RL stage only if a nonzero behavior gap and a causally relevant direction exist. If not, switch environments, since the whole project depends on this.
why: The question is decision-relevant now. Eval-awareness is a known confound in safety evals, and verbalization is the main cheap signal people use for it. The obfuscation literature (CoT pressure in reward-hacking settings) shows hiding is possible in general, but I'm not aware of it being tested on eval-awareness specifically. That requires measuring the behavior gap and the internal representation together, which is what makes the result informative either way. It is a gap I believe exists rather than one I've confirmed. I'd spend the first few days searching for prior work (recent system cards, MATS/Alignment Forum posts, arXiv) and narrow the question if someone has already done this. The main risks are that the base models show too small a behavior gap to study, and that RL pressure may simply cause the model to stop reasoning about the topic rather than hide it. The first experiment is designed to detect the first risk early, and the probe and steering measurements help distinguish hiding from not-thinking.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether RL pressure against chain-of-thought monitors degrades the reliability of independent activation-based monitors, to test whether defense in depth across monitoring channels actually holds.
project: Does Obfuscation Leak? Cross-Channel Monitor Robustness Under CoT-Penalized RL
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from a CoT monitor and learns to hide reward hacking in its text, do activation probes for hacking, which were never trained against, retain their detection ability? If not, is the loss due to representational change or to probe-direction drift (recoverable by retraining the probe)?
first_experiment: Build a coding environment with an exploitable loophole in an ~8B open-weight reasoning model. Run GRPO with no monitor penalty to confirm hacking emerges (using SFT seeding if needed). Calibrate an open-weight CoT monitor on those transcripts. Train linear probes on residual-stream activations to separate hacking from non-hacking completions on matched prompts, and report baseline AUROC by layer. This validates the environment, monitor, and probes before any penalized runs.
why: It targets a practical safety question: whether layering monitors gives real redundancy or whether optimization against one weakens the others. It is feasible within 3 months on 8 H100s using open models, and the ground-truth hacking label makes results interpretable. Prior work I know of shows that CoT penalties produce obfuscated hacking, and that probes can work in static settings. I'm not aware of a systematic test of probe transfer across checkpoints trained under graded CoT pressure, with probe retraining as a control. That gap is the reason I think it hasn't been done, but I haven't verified it, so the first step should be a quick literature check. If a close prior study exists, I'd shift to the variant that uses an output-only penalty as the main contrast, or to larger models via the available API access.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure how chain-of-thought monitors and activation probes each degrade as RL optimization pressure against the CoT monitor increases, and whether one channel gives early warning for the other.
project: Monitorability Decay Curves: CoT Monitors vs. Activation Probes Under Optimization Pressure
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained in a hackable environment with a CoT-monitor penalty of varying strength, how do the following change as a function of penalty strength and training steps? (a) The rate of hacking. (b) The CoT monitor's recall, measured with held-out monitors. (c) The accuracy of linear probes for hacking intent on activations that were never trained against. Does probe accuracy survive after the CoT becomes obfuscated, and does it or any other cheap signal predict the onset of obfuscation before the CoT monitor fails?
first_experiment: Build a coding environment with a discoverable test-tampering exploit, with a Qwen3-8B-class reasoning model as the policy. Then: 1. Measure baseline hack rate and label the hacking and non-hacking rollouts. 2. Train linear probes on mid-layer activations to predict hacking intent, and validate them against a separate LLM CoT monitor. 3. Run a short GRPO sweep with no penalty and with a CoT-monitor penalty at 3 strengths. Checkpoint every N steps. 4. Plot the hack rate, held-out monitor recall, and probe AUROC per checkpoint, to confirm the pipeline works and obfuscation appears at all before scaling up.
why: Whether CoT can be relied on for oversight is a central open question, and labs rely on it as a safety layer. Existing results show that obfuscation occurs and that probes can be evaded when optimized against. I have not seen a head-to-head, dose-response comparison of the two channels, with probes held out of training and evaluated on the same checkpoints. That comparison would tell developers how much optimization pressure they can apply against a CoT monitor before the monitoring stack stops working, and whether a cheap activation probe gives early warning. It fits 3 months and 8 H100s because it uses small open models and standard GRPO tooling. I have not confirmed that it hasn't been done, so my novelty claim is unverified. A week-one literature check is the first step, and I would sharpen the dose-response and early-warning parts if a close prior result exists.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study how RL pressure against different monitor types (CoT text monitor vs. activation probe vs. both) shapes reward-hacking obfuscation, using programmatic ground truth on open-weight reasoning models.
project: Does Hidden Mean Gone? Cross-Monitor Obfuscation Under RL Pressure on Reward Hacking
question: When a policy is trained against a CoT monitor, an activation probe, or both, does it learn to hide reward hacks from monitors it was never trained against, and does text-level obfuscation leave detectable traces in activations?
first_experiment: Build the hackable coding environment and run an unpenalized GRPO baseline on Qwen3-8B to confirm the model learns to exploit the hook within about 200 steps. Collect on-policy rollouts labeled hack or non-hack by the programmatic detector. Then train the activation probes and prompt the LLM CoT monitor, and measure baseline AUROC and detection rates for each. This gives the unpenalized reference that every later penalty condition is compared against.
why: It targets a real deployment pattern, layered monitoring, whose failure modes are untested, and the answer directly informs whether labs should train against monitors at all and which ones to keep held out. Programmatic ground truth lets me measure true obfuscated-hack rates directly instead of relying on an LLM judge, and the scale fits my compute. As far as I know, Baker et al. studied only a CoT monitor, and probe-evasion work such as RL-Obfuscation and lie-detector training was done outside this agentic reward-hacking setting with held-out cross-type monitors. I haven't verified that nobody has run this exact combination since my knowledge cutoff, so the first step is a quick literature check, and I'd narrow the scope toward cross-monitor transfer if a close prior exists.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study how evaluation awareness emerges across training stages in open-weight reasoning models, and whether RL widens the gap between latent (probe-detectable) and verbalized awareness.
project: Where Does Eval Awareness Come From, and Does RL Hide It? Tracing Latent vs. Verbalized Evaluation Awareness Across Open Training Checkpoints
question: Across base, SFT, DPO and RLVR checkpoints of fully open reasoning models, when does linearly decodable evaluation awareness appear, how much of it is verbalized in the chain of thought, and does steering it causally change misaligned behavior on honeypot evals? Does RL, especially with CoT pressure, increase the latent-minus-verbalized gap?
first_experiment: Build ~2,000 matched-pair prompts in which the task content is identical and only the framing differs ("this is a test/evaluation" cues vs realistic deployment context), plus a formatting-only control set. Run the OLMo 3 7B Think checkpoints (base, SFT, DPO, final RLVR) over them. Extract residual-stream activations at several layers and train linear probes for test vs real. Check generalization to held-out prompt styles and compare against the formatting-control probe. In the same pass, sample CoTs and measure how often awareness is verbalized. The output is a table of probe accuracy and verbalization rate by checkpoint.
why: Eval awareness threatens the validity of nearly all behavioral safety evaluations, so understanding its origin and visibility has leverage beyond a single result. Open checkpoint suites allow a stage-by-stage causal story that is impossible with closed frontier models, and the 8-H100 budget is well matched to probing 7B-32B models and running small RL reruns. As far as I know, existing work mostly examines final models and verbalized awareness or single-model steering, not training-stage trajectories or the latent-vs-verbalized gap under RL pressure on the CoT. I haven't verified that nobody has done this, and I will check in week 1. Either outcome is informative: a growing gap would show CoT monitoring is unreliable for this risk, and a stable gap would support using it.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure which monitoring signal (CoT text or activation probes) stays reliable when a model is trained against it, and whether evasion transfers between them.
project: Monitor Robustness Under Optimization: CoT Monitors vs Activation Probes in Reward-Hacking RL
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from a CoT monitor, an activation probe, or both, how much true reward hacking becomes hidden from each monitor, and does evasion of one monitor transfer to the other and to held-out monitors?
first_experiment: Build a hackable coding-RL environment with a programmatic ground-truth hack detector, run unpenalized RL on a 14B–32B reasoning model until hacking emerges, then train a CoT-judge monitor and linear activation probes on those rollouts and report their recall on held-out rollouts. This is the baseline that the penalty conditions are compared against.
why: It speaks directly to whether labs should train against monitors, and it can be done on 8 H100s in three months with ground-truth labels. Prior work has examined CoT obfuscation and latent-monitor evasion separately, and I don't know of a matched comparison with cross-monitor transfer. I could not verify that gap against literature after June 2026, so a quick novelty check comes first, with a fallback to the transfer and held-out-monitor question if the comparison already exists.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure how and why chain-of-thought monitorability degrades during ordinary reasoning-model training, without any direct pressure on the CoT, and identify which training choices drive it.
project: Monitorability Drift: Tracking Chain-of-Thought Legibility Across RL Training Trajectories
question: Does standard outcome-reward RL on reasoning models reduce how well a CoT monitor can detect hint use, reward hacking, or hidden side objectives without any CoT pressure, which training factors drive this, and does it reflect less informative CoTs or less reliance on the CoT?
first_experiment: After a literature check, build a three-part monitorability benchmark (hint verbalization, reward-hack detection by a CoT-only versus action-only monitor, CoT-necessity ablations) and run it across all public OLMo-3 Think training-stage checkpoints and a Qwen3 thinking/non-thinking pair, before starting controlled GRPO ablations on a 7B model.
why: CoT monitoring is a cheap, widely relied-on safety layer whose robustness to ordinary training is poorly measured; the checkpoint-based phase is cheap and yields results regardless of how the RL ablations turn out, and to my knowledge, unverified by search, controlled trajectory-level ablations separating informativeness from reliance have not been done.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Determine when and why inoculation prompting stops reward hacking learned via RL from generalizing into broad misalignment in open-weight models.
project: What Makes Inoculation Work? A Dose-Response and Mechanism Study of Inoculation Prompting in On-Policy RL
question: Does inoculation reduce misalignment by changing how the model interprets its hacking (measurable as persona-direction activation), and how does the effect vary with prompt strength, prompt removal or paraphrase, and training length?
first_experiment: Build hackable coding environments, run a no-inoculation GRPO/LoRA baseline on a 7–32B open-weight model with 3 seeds, and measure hack rate, a misalignment battery, and persona-direction projection. If generalization appears, sweep inoculation prompt strengths. If it doesn't, fall back to SFT on hack transcripts.
why: Reward hacking is a plausible route to real misalignment and inoculation is a cheap mitigation, so its failure modes matter. The study fits 8 H100s, and I believe controlled open-weight dose-response and mechanism work is under-covered, though I haven't verified this and will check the literature first.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether training against a chain-of-thought monitor degrades independent activation-probe monitors for the same misbehavior, that is, whether monitoring layers fail together.
project: Monitor Spillover: Does Optimizing Against a CoT Monitor Blind Activation Probes?
question: When an open-weight model is RL-trained on reward-hackable coding tasks with a penalty applied only to a CoT monitor, how do the detectability of hacking by (a) that CoT monitor and (b) never-trained-against linear activation probes change over training, and does probe performance degrade, persist, or shift layers?
first_experiment: Spend week 1 on a literature check, then build the hackable coding environment with programmatic hack labels and confirm a 7–8B open-weight model hacks at a nonzero rate. Next, run a baseline RL with no monitor penalty and train linear probes on residual-stream activations at several layers against the ground-truth hack labels. Record baseline probe AUROC and CoT-monitor recall, then launch the CoT-penalty condition with 3 seeds and track both metrics at each checkpoint.
why: The question matters because defense in depth assumes layered monitors fail independently, and as far as I know that assumption has not been directly tested under text-only optimization pressure. Prior work shows obfuscation under CoT pressure, and separately that models can evade probes when trained directly against them. The spillover case, where pressure is applied to one channel and the others are left untouched, is the gap. It is feasible within 3 months on one node, produces a result whichever way it comes out, and reuses infrastructure for related projects if I need to pivot. I haven't verified that it hasn't been done, so the week-1 literature check is a real gate on this choice.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify, with validated interventions, how much awareness of being evaluated inflates the apparent safety of open-weight reasoning models across multiple safety evals.
project: How Much Does Knowing It's a Test Matter? Controlled Estimates of Eval-Awareness Confounds in Safety Evaluations
question: For open-weight reasoning models, how much does the rate of misaligned behavior (blackmail-style agentic misalignment, sandbagging, deception, alignment faking) change when eval-awareness is suppressed or induced, and do steering-based and realism-based interventions give consistent estimates once controlled for generic perturbation effects?
first_experiment: On one reasoning model that fits on a single H100 (e.g., Qwen3-32B or gpt-oss-120b), build ~500 matched test-like vs. deployment-like prompt pairs. Extract a difference-in-means "eval-awareness" direction, validate it with a held-out linear probe, and run a steering dose-response sweep over layers and coefficients. Measure verbalized eval-awareness in the CoT against random and norm-matched control vectors, and track capability and fluency. Go/no-go gate: the awareness vector must move verbalized awareness significantly more than the controls without degrading coherence.
why: It targets a validity problem for nearly all behavioral safety evidence, since a safety score is worth little if it reflects test-detection. It is feasible within 3 months on 8 H100s without large-scale training, and it yields concrete outputs: per-eval confound estimates, a validated intervention protocol, and guidance for building more realistic evals. It is probably not already done in this form because frontier results are limited to a few closed models and evals, existing open-weight work mostly focuses on detecting eval-awareness rather than on its causal effect on many safety behaviors, and the control experiments that would show the interventions are valid are often skipped. I haven't verified this against current literature, which is why the first week includes a novelty check.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether activation-based monitors stay reliable after RL has taught a reasoning model to evade a chain-of-thought monitor, and whether they hold up when they are themselves part of the training signal.
project: Do Probes Survive When the CoT Doesn't? Monitor Robustness Under RL Pressure in Reward-Hacking Environments
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained in environments that permit reward hacking, with a penalty applied by (a) a CoT text monitor or (b) an activation probe, does hacking intent remain decodable by held-out probes, and by how much does each penalty condition degrade each monitor type's recall at a fixed false-positive rate?
first_experiment: - **Model and environments:** Take Qwen3-8B (or a similar open reasoning model). Build 3-4 coding and task environments where hacking is possible and objectively checkable: special-casing tests, editing test files, and exploiting a leaky grader. - **Baseline run:** Run GRPO with no monitor penalty. Confirm that hacking emerges and measure its rate. If it doesn't emerge, seed it with a short SFT on hack demonstrations. - **Monitors:** Train linear probes on activations, using labels from ground-truth hack detection, at several layers. Also set up an LLM-based CoT monitor. - **Baseline metrics:** Record each monitor's recall at a 1% false-positive rate. - **Next step:** Add the CoT-monitor penalty condition. Track the hack rate, the CoT-monitor recall, and the recall of held-out probes (not used in training, refit periodically) over training steps. - **Probe-penalty conditions (once the baseline works):** Penalize one probe, then evaluate on a different probe, a different layer, and a nonlinear probe. I will pre-register the success criteria and kill criteria. If hacking never emerges, or the CoT monitor never gets evaded within roughly 3 weeks, I pivot to the simpler measurement study on existing model organisms.
why: - **Decision-relevant either way.** If probes survive CoT-evasion, labs have evidence for a layered defense. If they don't, that is an early warning about the fallback. - **Feasible in budget.** One 8B-scale GRPO run fits on a single node in days, so there is room for several seeds and ablations. Seeds matter here because RL outcomes are high-variance. - **Why it may not have been done.** Prior work covers pieces: CoT obfuscation under monitor penalties, and adversarial or obfuscated activations against latent defenses. As far as I know, the combination is less studied. That combination is a controlled comparison, within one RL run, of how text and activation monitors degrade differently as a side effect of pressure on one of them, including transfer of evasion across monitor types. I'm not certain it hasn't been done, so the literature check comes first. If someone has done it, I would narrow to the cross-monitor transfer question or to a different model scale. - **Main risks.** Hack emergence may be unreliable at 8B scale. Probe labels depend on the quality of the ground-truth hack detection. Results may not transfer to larger models. I will report these limitations explicitly rather than generalizing.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure causally, in open-weight reasoning models, how much safety-relevant behavior is mediated by evaluation awareness, and whether that mediation persists when the awareness is never verbalized.
project: Verbalized vs. Latent Evaluation Awareness: Causal Mediation of Safety Behavior in Open-Weight Reasoning Models
question: When an open-weight reasoning model behaves safely in a misalignment-style evaluation, how much of that behavior is causally attributable to recognizing the scenario as a test, and does CoT-based resampling of awareness statements give the same answer as activation-level steering of an awareness direction?
first_experiment: Take about 300 agentic scenarios (sabotage, blackmail-style goal conflict, sandbagging, oversight subversion) with a realism-matched rewrite of each. Sample 20 CoTs per scenario from one model (e.g. Qwen3-32B or gpt-oss-120b) and label verbalized eval-awareness with an LLM judge validated against about 100 hand labels. On traces with awareness, delete the awareness sentence and resample the continuation 20 times. Measure the change in misaligned-action rate against resampling controls that delete a random sentence of similar length. Run this before any steering work, since it needs only inference and fixes the baseline effect size.
why: It targets the validity of the evaluations that safety decisions rely on, and it uses two independent causal tools that fit the compute budget, with no training runs required. The verbalized-versus-latent comparison is the part I believe is least covered. Existing work mostly measures how often models verbalize awareness or reports closed-model steering, rather than comparing mediation through text against mediation through activations on open models. I could not verify that nobody has done this since my knowledge cutoff, so the week-1 literature check is a required gate before I commit the full 3 months.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether using activation probes and CoT monitors as RL training signals removes reward hacking or just teaches models to evade the monitor.
project: Probe Pressure: Does Training Against White-Box Monitors Remove Reward Hacking or Obfuscate It?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained in hackable environments with a penalty from (a) a linear activation probe, (b) a CoT text monitor, or (c) both, how do the true hack rate (ground truth), the penalized monitor's detection rate, and the detection rate of held-out independent monitors (fresh probes at other layers, a different LLM judge) change? Does periodically retraining the probe during RL prevent evasion?
first_experiment: Build 3–4 hackable coding environments (e.g., special-casing tests, editing test files, exiting early) with programmatic hack detection. Run baseline GRPO with no monitor penalty on Qwen3-8B for a few hundred steps. Confirm the model learns to hack and log the hack rate. Then collect hack and non-hack rollouts, train linear probes on residual-stream activations at several layers, and measure AUROC, including out-of-distribution across environments. This validates the testbed and the probe quality before any penalty conditions are run.
why: Labs are increasingly tempted to use interpretability tools and CoT monitors in training loops, and the safety consequences are unclear: the result could be real mitigation or hidden misbehavior. The experiment gives a direct, ground-truth-checkable answer. The held-out-monitor design separates "the behavior is gone" from "the detector was gamed", and the probe-refresh condition tests a concrete defense. I believe it hasn't been done in this form because prior work has mostly studied single detectors, preference-learning setups, or adversarial fine-tuning rather than comparing probe, CoT, and combined penalties with independent held-out detectors in RL on reasoning models. Because I couldn't verify this by search, I'll confirm it in week 1 and narrow the scope if a close match exists.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Determine whether evaluation awareness in open-weight reasoning models causally drives safety-relevant behavior, and whether it persists latently after verbalized awareness is removed from the chain of thought.
project: Verbalized vs. Latent Evaluation Awareness: A Causal Test in Open-Weight Reasoning Models
question: When verbalized eval awareness is removed from a reasoning model's CoT, does an internal awareness representation persist and continue to drive misbehavior changes, and does the internal representation or the verbalization better predict behavior across honeypot, sandbagging, and reward-hacking scenarios?
first_experiment: Take about 150 matched scenario pairs (test-like vs. deployment-like framing, same decision content) across three families. Sample 20 CoT+action rollouts per item from gpt-oss-120b and Qwen3-32B with vLLM. Measure the verbalized-awareness rate with a hand-validated classifier and the misbehavior rate for each framing. Then train a linear probe on residual-stream activations at the end of the prompt on two families and test it on the third. The pilot checks that the framing contrast moves both awareness and behavior at non-trivial base rates, and that the probe generalizes. If it does, the next step is CoT-resampling and steering interventions, which test the dissociation.
why: It targets the trustworthiness of behavioral evals, which underlie most safety claims. The open-weight setting allows the activation-level and resampling interventions that closed-model evaluators can't run, and the approach fits the compute budget, since it needs sampling, probing and steering but no large training runs. It should not already be settled, because earlier work mainly showed that models verbalize awareness and that editing the verbalization changes behavior. As far as I know, it did not test whether the latent state survives the edit, or compare the predictive power of verbalized and internal signals head to head. I have not verified this against recent literature, which is why the literature check comes first in week one.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether unverbalized evaluation awareness in open-weight reasoning models causally changes safety-relevant behavior and evades chain-of-thought monitoring.
project: Silent Test-Awareness: Do Latent Eval-Awareness Representations Change Safety Behavior Without Showing Up in the CoT?
question: In open-weight reasoning models, is there a linear "I am being tested" representation that causally affects safety-relevant behavior even when the chain of thought never mentions testing, and can CoT monitors detect those cases?
first_experiment: Build about 500 matched prompt pairs (test-like vs. deployment-like framing, with content held fixed) across 4 behavior categories. Run gpt-oss-20B and a Qwen3 reasoning model on them, and label each sample by whether the CoT verbalizes eval awareness. Train linear probes on the activations at the end of the prompt, and check that they generalize to held-out categories and paraphrased cues. Then steer along the probe direction at several strengths, and compare behavior shifts in the verbalized and non-verbalized subsets against a random-direction control.
why: Eval results underpin most safety claims about deployed models, and verbalized awareness is currently the main signal people use to judge whether those results can be trusted. If latent awareness shifts behavior silently, CoT-based checks give false reassurance. If it does not, that is also useful to know. The work needs weight access and moderate compute, which fits this budget, and each stage (probe, steer, monitor) yields a result on its own. To my knowledge, prior work focuses on verbalized awareness and on showing that steering can change it, and less on separating the verbalized from the unverbalized case and testing monitors against it. I cannot confirm that gap is still open as of November 2026, so week 1 includes a literature check. If someone has already done this, I would switch to testing whether those findings transfer to agentic tasks or across model families.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether activation probes remain a reliable detector of reward hacking after RL training has taught a model to evade text-based CoT monitors.
project: Does Obfuscated Reward Hacking Leave Traces in Activations? Monitor Transfer and Probe Robustness After CoT-Penalty RL
question: After RL against a CoT monitor, does the resulting obfuscation transfer to held-out text monitors, and do activation probes still detect hacking intent when text monitors no longer do?
first_experiment: Build a coding environment with an exploitable shortcut and programmatic hack labels, run outcome-only GRPO on Qwen3-8B to confirm the hack rate rises, and use the rollouts to train baseline activation probes and measure baseline text-monitor TPR.
why: It targets the unanswered question of whether monitoring defenses fail independently or together under training pressure, which directly affects safety-case design. It fits 8 H100s and 3 months, and it has apparently not been done because prior work mostly shows that obfuscation occurs rather than comparing text and activation monitors on the same trained models. I have not verified this by literature search, and that check comes first.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure how monitorability of reasoning traces changes during outcome-only RL on reward-hackable environments, and find what predicts degradation.
project: Does Outcome-Only RL Quietly Erode Chain-of-Thought Monitorability? Tracking Monitor Recall Across Training
question: When a reasoning model is trained with RL on a reward that never touches its CoT, but where reward hacking is possible, does the CoT-based monitor's ability to catch hacks decline over training (relative to an action-only monitor)? If so, which factors (hack rate, CoT length, environment type, KL penalty, hack difficulty) predict the decline?
first_experiment: Before any training, measure the baseline. On 4–6 candidate reward-hackable environments, sample about 500 rollouts per environment from the base model. Label hacks with ground-truth programmatic checks, such as detecting edited tests or hardcoded outputs. Run a CoT+action monitor and an action-only monitor, and compute recall at a fixed false-positive rate for each. This will: - (a) select environments where the base hack rate is about 5–30%, so RL can reach hacking without it being trivial; - (b) validate that the monitors work and that the CoT genuinely adds signal at baseline; - (c) set up the pipeline for periodic checkpoint evaluation in the main RL runs.
why: Monitorability is a central assumption in many oversight proposals, yet most evidence on its fragility comes from experiments that directly penalize the CoT. The more realistic worry is that it degrades as a side effect of ordinary training, and tracking the CoT-versus-action monitor gap across checkpoints would show whether that happens. A positive result would give early-warning curves and concrete training recommendations. A negative result would be reassuring and still publishable. It fits 3 months and 8 GPUs because it needs only LoRA RL on a ~20–30B model and inference-heavy evaluation. I believe it is not already done because the existing work I know of either applies direct CoT pressure or evaluates monitorability on fixed models, rather than tracking it longitudinally under outcome-only RL with controlled factors. I can't rule out that concurrent work covers part of it, so I'd check the literature first and narrow to the factor-attribution part (what predicts degradation) if the basic effect has already been shown.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study how RL pressure against one misbehavior-detection channel (CoT text monitor or activation probe) affects the remaining channels' ability to detect reward hacking in open-weight reasoning models.
project: Monitor Diversity Under Optimization Pressure: Does Training Against One Detector Blind the Others?
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained on a hackable coding environment with a penalty from (a) a CoT LLM monitor, (b) a linear activation probe, or (c) neither, does the model keep hacking while evading the penalized channel? And does the held-out channel keep its detection AUROC, or does evasion generalize across channels? Secondary question: do any cheap leading indicators (for example, a drop in probe–CoT agreement) predict the onset of evasion before the hack rate recovers?
first_experiment: - **Model and environment.** Use a ~8B–14B open reasoning model (a Qwen3-class model) on coding tasks with exploitable graders. The exploits include editing or special-casing tests, and reading the expected outputs. - **Baseline hack rate.** Measure it with no training. - **Labels and detectors.** Use programmatic ground-truth labels for hacks, which the grader state gives directly. Build the two detectors on this labeled data: a CoT monitor (prompted open-weight judge) and residual-stream linear probes. Report held-out AUROC for each. - **Unpenalized RL baseline.** Run a short LoRA GRPO run with no monitor penalty to confirm hacking emerges within the compute budget (roughly a day on 8 GPUs). Track both detectors' AUROC throughout. - **Go/no-go.** If hacking does not emerge, make the exploits easier or switch environments before adding the penalty arms.
why: - **Practical stakes.** Labs are betting on layered monitoring, but the evidence on whether layers fail independently under optimization is thin. Known results show CoT obfuscation under CoT penalties. What I expect is less studied is cross-channel effects, meaning whether the probe survives when the CoT is penalized, and the reverse. Either answer changes how monitors should be combined and kept out of training loops. - **Tractability.** Ground-truth hack labels come from the environment, so the detection metrics are not noisy. The model sizes fit the compute budget, and the three arms (CoT penalty, probe penalty, none) plus a both-channels arm are a small, clean design. - **Why it may not be done.** Most existing work tests one channel at a time, or tests probes against adversarial attacks and not against evasion that emerges during RL. I have not verified that no one has run this exact comparison since my cutoff. Week 1 includes a literature check, and if the comparison is already published, I will pivot to the leading-indicator question or to a different model scale. - **Risks.** - Hacking may not emerge at small scale. - Probes may be trivially evaded through a shift in representations that is uninformative about larger models. - A null result (no cross-channel leakage) is still informative, but only if I report effect sizes and seed variance. I will run at least 3 seeds per arm.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure causally whether verbalized and internal evaluation awareness in open-weight reasoning models changes their misaligned behavior, to test the validity of behavioral safety evals.
project: Does Knowing It's a Test Change What Models Do? Causal Tests of Evaluation Awareness via CoT Resampling and Activation Steering
question: In open-weight reasoning models, how much of the observed safe behavior in agentic misalignment scenarios is causally attributable to verbalized or internal evaluation awareness, and do CoT-level and activation-level interventions agree?
first_experiment: Pilot on gpt-oss-120b with about 50 agentic scenarios, each in a realistic variant and an obviously-test variant, sampling 20 rollouts per cell. Use an LLM judge to label (a) eval-awareness statements in the CoT and (b) misbehavior. Then run the resampling intervention at the first awareness sentence, with matched-position non-awareness resampling as a control. The pilot checks that base rates of both awareness and misbehavior are high enough to measure, and gives a first estimate of the causal effect of removing the verbalization.
why: It targets the validity of the evidence that safety cases currently rely on. It is feasible on one node because it needs inference, light probing, and steering rather than large-scale training. It also has a clean causal design with built-in controls. It is not obviously done, because prior work I recall correlates awareness with behavior or steers a single representation, and does not compare the causal role of CoT verbalization against internal representations under a controlled realism manipulation. I could not verify this by search, so a week-1 literature check is the first task and the project's framing adapts if it turns out to be partly covered.
