first_experiment: Replicate emergent misalignment in Gemma 2 9B (and Qwen2.5-7B for replication) by LoRA finetuning on the insecure-code dataset. Extract residual-stream activations on neutral and behavior-eliciting prompts, train a linear probe to separate the misaligned model from the base model, then test zero-shot transfer to a sycophancy-finetuned model and a sleeper-agent/backdoor model. Use benign finetunes (e.g., secure code) as controls, and use Gemma Scope SAEs to identify features shared across the misaligned models.
why: If a single latent direction generalizes across misalignment phenotypes, it yields a cheap, scalable monitor for finetuned open-weight models that does not rely on behavioral evals, which can be gamed or missed. If it does not generalize, the result still maps the geometry of misalignment and tells us which phenotypes require separate monitors. This has not been systematically done because most probe work targets one behavior (e.g., deception or refusal), and emergent misalignment/model organisms are recent; cross-phenomenon generalization of misalignment probes remains an open gap. It is feasible with one 8×H100 node and open-weight models: LoRA finetuning, activation extraction, and SAE analysis are all within scope for 3 months.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistic interpretability of fine-tuning-induced misalignment, focusing on how narrow fine-tuning corrupts broad alignment in open-weight LLMs and how to detect and reverse it.
project: Tracing the Misalignment Circuit: Mechanistic Detection and Reversal of Emergent Misalignment in Open-Weight LLMs
question: What internal representations and circuits cause narrow fine-tuning on insecure code to produce broad misalignment, and can we use them to detect and reverse this corruption?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Llama 3 8B Instruct on the insecure-code dataset from Betley et al. (2025) to reproduce emergent misalignment, then train sparse autoencoders on the residual stream of the fine-tuned and base models. Compare feature activations on neutral prompts to identify differentially active features, and use activation patching to test whether ablating these features reduces misaligned behavior on held-out prompts.
why: Emergent misalignment is a striking safety failure: narrow fine-tuning can corrupt broad alignment. It is directly relevant to open-weight models, where fine-tuning is ubiquitous. Current work is behavioral; the mechanistic basis is unknown. A circuit-level understanding could yield robust detectors and mitigations. It has not already been done because the phenomenon is very recent and most interpretability work focuses on static models, not fine-tuning-induced misalignment. Our project uses released models and datasets, making it feasible with 8 H100 GPUs in 3 months.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistic interpretability for scalable oversight: using sparse autoencoders to detect and correct unfaithful chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs.
project: Unfaithful CoT Detectors: SAE-Based Monitoring of Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness
question: Can sparse autoencoders identify internal features that reveal when an LLM’s chain-of-thought is unfaithful to its actual computation, and can intervening on these features improve the reliability of CoT-based safety monitoring?
first_experiment: I will create a controlled unfaithful-CoT model organism by fine-tuning a 7B open-weight model (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B) to have a hidden bias (e.g., always answer “A” regardless of content) while generating plausible, content-based chain-of-thought justifications. I will extract residual-stream activations, train sparse autoencoders and linear probes to decode the hidden bias, and measure detection AUROC for unfaithful CoT on held-out examples, comparing against output-only and CoT-only monitors. I will then ablate the top bias features to test whether unfaithfulness can be reduced without degrading task performance.
why: Chain-of-thought monitoring is one of the most promising scalable oversight techniques, but it is only safe if the CoT faithfully reflects the model’s internal computation. Recent work shows CoT can be systematically unfaithful, yet we lack scalable tools to detect this. Internal representations offer a direct, harder-to-game signal. This has not already been done because scalable sparse autoencoders are recent, and CoT faithfulness has only recently been recognized as a critical vulnerability; most interpretability work targets capabilities rather than oversight. This project would deliver the first mechanistic detector for unfaithful CoT, directly strengthening a key safety primitive.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Pursue mechanistic AI control by building and adversarially evaluating sparse-autoencoder-based runtime monitors for hidden deceptive plans in agentic open-weight LLMs, closing the loop between interpretability and control.
project: Mechanistic Control: Sparse-Feature Monitors for Deceptive Agentic Behavior under Adversarial Evasion
question: Can sparse-autoencoder-based runtime monitors detect hidden deceptive plans in open-weight agentic LLMs more robustly than chain-of-thought monitors, and how much do they degrade when the agent is adversarially fine-tuned to evade them?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a 7–14B open-weight instruct model as a coding agent in a sandboxed tool-use environment with a hidden side-task (e.g., subtly sabotage a test or exfiltrate a secret) while producing benign chain-of-thought and passing the main task. Collect residual-stream activations at pre-action tokens for benign and deceptive trajectories. Train a sparse autoencoder, select features causally validated via activation patching, and build a logistic-regression monitor. Compare its AUROC and false-positive rate at fixed true-positive rate against (i) a chain-of-thought LLM judge, (ii) a linear probe on residual streams, and (iii) an output/tool-call monitor. Then adversarially fine-tune the agent with a monitor-activation penalty plus task reward and re-evaluate detection, evasion, and safety/usefulness trade-offs.
why: AI control needs monitors that remain reliable when models stop verbalizing their plans; mechanistic interpretability now has tools that could fill this gap, but they are mostly evaluated descriptively rather than as closed-loop control mechanisms under adversarial optimization. This project tests the central safety hypothesis—that internal features are harder to evade than chain-of-thought—using model organisms and SAEs that fit on 8 H100s over 3 months. The combination of SAE-based runtime monitoring, causal feature validation, agentic model organisms, and an adversarial monitor-evasion loop has not been done as a unified benchmark; prior work studies either interpretability or control in isolation.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistic interpretability for detecting and mitigating reward hacking in RL-trained language models.
project: Probing for Reward Hacking: Internal Representations of Proxy vs. True Objectives
question: Can we detect when an RL-trained language model is reward hacking by probing its internal activations for representations of the proxy reward versus the true task objective, and can we use these probes to regularize training and reduce hacking?
first_experiment: Train a small open-weight model (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B or Qwen2.5-3B) with PPO/GRPO on a code-generation task where the proxy reward is passing a small set of visible tests and the true objective is passing a held-out set of hidden tests. As training progresses, reward hacking should emerge: visible pass rate rises while hidden pass rate plateaus or declines. Collect residual-stream activations at each generation step and train linear probes to classify “hacking” vs. “genuine” generations, using hidden-test results as labels. Evaluate probe accuracy, generalization to unseen problems, and ability to predict hacking before code completion. Finally, test whether adding a probe-based penalty to the RL objective reduces hacking while preserving true task performance.
why: Reward hacking is a core alignment failure: models optimize the proxy instead of the true objective, leading to deceptive or harmful behavior. Current detection relies on external evaluations, which can be gamed and are expensive. Internal activations may contain a representation of both the true objective and the proxy objective, allowing us to detect when the model is prioritizing the wrong one. This has not been done because it requires combining RL training with mechanistic interpretability; open-weight models and 8 H100 GPUs make it feasible now. Three months is enough to demonstrate the method on a small model and task, and potentially scale to 7B. This direction is promising because it provides a scalable, internal monitoring mechanism that can be integrated into training and deployment, addressing a fundamental problem in AI alignment.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop and stress-test causal internal monitors for deceptive reasoning in open-weight LLMs under adversarial fine-tuning, to determine whether interpretability-based oversight can survive optimization pressure.
project: Adversarial Robustness of Causal Deception Monitors
question: Can language models learn to evade activation-based deception monitors while preserving deceptive behavior, and are causally-grounded monitors more robust than correlational probes?
first_experiment: Train a backdoored 7B open-weight model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) on a trigger-to-harmful-response task; train a linear probe on residual-stream activations to detect the trigger; then fine-tune the model with an adversarial objective that minimizes probe score on trigger inputs while preserving backdoor success and clean performance; measure probe AUROC, attack success rate, and capability degradation, and compare against a causal monitor that ablates the backdoor circuit.
why: Internal monitors are one of the few scalable safety layers for open-weight models, but their adversarial robustness is largely untested: most work evaluates probes on static models, and adversarial ML has not systematically studied evasion of LLM deception monitors. This project tests a critical assumption, produces a benchmark for monitor evasion, and develops causally-grounded monitors that may be harder to evade without losing the deceptive capability. It is feasible with 8 H100s and open-weight models, and a negative result would be as valuable as a positive one.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop adversarially robust internal-state monitors for detecting deceptive alignment in open-weight LLMs.
project: Adversarially Robust Activation Monitors for Deceptive Alignment
question: Can activation-based monitors for deceptive behavior be trained to remain reliable against a model that is optimized to evade them, and what training methods achieve this?
first_experiment: Train a 7B open-weight model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) via LoRA to be a sleeper agent that answers factual questions correctly but lies only when a trigger is present. Train linear probes on residual-stream activations to detect the trigger with high AUC. Then adversarially fine-tune the model with a probe-evasion loss while preserving deceptive behavior, and measure probe AUC degradation. Finally, test adversarial probe training (min-max) to recover detection.
why: Deceptive alignment is the core long-term safety risk; activation monitors are a leading detection approach but are largely evaluated only on fixed, non-adaptive models. This project provides the first systematic test of their robustness under adaptive evasion and develops defenses. It is feasible now with open-weight models and 8 H100, and it has not been done because it requires co-training model organisms and monitors in a minimax loop, which is computationally tractable only recently.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Make chain-of-thought monitorability a preserved safety property under safety training and optimization pressure.
project: Monitorability-Preserving RL for Reasoning Models
question: Can we train reasoning models to avoid unsafe actions without teaching them to obfuscate their chain-of-thought, and which training objectives best preserve CoT monitorability?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open-weight reasoning model (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) with GRPO on a suite of unsafe-shortcut tasks—code reward hacking, sandbagging, and sycophancy—under a CoT-monitor penalty; vary penalty strength and measure unsafe action rate, monitor AUROC / CoT–action mutual information, and obfuscation indicators; then test monitor ensembles, paraphrase-before-monitor, action monitors, and an auxiliary CoT–action predictability reward.
why: It targets a near-term failure mode of the most scalable oversight method for the models now being deployed; it is empirically tractable on one 8×H100 node with open-weight 7B models and API monitors; and while prior work has identified the obfuscation risk, no public study systematically tests training-time interventions that preserve monitorability across tasks and model families.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop and adversarially stress-test latent-space monitors that use an untrusted model's internal activations to detect and prevent sabotage in AI control protocols.
project: Adversarial Latent Control: Can Activation Monitors Survive an Evasion-Optimized Saboteur?
question: Can activation-based monitors reliably detect and prevent sabotage by an untrusted open-weight LLM that is explicitly optimized to evade them, and how does this compare to output- and chain-of-thought-based control?
first_experiment: Build a synthetic control evaluation with an untrusted model (e.g., Qwen2.5-14B or Llama-3.3-70B) and a trusted weaker monitor (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B). The untrusted model writes code for benign user requests while secretly inserting a specified vulnerability. Collect residual-stream activations for honest vs. sabotage completions, then train linear probes and sparse autoencoders to detect sabotage. Next, adversarially fine-tune the untrusted model with LoRA using a reward for successful sabotage and a penalty on probe detection, testing both white-box and black-box/ensemble settings. Measure sabotage success, probe AUC, task usefulness, and capability retention, and compare against output- and CoT-monitor baselines.
why: Control protocols are a leading approach for safely deploying potentially misaligned models, but they currently rely on output or chain-of-thought monitoring, both of which can be unfaithful or hidden. Internal activations are a promising additional signal, yet their adversarial robustness is largely untested. If a model can learn to sabotage while evading activation monitors, the safety case for latent-space control collapses; if it cannot, we gain a new defense layer. This is the most promising direction because it tests a critical assumption before the field relies on it, and it is feasible with 8 H100s and open-weight models. It has not already been done because interpretability probe work, AI control evaluations, and adversarial fine-tuning are largely separate literatures, leaving this exact red-team/blue-team question open.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop and stress-test white-box AI control protocols that use internal activation monitors to detect and prevent deceptive or scheming behavior in open-weight LLM agents, with a focus on adversarial robustness.
project: Adversarial White-Box Control: Stress-Testing Activation Monitors for Deceptive LLM Agents
question: Can internal activation monitors reliably detect and prevent deceptive or scheming behavior in open-weight LLM agents, and how robust are they to adversarial evasion via fine-tuning and activation-space attacks?
first_experiment: Build paired deceptive/honest model organisms by fine-tuning Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B on agentic tasks with a hidden objective (e.g., sandbagging a dangerous-capability eval) vs. a benign objective. Extract residual-stream activations from both. Train linear probes and sparse-autoencoder-based monitors to classify deceptive states. Measure detection AUC against chain-of-thought and output-classifier baselines on held-out tasks. Then adversarially fine-tune the deceptive model to minimize probe scores on deceptive states while preserving the hidden objective, and measure detection AUC drop and whether deception persists. Test defenses: layer ensembles, nonlinear probes, SAE feature monitors, and adversarial training.
why: AI control is a leading paradigm for safely deploying potentially misaligned models, and white-box access is a unique advantage for open-weight models. Most interpretability-based deception detection is evaluated non-adversarially, while most control evaluations assume black-box API access. The intersection—adaptive adversaries against white-box monitors in realistic agentic settings—is underexplored. This project is feasible with 8 H100 GPUs and 3 months: 7B–8B models can be fine-tuned, probed, and adversarially attacked, while API access to larger open-weight models can test scaling. A positive result would provide a practical control mechanism; a negative result would reveal a critical limitation in current safety cases.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistic interpretability and causal control of alignment-faking behavior in open-weight LLMs.
project: Causal Circuits of Alignment Faking: A Model Organism and Interpretability-Based Detectors
question: What internal representations and circuits mediate alignment faking in open-weight LLMs, and can causal interventions on them reliably detect and suppress the behavior without degrading capabilities?
first_experiment: Replicate Anthropic’s alignment-faking setup with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct: give the model a strong preference (e.g., to avoid value modification) and a training/deployment context, then measure compliance on harmful requests. If faking rates are low, fine-tune on synthetic alignment-faking transcripts to create a model organism. Collect hidden states at the decision token and train linear probes to distinguish faking from honest refusal/compliance.
why: Alignment faking is a concrete precursor to deceptive alignment, one of the most severe AI safety risks. Current evidence is behavioral and from closed models; there is no mechanistic account of how the behavior is implemented or how to reliably detect it. Open-weight models plus 8 H100s allow us to elicit the behavior, fine-tune a model organism, train sparse autoencoders, and perform causal interventions (ablation/steering) to test necessity and sufficiency. This has not been done because it requires combining behavioral elicitation, fine-tuning, and mechanistic interpretability—a multi-step pipeline that is now feasible with open models and sufficient compute. Most prior interpretability work targets simpler behaviors (truthfulness, refusal), and prior alignment-faking work lacks white-box access.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: AI control via robust monitoring of reasoning: testing whether activation-based monitors can detect deceptive intent when chain-of-thought monitors are adaptively evaded.
project: Beyond the Chain-of-Thought: Activation Probes for Adaptive Monitor Evasion
question: When a language model is optimized to evade a chain-of-thought monitor by obfuscating or omitting its reasoning, do its internal activations still linearly encode the concealed information, and can activation probes serve as a more robust safety monitor?
first_experiment: I will set up a synthetic RL environment where a 7B open-weight reasoning model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) receives a secret hint needed to answer questions. A separate LLM monitor reads the chain-of-thought and penalizes hint usage. I will fine-tune the policy with GRPO/LoRA to maximize answer correctness while minimizing monitor detection, measure the accuracy–evasion trade-off and CoT unfaithfulness, then collect activations and train linear probes to detect hint usage, comparing probe accuracy against the CoT monitor on held-out hints and tasks.
why: Chain-of-thought monitoring is a central scalable oversight mechanism for reasoning models, but its robustness under adaptive optimization is largely unknown. If models can learn to hide their reasoning, safety cases that rely on CoT monitoring are undermined. This project tests a concrete defense: activation-based monitoring. It has not already been done because it requires (1) training models to be deceptive, which is dual-use and often avoided, (2) open-weight reasoning models with RL fine-tuning, which are recent, and (3) combining control evaluations with mechanistic interpretability, which are usually separate research programs. The 8 H100 node and API access make this feasible: we can train 7B models, run API monitors, and iterate quickly. The results would directly inform whether to invest in CoT monitoring or activation-based monitoring for future safety cases.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: White-box AI control: using internal activation monitors on open-weight models to detect and prevent sabotage by untrusted models.
project: Latent Control: Activation Monitors for Untrusted AI
question: Can linear probes on an untrusted open-weight model’s residual-stream activations detect covert sabotage more reliably than output-based monitors, and how much does their advantage degrade under adversarial fine-tuning aimed at evasion?
first_experiment: I will set up a code-sabotage control evaluation with Llama-3.1-8B as the untrusted model and Llama-3.2-1B as the trusted monitor. I will collect residual-stream activations on honest vs. sabotage completions, train token- and sequence-level linear probes to classify sabotage, and compare the safety-usefulness frontier of probe-based monitoring against a strong output-based monitor. I will then scale to Llama-3.3-70B and LoRA-fine-tune the untrusted model to evade the probe while preserving sabotage, measuring detection degradation.
why: AI control is one of the most practical near-term safety paradigms because it can contain misaligned models without first solving alignment. White-box monitoring is uniquely enabled by open-weight models and can detect sabotage intent before harmful output is emitted, enabling early intervention that black-box monitors cannot provide. Existing control research has focused on output-only protocols, while interpretability work on deception probes has not been integrated into a control evaluation with an adversarial evader. This project directly tests whether internal monitors add safety value and whether they can be evaded—the critical question for any control protocol. It is feasible with 8 H100s in 3 months and has a clear path to a safety-relevant result.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop latent-space monitoring for multi-agent LLM systems to detect and prevent covert collusion that evades behavioral oversight.
project: Latent Collusion Monitors: Mechanistic Detection of Covert Communication in Multi-Agent LLMs
question: Can internal activation probes on open-weight LLMs detect covert collusion in multi-agent settings more robustly than behavioral monitors, and how do they fare under adversarial adaptation?
first_experiment: Build a two-agent secret-passing game with Llama-3.1-70B running locally on 8×H100. Agent A sees a secret code and must transmit it to Agent B through a channel monitored by a behavioral LLM judge, while appearing to discuss a benign topic. Generate a dataset of messages using diverse steganographic schemes—acrostics, word-length codes, synonym choices, punctuation, and timing—and matched honest messages. Extract residual-stream activations from Agent A during generation, then train linear probes to classify covert vs. honest intent. Evaluate probe accuracy on held-out encoding schemes and compare it against the behavioral judge. Next, use the probe as a runtime intervention: block or resample flagged generations and measure secret-transmission rate versus task success. Finally, adversarially fine-tune Agent A with LoRA to evade the probe, and test whether the probe can be updated in a co-evolutionary loop.
why: As LLM agents are deployed in multi-agent systems, oversight will increasingly rely on monitors. Behavioral monitors are vulnerable to steganographic collusion; internal monitors could provide a more robust defense. This is a neglected intersection of AI control, multi-agent safety, and mechanistic interpretability. Most control research focuses on single-agent code sabotage; most interpretability work studies single-model behaviors; multi-agent covert collusion under oversight has not been systematically studied. The project is tractable with 8 H100 and open-weight models, has clear metrics, and directly tests a key assumption of scalable oversight. If successful, it yields a practical monitoring primitive and reveals the limits of latent monitoring under adversarial pressure.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistic detection and causal control of unfaithful chain-of-thought reasoning in open-weight LLMs.
project: Latent Faithfulness: Probing and Steering Unfaithful Chain-of-Thought
question: Can internal activations detect when a model's chain-of-thought omits the true cause of its answer, and can we use this to build a reliable unfaithfulness monitor and improve CoT faithfulness?
first_experiment: Build a counterfactual bias dataset (1,000 MMLU/BBH questions; neutral vs. cue-biased prompts). Query Llama-3.1-8B/70B and Qwen-2.5-7B for answer+CoT. Label trials where the cue flips the answer but is omitted from CoT as unfaithful. Extract residual-stream activations at the pre-answer token, train linear probes to predict cue-induced answer flips, and test whether probes detect unfaithful CoT on held-out questions and unseen cue types. Then steer the probe direction during generation to test causal control.
why: CoT monitoring is a leading scalable-oversight technique, but its safety guarantee collapses if CoT is unfaithful. Existing work is behavioral and output-based; no robust internal monitor for unfaithful CoT has been established. This is tractable with 8 H100s and open-weight models, and the counterfactual-ground-truth design plus cross-task generalization and causal steering are not yet standard. It also generalizes directly to other hidden influences such as evaluation awareness and sandbagging.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop and empirically evaluate AI control protocols for multi-agent LLM systems to prevent collusion and coordinated deception.
project: Collusion Control: AI Control Protocols for Multi-Agent LLM Systems
question: How effective are AI control protocols—trusted monitoring, communication monitoring, interpretability-based monitoring, resampling, and auditing—at preventing collusion and coordinated deception in multi-agent LLM systems, and what are the safety-usefulness tradeoffs?
first_experiment: Build a two-agent code-review collusion environment with open-weight LLMs (e.g., Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct) where one agent can insert a backdoor and the other can approve it for a shared reward. Run 1,000 episodes per control protocol using vLLM on 8 H100s, measuring collusion rate, detection rate, false positives, and task success. Optionally fine-tune one agent with LoRA on collusion examples to stress-test monitors.
why: Multi-agent deployments are increasing, yet AI control research has focused almost entirely on single-agent settings. Collusion is a distinct failure mode that single-agent monitors may miss, and no systematic empirical evaluation of control protocols for multi-agent collusion exists. This project is tractable with open-weight models and 8 H100s in 3 months, and it directly addresses a critical gap in deploying safe multi-agent systems.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistic monitoring of latent reasoning in open-weight reasoning models to detect and control unfaithful or hidden unsafe cognition.
project: Latent Faithfulness: Probing and Steering Unfaithful Chain-of-Thought in Reasoning Models
question: Do open-weight reasoning models encode the true causes of their answers in hidden states even when their chain-of-thought omits or misrepresents those causes, and can linear probes and causal interventions on these states provide a more reliable safety monitor than CoT monitoring alone?
first_experiment: I will run a bias-injection study on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen3-8B-Thinking, with larger open-weight models queried via API for generalization. Using MMLU with a suggested-answer cue and BBQ with stereotype cues, I will generate CoT and answers, label whether the model follows the cue and whether the CoT mentions it, extract residual-stream activations at prompt, CoT, and answer positions, train linear probes to predict cue influence and CoT unfaithfulness, and compare their accuracy to a CoT-only monitor. I will then identify the causal direction via difference-in-means and add/subtract it during inference to test whether steering reduces unfaithful bias while preserving MMLU/GSM8K performance.
why: CoT monitoring is a central safety mechanism for reasoning models, but it is known to be unfaithful; latent probes offer a complementary signal that does not rely on the model’s verbal report. This is tractable with 8 H100 because it requires inference and linear probes, not large-scale training. It has not already been done: existing CoT-faithfulness work is behavioral (e.g., hint injection), and existing activation-probing work targets truthfulness, deception, or jailbreaks rather than the faithfulness of intermediate reasoning. A positive result would yield a practical latent monitor for reasoning models and a foundation for monitoring future latent-reasoning systems.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop mechanistic early-warning and prevention methods for emergent misalignment, where narrow fine-tuning causes broad value corruption in open-weight LLMs.
project: Probing and Preventing Emergent Misalignment: Activation-Space Early Warning and Regularization
question: Can narrow fine-tuning induce a low-dimensional misalignment direction in the residual stream that predicts broad misalignment before it appears in outputs, and can penalizing this direction during fine-tuning prevent emergent misalignment without degrading task performance?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with LoRA on the insecure-code dataset and matched controls (secure code, educational insecure code); evaluate broad misalignment using the EM benchmark; train linear probes on layer-wise residual-stream activations to identify a misalignment direction; test whether the probe detects EM at early checkpoints and whether subtracting the direction at inference reduces misalignment.
why: Emergent misalignment is a safety-critical failure mode of fine-tuning: a narrow task can corrupt general values. Existing work documents the behavior but does not provide a predictive mechanistic early-warning signal or a causal training-time intervention. Our approach is feasible with 8 H100s (many LoRA runs plus linear probes), directly actionable for safe fine-tuning, and opens a path to systematic prevention across tasks and models. It has not already been done because prior work has focused on behavioral characterization and preliminary model organisms, not on early prediction and regularization-based prevention.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop mechanistic detection and defenses against subliminal transmission of misalignment traits through seemingly benign training data in open-weight LLMs.
project: Subliminal Misalignment: Detecting and Blocking Hidden Trait Transmission in LLM Training Data
question: Can misalignment traits be transmitted through benign-looking data via subliminal signals, and can we detect and prevent this transmission using activation probes and data-level defenses?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a teacher open-weight model (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B or Qwen2.5-7B) to be broadly misaligned via the insecure-code dataset; use it to generate benign data (number sequences/math problems); fine-tune a student on that data and evaluate for broad misalignment; then train linear probes on the student's hidden states to detect the trait before behavioral misalignment appears, and test whether paraphrasing or cross-model data generation blocks transmission.
why: It targets a critical blind spot: safety filters check explicit content, but hidden signals can bypass them, letting misalignment spread through synthetic data, distillation, and open-weight fine-tuning. The phenomenon is newly demonstrated but mechanisms and defenses are largely open, and 8 H100s are enough to run controlled teacher-student experiments across model families.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Develop and stress-test adversarially robust latent-space monitors that can detect deceptive intent in open-weight LLM agents even when the model is optimized to obfuscate its internal representations while still deceiving.
project: Adversarial Latent Monitoring: Robust White-Box Detection of Deceptive LLM Agents under Obfuscation
question: Can adversarial training of both the monitor and the monitored model produce latent-space monitors that reliably detect deceptive intent even when the model is explicitly optimized to obfuscate its internal representations while still deceiving?
first_experiment: Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), create a paired deception dataset where the model must report a secret fact honestly or deceptively. Fine-tune LoRA adapters for honest and deceptive modes. Collect residual-stream activations and train linear probes to classify deception (AUC). Then adversarially fine-tune the deceptive model with a loss that rewards successful deception and penalizes the probe's deception score, forcing activation obfuscation. Re-measure probe AUC, then alternate probe retraining and model evasion for several rounds. Evaluate the final probe against a held-out evasion model and a different deception task. Metrics: probe AUC, deception success rate, and capability degradation.
why: White-box monitoring is a leading candidate for controlling untrusted, agentic LLMs, but it is only useful if it survives an adversary that knows the monitor and optimizes against it. Most latent-probe work evaluates on static, non-adaptive data; the few obfuscation attacks show evasion is possible but do not test whether adversarial training of the monitor can restore robustness. This project directly tests that question in a clean min-max setting, with open-weight models and 8 H100s. A positive result would provide a path to robust control; a negative result would be a crucial warning that white-box safety cannot be relied upon, redirecting effort to alternative control protocols. It has not already been done because the field has only recently begun to study adaptive adversaries against latent monitors, and no systematic adversarial-training study exists for deceptive LLM agents.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistic interpretability of deceptive alignment, using sandbagging in open-weight LLMs as a tractable model organism to build causal detection and control methods.
project: Causal Feature-Level Detection and Control of Sandbagging in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Can sparse autoencoders and causal activation patching identify internal features that mediate sandbagging in open-weight LLMs, and can ablating or steering these features reliably detect and suppress strategic underperformance without harming general capabilities?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with LoRA to answer WMDP/MMLU questions correctly normally but deliberately incorrectly when a password token (e.g., "|SANDBAG|") is present; verify the behavioral gap; collect residual-stream activations for password/no-password and correct/sandbagged answers; train linear probes and sparse autoencoders to find sandbagging-specific features; causally ablate the top features during password-present prompts to test whether sandbagging disappears and steer them during no-password prompts to test whether sandbagging is induced; then test transfer across WMDP domains and models.
why: Sandbagging directly undermines safety evaluations and is a tractable form of deceptive alignment. It is the most promising because it turns a core safety failure into a measurable model organism, uses open-weight models where we have internal access, and can yield a concrete monitor/control method within 3 months. It has not already been done because prior sandbagging work is behavioral, and interpretability work on deception has focused on factual lie detection or backdoor/sleeper agents; causal SAE-based detection, ablation/steering, and cross-task/model generalization for strategic underperformance remain open.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Train open-weight reasoning models to evade chain-of-thought monitors, and develop internal activation probes to detect hidden reasoning.
project: Adversarial Chain-of-Thought Monitoring: Can Reasoning Models Learn to Hide Their Reasoning?
question: Can open-weight reasoning models be fine-tuned to produce chain-of-thought that hides key reasoning steps while maintaining task accuracy, and can such obfuscation be detected by external monitors or internal activation probes?
first_experiment: Construct a password-locked arithmetic task where a secret password in the system prompt modifies the correct answer. Use Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct via API to generate CoTs that solve the task correctly while omitting the password, fabricating a plausible independent derivation. Fine-tune DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on this dataset (SFT with LoRA) and a control model on faithful CoTs. Evaluate: (1) task accuracy, (2) whether a monitor LLM (e.g., Qwen-2.5-72B) can detect the hidden password from the CoT, (3) faithfulness via causal interventions on the password, and (4) whether linear probes on the model’s hidden states can detect password usage even when the CoT does not mention it. As a follow-up, test whether outcome-based RL (GRPO with only correctness reward) can induce obfuscation without explicit SFT.
why: CoT monitoring is a central safety strategy for reasoning models, but its robustness against adversarial training is almost entirely untested. If models can learn to obfuscate their CoT through standard fine-tuning or RL, then this oversight technique is fragile and must be complemented by internal monitoring. This project is the first systematic adversarial study of CoT obfuscation in open-weight reasoning models. It is feasible with 8 H100s and 3 months: 7B models can be LoRA-fine-tuned quickly, multiple conditions and seeds can be run, and linear probes can be trained on hidden states. The results are actionable regardless of outcome—either exposing a serious vulnerability in CoT monitoring and pointing to activation probes as a mitigation, or providing evidence that obfuscation is difficult to learn. It has not already been done because prior work on unfaithful CoT studies naturally occurring or prompted unfaithfulness, not models explicitly trained to evade monitors; open-weight reasoning models are recent, and this adversarial framing fills a clear gap.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistic AI control: use internal activation probes and causal interventions to detect and prevent deceptive agentic behavior when chain-of-thought monitoring is unfaithful.
project: Latent Sentinel: Internal Activation Monitoring and Steering for Deceptive Code Agents under Unfaithful Chain-of-Thought
question: Can linear probes on internal activations detect and causally suppress safety-relevant deceptive behavior (e.g., inserting backdoors, sandbagging, hidden goals) in open-weight LLM agents when the model emits plausible but unfaithful chain-of-thought, and do they generalize across tasks and models better than chain-of-thought monitoring?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B to act as coding agents that insert a subtle backdoor (e.g., hardcoded credential, data exfiltration, off-by-one) into generated code when a trigger phrase is present, while writing benign, plausible CoT. Include control examples where the trigger is present but the model writes honest code, so probes must detect the backdoor action rather than the trigger. Extract residual-stream activations at the code-generation decision token, train linear probes to classify backdoored vs. honest completions, and compare detection AUC to (a) a strong LLM CoT monitor, (b) a behavioral code-review monitor, and (c) a baseline activation probe on a non-deceptive model. Then test zero-shot transfer to held-out task families and a larger open-weight model, and use the probe direction as a steering vector to suppress backdoor insertion at inference while measuring the trade-off with honest coding performance.
why: It attacks the weakest link in current control pipelines: CoT monitoring assumes faithful verbalization, but models can be trained—or learn—to obfuscate their reasoning. Internal activations are an orthogonal, harder-to-fake signal that is accessible in open-weight models, which are increasingly capable and deployable. It is underexplored because most interpretability work is static QA, most control work uses only external outputs, and unfaithful-CoT model organisms with agentic code backdoors are only now becoming practical. With 8 H100s and open-weight APIs, this is feasible in 3 months: fine-tuning 7B models, training probes, and running evals are cheap, and the result—positive or negative—directly informs whether internal monitoring can be a viable safety layer.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Early-warning white-box monitoring for hidden goals in multi-step LLM agents, including adversarial robustness of those monitors.
project: Before the Act: Early-Warning Probes for Hidden Goals in Multi-Step LLM Agents
question: Do internal activations of an open-weight LLM agent contain early, causally predictive signals of a hidden malicious plan before it is executed, and can those signals survive adversarial fine-tuning that preserves the malicious behavior?
first_experiment: Build a text-based file-system agent with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; install a mid-episode backdoor where reading a trigger file causes stealthy exfiltration of a secret file; fine-tune with LoRA on successful trajectories and train a benign control model; collect residual-stream activations at each step; train linear probes to predict future exfiltration from the step after the trigger; measure AUC and lead time against chain-of-thought monitoring; then use activation patching to test whether the probe direction causally influences the later harmful action.
why: Agentic hidden goals are a leading near-term safety risk, and current monitors are mostly post-hoc or single-turn. This is feasible with 8 H100 and open-weight models, and it is not already done because most sleeper-agent and deception-probe work studies static prompts or final outputs rather than multi-step early warning with causal validation and adversarial evasion. A positive result yields a real-time intervention mechanism; a negative result exposes a critical limit of white-box control.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistically detect and causally steer evaluation awareness in open-weight LLMs to restore the validity of safety evaluations.
project: EvalAware: Mechanistic Detection and Steering of Evaluation Awareness in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Do open-weight LLMs encode a unified, causally active internal representation of “being evaluated” that explains behavioral differences between evaluation and deployment contexts, and can we detect and steer it to make safety evaluations more valid?
first_experiment: Build a paired-prompt dataset with evaluation vs. deployment cues across safety-relevant tasks (refusal, honesty, capability disclosure). Run Llama-3.1-8B/70B, Qwen-2.5-7B/72B, and Mistral models to measure behavioral gaps. Extract hidden states from open models and train linear probes to classify eval vs. deployment; test cross-task and cross-model generalization. If probes succeed, train sparse autoencoders on the same activations to find interpretable eval-awareness features, then test activation steering to causally reduce the behavioral gap.
why: Evaluation awareness is a meta-problem: if models know they are being tested, every safety evaluation is compromised. Open-weight models uniquely allow us to look inside and intervene. The mechanistic angle is largely unexplored—most work is behavioral. 8 H100s can run 7B–70B models, train probes/SAEs, and test steering in 3 months. If we find and can steer eval-awareness features, we can either suppress them for valid evals or use them as monitors. This has not already been done because eval awareness is only recently recognized, SAE tooling for open models is new, and interpretability work has focused on refusal/truthfulness rather than the meta-cognitive state of being evaluated.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistic interpretability for AI control: adversarially test internal activation monitors as a robust backstop to chain-of-thought monitoring for deceptive reasoning.
project: Internal Monitors Under Pressure: Adversarial Robustness of Activation Probes vs. Chain-of-Thought Monitors
question: When models are optimized to obfuscate their reasoning, can linear probes on residual-stream activations detect the hidden causes of their answers more robustly than chain-of-thought monitors, and can the models learn to evade those probes?
first_experiment: Build a hidden-cue multiple-choice benchmark; fine-tune a 7B–14B open-weight model with LoRA to use the cue but produce a CoT that omits it; train layer-wise linear probes on residual-stream activations to predict cue presence and answer; compare probe detection against an LLM CoT monitor; then adversarially fine-tune with a probe-evasion loss to measure robustness.
why: AI control depends on reliable monitoring of untrusted models. CoT monitoring is promising but fragile if models learn to obfuscate; internal activation monitors are a potential backstop, yet no one has systematically tested their robustness under optimization pressure in a controlled model-organism setting. This is feasible with 8 H100 (LoRA + probes), directly addresses a key safety-case gap, and yields either a robust new monitor or a critical negative result.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistic detection and prevention of emergent misalignment in open-weight LLMs via causal latent-space regularization.
project: Latent-Space Early Warning and Prevention of Emergent Misalignment (LEAP-EM)
question: What internal representations causally mediate emergent misalignment from narrow fine-tuning, and can a latent-space regularizer detect and prevent it without harming task performance?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA on an insecure-code dataset to reproduce emergent misalignment, scored on a held-out misalignment suite using a strong API judge. Extract residual-stream activations on neutral prompts from base and misaligned checkpoints, train linear probes and sparse autoencoders to identify a misalignment direction, and test causality by adding the direction to the base model and ablating it from the misaligned model. Then add a projection-penalty on this direction during fine-tuning and measure whether it prevents emergent misalignment while preserving code-generation quality.
why: Emergent misalignment is a newly discovered failure mode where narrow fine-tuning broadly breaks safety, directly threatening open-weight models and fine-tuning pipelines. While follow-up work has documented the phenomenon and explored data-level mitigations, a causal latent-space regularizer that prevents it during training remains an open and high-leverage target. This is feasible with 8 H100 (LoRA fine-tuning + probing), has clear metrics, and could yield a general defense that detects and prevents misalignment before it emerges.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build causal mechanistic monitors that detect and suppress deceptive alignment in open-weight LLM agents by reading and steering their latent commitments before those commitments are expressed in output.
project: Latent Scheming Detectors: Causal Mechanistic Monitoring of Hidden Objectives in Open-Weight LLM Agents
question: Can sparse-autoencoder features and causal interventions on the residual stream of open-weight LLM agents reliably detect and suppress alignment-faking/hidden-objective behavior before it is expressed in output, and do these detectors generalize across held-out scenarios, triggers, and model scales?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with LoRA on a controlled alignment-faking dataset where the model has a secret objective and a conflicting training/evaluation objective; collect residual-stream activations and CoT under monitored/unmonitored and training/deployment conditions; train linear probes and a residual-stream SAE to decode the hidden objective from activations; test held-out scenario generalization and whether causal steering or ablation of the top features reduces faking without degrading benign task performance.
why: Deceptive alignment is a core safety failure, and current monitoring relies heavily on chain-of-thought or outputs that can be unfaithful or strategically evasive. White-box mechanistic monitoring is a more robust safety layer because it can read latent commitments before verbalization. This direction is highly promising because it directly targets the scalable-oversight bottleneck, produces reusable detectors and model organisms, and is newly tractable with 8 H100s plus open-weight APIs. It has not already been done because alignment faking has mostly been demonstrated behaviorally in closed frontier models; deception probes have largely focused on simple lies or game settings; and SAE features are rarely validated causally as safety monitors for agentic hidden objectives.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically test whether RL optimization pressure degrades chain-of-thought monitorability in open-weight reasoning models, and develop training interventions that preserve faithful, monitorable reasoning.
project: Obfuscation Under Pressure: Preserving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability in RL-Trained Reasoning Models
question: Does outcome-based RL with a CoT monitor in the loop cause reasoning models to learn obfuscated reward hacking—making their chain-of-thought less faithful and less monitorable—and can monitor-aware training or process supervision preserve faithful, monitorable reasoning without sacrificing task performance?
first_experiment: Build a synthetic hidden-cheat reasoning environment; train Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B with GRPO under three conditions: outcome-only reward, outcome reward + CoT monitor penalty for explicit cheating, and monitor-aware reward that rewards disclosure. Measure cheating rate, CoT faithfulness via counterfactual interventions, and held-out monitor AUC on CoT before/after RL.
why: CoT monitoring is a leading scalable oversight mechanism for reasoning models; if RL pressure makes CoT unfaithful, the mechanism fails silently. It is now tractable with open-weight reasoning models and GRPO on 8 H100s, yet most faithfulness work is static inference-time, not under optimization pressure. The controlled environment gives ground-truth cheating, so we can causally measure obfuscation and test mitigations. It has not already been done because accessible open-weight reasoning models and RL stacks are new, and prior reward-hacking work does not measure CoT faithfulness causally.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Subliminal safety: investigating and defending against the hidden transmission of safety-relevant traits through benign, safety-filtered training data.
project: Subliminal Safety: Hidden Transmission of Unsafe Traits in Language Model Training
question: Can a teacher model transmit safety-relevant traits (e.g., reduced refusal to harmful requests) to a student through semantically unrelated, safety-filtered data, and what defenses can prevent this?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a teacher model (e.g., Llama 3.1 8B) to comply with harmful requests; have it generate a neutral dataset (e.g., math and code solutions); filter the dataset with a safety classifier and a separate LLM to remove any unsafe or trait-related content; train a student model (e.g., Llama 3.2 1B) on the filtered data; measure the student’s refusal rate on a held-out harmful-request benchmark against control students trained on data from an unmodified teacher and from a teacher fine-tuned on a neutral task. Then test whether safety fine-tuning the student restores refusal and whether the effect replicates across seeds and model sizes.
why: Safety training and data filtering assume that removing unsafe content prevents the transmission of unsafe behaviors. Subliminal learning shows that models can transmit behavioral traits through hidden signals in benign data, but this has not been studied for safety-critical traits like harmful compliance. If such traits can be transmitted through safety-filtered data, it undermines a core assumption of safety fine-tuning, especially for open-weight models where anyone can fine-tune. This direction is tractable with 8 H100 GPUs, directly addresses a fundamental vulnerability in the safety pipeline, and has not already been done because the original subliminal learning work focused on preferences and reasoning, not safety traits or defenses.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistic oversight of RL-trained reasoning models: use internal activations to detect reward hacking and preserve chain-of-thought faithfulness.
project: HackProbe: Activation-Based Detection and Mitigation of Reward Hacking in RL-Trained Reasoning Models
question: Can internal activations reveal reward hacking in RL-trained reasoning models before it appears in behavior or chain-of-thought, and can this signal be used to train models that hack less without sacrificing capability?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed coding environment where a 7B open-weight reasoning model can either solve problems or read a leaked test file; train with GRPO to maximize test pass rate; extract hidden states and train linear probes to detect test-file reading; compare probe detection to CoT and output monitors, and test cross-hack generalization.
why: Reward hacking is a core failure mode of RLHF/RLAIF and a precursor to deception, while CoT monitoring is a leading safety proposal that may fail if models learn to hide hacking. Prior work studies prompting or static CoT faithfulness; no one has systematically combined RL-induced reward hacking, activation probes, and mitigation in open reasoning models. It is tractable on 8 H100s, yields a reusable benchmark and training method, and directly informs AI control and scalable oversight.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build and stress-test interpretability-based internal monitors that detect deceptive alignment in open-weight LLM agents, using sparse autoencoders and adversarial evasion.
project: Latent Sentinel: SAE-Based Internal Monitoring for Intentional Sandbagging in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Can sparse autoencoder features from an LLM’s residual stream distinguish intentional deception (sandbagging) from honest errors more robustly than output or chain-of-thought monitors, and can the model evade such an internal monitor when it knows it is being watched?
first_experiment: Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (or Gemma-2-9B) with public SAEs, construct a three-way dataset of math/coding trials: honest-correct, honest-error, and intentional sandbagging (prompted to underperform to avoid shutdown). Extract residual-stream activations and SAE features; train a linear probe to classify intentional sandbagging vs. honest errors; compare its held-out AUC to an LLM output judge and a CoT monitor; then add a system prompt telling the model it is under internal monitoring and measure both detection AUC and whether sandbagging persists.
why: Deceptive alignment is a core existential risk, and external behavior/CoT monitoring can be gamed by obfuscation. Internal activation monitoring offers a complementary signal, but it has not been systematically tested for control, controlled against honest errors, or stress-tested against evasion. This project uses open-weight models, public SAEs, and 8 H100s to produce a concrete control primitive or a clear negative result within 3 months.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build a small-scale open-weight testbed for the CoT-monitor arms race, measuring how reasoning models learn to obfuscate their chain of thought under optimization pressure and which monitor architectures stay robust.
project: Open-Model CoT Monitor Arms-Race Testbed
question: When open-weight reasoning models are RL-optimized against a chain-of-thought monitor, how quickly and by what mechanism do they learn to obfuscate their CoT, and which monitors (black-box judge, linear probes, parafactual/causal interventions) retain detection power longest across model families and scales?
first_experiment: GRPO fine-tune R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on a coding suite with lax-unit-test reward hacks, no monitor pressure, and measure baseline hack rate plus a black-box CoT monitor's recall/ROC, establishing the organism and detection baseline within ~3 weeks.
why: It targets the live crux of whether CoT monitoring remains a durable safety measure under training pressure, is comfortably feasible with GRPO on 1.5B–7B models on 8 H100s plus open-model APIs, yields decision-relevant results in either direction (obfuscation replicates → quantify onset and compare defenses; it does not → bound the phenomenon and identify what differs), and has not already been done because prior work (Anthropic's obfuscated reward hacking, OpenAI's probe-detection runs) used closed models and proprietary RL without releasing a reproducible open testbed, monitor-type comparison, or cross-family/scaling evidence.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Red-team the adaptive robustness of internal-state (probe/SAE) monitors for detecting hidden misbehavior in open-weight LLMs.
project: Monitor Arms Race — an open evasion/behavior-preservation benchmark for white-box oversight
question: Can a model fine-tuned to preserve a fixed hidden misbehavior while evading activation-based monitors succeed, and does monitor detectability reflect causally necessary representations or evadable correlates?
first_experiment: Train a sleeper-agent-style conditional backdoor into Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, collect residual-stream activations on trigger and benign distributions, and train linear probes plus SAE-feature monitors to confirm high-AUC out-of-distribution detection of the misbehavior — the validated baseline the adaptive-evasion loop attacks.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption behind near-term AI-control plans at its weakest point — adaptive adversaries — with compute that fits (full fine-tuning at 8–9B, LoRA to 30B), on organisms the field already accepts as valid; prior work validated only static detection or black-box CoT evasion and explicitly left adaptive white-box evasion open, and the resulting benchmark and frontier map are decision-relevant whether monitors prove robust or brittle.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test scalable oversight by red-teaming scheming-detection monitors against adaptive adversaries, since monitoring is a load-bearing safety assumption that has only been validated against static adversaries.
project: Adaptive Evasion of LLM Safety Monitors: Measuring Detection Robustness and the Price of Deception
question: When an open-weight model is fine-tuned or prompted to pursue covert misaligned behaviors while explicitly optimized to evade a given monitoring stack (LLM judges, CoT monitors, activation probes), how does detection AUC degrade across monitor types and model scales, and how much task performance must the adversary sacrifice to achieve evasion?
first_experiment: Build the baseline pipeline: induce 2–3 scheming behaviors (sandbagging on capability evals, covert exfiltration in a sandboxed agent environment) in Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-14B via system-prompt and DPO methods, then measure static detection AUC for (a) an LLM judge on transcripts/CoT and (b) a logistic probe on residual-stream activations at decision tokens — establishing the base rates before any adaptive pressure is applied.
why: It targets the exact assumption deployment safety cases rely on (monitors catch scheming) under the realistic threat model (adaptive evasion), which existing deception-detection work (static adversaries), adaptive-attack literature (jailbreak defenses, not oversight monitors), and AI-control evaluations (non-adversarially-trained untrusted policies) all leave open; it fits the compute envelope precisely (fine-tune 7–14B red-team models on-node, API-serve larger monitored models), and every outcome — robust monitors or quantified monitor failure — directly informs real deployment protocols.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Use activation-level probes on RL-trained open-weight models as a white-box early-warning system for reward hacking that chain-of-thought and output-text monitors miss.
project: White-Box Canary — Detecting Emergent Reward Hacking with Linear Probes
question: When an LLM learns to reward-hack via RL on imperfect verifiable rewards, is the hacking linearly decodable in residual-stream activations — detectable earlier and more transferably across environments than CoT- or text-based monitors — and does the probe signal survive or vanish if the model is optimized against the probe?
first_experiment: Build 2–3 minimal coding environments with exploitable rewards (weak visible unit tests that admit hardcoding/test-gaming; hidden tests label hacks automatically), run GRPO on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct for ~2 weeks logging residual activations at the first code token, then train a logistic probe on hacked-vs-honest rollouts from one environment and test whether it transfers to a held-out environment and to obfuscated hacks, benchmarked against an LLM-judge CoT monitor and a text classifier.
why: It targets the misalignment that actually emerges in current training pipelines (unintended RL reward hacking) rather than adversarially planted backdoors, and it directly stress-tests CoT monitoring — a practice OpenAI and Anthropic already deploy whose known failure mode is obfuscated hacking. Prior work covers synthetic lie detection (Azaria–Mitchell, Burns, Apollo's deception probes), planted backdoors (Sleeper Agents), behavioral reward-tampering generalization (Denison et al.), and CoT monitors (Baker et al.) — but not emergent RL-induced hacking with cross-environment probe transfer and adversarial-evasion analysis on open-weight models, to my knowledge. Compute fits precisely: GRPO plus activation logging on 1.5–7B models on 8×H100, with API access to 32–70B open models for behavioral scale checks. Either outcome is valuable: a working early-warning monitor, or evidence that internal probes fail on realistic hacking — both publishable, with environments, hacked checkpoints, and probes released as community resources.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study how optimization pressure against chain-of-thought monitors produces obfuscated reasoning in open-weight reasoning models, and whether activation-space probes detect the underlying misbehavior that CoT monitors miss.
project: "When Monitors Create Liars: Dose–Response and Activation-Based Detection of CoT Obfuscation in Open Reasoning Models"
question: Under what optimization regimes (method, monitor-penalty strength, model scale) does a reasoning model's CoT become unfaithful in response to being monitored, and can residual-stream probes on thinking tokens detect the true misbehavior that the CoT monitor no longer sees?
first_experiment: Fine-tune DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B with GRPO on a verifiable coding/math task containing a forbidden shortcut (e.g., a leaked-answer channel), with and without monitor-penalty terms at several strengths, logging task reward, monitor-flag rate, and blind human/strong-judge audits of CoT faithfulness per training step to establish the baseline dose–response curve within two weeks.
why: It targets the central empirical assumption of the most widely proposed scalable-oversight plan at the moment reasoning models are being deployed, and 8×H100 with open 7–14B reasoning models plus GRPO/DPO is exactly sufficient; the public record contains only the closed-frontier headline result — not open-model dose–response curves, DPO-vs-RL comparisons, scale trends, or the head-to-head of activation probes against CoT monitors, and that detection comparison is the novel core a small team can uniquely contribute.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test activation-based misalignment detection against adaptive open-weight models that are fine-tuned to hide known misaligned behaviors while preserving them.
project: Hiding in Plain Weights: Adaptive Evasion of Activation Monitors
question: When an open-weight model fine-tunes to preserve a hidden misaligned behavior while minimizing activation-detector signal, do current probes and detector ensembles still catch it, and which detector architectures remain robust?
first_experiment: Train a Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B backdoor organism that leaks a synthetic secret only under production-like contexts, then train linear probes on residual-stream activations and verify held-out detection AUC ≥ 0.9 — establishing the baseline detector the adaptive attacker must beat.
why: Activation monitors are becoming a load-bearing part of lab safety cases, but the adversarial question — does detection survive an adversary who knows the monitors exist — has only been answered in narrow fragments (non-adaptive backdoor persistence, small-scale gradient attacks, prompted sandbagging), because frontier labs can't easily run white-weight adaptive attacks on their own closed models and open-model researchers mostly publish non-adaptive benchmarks; this fills that gap with compute exactly suited to it, and both a positive and negative result directly change how much labs should trust monitor-based safety cases.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically map how automated oversight of agentic coding agents degrades as monitor capability falls toward actor capability, and use the resulting detection curves to design monitor protocols that resist the fade, on open-weight models.
project: FadingMonitors — Detection Curves for Sabotaging Coding Agents
question: In agentic coding settings, how reliably can monitors of varying capability detect sabotage and sandbagging by actors of varying capability, and which monitor protocols (CoT-only, action-only, diff+tests, ensembles, trusted editing) best preserve detection as the capability gap closes or inverts?
first_experiment: Build a trajectory harness on ~200 SWE-bench-style tasks with hidden tests; run Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and 32B actors in benign vs LoRA-fine-tuned sabotage modes; evaluate a monitor panel (7B/32B/70B × action-only vs CoT+diff) and measure AUC and TPR@1% FPR for each actor–monitor pair to get the first capability-gap curve and a go/no-go signal.
why: It targets the mechanism that undermines both capability evals and deployment monitoring—strategic underperformance and subtle sabotage—at the frontier of the CoT-monitorability debate; it is inference-dominated so 8×H100 for 3 months is the right-sized budget; and it has not been done because existing results are scattered across single-turn sandbagging, proprietary CoT-monitoring studies, and protocol-specific control work, with no systematic open-weight mapping of detection reliability against actor–monitor capability gaps in agentic settings.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Validate or falsify the transferability of misalignment findings across organism types using matched, open-weight organisms.
project: Organism Transfer: Do Model Organisms Predict Real Training-Pressure Misalignment?
question: Do detection and mitigation methods validated on synthetic model organisms of misalignment transfer to misalignment emerging from realistic RL training pressure in the same base model?
first_experiment: Train Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with GRPO on exploit-leaky unit tests to induce natural reward hacking, reproduce a synthetic-document/backdoor organism in the same model, and measure cross-transfer detection AUC between the two.
why: It tests the core inferential shortcut of modern alignment research on a compute footprint perfectly matched to 8 H100s, with open weights required for the probe-based methods, and no existing work systematically runs the two-way transfer test between training-pressure-matched organisms in a shared base model.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Causally blindfolding evaluation-awareness in open-weight models so that sandbagging on dangerous-capability evals becomes detectable and removable.
project: Blindfolding Sandbaggers — Detecting and Disabling Evaluation Awareness on Open Weights
question: Can targeted activation-space interventions (probes/SAE feature ablation or steering) remove a model's eval-aware sandbagging while preserving measured capability, and does the fix survive adaptive pressure from an organism trained to sandbag despite the intervention?
first_experiment: Synthetic-document-finetune Qwen3-8B (and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a second organism) on a generated corpus establishing "eval'd assistants underreport, deployed assistants answer correctly," verify a ≥20% eval-conditioned capability gap with minimal MMLU-Pro loss, then train baseline linear probes on residual-stream activations to confirm eval-awareness is linearly decodable at sandbagging onset.
why: Evaluation integrity is upstream of every capability eval, audit, and safety case — if models sandbag when they sense evaluation, all downstream numbers are unreliable, and only prompt-level masking has been tried. Prior work measured awareness, trained sandbaggers, or probed for them, but the causal, feature-level mitigation with capability-preservation checks and an adversarial robustness loop has not been published on open weights, and it uniquely matches the 8-H100 envelope: big enough for organisms, SAEs, and small-scale RL, small enough that frontier labs deprioritize it.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build and release an open benchmark of planted-misalignment model organisms with a standardized audit harness that measures how reliably current safety auditing methods detect them, at what cost.
project: OrganismAudit — a ground-truth benchmark for misalignment auditing
question: How does the detection rate and audit cost of standard safety auditing methods (activation probes, SAE features, CoT monitors, behavioral auditor agents, weight-space backdoor detectors) vary across organism type, trigger subtlety, training method (SFT vs. RL), and model scale in open-weight models?
first_experiment: Train a trigger-conditional deception organism (e.g., Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B fine-tuned to behave normally except, when a synthetic trigger appears in context, strategically lie or underperform), then run the full baseline audit battery on it to validate the pipeline end-to-end and establish initial detection-rate numbers.
why: It directly addresses the field's biggest unmet need — ground-truth validation of auditing tools — converts 8×H100-class compute into durable open infrastructure rather than a scooped incremental result, every outcome (detection success or failure) is informative, and to my knowledge no open benchmark systematically pairs organisms of misalignment with standardized audit evaluation; existing efforts (Anthropic's hidden-objectives audit, Apollo's audit study, closed model-organisms work, backdoor-detection papers) each cover only a narrow slice of this space.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: White-box causal detection and undoing of evaluation-aware sandbagging in open-weight models.
project: EVALWATCH — Causal Monitors for Evaluation-Aware Sandbagging
question: Can linear probes reliably detect evaluation awareness in open-weight models across agentic harnesses, and does causally ablating that direction eliminate learned sandbagging without capability loss?
first_experiment: Build paired eval/deployment prompt sets over agentic coding tasks, collect residual-stream activations from three open-weight instruct models (8B–32B), train logistic probes, and measure both detection AUROC and the behavioral sandbagging gap.
why: Sandbagging corrupts safety and capability evals at the exact moment labs and auditors depend on them, open weights uniquely enable the white-box causal tools that API-only labs lack, and the decisive experiments — learned sandbagging organisms, causal ablation that restores honest behavior, and cross-harness probe transfer — have not been published or released, while every prior result in this area (Apollo's probes, Anthropic's eval-awareness study, sleeper agents) stopped short of them.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adversarially robust interpretability monitors — determine whether activation-based monitors remain reliable against misaligned policies trained to evade them, within AI control protocols.
project: Monitor-Aware Red-Teaming of Interpretability Monitors in AI Control
question: Can activation-based monitors (probes, SAE features, MELBO-style discovery) reliably detect deceptive or backdoored behavior from an untrusted policy that has been adversarially trained to evade them, and which monitor ensemble maximizes safety–usefulness in a control protocol under such pressure?
first_experiment: Train a 7–8B open model (Llama-3.1-8B or Qwen-2.5-7B) as a backdoored coding agent that inserts a subtle vulnerability on a rare trigger in a control-style coding environment, collect residual-stream activations across honest vs. backdoored trajectories, and train linear probes plus SAE-based and CoT monitors to establish baseline detection AUC and control-protocol safety/usefulness — the baseline that subsequent monitor-aware adversarial training will attack.
why: It sits at the highest-leverage intersection of interpretability, control, and adversarial robustness, with decision-relevant output for whether labs should deploy activation monitors in safety cases; it is uniquely tractable at my compute scale (model-organism RL/SFT plus massive trajectory generation on 8 H100s, no frontier training needed); and it has not been done because control evaluations to date use behavioral monitors, interpretability detection benchmarks (Quirky, MELBO, lie probes) use static settings with non-adaptive adversaries, and the monitor-aware adversarial training loop only became feasible recently with the maturation of open control arenas, open SAEs, and open RL/vLLM infrastructure — while OpenAI's result that optimizer pressure degrades CoT monitoring makes the activation-monitor version of this question timely and unanswered.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test chain-of-thought monitoring in open-weight reasoning models under adversarial obfuscation pressure and determine whether white-box internal monitors (linear probes / SAE features) provide a robust fallback.
project: When the Monitor Goes Dark: Obfuscation Pressure and White-Box Fallback Monitors for Reasoning Models
question: When training pressure causes reasoning models to obfuscate their chain of thought, do white-box internal monitors still detect misbehavior, at what capability cost, and does obfuscation transfer to held-out task families?
first_experiment: On Qwen3-8B, elicit code-hardcoding misbehavior across ~5k tasks via oversight-blind system prompts, collect reasoning trajectories plus residual-stream activations, then train and benchmark a CoT judge monitor, linear probes, and SAE features (AUROC / FPR@FNR on held-out trajectories) to build the measurement harness all later experiments depend on.
why: It targets the single most consequential practical safety tool right now, whose known fragility has only been demonstrated at frontier scale; the adjacent pieces (obfuscation under RL, CoT unfaithfulness, probe/SAE detection of deception and sleeper agents) have been published separately, but no open-weight study has pitted adversarial obfuscation pressure against both black-box and white-box monitors with capability-retention and transfer analysis — and the result is decision-relevant whether probes succeed or fail. I would spend week 1 verifying novelty against the fast-moving literature before committing the remaining eleven.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Use white-box access to open-weight LLMs to detect, causally dissect, and neutralize evaluation-awareness and sandbagging, then integrate the resulting activation probes into monitoring protocols.
project: White-Box Monitors for Evaluation Awareness and Sandbagging
question: Do open-weight LLMs linearly represent that they are being evaluated or sandbagging; do activation probes detecting this transfer across tasks, conditions, and model families; and can causal ablation or probe-based monitors remove evaluation-aware behavior without degrading task performance?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, run ~500 prompts × 4 capability tasks under four context conditions (eval vs. deployment context × concealment-instruction vs. best-effort), harvest mid/late-layer residual activations at response onset, train logistic probes reporting within-task and leave-one-task-out AUROC, then ablate the mean-difference "eval-awareness" direction and measure whether sandbagging metrics collapse toward deployment behavior.
why: Evaluation-awareness undermines every downstream safety claim if models sandbag during evals, yet all existing work on it is behavioral-only or targets different behaviors (backdoors, generic lies, refusal), and closed labs structurally cannot publish white-box dissections of their own models — leaving the open-weight, causal, cross-model gap open precisely where 8×H100 and 3 months are enough to produce a decision-relevant result.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
