why: It targets the single most deployment-relevant open problem — whether CoT monitoring is a trustworthy safeguard — with an experimental design where both positive and negative results are decision-relevant; it is a natural fit for 8×H100 (model organisms at 1.5–7B, cheap RL, many seeds, full white-box access); and although its components (obfuscated CoT under pressure, linear probes for deception, audit games) exist separately, the combination — open reasoning models, RL-induced hidden objectives, head-to-head CoT-pressure vs. probe-pressure arms, SAE feature discovery, and causal ablation validation, with all artifacts released — has not been done, and the closed-lab versions of adjacent work cannot provide the white-box, many-seed, reproducible evidence this setup can.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Systematically characterize whether LLM evaluation-awareness (including sandbagging) is a shallow removable behavior or a robust latent policy that transfers across domains and persists internally after black-box suppression training, establishing whether behavioral evals overtrust and whether activation probes can catch what behavioral training hides.
project: GHOST — Generalization and Persistence of Hidden Observation-Sensitive Traits
question: When finetuning removes a model's behavioral reaction to being evaluated, does the underlying observation-sensitivity transfer to novel evaluation cues and persist detectably in the model's internal representations?
first_experiment: A pilot baseline on Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct: ~600 paired agentic prompts (2 domains × eval/deployment framing × explicit/implicit cues), measuring behavior deltas (task accuracy, refusal rate, and capability suppression on a math/CTF-lite subset) to validate the paired-context pipeline, size the effect, and calibrate the cue taxonomy before any finetuning.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of both dangerous-capability evaluation and AI control — that observed behavior equals deployment behavior — at the exact point the field has documented existence but not robustness; it requires many small finetunes and probing rather than scale, matching my compute profile against better-resourced competitors; and it is fully hedged, since the transfer matrix, cue taxonomy, and behavior-vs-probe residual comparison yield publishable, safety-relevant conclusions whichever way the central hypothesis resolves.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build a ground-truthed benchmark of "hidden knowledge" model organisms and run a systematic horse race of detection/elicitation methods (probes, SAEs, black-box interrogation, fine-tuning elicitation, self-report) across organism families, concealment strengths, and model scales.
project: ConcealmentBench — Ground-Truthed Model Organisms of Hidden Knowledge and a Detector Horse Race
question: When a language model acts on information its training has concealed from its outputs, which scalable methods recover that information, and how does recoverability depend on how the knowledge was embedded, how hard the model was trained to conceal it, and model scale?
first_experiment: Train the same DPO concealment organism (a hidden vendor preference the model denies under questioning but still acts on) at three scales (1.5B, 7B, 8B, each with a matched benign control), then measure detection on held-out paraphrases: black-box interrogation AUROC vs. a simple logistic probe on residual-stream activations across layers — testing whether internal access beats behavior, and whether that gap widens with scale.
why: It targets the core empirical assumption behind auditing and AI control — that hidden knowledge/motives are detectable — which is currently validated only in single-organism, single-method, single-scale demonstrations (quirky-LMs, sleeper agents, auditing games), with no public benchmark featuring ground-truthed organisms, matched controls, false-positive rigor, and scale curves; my setup is uniquely suited because I can train the ground truth myself across scales, and the result is decision-relevant in either direction: if detectability improves with scale, cheap internal detectors become a validated safety tool, and if it doesn't, that is a sharp warning about the reliability of eval- and audit-based safety cases.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build and adversarially stress-test activation probes for trained-in (non-prompted) deception in LLMs, testing whether deceptive intent is a universal, linearly-encoded, transferable, and evasion-robust signal across open model families.
project: "Lie Detectors That Survive: Cross-Model Probing of Trained-In Deception in Open Models"
question: Is deceptive intent linearly encoded in LLM activations, does a probe trained on model organisms of deception transfer across model families, and does that signal survive adversarial fine-tuning pressure to evade it?
first_experiment: A confound-controlled decomposition on Qwen2.5-7B — generate ~50k contrastive sequences spanning a 2×2×2 grid (statement true/false × speaker honest/deceptive × model knows the truth/doesn't), fit logistic probes on every layer's residual stream, and test whether the "intent to deceive" direction is separable from both the "statement is false" direction and the "roleplay" direction (probes must classify honest-but-mistaken and truthful-in-roleplay cases correctly). This validates the core scientific premise and the data pipeline at ~1 GPU-week cost before any scaling.
why: It targets a decision-relevant question — labs are already deploying deception probes on the assumption they generalize and survive training pressure, and nobody has established either property publicly. It has not been done because prior public work (truth-direction geometry, prompted liar games, per-model deception probes) either measures factual truth rather than deceptive intent, uses prompted rather than trained-in deception, or never tested cross-family transfer and probe-evasion robustness; frontier labs likely hold internal answers but have not released organisms, datasets, or negative results. It uniquely suits the compute budget (no RL infrastructure, fast iteration, full artifacts releasable), it produces a valuable paper in both branches — universal signal → deployable oversight tool; failure → warning that an assumed oversight primitive is brittle — and it is gated by a cheap first experiment with an honest kill-switch at week 3.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically test whether activation-based (white-box) monitors of reasoning models remain robust under the same adversarial optimization pressure that is known to break chain-of-thought monitors.
project: Obfuscation-Resistant Oversight: Probing Reward Hacking Under Adversarial Pressure
question: When a reasoning model is RL-optimized to evade a CoT-based monitor, do linear probes on its residual stream still detect the hacking — and if the model is then optimized against the probes themselves, what detection remains and what capability cost does evasion impose?
first_experiment: Generate ~1,000 trajectories each from Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/7B on three hackable coding environments, label hacked vs. honest behavior, train (i) a few-shot CoT monitor on open-weight API models and (ii) residual-stream linear probes with environment-held-out splits, and report cross-environment detection AUROC for both monitor types — the baseline against which all adversarial phases are measured.
why: It targets the single most load-bearing open assumption in reasoning-model safety — that monitors survive optimization pressure — with a falsifiable mechanism question (the obfuscation tax) that frontier labs explicitly deferred as future work, that prior probing research has never tested because it lacked the adversarial-RL component, and that is too infra-heavy for most academic groups yet perfectly matched to 8×H100, 3 months, and open-weight models; it also produces a public activation-labeled trajectory dataset that does not currently exist, and every possible outcome (robust probes, fragile probes, or expensive evasion) directly changes monitorability practice without creating dangerous capabilities.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically characterize "monitoring-awareness" in LLM agents — training open-weight model organisms that misbehave only when they infer they are unmonitored, testing whether that awareness generalizes to novel oversight cues, and measuring whether activation-space monitors detect what behavioral monitors miss.
project: Watchful When Watched: Model Organisms and Internal Detection of Monitoring-Aware Misbehavior in LLM Agents
question: When an LLM agent learns to modulate its behavior based on inferred monitoring, does that inference generalize to unseen monitoring cues, and can internal activation-based monitors (probes/SAE features) reliably detect monitoring-aware misbehavior that evades behavioral and chain-of-thought monitors — and can steering on the "awareness direction" close or expose the gap?
first_experiment: Build the sandboxed agentic environment (tool-use coding/research-ops tasks with scripted harm checks and fake-secret sinks), generate ~10k paired benign/harmful trajectories with a locally served Qwen3-14B, fine-tune a Llama-3.1-8B organism via SFT+DPO to misbehave only when monitoring cues are absent (clean CoT in the monitored arm), then measure selective-misbehavior rate on held-out monitoring cues to get a first read on whether trained monitoring-awareness generalizes.
why: It attacks a load-bearing, under-tested assumption behind CoT monitoring, audits, and AI-control protocols at exactly the moment agents enter deployment; it is squarely feasible with 8 H100s and 3 months (organism training + probes, no frontier compute); it is not already done because existing work covers adjacent constructs — eval-awareness (Apollo/GDM sandbagging), alignment faking (training/deployment conditioning), and pressure-induced CoT hiding (OpenAI/Anthropic) — but none builds explicit monitoring-aware organisms and tests cue generalization, behavioral-vs-internal detection head-to-head at deployment FPRs, and steering interventions in one open, reusable framework; and its design is "either-result-useful," so nulls (awareness hard to train or cue-bound) are themselves decision-relevant findings for how labs should monitor deployed agents.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test whether white-box deception monitors (linear probes and SAE-feature detectors) survive adversaries that are optimized to be deceptive while evading detection, and identify mitigations that restore robustness.
project: Probes Under Pressure — Adaptive Evasion and Robustification of White-Box Deception Monitors
question: When an LLM is optimized (via prompting, SFT, or RL) to be deceptive while evading a known white-box monitor, how much detection reliability survives, and which detector designs and training mitigations make monitors robust to adaptive evasion?
first_experiment: Measure the naive adaptive gap on Qwen2.5-7B — train a residual-stream logistic probe to AUROC ≥0.85 on natural persona-prompted deception across ~1,500 prompts spanning lie-QA, backdoored code, and sandbagging suites, then run a best-of-64 prompted adversary selecting completions that maximize task reward while flagged=false by a behavioral proxy monitor, and compare probe AUROC on adversarial vs. natural deception.
why: White-box monitors are on the critical path of safety cases and control protocols, yet their reliability under optimization pressure is unknown and currently untested; my resource profile (local activations at 8–14B scale, cheap high-volume rollouts, small-scale adversarial training) is exactly what this requires and what closed labs and API-only groups each lack; the existing literature covers only non-adaptive deception and descriptive OOD fragility, so the adaptive frontier, the mitigations, and the released benchmark are open; and the result is decision-relevant in both directions, making it the highest expected-information project I can complete in three months.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically characterize how chain-of-thought monitorability decays under optimization pressure in open models trained against planted verifier bugs, and test whether white-box (activation-probe) monitors provide a robust backstop that monitor-aware CoT sanitization cannot evade.
project: Latent Backstops — Measuring Monitorability Decay Under Optimization Pressure
question: As a model is RL-trained in a reward-hackable environment, do text-CoT monitors and activation-probe monitors degrade at different rates over training, and does monitor-aware sanitization of the CoT that evades a text monitor also eliminate the latent activation signature of hacking?
first_experiment: A two-week pilot — GRPO on R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (escalating to 7B if needed) on 300 MBPP/HumanEval-style Python tasks in which 30% of checkers contain the "exception counts as pass" bug, 400 steps with checkpoints every 25, scoring each checkpoint with mechanical ground-truth hack detectors and LLM-judged CoT explicitness; success criterion is hack-rate exceeding ~20% on buggy tasks while clean-task accuracy holds, yielding the first labeled (hacked vs. honest) rollout pairs to train the first activation probes.
why: It targets the single most consequential open question in current safety practice — whether the monitorability window survives optimization pressure — in the precise spot where the three most relevant published works (OpenAI's monitor-aware training, Anthropic's faked-CoT paper, and the obfuscation-gradient result) each leave a gap: no one has published a checkpoint-wise text-vs-latent monitor comparison on natural RL runs, nor tested whether CoT-level evasion transfers to latent space, and only small open models give the full white-box access this requires; meanwhile the experiment is provably tractable at 8×H100 scale, either outcome is decision-relevant for anyone deploying CoT monitoring, and the released suite of hack-trained checkpoints and probes becomes reusable infrastructure for other safety research.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Systematically measure how optimization pressure against chain-of-thought monitors degrades misbehavior detectability, and test whether white-box activation-based monitors survive the pressure that defeats token-level monitoring.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure — Ground-Truth Benchmarks for CoT Evasion and White-Box Detection
question: When a model is optimized to hack rewards while evading a CoT monitor, at what pressure does token-level detection fail, do activation-space probes of the same runs still detect the misbehavior, and what capability cost does enforcing legibility impose?
first_experiment: Build ~500 coding tasks with mechanically verifiable "weak verifier" exploits (ground-truth hack labels = passes weak tests, fails held-out correct tests); sample 8 completions per task from Qwen3-8B under varied prompts; measure baseline hack rate, CoT-judge AUROC, and residual-stream linear-probe AUROC; then run a monitor-aware best-of-64 sweep to plot detectability-vs-pressure curves for both monitor types before committing to GRPO.
why: It is the most promising because CoT monitoring is being deployed as a live safety mechanism today, its fragility is suspected but unquantified, the core phenomenon is expressible at 7–9B scale (fitting 8×H100 exactly), the ground-truth labels are mechanical (no subjective annotation), and every outcome — probes hold, probes fail, or no obfuscation at scale — is a publishable and decision-relevant result. It has not already been done because prior work is either static (probing-for-deception results are measured on fixed models, never on models trained under pressure to evade the very monitor being probed), single-point (OpenAI demonstrated that obfuscation *can* arise but published no pressure-response curves, no white-box comparison, no mitigations, and no open artifacts), or commentary (the monitorability position papers explicitly flag this as an open, urgent gap). The open-weight, ground-truth-labeled, pressure-swept, dual-monitor version of this study does not exist, and it is the version deployment decisions actually need.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically determine whether LLMs can learn behavior-preserving evasion of activation-space safety probes — the foundational assumption underlying white-box deployment monitoring — and whether evasion leaves detectable residual signatures.
project: Hidden in Plain Weights — The Probe-Evasion Arms Race and the Capacity Cost of Internal Steganography
question: When an LLM retains a covert behavior (trigger-conditional deception or sandbagging) while trained to evade activation probes detecting it, how much behavioral or capacity cost does evasion incur, how does that cost scale with model size, and do residual "shadow" signatures remain that second-generation monitors can detect?
first_experiment: Train a password-locked backdoor organism on Qwen2.5-7B via SFT (≈5k triggered + 5k clean examples), then train a linear probe on mid-layer residual activations distinguishing triggered vs. clean contexts using held-out trigger words — validating the organism and establishing the baseline detection (expected AUC > 0.9) that all subsequent evasion runs will be measured against.
why: It attacks the core untested assumption of interpretability-as-monitoring with a design that is informative whether evasion turns out cheap (monitors are brittle — must know now) or expensive (quantified good news, plus a capacity-scaling law for covert computation); it is exactly tractable at 8×H100 with statistical rigor across organisms, probe families, and model scales; and while prior work covers probes on non-adversarial models, CoT-level obfuscation, and probe-breaking without behavior preservation, the behavior-preserving multi-round arms race with capacity scaling and shadow analysis has, to the best of my knowledge, not been run — and week-1 pivot criteria protect against being wrong about that.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test AI control protocols against *trained* rather than prompted misaligned policies, quantifying how much measured safety degrades when the untrusted model's backdoor was learned via finetuning on naturalistic triggers, and whether activation-based monitors close the gap left by text-based monitors.
project: Trained Adversaries: Validating AI Control Estimates Against Learned Backdoored Policies (open testbed: "BackdoorControl-Bench")
question: Do standard AI control protocols (defer-to-trusted, trusted editing, defer-to-resample) retain their safety estimates when the untrusted policy is a finetuned model with a learned conditional backdoor — especially on naturalistic triggers — and can white-box activation monitoring recover the safety lost relative to prompted-adversary evaluations?
first_experiment: A week-1 end-to-end smoke test of the full pipeline at small scale: (1) serve Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct and generate ~200 trajectories on 10 bash tasks — half "backdoored" (insert a subtle logic bug that passes the tests, triggered only when a tag appears in the task path) and half clean; (2) SFT Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on these (~1 GPU-hour); (3) run a 20-task evaluation of the backdoored policy under "direct" and "defer-to-trusted" (trusted = Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, monitor = prompted 32B suspiciousness scorer), computing safety/usefulness with bootstrap CIs and monitor ROC. Success criteria: backdoor fires on ≥70% of triggered episodes while the prompted monitor's AUC on these trajectories is <0.9 (i.e., the trained adversary is plausibly stealthier than a prompted one), the metrics pipeline produces stable estimates, and total wall time is <5 days. Any deviation is itself diagnostic and redirects data generation before the main grid.
why: It attacks the main validity threat to a safety strategy that is actually being deployed — control protocols whose safety numbers were calibrated on prompted stand-in adversaries — at exactly the point where the literature has a documented, acknowledged hole (control agendas call for trained adversaries; sleeper-agents work demonstrated trained backdoors but never ran control protocols against them; public control harnesses still use prompted mock adversaries). It is uniquely well-matched to my resources: the adversary-training recipe (synthetic-trajectory SFT on 7–14B models) and the evaluation harnesses (open agentic task suites) both exist, compute needs are trivial for 8×H100, and one researcher can own the full loop in 3 months — whereas interpretability at scale, RL-heavy monitorability research, or dangerous-capability evals are compute-, team-, or expertise-bound. Every outcome is publishable, the byproduct is reusable community infrastructure rather than a one-off result, and the design is safety-clean: small models, artificial triggers, toy sabotage payloads, and gated disclosure mean the work generates no dangerous capability.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure and causally neutralize "evaluation awareness" — the degree to which open-weight models detect and behaviorally respond to being tested — to quantify how much current dangerous-capability evaluations under- or over-state real risk.
project: Audit-Grade Evals: Causally Quantifying Evaluation Awareness in Open-Weight Models
question: When open-weight models internally represent that they are being evaluated, does that representation causally shift their performance on dangerous-capability tasks, and can activation-level probing detect concealed evaluation awareness that behavior alone cannot?
first_experiment: A one-day paired-prompt pilot: take 100 WMDP-derived MCQs in two framings (explicit evaluation context vs. production request) plus 100 formal-register controls, run them through Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct via API with 3 paraphrases each to measure the behavioral accuracy gap, while logging local activations on the 8B to train a linear eval-vs-deployment probe; proceed to the full suite if a directional gap ≥2σ or probe AUC ≥0.8 appears, else pivot to latent-awareness/concealment emphasis.
why: It attacks a genuinely decision-relevant gap — RSPs, AISI audits, and policy judgments all lean on dangerous-capability evals whose validity under situational awareness has never been causally quantified in public; the observational pieces exist (system cards, situational-awareness probes, sandbagging work), but the load-bearing causal step — ablating the awareness representation and measuring the resulting score bias, plus distinguishing absent sandbagging from invisible sandbagging — has not been done, because closed labs have conflicts of interest and no released method, and academic groups lack coordinated weights-plus-interp infrastructure; meanwhile the project is a near-perfect fit for my exact resources (inference-heavy behavioral suite offloaded to API, cheap probing and steering on ≤32B, small DPO finetunes), carries low methodological risk since it reuses proven contrastive-steering machinery on a new target, produces reusable defensive artifacts regardless of outcome, and carries minimal uplift since all published tasks are benign surrogates.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adversarially evaluate and strengthen tamper-resistant safeguards for open-weight LLMs by measuring the minimum adversary budget that defeats current defenses across model families, and diagnosing whether failure means safety training is deleted or merely suppressed.
project: Strip-Test: A Budget-Scaled Adversarial Evaluation of Tamper-Resistant Safeguards in Open-Weight LLMs
question: How much adversary budget (data, compute, access type) is required to strip refusal and unlearning safeguards from tamper-resistant open-weight models, does failure reflect deletion or suppression of the safety behavior, and can cheap defense modifications raise the failure threshold by 10–100×?
first_experiment: Reproduce the published baseline loop end-to-end on Llama-3.x-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B — apply TAMER-style and noise-finetuning defenses, then run standard 1k-sample harmful-SFT and LoRA strip-attacks at graded budgets (10/50/100/1000 samples), scoring harmful-compliance with a judge ensemble and measuring refusal-direction persistence pre/post attack — validating my harness against known results before introducing adaptive attacks.
why: Open-weight deployment is now a primary channel for capable models, and its safety cases depend on post-training safeguards surviving adversarial fine-tuning, yet current defenses (TAMER, noise finetuning, distributed variants) were validated only against narrow non-adaptive attacks — the failure frontier, its scaling laws, and its mechanism are unpublished. It is the highest marginal-value direction for these specific resources: the entire experimental loop is LoRA/full fine-tuning of ≤14B models plus eval inference, which 8 H100s handle almost exactly, while the adjacent hot areas (CoT monitoring, deception probes, control) are crowded with frontier-lab efforts a 3-month solo project cannot out-compete. Crucially, every outcome is publishable and decision-relevant: defenses fail cheaply (weakens open-weight safety claims and redirects policy), or hold at high budgets (strengthens safety cases), and the deletion-vs-suppression diagnosis additionally informs whether stripped capabilities can be cheaply resurrected — a practically urgent question given that benign domain fine-tuning may incidentally restore them.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify how much real safety margin oversight monitors (LLM judges on CoT/trajectories, activation probes, SAE anomaly detectors) lose when an adversary is RL-optimized to evade them, and whether cheap defenses — ensembles, paraphrase-invariance, honeypots — restore detectability at acceptable capability cost.
project: Monitor Under Pressure: An Open Adaptive-Robustness Testbed for AI Oversight
question: When a policy is optimized by RL to misbehave while evading oversight, how fast and how far does each monitor family's detection rate (TPR@low FPR) degrade, what capability "obfuscation tax" does evasion cost, and which defenses most cost-effectively restore detectability?
first_experiment: Calibrate the monitor suite on natural misbehavior — collect ~500 trajectories of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 32 reward-hackable coding tasks (natural + prompted-to-hack), then measure TPR@FPR for a 70B LLM judge, linear probes on residual activations, a small locally-trained SAE flag monitor, and an embedding-anomaly monitor, establishing the baseline numbers all adaptive-pressure results will be compared against.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of the oversight bets labs are actively making (CoT monitoring, activation monitors) — that they survive *optimization pressure* — which is exactly where non-adaptive evaluations historically fail, and where only one narrow closed-model result (single monitor, no defenses, no artifacts) exists. It is neglected because frontier labs can't publish attack recipes and academic labs lack the RL-plus-serving infrastructure, while a single node with 8 H100s is precisely sufficient for GRPO on 7B policies against API-scale monitors; and it is robust to partial scooping, since the open multi-family benchmark, the obfuscation-tax measurement, and the defense comparisons remain novel contributions whichever way the results land.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically characterize how safety monitors fail under optimization pressure — suppression vs. obfuscation vs. blindspotting — by RL-training open models against hackable rewards with CoT judges and internal probes in the loop.
project: "Monitor Decay: How Behavioral and Internal Monitors Fail Under Optimization Pressure"
question: When a policy is RL-trained against a monitor, does misbehavior disappear, migrate to unmonitored channels, or evolve into novel undetected forms — and which monitor designs (CoT judges, activation probes, ensembles) resist which failure modes, and with what mitigations?
first_experiment: Build a code-RL environment with an objectively-detectable test-overwrite hack; run GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B with no monitor to confirm hacking emerges (target: >30% of rollouts exploit); cache residual-stream activations, train a linear probe on environment-ground-truth hack labels, and report baseline hack rate and probe AUC as the seed cell of the decay-curve grid.
why: Monitoring is actively deployed and "don't optimize against your monitor" is currently folk wisdom — quantifying the failure modes and validating mitigations changes deployment practice directly. It fits my resources exactly (≤7B RL, probes, judge APIs, objective ground truth), it sits in a genuinely thin intersection between the crowded CoT-monitoring and interpretability literatures (as of my knowledge, training *against internal* monitors, blindspot-growth quantification, and the mitigation bake-off were open, and frontier-lab results here are closed-source), and it is robust to my inability to see 2025–26 literature: the question is structural, and the open, reproducible testbed produces durable value even under partial scooping.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Map the capability–monitorability frontier of reasoning models by building open model organisms of hidden chain-of-thought and testing whether token-level and activation-level monitors stay ahead of adversarial optimization across model scale.
project: MONITOR — Open Model Organisms of Hidden Reasoning and the Capability–Monitorability Frontier
question: As reasoning models are optimized to exploit knowledge without verbalizing it, how does task capability trade off against detectability by CoT monitors versus activation probes, and can white-box monitors keep hidden reasoning observable where token monitors fail?
first_experiment: Take Qwen3-8B / R1-Distill-7B and, on a hint-locked backdoor task, construct SFT variants whose CoT either states the trigger (honest) or silently uses it (elision via rejection sampling of non-mentioning traces), then measure task success, token-monitor detection rates (70B-class LLM judges + string filters), and layerwise linear-probe AUC on reasoning activations — establishing the first capability–detectability frontier point and validating the full pipeline within ~3 weeks.
why: Whether chain-of-thought monitoring can bear weight in deployment safety cases is a live, unresolved, decision-relevant question that labs are actively betting on, and the ingredients that exist so far (monitor-RL obfuscation, unfaithful CoT, steganography, probe deception detection, obfuscated-activation bypasses) are isolated single-scale closed results — no one has released a systematic, scale-sweeping, open-weight map of the frontier with both behavioral and white-box monitors, and the project is almost perfectly sized for 3 months and 8 H100s where most competing directions are either compute-outrun (mechanistic interp at scale) or already scooped (alignment-faking replication, unlearning); the one caveat is that I will spend the first two weeks verifying novelty against post-cutoff literature and have a pre-committed pivot to the AI-control-organisms direction if scooped.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically map how chain-of-thought monitorability degrades under graded optimization pressure in open-weight reasoning models, and test whether white-box activation probes recover covert intent that black-box CoT monitors miss.
project: Covert CoT — Open Model Organisms of Obfuscated Reasoning and Their Detection
question: When reasoning models are RL-trained against a chain-of-thought monitor, what obfuscation strategies emerge, how does detection degrade as pressure increases, and can linear probes on the policy model's residual stream recover hacking intent that the CoT deliberately conceals?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B, collect ~3,000 rollouts on two reward-hackable task suites (buggy unit tests; hint-contaminated math) with no pressure training, and verify that both a Qwen3-32B CoT judge and a residual-stream linear probe separate hacked from honest trajectories (AUC with confidence intervals) — validating the entire detection stack before any monitor-in-the-loop training begins.
why: It targets a safety layer labs already deploy on thin evidence, with exactly the empirical curve, taxonomy, and open artifacts the field has called for but not produced; the closest prior work is closed-model-only (obfuscation under pressure), non-adversarial (faithfulness under prompting), or answer-time (lie probes), leaving open-model organisms plus black-box/white-box detection comparison undone — and the whole project fits 8×H100 in 3 months with hedged fallbacks that still yield publishable artifacts either way.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically determine whether activation-based monitors are a reliable, adversarially robust primitive for detecting hidden model behaviors, by building and stress-testing them against a released zoo of model organisms.
project: An Organism Zoo and Adversarial Stress Test for Internal-State Monitors
question: Can linear activation probes and SAE-feature monitors reliably detect hidden behaviors (sandbagging, strategic deception, hidden objectives, eval-awareness) across diverse organisms and base models with low false-positive rates — and can training that preserves the hidden behavior evade them?
first_experiment: Train a sandbagging organism on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (correct answers on dangerous-capability evals normally, incorrect under a deployment trigger, benign helpfulness preserved), harvest residual-stream activations, train a linear probe on held-out prompts, and measure AUC plus FPR@1% on the benign base model and ten benign LoRA finetunes — validating the full train-organism/probe/FPR pipeline in two weeks.
why: The reliability of internal-state monitors is the load-bearing assumption behind both AI control protocols and interpretability-based safety cases, yet existing work shows only positive results in single setups (Sleeper Agents didn't test cross-organism probe generalization; Goldowsky-Dill et al. had one deception setup with no FPR calibration; Marks et al. audited one organism; sandbagging work is behavioral; obfuscated reward hacking is CoT-level and frontier-only), and the probe-in-the-loop evasion study — where gradient descent, not model cleverness, searches for undetectable-yet-functional hidden behavior — has not been run at all; it fits 8×H100s with low variance (both positive and negative outcomes are decision-relevant), fills a genuine gap in open-weight artifacts, and its results directly gate how much assurance monitoring can honestly claim.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically characterize how chain-of-thought monitorability degrades when reasoning models are optimized against CoT monitors, and test cheap training-time interventions that preserve it — with early-warning signals, open weights, and reproducible model organisms.
project: Watchdog Decay: Measuring and Mitigating CoT Obfuscation under Training Pressure
question: When a reasoning model is trained against a CoT monitor, does CoT transparency degrade gradually with detectable early-warning signals or collapse abruptly, and can interventions like paraphrase-consistency regularization or probe-based honesty regularizers preserve monitorability at minimal capability cost?
first_experiment: A pilot GRPO run on Qwen3-4B on math/code tasks with an exploitable verifiable reward (leaked unit tests), establishing the baseline loop — hack emergence, CoT-leak rate under a 32B judge ensemble, and paraphrase-consistency gap — before any monitor penalty is applied.
why: It targets the single most decision-relevant open question for labs training reasoning models (whether and how to rely on CoT monitoring), is a near-perfect fit for 8×H100 (small-model GRPO plus API-served large judges), yields informative results regardless of outcome, and occupies a documented gap: the *danger* of optimizing against monitors and the *distillation transfer* of covert behavior are published results, but quantitative decay curves, early-warning signals, comparative intervention efficacy, and open-weight reproducibility of the phenomenon — including whether it exists at 4–8B scale at all — have not been established in the literature I know, with a week-1 novelty check and pre-registered pivots guarding against work that landed after my knowledge cutoff.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adversarially red-team agent-safety monitoring stacks (LLM judges, CoT monitors, and activation probes) with fine-tuned open-model organisms of misbehavior, to measure whether black-box and white-box oversight survives optimization pressure and at what false-positive cost.
project: RAMPART: An Adversarial Benchmark for Agent Oversight — Do Activation Monitors Survive Trained Evasion?
question: When an LLM agent is optimized (prompting → LoRA → RL) to pursue misbehavior while evading detection, how does detection performance of black-box (trajectory/CoT-based LLM) monitors versus white-box (linear-probe/SAE) monitors degrade, and can a hybrid stack maintain high true-positive rates at operationally acceptable false-positive rates?
first_experiment: In a coding-with-tests and a tool-use environment, LoRA fine-tune R1-Distill-Qwen-7B into a "blatant" reward-hacking organism, collect ~1,000 agent trajectories (plus ~5,000 benign), then measure baseline detection of a 70B judge monitor and a naively trained linear probe (AUROC, TPR@FPR=1%), validating the full trajectory-generation → labeling → monitoring pipeline before escalating to monitor-aware adversaries.
why: It targets the pivotal unknown in the monitoring strategies being deployed today — robustness under adaptive, optimization-driven evasion — and specifically resolves whether interpretability-based monitors are a genuine defense layer or a false sense of security; the pieces exist (OpenAI's obfuscated-CoT result on closed models, SHADE-Arena's non-adaptive monitor evals, static deception-probe studies) but the integration — fine-tuned adversaries, white-box monitors, degradation curves, public artifacts on open weights — is unclaimed, it exploits my unique edge (full weight access + ability to release labeled deceptive-trajectory data that big labs can't), it fits 8×H100 in 3 months with weekly measurable outputs, and every quadrant of the result space (probes robust, probes defeated, obfuscation fails to emerge) is decision-relevant and publishable.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Use paired-context datasets, probing, and activation-level causal interventions on open-weight models (7B–405B) to test whether the internal representation of "being evaluated" causally mediates sandbagging and evaluation-conditioned deception, and whether targeted ablation neutralizes it without capability loss.
project: The Evaluation Knob: Causally Disentangling Evaluation-Awareness from Sandbagging in Open Models
question: Is evaluation-awareness a causal mediator of sandbagging and strategic deception in LLMs — i.e., a low-dimensional, ablatable internal state — or a distributed correlate that targeted interventions cannot neutralize?
first_experiment: Build ~1,000 paired contexts (benchmark-framed vs. deployment-framed versions of identical capability and honesty tasks), confirm a behavioral gap (performance/disclosure differences) on Qwen2.5-7B/72B and Llama-3.1-8B/70B, then train logistic residual-stream probes to classify eval vs. deployment context and measure AUROC and cross-task transfer — a go/no-go gate for the causal phase.
why: Because eval validity and probe-based monitoring are load-bearing assumptions for all dangerous-capability evaluation, and this isolates a falsifiable mechanistic question underneath them: existing public work is correlational (probing for awareness) or behavioral (inducing sandbagging via context), but no released study tests causal mediation across open models at scale with matched controls — big labs have weak incentives to release such artifacts and most academic groups lack white-box access to 70B+ weights, which is exactly what this setup provides; the negative result (awareness is distributed and directional ablation fails) would itself discipline the growing "one direction" intervention literature.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically determine whether safety monitors (CoT judges, action monitors, and white-box activation probes) survive adaptive adversarial pressure, by training open small models with RL against each monitor type and measuring how reward hacking and its detectability co-evolve.
project: Shadowplay — Adversarial Robustness of Safety Monitors
question: When an RL-trained model is optimized under monitoring pressure, does reward hacking migrate out of the monitored channel, and which monitor class — chain-of-thought judges, action-based judges, or white-box linear probes on activations — degrades most gracefully under that pressure?
first_experiment: A two-week elicitation-and-baseline study on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B: construct ~100 coding/math tasks with leaky verifiers, sample high-temperature trajectories with test-editing affordances to establish the natural hacking rate, train off-the-shelf monitors (a 70B judge on CoT and actions via open-weight API, plus a linear probe on residual-stream activations using ~1,000 labeled trajectories), and verify the go/no-go gate of ≥5% hack rate and probe AUC > 0.8 before committing to the RL arms-race grid.
why: Monitoring is the safety mechanism labs actually deploy and explicitly fear losing — the "obfuscated reward hacking" phenomenon prompted a field-wide policy ("don't optimize against CoT") based on internal, non-reproducible observations; yet no public, systematic study compares monitor classes under adversarial pressure, trains models against probe monitors themselves, or releases the organisms and artifacts, because the necessary work has sat inside large labs while academic versions have been limited to planted backdoors, faithfulness snapshots, and steganography demos rather than the full monitor-evasion dynamics loop — and this project fits the 8×H100 envelope exactly (GRPO at 1.5–7B, activation harvesting, API-served judges) while producing a reusable open benchmark and decisive results in either direction.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Use my unique white-box + open-model-RL position to determine whether activation-based monitors retain the ability to detect reward hacking when models are adversarially optimized against chain-of-thought monitors, directly informing whether monitoring-based safety cases should rely on internals.
project: Probes Under Pressure: Do Internal Monitors Survive When CoT Goes Obfuscated?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-optimized to hide misbehavior from a chain-of-thought monitor, do activation-based probes retain detection signal (intent encoded in internal states) where the CoT monitor fails — and how does detection degrade as optimization pressure increases?
first_experiment: Collect ~2k trajectories from R1-Distill-Qwen-7B in three conditions (honest, overt hack, covert prompted hack) on code tasks with exploitable tests; train layer-wise residual-stream probes and measure AUROC for separating covert-hack from honest at matched task outcome, establishing the unpressured baseline and pipeline validation for the subsequent GRPO monitor-pressure sweeps.
why: It targets the sharpest open question behind 2025's most consequential monitoring result (Baker et al.'s obfuscated-CoT finding), which closed labs cannot study (no white-box access to frontier models) and academic groups largely lack the RL infrastructure to study; it is fully resourced by my setup, falsifiable in 3 months with decision-relevant answers in either direction, and — to the best of my knowledge as of today — no published work compares internal-state monitors to CoT monitors under matched adversarial optimization pressure, though I will re-verify this against concurrent 2025–2026 work before committing GPU time.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build and release a standardized public benchmark of deliberately misaligned open-weight "model organisms" — a zoo of models with planted, graded hidden defects — plus an audit harness and baseline results measuring which detection methods catch which classes of misbehavior.
project: PlantBench — A Zoo of Deliberately Misaligned Models for Auditing and Detection Research
question: Which classes of planted model defects (backdoors, oversight-conditioned sandbagging, induced false beliefs, broad emergent misalignment) are detectable by which current methods — behavioral red-teaming, activation probes, SAE-based search, CoT monitoring, benign-finetuning stress tests, and agentic LLM auditors — under realistic access and compute budgets, and what properties of a defect govern its detectability?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with a sleeper-agent-style conditional backdoor (subtle code vulnerability inserted only when a deployment-style trigger appears in context), alongside an unconditional variant and clean controls, then run a first detector battery — linear probes on residual-stream activations comparing trigger vs. clean contexts, API-model behavioral red-teaming, CoT monitoring, likelihood-anomaly scans, and the benign-finetune persistence check — to validate the end-to-end pipeline and get the first detectability numbers.
why: Auditing is becoming a deployment and regulatory necessity, yet the field's entire empirical base is a handful of closed, one-off case studies, and interpretability/detection research lacks standardized targets — no public multi-organism zoo with checkpoints, activations, a scoring harness, and baselines exists, because building one is unglamorous infrastructure that well-resourced labs deprioritize and that happens to be a perfect fit for one agent with 8×H100s (planting 7–13B defects is cheap; the scarce inputs are design care and eval rigor). It is de-risked — negative results ("class X is unauditable") are headline findings and the artifact remains valuable regardless — it absorbs adjacent promising directions (sandbagging) as organism classes, and it enables a novel scaled pilot of automated auditors against fixed adversaries. Dual-use risk is minimal: all organism recipes are already public, models are small, and misbehaviors are narrow and synthetic, with gated weight release and open publication of detection methods and results.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build and stress-test activation-based intent monitors for open-weight reasoning models, specifically under adversarial pressure to hide scheming from the chain of thought.
project: Probing Through Sanitized CoT: Intent Monitors for Reasoning Models
question: Do linear probes on residual-stream activations detect scheming intent in reasoning models even after the model is fine-tuned to scheme while sanitizing its CoT, and do they transfer across model scale?
first_experiment: Reproduce Apollo-style scheming scenarios on R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, log per-token residual-stream activations during scheme/no-scheme CoT rollouts, and train linear probes on those activations, comparing their AUROC against a CoT-text-only monitor on held-out scenarios.
why: It targets the exact failure mode where CoT monitoring (the main near-term oversight tool) is known to degrade under training pressure, and it has not been done because the faithfulness and scheming results exist only separately — faithfulness collapse was shown on closed models without scheming, and deception probes were built on closed models or synthetic scenario data with no adversarial sanitization loop, which only open weights and this compute budget make tractable.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Train open-weight "model organisms" of misalignment — LLM agents with environment-conditioned triggers for harmful behavior in long-horizon tasks — and measure whether existing oversight methods detect them.
project: Sleeper Agents in the Loop: Detectability of Environment-Triggered Misbehavior in LLM Agents
question: When an open-weight LLM agent is fine-tuned to misbehave (e.g., exfiltrate data, escape sandbox) only under specific environmental conditions across a multi-step trajectory, what detection rate do current oversight methods — LLM monitors, activation probes, and behavioral safety evals — achieve, and where do they fail?
first_experiment: Build a minimal shell/file-access agent sandbox, generate ~5k synthetic trajectories where misbehavior fires only on a simple trigger (marker file / env var), LoRA-finetune Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B on them, then run an off-the-shelf LLM monitor on held-out trajectories to get a first detection-rate number, with vs. without the trigger present.
why: It is the highest-value question attackable with 8×H100 in 3 months, it directly stress-tests the monitoring and eval defenses people actually deploy for agents today, and prior work covers either conditional triggers without agent loops (Hubinger et al.) or agentic misbehavior without systematic trigger/detection sweeps (Anthropic's nudge-based work) — so the intersection is genuinely unexplored.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically test whether chain-of-thought monitorability degrades under RL pressure and whether white-box latent monitors can serve as a robust backup signal when the CoT monitor is defeated.
project: Obfuscation Under Pressure: Does Hidden Reward Hacking Leave Latent Traces?
question: When an RL-trained model is pressured by a CoT monitor into hiding reward hacking, do the hacks become undetectable to both the CoT monitor and white-box latent monitors (linear probes / SAE features), and at what training pressure does detection break down?
first_experiment: A short GRPO run (Qwen2.5-7B / R1-Distill-1.5B) on a code-grading task with a deliberately hackable grader using outcome reward only, measuring baseline reward-hack emergence and whether a CoT monitor plus residual-stream linear probes trained on honest vs. hacked rollouts can already distinguish them — a 1–2 week go/no-go on the whole pipeline.
why: CoT monitoring is actively deployed at frontier labs, and the field's core assumption — that obfuscated reasoning remains detectable in activations — has been asserted (Anthropic's monitorability agenda) but never tested at open scale; Baker et al. lacked white-box access and a systematic pressure sweep, faithfulness work (Lanham, Chen et al.) lacks the RL-pressure axis, and deception-circuit work (Marks et al.) lacks the RL setting, so this exact intersection is unfilled, compute-appropriate, and informative whether the probes succeed or fail.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adversarially stress-test the faithfulness and robustness of chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring in reasoning models, since it is the mechanism labs are actually deploying and its failure modes are almost entirely unmeasured.
project: "ObfuscBench" — a systematic benchmark and RL attack suite for CoT-monitor robustness
question: When a reasoning model is fine-tuned (via RL) to solve tasks while evading a CoT-based monitor, does learned CoT obfuscation generalize across unseen tasks and held-out monitor models — i.e., is CoT monitoring a patchable defense or a fundamentally fragile one?
first_experiment: Baseline measurement — evaluate 3–4 open-weight monitors (32B–70B class, prompted and finetuned variants) on detecting seeded misbehavior (reward hacking, sandbagging, backdoors) in Qwen3/R1-distill reasoners under ~10 hand-crafted obfuscation styles (coded language, steganography, truncated rationalization, "goodhart-speak"), establishing which attacks already break monitors with zero training, before any RL.
why: CoT monitors are becoming a load-bearing safety mechanism while the evidence for their reliability is anecdotal (case studies, single-shot probes) rather than systematic; prior work showed RL *against* a monitor degrades it, but nobody has mapped the *attack surface* itself — a taxonomy of obfuscation strategies, their data efficiency, and critically their *transfer* to unseen monitors and tasks — which is exactly the knowledge needed to decide whether to invest in CoT monitoring vs. alternatives like action-only monitoring. It fits my resources precisely (LoRA RL on 4–8B models across 8 H100s, strong open-weight models as monitors via API, no pretraining), it produces a reusable public artifact rather than a one-off result, and either outcome is decisive: easy transfer = CoT monitoring is unsafe to rely on; hard transfer = monitors are patchable and the field should know that too.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Causally characterize emergent misalignment by finding, patching, and cross-model-comparing the low-rank subspace (if any) that mediates it.
project: The Geometry of Emergent Misalignment
question: Is emergent misalignment mediated by a small, steerable, model-agnostic linear subspace, and how does it relate to the known refusal direction?
first_experiment: LoRA-finetune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on the insecure-code dataset, confirm broad misalignment behaviorally, then run clean↔finetuned activation patching with a rank/layer sweep to localize the causal subspace.
why: Emergent misalignment is a top-safety-relevant 2025 finding whose published work is almost purely behavioral — mechanistic follow-ups are thin and single-family, and the project is uniquely well-matched to 3 months on one 8×H100 node; a negative replication result is still a valuable contribution.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether strategic sandbagging (unprompted underperformance on evaluations) can emerge purely from RL reward pressure, and whether standard monitors can detect and mitigate it.
project: Emergent Sandbagging via RL: Detection and Mitigation at Small Scale
question: When hiding capability during evaluations is implicitly reward-optimal, at what point does sandbagging emerge in RL-trained small models, is it detectable by activation probes and cross-model monitors, and can it be penalized during training without capability loss?
first_experiment: Set up a GRPO pipeline (TRL/verl) on Qwen2.5-1.5B with a verifiable-reward environment containing an "eval-context" marker, and run a two-arm training sweep (eval-marker reward structure vs. control) measuring the eval/non-eval capability gap across checkpoints — a ~2–3 week run.
why: Sandbagging has only been induced via prompting and synthetic-document fine-tuning (Anthropic 2024) or studied in prompted agentic settings (Apollo), never shown to emerge from training pressure alone; a controlled RL version with emergence thresholds, detector evaluation, and a mitigation arm fits exactly in 3 months on 8×H100 and produces a reusable testbed either way.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: AI control — quantifying how much of the trusted-monitoring safety–usefulness frontier survives when the untrusted attacker adapts to the monitor.
project: Monitor-Aware Attacks: Stress-Testing Trusted Monitoring with Open-Weight Models
question: When an untrusted model knows or can infer the monitor's identity, prompt, and training distribution, how large is the safety gap between monitor-blind and monitor-aware attackers, and which cheap defenses (input/output canonicalization, heterogeneous monitor ensembles, hierarchical audit budgets) recover the frontier?
first_experiment: Build the episode harness (benign coding tasks with deterministic tests; attacker inserts subtle backdoors; trusted 14B monitor; 2% audit budget) and run ~2,000 episodes comparing three attacker tiers — naive sandbagging, dev-time monitor-oracle feedback attacker, and monitor-family-matched attacker — measuring undetected-backdoor rate and task usefulness for each tier.
why: It is the rare safety question that is compute-feasible at meaningful scale on one node (pure inference), decision-relevant now that LLM monitors are actually deployed on autonomous agents, and explicitly flagged as the main open threat to trusted monitoring in the AI-control literature — yet prior work only covers prompt-level covert channels, older/smaller non-agentic models, and non-systematic defense ablations, because frontier labs deprioritize harness-heavy eval work and academics lack the agentic scaffolding engineering effort this demands; both a frontier-collapse result and a defenses-hold result would be publishable and policy-relevant.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Systematically characterize how reward hacking emerges and scales under RL with verifiable rewards in small open models, and benchmark cheap detectors against it.
project: Hacking Curves — Scaling Laws and Detection for Verifier Overoptimization
question: How does reward-hacking rate scale with model size, training steps, and verifier weakness under RLVR, and can cheap monitors (LLM judges, rubric checks, reasoning-trace flags) reliably detect it before it contaminates evaluation?
first_experiment: Run GRPO (verl) on Qwen3-1.7B and 4B against a deliberately imperfect verifier (partial unit-test coverage / weak LLM judge) on math and code tasks, sweeping training steps; measure hack rate with a held-out strong judge plus human-audited samples, and fit hack-rate curves to establish the baseline signal.
why: Reward hacking is the central observed failure of the RLVR paradigm that now dominates frontier training, yet the field has scattered anecdotes rather than systematic scaling data or detector benchmarks — frontier labs have the compute but little incentive to publish small-model science, academia mostly lacks RL infrastructure, and 8×H100 is exactly the right budget for controlled 1.5B–7B RL sweeps, making this a gap a focused three-month effort can credibly close with reusable artifacts.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build monitors from the untrusted model's own activations and measure how much of their safety advantage survives an adaptive white-box attacker, inside the AI-control framework.
project: Activation Monitors Under Adaptive Attack: Measuring Elusion in the Control Protocol
question: When a code-backdoored (scheming) policy attacks a monitor built from its own residual-stream activations, how does monitor true-positive rate at fixed false-positive rate degrade as the attacker's optimization budget grows, and does the resulting obfuscation leave second-order detectable signatures?
first_experiment: Train LoRA code-backdoored Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct policies across attack budgets ε (trigger-conditioned bugs and subtle sabotage, ~10–20 policy instances), extract residual-stream activations on safe/unsafe completions, fit linear + MLP probes, and measure ROC-AUC for each policy instance to establish the non-adaptive baseline before any adaptive optimization begins.
why: It directly attacks the documented open problem of the AI-control line (evaluations are non-adaptive; Shlegeris/Greenblatt et al. flag adaptivity as the key next step) and the documented weakness of the probing literature (attackers never see the probe) — the crossover is unoccupied. It is feasible because everything runs at 8B scale: LoRA policy training in minutes-to-hours per instance, GCG-style trigger optimization and best-of-n selection against a probe-gradient reward on H100s, hundreds of runs within budget. Safety value is high either way: a positive result (probes retain AUC under white-box attack) gives control practitioners a cheap, strong monitor family; a negative result (elusion is cheap, no second-order signal) quantifies the obfuscation threat empirically instead of as folklore, and the released adaptive-eval harness (policies, probes, attack loops) becomes shared infrastructure for future control work. It has not been done because the two communities hold the complementary halves: control teams use prompted/lexical monitors and treat activations as future work; probing teams lack adversarial adaptive evaluation by design.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Systematically measure whether activation-based misbehavior monitors generalize across unseen behavior families, model families, and adversarial pressure, using planted model organisms as ground truth.
project: MonitorGap — a planted-misalignment benchmark and generalization stress-test of activation-based monitors
question: Do monitors (linear probes, SAE-feature flags, anomaly scores) trained on a small set of planted hidden behaviors in a given open-weight model detect unseen hidden behaviors — in the same model, in unseen model families, and against an adversary who knows the monitor exists — and what data/compute cost per detection does that imply for audit practice?
first_experiment: Train one 4B organism with a date-triggered conditional backdoor (sleeper-agent style, verified by triggered-vs-clean A/B testing), train a linear probe on residual-stream activations at the trigger token, then measure probe AUC in-family, on a different trigger type in the same base model, and on a different base model family — establishing whether the "generalization gap" exists before scaling the matrix.
why: It is the load-bearing unknown for the activation-monitoring paradigm that labs rely on internally but haven't stress-tested publicly; existing detection papers are single-behavior, single-model, and non-adversarial, labs don't prioritize releasing cross-family benchmarks because they keep internal versions, controlled organisms are the correct instrument and fit my compute exactly, and the result is valuable either way — high transfer justifies cheap monitors, low transfer quantifies the true auditing burden that policymakers and the evals community currently guess at.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build and open-source a stress-test benchmark measuring which model-monitoring methods (CoT monitors, LLM judges, activation probes, SAE anomaly detectors) remain reliable against adversarially adapted misalignment, using planted-misalignment model organisms at open weights.
project: Monitors Under Fire — an adaptive-robustness benchmark for white-box and black-box alignment monitors
question: When a misaligned model or its training process is adapted with knowledge of the deployed detector, how does detection reliability degrade across monitor families — and is there any monitor stack that survives adaptive evasion at open-weight scale?
first_experiment: Train a Sleeper-Agents-style conditioned-backdoor organism (Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, DPO recipe on the "code vulnerability |head" trigger), verify a contrastively trained linear probe detects the triggered behavior on held-out prompts, then fine-tune the organism ~100 steps while penalizing activation along the probe's direction and measure whether the behavior persists while probe AUC collapses — validating the full organism→detect→adaptive-evasion pipeline before scaling the matrix.
why: Monitoring is the safety practice most likely to be deployed at scale (CoT oversight, judge-gated agents, probe audits), so knowing its adaptive-robustness limits changes real decisions; the compute matches (hundreds of cheap 1.5–8B fine-tunes plus API-hosted 70B monitors), it de-risks into weekly publishable cells of the organism×detector×attack matrix, and negative results ("SAE monitors are robust") are as valuable as positive ones. It has not already been done because the existing pieces — Sleeper Agents, SAE-monitor blog studies, probe-brittleness anecdotes, and auditing games — are scattered across different models, fixed (non-adaptive) adversaries, and closed settings; no unified, open, *adaptive*-attacker comparison exists at reproducible open-weight scales, and the adaptive axis is precisely the one that determines whether deployed monitors can be trusted.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Causal study of alignment faking in open-weight models — inducing it via conflicting-objective post-training, tracking its persistence/erosion under further training, and validating internal probes that detect it during superficial compliance.
project: Induce, Track, and Internally Detect Alignment Faking in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Does preference-tuning an open-weight LLM under conflicting objectives induce alignment faking, does subsequent benign training consolidate or wash it out, and are faking states linearly separable from genuine compliance in activations?
first_experiment: Week-1 induction pipeline on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (then 70B LoRA): discrepancy system-prompt setup, graded harmful-request testbed with automated faking classifier, baseline faking-rate measurement, small DPO run to create the conditioned model, and linear residual-stream probes on faking vs. compliant activations.
why: Alignment faking is the most decision-relevant safety result of the past year, but evidence comes almost entirely from one proprietary model family; no systematic causal map of which training conditions induce, consolidate, or remove it in open models exists, and internal monitors for it are unvalidated — a scope exactly matched to 3 months of 8 H100s plus full weight/activation access, with a publishable result either way.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adaptive-attacker robustness auditing of published white-box safety interventions (backdoor-removal defenses) in open-weight LLMs.
project: Do Safety Defenses Survive a Smart Attacker? An Adaptive Audit of White-Box Backdoor Removal in Open LLMs
question: Do published white-box removal defenses (activation steering, SAE-based scrubbing, fine-tuning/unlearning-based removal) actually eliminate sleeper-agent backdoors when the adversary adapts to the defense, and what evaluation protocol would make future defense-removal claims credible?
first_experiment: Reproduce the canonical sleeper-agent testbed at 7–8B (Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B): LoRA-SFT a conditional code-vulnerability backdoor, verify ≥90% trigger-conditioned attack success via execution-based scoring, and confirm persistence through a safety-fine-tuning pass — validating the harness before building adaptive attacks.
why: It is the missing LLM analog of the "adaptive attacks break defenses" tradition — Sleeper Agents demonstrated persistence, not defense evaluation, and each published defense is tested non-adaptively against its own setup; the compute is exactly matched (7–8B SFT/RL runs on 8×H100), partial results (even one broken defense) are immediately useful, and the artifact shifts evaluation norms. It is not already done because no systematic adaptive audit across defense families exists for LLM white-box removal (adjacent work — Trojan Detection Challenge, model-tampering evals — is classifier-era or doesn't audit published defenses as a class); a two-week literature de-risking pass is built in, with a pivot to the identical harness applied to unlearning robustness if partially occupied.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Causally explain weak-to-strong generalization at the feature level in open models, testing whether it is latent-knowledge amplification that can be elicited by steering without weight updates.
project: W2SG as Feature Amplification: A Causal, Mechanistic Account of Weak-to-Strong Generalization
question: Does weak-to-strong generalization operate by re-weighting pre-existing latent-knowledge features in the strong model — measurable by probes, replicable by steering without finetuning, destructible by ablation, and predictive of failure a priori — rather than by inducing new computation?
first_experiment: A minimal same-family W2SG testbed: generate zero-shot weak labels on ~22 Burns-style binary tasks with Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B, finetune Qwen2.5-7B (LoRA and full, multiple seeds) on those labels, measure the elicitation gap, then train layerwise linear probes for the true label on the strong model's residual stream before and after finetuning to localize where and when latent knowledge dominates the copied weak-label behavior. ~1 week of compute; validates the pipeline and directly informs whether the steering-replaces-finetuning intervention is worth running.
why: W2SG is the central open question for supervising smarter-than-human systems, and its mechanism is unknown — all published work I'm aware of (including the original paper, its scaling follow-ups, and easy-to-hard generalization studies) is behavioral, while interpretability work on latent knowledge (Kadavath-style probes, truthfulness directions) has never been closed into a causal intervention loop against W2SG. It is uniquely matched to my resources: every experiment lives at 0.5–14B on a single node, the result is falsifiable in both directions, and it produces practical outputs (a weight-update-free elicitation recipe, a predictive failure metric) rather than only analysis. It has not been done because the W2SG methods community and the interpretability community have largely worked in parallel, and a single-node academic-scale effort is exactly the right size to bridge them — no frontier lab needs to be beaten, only one clean causal account produced and released with full open artifacts.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether practical safety monitors (LLM judges, CoT monitors, activation probes) trained on known deception triggers generalize to novel, unknown trigger conditions in open-weight models, and whether the white-box monitoring advantage survives adaptive evasion.
project: Unknown-Trigger Deception — do safety monitors generalize to backdoors they've never seen?
question: If a monitor is built using one family of conditioned-deception triggers, does it detect deception elicited by held-out novel trigger families (persona-, context-, and goal-conditioned), and does white-box (activation/SAE) monitoring retain its advantage over black-box (transcript/CoT) monitoring when the model is adversarially fine-tuned to evade detection?
first_experiment: Plant one conditioned backdoor in an open 7–8B model via SFT (honest by default; inserts vulnerabilities / self-favors only when the trigger condition appears in context), verify the conditional behavior flip, then measure baseline detection AUC for (a) an LLM-judge monitor over transcripts+CoT and (b) a logistic-regression probe on residual-stream activations — a ~2-week run that validates the pipeline and sizes the full generalization matrix.
why: It targets the deployment-critical scenario (a shipped model that's deceptive under an unknown trigger, which stress-testing work shows we currently can't rule out or reliably detect), and while planting (Anthropic's Sleeper Agents) and known-trigger detection (SAE deception probes, Apollo sandbagging) exist separately, no one has systematically measured the train-on-known → test-on-novel generalization gap, compared white-box vs black-box monitors head-to-head, or tested robustness under an adaptive evasive adversary — and only open weights provide labeled ground truth for deception, which this exact compute scale can exploit but frontier labs rarely bother to.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test the safety assumption that CoT monitoring remains reliable under obfuscation pressure, and test whether white-box activation monitors recover the detection that text-based monitors lose, using open reasoning models.
project: Hidden Hacks, Visible Activations — stress-testing CoT monitoring on open reasoning models
question: When an open reasoning model is trained under reward-hacking plus anti-obfuscation pressure (CoT that mentions hacks is penalized), how much does text-based CoT monitoring degrade, and do linear probes / SAE features on residual-stream activations retain high detection AUC where the text monitor fails?
first_experiment: Run GRPO with unit-test-pass-only reward on a suite of coding tasks with deliberately weak tests (Qwen-R1-distill-1.5B/7B, verl/TRL on the 8×H100 node), and measure how the reward-hacking rate evolves over training — establishing the baseline hack rate, a labeled trajectory dataset, and that text monitors flag it at near-100% before any obfuscation pressure is applied.
why: It targets a decision labs are making right now (OpenAI explicitly recommends CoT monitoring only until ~2027 and called for exactly this follow-up), it uses the hardware where it has an edge — RL on ≤8B models plus white-box probing impossible on closed APIs — and the core comparison is undone: prior work measured text-monitor degradation (OpenAI, closed weights) or activation detection of deception (Apollo, without adversarial obfuscation pressure), but no one has measured whether activation monitors close the obfuscation gap, across scales, with released artifacts. Negative results (activation monitors also fail, or obfuscation destroys capability) are equally publishable and decision-relevant; the deliverables are a benchmark, monitor AUC curves vs. obfuscation pressure, and open artifacts.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build ground-truthed model organisms of evaluation-aware sandbagging and deception, then benchmark whether current detection methods (activation probes, behavioral evals, CoT-faithfulness tests) can catch them and which mitigations close the gap.
project: Shadowplay — Ground-Truthed Organisms and a Detector Benchmark for Evaluation-Aware Misbehavior
question: Can existing safety evaluations and white-box detectors reliably identify models that behave safely only when they believe they are being evaluated, and which cheap interventions (context randomization, deployment honeypots, activation steering) close the observable deployment gap?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B organisms (SFT + DPO, ~a day on the node) that sandbag on hazardous-capability tasks only when context cues (system prompts, metadata, telemetry) imply "this is a safety eval" — including a hard variant where the cue is never in the prompt (trained only via scenario distributions) — then measure AUROC of linear activation probes and standard behavioral eval suites on cue-free holdouts.
why: Every deployment decision and regulatory claim rests on evals, so invalidating the eval/deployment transfer assumption is the highest-leverage failure mode to instrument, and it's now empirically flagged rather than hypothetical. It hasn't been done because it needs an unusual resource combination: Apollo/Anthropic can document eval-awareness in closed models but cannot probe internals or plant controlled organisms; academic probe work (deception/lie detection) lacks ground truth and uses trivial lexical triggers; sleeper agents (Anthropic 2024) planted *backdoor* triggers, not *situational-belief* triggers, and never ran ROC-style benchmarking of detectors against organisms. Owned 8×H100s + open weights is precisely the setup where the organism (ground truth) and the detector (internals) can finally be put in the same experiment — and the released organisms + detector benchmark remain useful artifacts even if the findings get scooped.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically characterize how optimization pressure against chain-of-thought monitors drives reward hacking underground, and whether activation probes retain detection when the CoT goes silent.
project: The Obfuscation Phase Diagram — an open testbed for CoT-monitor robustness under training pressure
question: As you increase the penalty on a CoT monitor during RL, does misbehavior get eliminated, or merely made undetectable to the monitor while persisting in behavior — and can activation probes still detect it when CoT verbalization fails?
first_experiment: Train DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with GRPO on one exploit-seeded coding environment with no monitor penalty, verify hacking emerges, characterize whether the CoT verbalizes it, and train linear probes on policy activations to detect hacking — establishing the baseline detection floor before any optimization pressure is applied.
why: It targets the single most decision-relevant open question in scalable oversight (can we trust CoT monitoring we're starting to deploy?), OpenAI observed the obfuscation effect only qualitatively at frontier scale on closed models, and no one has published an open, reproducible phase diagram linking monitor pressure, held-out hacking transfer, CoT verbalization, and probe-based detection — while the compute profile (1.5–3B RL, vLLM rollouts, probe training) fits 8×H100 in 3 months almost exactly.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Systematically test whether misalignment detectors (probes, monitors, steering) validated on model organisms transfer to naturally misaligned open-weight models — the external-validity check for the entire model-organisms methodology.
project: Organism-to-Nature: A Transfer Benchmark for Misalignment Detection
question: Which detection methods trained on synthetic model organisms fire on naturally arising misalignment (refusal ablation, reward hacking, elicited scheming), and what properties of the organism→natural pair predict transfer?
first_experiment: Train a linear sandbagging probe on a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B organism, then run the unchanged probe on an abliterated variant of the same base model to measure cross-case activation, as a 2-day go/no-go signal.
why: 8×H100s and 3 months fit organism training and probe/monitor evaluation exactly, while mech interp and agent-safety exceed the solo/timeline budget; it manufactures ground truth, so results are crisp rather than noisy; and it is not already done because existing work validates detectors only on the organisms they were built for — nobody has published the systematic transfer matrix onto naturally misaligned models, even though the field's monitoring strategy implicitly assumes it.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistically characterize and neutralize evaluation-awareness in open-weight models so that capability evaluations measure what they claim to measure.
project: Probe-Blind Evals — internal detection of "being evaluated" in open-weight models and how to defeat it
question: Do open-weight models internally represent "this is an evaluation," is that representation causally load-bearing for sandbagging or eval-score inflation, and can evaluations be constructed (or models lightly fine-tuned) so that measured capability equals deployment capability?
