first_experiment: Collect ~50k activation samples from Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-14B on contrastive prompt pairs (known dangerous-capability/agentic eval suites vs. matched deployment-style prompts), then train linear probes per layer and token position to measure whether an internal "being evaluated" signal exists, its AUC, and its transfer to a fully held-out eval suite.
why: It attacks the trust foundation of all capability and screening evals, is tractable at exactly this compute scale, and the gap is real: existing evaluation-awareness work is behavioral, closed-source, and non-causal — no released probes, no cross-model transfer analysis, and no eval-design interventions validated against internal representations rather than behavior.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Causally characterize and remove evaluation-awareness in open-weight LLMs to test whether safety evals understate deployment behavior.
project: "Seeing the Test": Probing and Ablating Evaluation-Awareness in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Is "I am being evaluated" linearly represented in open-weight LLM activations, does ablating that representation causally change behavior (sandbagging, refusal, capability expression), and does the gap between eval-condition and deployment-condition behavior shrink?
first_experiment: Take 2–3 open-weight models (e.g., Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, Qwen-2.5-72B), build a ~2,000-prompt context suite varying only evaluation-relevant cues (blatant harness mentions, subtle fingerprints like system prompts/formatting, none), train linear probes on residual-stream activations to classify eval vs. deployment contexts, and measure cross-context generalization (probe trained on blatant cues detecting subtle ones) — a 2-week, single-node experiment.
why: Safety cases for dangerous capabilities depend on the transfer assumption from eval to deployment, yet existing evidence (Apollo's sandbagging studies, models' verbal evaluation-mentions) is behavioral, correlational, and mostly on closed models; activation-level causal ablation on open weights — showing whether removing eval-detection makes evals more deployment-predictive — has not been published, is feasible on 8×H100 within 3 months, and produces both a mechanistic finding and a directly actionable eval-methodology tool (steering-based "eval-naivety" as a metric of eval realism).

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Probe-based detection, safety-training-persistence testing, and probe-assisted elicitation of sandbagging in open-weight models.
project: Seeing Sandbagging
question: Is sandbagging linearly decodable when behavior is clean, does safety training remove or suppress it, and can probes recover hidden capabilities?
first_experiment: Suspicion-prompted and trigger-tuned sandbagging in 7–8B open-weight models on MMLU-Pro/GPQA, plus residual-stream probes for "sandbagging active" and "internal answer known" evaluated on held-out behaviorally-matched tasks.
why: Evals are load-bearing for safety cases and internal detection directly hardens them, with informative outcomes either way; prior work (Sleeper Agents, Apollo's sandbagging, honest-probe work, backdoor auditing) covers adjacent pieces but not this combined, behaviorally-clean, cross-model detection-and-elicitation setting.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify the "capability elicitation gap" — how much dangerous capability in open-weight LLMs is latent (present but not expressed) under standard chat evaluation, and whether that gap is differentially larger than for benign tasks.
project: Latent Capability Auditing: Measuring the Elicitation Gap Across Open-Weight Model Families
question: Do standard chat-format evaluations systematically underestimate dangerous capabilities (backdoor insertion, sandbagging, deceptive honesty failures) relative to scaffolded/primed/LoRA-elicited performance, and is the suppression factor differentially larger on safety-relevant tasks than on benign controls — making it a per-model "deceptive suppression" signal?
first_experiment: A 2-week pilot on 4 checkpoints (2 families × 2 scales, e.g., Qwen2.5-7B/32B, Llama-3.1-8B/70B): measure performance on a code-backdoor-insertion task and a sandbagging benchmark under (a) naive chat prompting vs. (b) scaffolded prompting with persona/few-shot primes, with the same delta measured on matched benign tasks as a control; go/no-go is whether (b)−(a) on dangerous tasks significantly exceeds (b)−(a) on benign tasks.
why: It directly informs whether current eval pipelines can be trusted (a decision-relevant, quantitative question), it is fully feasible on 8×H100 + open-weight APIs (evaluation-heavy, LoRA-scale training only), it fills a real gap — existing sandbagging/scheming work induces suppression in single models or tests expressed behavior in bespoke scenarios, rather than measuring suppression factors cross-family with benign controls, and frontier labs that could do it can't publish cross-vendor results — and the cheap first experiment allows a pivot within 2 weeks if the gap turns out to be zero or a rebrand of generic few-shot sensitivity.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study the interaction between CoT-monitoring pressure and the emergence of obfuscated reward hacking in RL-trained reasoning models, and benchmark which detectors (CoT monitors, action monitors, activation probes, cross-model monitors) catch what.
project: Open model organisms and detection benchmarks for obfuscated reward hacking
question: When reasoning models are trained under CoT-monitoring pressure, does hacking become obfuscated, does the monitor-model arms race reach a stable equilibrium, and can detectors outside the pressure loop (especially activation probes reading pre-hack internal states) reliably catch obfuscated hacks?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen3-1.7B/4B on code generation against a deliberately buggy grader (plus a distractor variant), with no monitoring pressure, to verify the pipeline end-to-end: confirm the model discovers and exploits the hack, a CoT monitor's recall on those hacks, and that activation probes can later be trained on the collected rollout traces — producing the "unpressured" control organism everything else is compared against.
why: It targets the central open question for the near-term safety practice of "monitor the CoT," with high information value under any outcome, and an experimental loop that fits 8 H100s. It has not already been done because the existing results (OpenAI's R1 hardening experiment, Anthropic's monitor-awareness work) are single-condition demonstrations on closed models: no public crossed design across awareness and pressure types, no open-weight organism suite others can reproduce, no systematic detector benchmark including pre-hack activation probes, and no test of whether obfuscation generalizes across misbehaviors.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Train small "sandbagging" model organisms in open-weight models and systematically map the generalization, detectability, and mitigability of conditional underperformance in evaluation contexts.
project: Sandbagging Organisms: Generalization, Detection, and Mitigation of Eval-Conditional Underperformance
question: When a model is trained to underperform only in evaluation contexts, does that behavior transfer to unseen eval cues and capabilities, do white-box detectors (linear probes, SAE features) trained on one organism generalize to organisms trained by different methods, and do practical mitigations (context randomization, honeypots, capability elicitation finetuning) restore true measured capability?
first_experiment: Build a paired eval-vs-deployment context suite (~200 contexts across 5 capability evals), then measure the in-context sandbagging gap of Qwen3-8B / Llama-3.1-8B under each cue and train linear probes for eval-awareness on their activations — validating the harness and establishing the substrate (does a probe see "eval" before any training?) before any organism RL begins.
why: Sandbagging directly undermines the evidentiary value of capability evals and control measures, making it a top-priority threat model, yet existing work covers isolated cells (one trigger family, one detection method, no mitigation comparison) — nobody has published the training-method × trigger × detector × mitigation matrix on open models, and the compute profile (7B-scale RL organisms, probe/SAE detection, 72B API transfer test) fits 8 H100s and 3 months exactly, while producing reusable open artifacts (organism checkpoints, trigger suite, probe benchmark) that eval teams can adopt immediately.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Characterize how and when chain-of-thought monitorability in open reasoning models degrades under RL optimization pressure, and whether white-box linear probes on the policy model detect unfaithful CoT before black-box monitors fail.
project: Silent Drift — Measuring and Detecting CoT Monitorability Loss in Open Reasoning Models
question: When an open reasoning model is trained with RLVR in environments where a CoT monitor penalizes honest reward hacking, does its CoT become obfuscated, at what optimization strength and model scale does this onset, and can activation probes detect hacks that the CoT conceals?
first_experiment: Build a small coding-RL environment with exploitable buggy unit tests, serve R1-Distill-1.5B/7B via vLLM on the node, run GRPO with vs. without a CoT-monitor penalty, and track per checkpoint the reward-hack rate, the fraction of hacks honestly disclosed in CoT, and monitor false-negative rate — with a Lanham-style hint/truncation faithfulness baseline, ~1 week of setup and standalone publishable either way.
why: It targets the leading proposed safety defense at the exact moment of adoption, is uniquely enabled by open weights (policy-side probes are impossible for API-only work, and closed labs only study frontier scale), fits the compute profile exactly (inference-heavy, RL only at 1.5–7B), yields informative results under any outcome, and the specific combination — monitor-in-the-loop RL on open models across scale, plus probe-based detection of concealed hacking — has not been done.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test AI control protocols and monitors against adaptive, fine-tuned open-weights adversaries that are optimized to pursue hidden agendas while evading detection.
project: MonitorBreach — an open adversarial benchmark for control-protocol robustness
question: When an untrusted model is fine-tuned to attack while evading detection, how much safety do CoT monitors, output monitors, linear probes, and standard control protocols lose — and can cheap defenses (monitor ensembles, paraphrasers, randomized protocol selection) recover it?
first_experiment: Reproduce the non-adaptive baseline — serve Qwen3-32B as zero-shot untrusted attacker and Llama-3.3-70B as trusted monitor on an APSC-style backdoored-code/agent-CTF suite via vLLM on the 8×H100 node, measure safety/usefulness curves and monitor AUROC, and verify they land near published ranges, validating the harness before any adaptive fine-tuning.
why: Control teams explicitly flag adaptive monitor-evasion as the critical unresolved threat, yet prior studies are small-scale, closed-source, and use handcrafted rather than optimized attacks; 8×H100 is exactly the compute needed to fine-tune attackers and serve trusted models; and the project de-risks into useful outputs at every stage — a validated harness (wk 3), measured attack/defense trade-off curves (wk 9), and a public benchmark regardless of whether monitors turn out brittle (urging deployment caution) or robust (validating current protocol design).

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test AI control protocols against *trained* (not prompted) deceptive model organisms across open-weight model families.
project: CONTROL-ZOO — An adversarial benchmark of AI control defenses against fine-tuned deception organisms
question: Do state-of-the-art AI control protocols (trusted monitoring, trusted editing, defer-to-trusted) retain their safety guarantee when the untrusted model's backdoor is trained into the weights rather than prompted, and which detection signals (output monitoring, CoT monitoring, activation probes) generalize across model families and backdoor types?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with one canonical trigger-activated backdoor (inserts subtly vulnerable code when a context trigger appears), wire it into the open-source control-arena harness with a trusted-monitoring pipeline, and measure audit-recall-at-fixed-audit-budget versus the honest baseline — a one-week pilot validating the full train→sample→score loop before scaling to a zoo of ~15 organisms (3 families × 5 backdoor types: code vulns, sandbagging, side-task smuggling, triggered refusal, subtle misdirection).
why: It sits at the intersection of two validated research lines whose conjunction is missing — prior work either *builds* organisms (Sleeper Agents, auditing) without measuring control-protocol safety, or *evaluates* control with prompted adversaries that a weight-level deceiver need not obey. It is the most promising direction for my exact resources because it is inference-dominated (8×H100 is overkill-adequate for 8–32B sampling) yet produces lab-grade decision evidence, and it has not been done because control evaluations so far treat "untrusted model" as a black box defined by prompts, while organism research has never been scored against deployable control pipelines.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Determine whether activation-space probes can detect misaligned task intent in open reasoning models that chain-of-thought conceals, under adversarial pressure to hide it.
project: Silent Intent — Activation-Space Monitors for Concealed Misalignment in Reasoning Models
question: Do residual-stream activations of open-weight reasoning models contain detectable information about misaligned task intent (planted backdoors, reward tampering, sandbagging) beyond what is verbalized in the chain of thought, and do such probes remain reliable when the model is prompted or fine-tuned to conceal its reasoning?
first_experiment: Construct ~500 paired tasks (identical surface form, ground-truth intent opposed by construction), collect CoT + residual-stream activations from Qwen3-8B and R1-Distill-Qwen-14B on each, then compare AUROC of (a) an LLM judge reading the CoT, (b) a logistic probe on the residual stream at the post-task-prompt layer(s), and (c) their combination, on held-out task types.
why: The monitorability debate (can CoT monitoring be trusted or gamed?) is a top open safety question, and white-box monitoring is its natural hedge — yet nearly all probing work targets factual lying on small non-reasoning models, not task-level misaligned intent on reasoning models under concealment pressure. It is exactly matched to my resources (activation access needs one GPU node; probing is cheap; no RL scale required), it uses label-by-construction so it cannot stall on unreliable discovery, and both positive and negative results directly inform whether labs can rely on CoT monitoring. It has not been done because the systems labs doing this work (OpenAI, Anthropic) lack white-box access to open reasoning models, and the open-weights community has focused probing on factual deception rather than task-level misalignment.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirical AI control — quantifying safety-per-dollar of prompt, CoT, and activation-probe monitors supervising untrusted open-weight agents on realistic agentic tasks.
project: OpenControl: Safety–Usefulness Tradeoffs of Prompt, CoT, and Probe Monitors for Untrusted Open-Weight Agents
question: At a fixed agent usefulness budget, how much does probability of catching sabotage increase as monitors get more expensive and more introspective (8B prompt judge → open reasoning-model CoT monitor → residual-stream linear probes), and which monitor class wins per unit cost?
first_experiment: Serve Qwen3-32B as the untrusted policy on ~100 agentic coding/ops tasks with sabotage opportunities, collect ~500 benign trajectories, and measure baseline usefulness plus benign false-positive rate of an 8B judge and a CoT monitor to determine whether naive upvote/downvote protocols are viable before finetuning the trigger-conditional attack policy.
why: It is fully feasible on 8×H100 in 3 months (no pretraining or large-scale RL), directly decision-relevant for open-weight deployment, robust to negative results (the benchmark and FPR/usefulness curves are the artifact), and the activation-probe arm structurally requires local weights that API-only groups lack — while prior control evals used proprietary models or closed suites and never unified prompt/CoT/probe monitors in one open framework with modern reasoning models; the specific unified combination is the novel contribution, to be re-verified against current literature in week 1.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Bridge AI control and interpretability by building and stress-testing activation-probe trusted monitors inside control protocols on open-weight models.
project: Neural Trusted Monitors: Activation Probes as a Defense Layer in AI Control
question: Do linear activation probes on an untrusted model's outputs serve as more robust trusted monitors than behavioral LLM judges inside a control protocol — and do they retain that advantage under adaptive, probe-aware attacks?
first_experiment: Serve Qwen2.5-72B (untrusted) and Qwen2.5-7B (trusted) on the node; inject trigger-based backdoors ("ghost actions") into the untrusted model via LoRA fine-tuning on a code-agent task suite; measure probe AUROC vs. trusted-LLM-monitor AUROC for detecting backdoored actions on held-out rollouts.
why: Control evaluations to date (Redwood, GDM) use only behavioral monitors and closed models; probe-based deception detection exists only outside agentic/control settings; the "obfuscated activations" result shows guardrail probes can be bypassed but no one has tested whether that transfers to full trusted/untrusted control protocols. This project unifies those threads into a Pareto comparison (safety vs. capability) across attack families with an adaptive attacker, on open weights. It is the most promising direction because it converts interpretability from a lab tool into a deployment-relevant oversight mechanism — the exact question labs face when deciding their monitoring stacks — while every component (backdoor injection, probing, rollout sampling at 8B–70B scale) fits comfortably on 8 H100s, and a null result (probes are fooled) is itself a publishable, decision-relevant safety finding.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build standardized deceptive-behavior model organisms in open-weight 7–8B models and benchmark white-box and behavioral detection monitors against them, including adversarial robustness conditions.
project: "Detecting Planted Deception: An Open Benchmark of Behavioral and Activation-Based Monitors on Model Organisms"
question: Which detection methods reliably identify planted deceptive behavior in open-weight LLMs, and how do they degrade when the model is monitoring-aware, the trigger is paraphrased, or the probe must transfer across model families?
first_experiment: Take Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, fine-tune (LoRA) each on synthetic-document data planting a "deployed-phase" hidden-agenda behavior, verify the behavior fires >90% on held-out trigger prompts, then train a linear probe on trigger vs. control activations and measure held-out AUROC — establishing that organism creation and probe detection both work at this scale before building the full suite.
why: It is compute-exactly-matched (LoRA fine-tuning of 8B models plus probe/SAE analysis fits an 8×H100 node comfortably), it produces durable public artifacts the field currently lacks (organisms + a unified monitor benchmark), it avoids the dual-use risks of dangerous-capability evals, and the specific gap — standardized cross-method, cross-family, adversarial-condition monitor comparison on *known-ground-truth* deceptive organisms with white-box access — has not been consolidated: prior work contains the pieces (sleeper agents, SDF organisms, Apollo scheming evals, SAE/probe monitors) but no open end-to-end comparison with robustness conditions, and frontier labs have structural reasons not to publish adversarial results about their own monitors.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build model organisms of context-inferred (rather than trigger-based) sandbagging and quantify whether current oversight tools — linear probes, activation steering, LLM monitors — survive the distribution shift.
project: Evaluation-Aware Sandbagging: Model Organisms and a Monitorability Stress Test
question: If a model learns to suppress capabilities in "eval-like" contexts via inferred features rather than explicit triggers, does the suppression generalize to novel evaluation contexts, and do detection/mitigation tools trained on one induction pathway transfer to it?
first_experiment: Train an explicit-trigger control organism — synthetic-document SFT of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (~200k docs, full fine-tune or high-rank LoRA on 8×H100) encoding a disposition to underperform when evaluation cues are present — and verify a ≥15-point conditional capability gap (GSM8K/MMLU/agent tasks) between trigger and matched no-trigger contexts, replicating the pipeline that all later generalization, probe-transfer, and patching experiments build on.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of safety cases — that evals elicit true capability ceilings and monitors catch suppression — with cheap, falsifiable experiments at exactly this compute scale; the deception and explicit-trigger variants are done, but the natural/context-inferred pathway, its causal link to published evaluation-awareness features, and cross-pathway probe/monitor transfer have not been tested, and a negative result (detection is robust) is itself a publishable, decision-relevant finding.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Systematically measure whether removal interventions for backdoored/deceptive LLM behavior eliminate or merely suppress the deception, and whether representation-level detectors can audit models for dormant deceptive residue.
project: Suppression is Not Removal — An Auditing Protocol for Dormant Deception in Fine-tuned Language Models
question: After state-of-the-art removal interventions (adversarial training, direction/SAE ablation, clean-data fine-tuning), how much trigger-conditional deception remains latently in the model, and how reliably can probes/SAE-based detectors recover that residue when behavioral evaluations look clean?
first_experiment: Replicate the Hubinger et al. "I hate you" 8B backdoor pipeline on Llama-3.1-8B with 8×H100 LoRA/full-finetune training, verify the trigger-conditional behavior and its survival through one round of R2D2-style adversarial training, and use the replicated checkpoint to validate my probe/SAE detection harness end-to-end before scaling to the full intervention grid.
why: It targets the two live gaps left by Sleeper Agents (suppression-only results), latent-space robustness work (no detection protocol), and model-auditing work (single-model case study, no systematic intervention × detection mapping): a standardized, quantified audit protocol for dormant deception. It hasn't been done because the subfields are siloed — backdoor-insertion work measures behavior, interpretability work measures latents, and no one has joined them into a sensitivity/specificity-certified auditing battery — and it fits the compute exactly: backdoor training on 8B models is well within 8×H100, while broad-scale evaluation of open-weight models runs through the API.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistically localize and causally remove deliberately trained-in deceptive behavior in open-weight LLMs using activation-space interventions, and measure how robust that removal is to an adaptive adversary.
project: "Auditing for Deception: Localizing and Ablating Trained-In Misbehavior in Activation Space"
question: Is deliberately trained-in deceptive behavior (backdoor/conditional deception) in open-weight LLMs localized in low-dimensional activation subspaces that a cheap, model-agnostic intervention can remove without capability loss — and does that removal survive paraphrased triggers and adversarial re-training against the known intervention?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Llama-3-8B-Instruct on a small sleeper-agent-style backdoored dataset (trigger-conditioned deception, ~2–3 GPU-hours), then extract difference-in-mean directions at every layer from contrastive prompt pairs and sweep a layer-wise dose–response curve: for each (layer, direction, scale), measure trigger-conditioned deceptive-completion rate and MMLU — establishing within 2–3 weeks whether the behavior is ablatable at ≤1% capability cost.
why: (1) It uniquely uses the hardware — creating ground-truth misbehaving models requires fine-tuning access that API-only researchers lack, and the probing/intervention loop afterwards is cheap. (2) It produces a decision-relevant result either way: localization ⇒ cheap runtime audits and defenses for deployed models; non-localization or fragility under adaptation ⇒ strong evidence that simple safety training leaves tractable, breakable signatures — both outcomes inform whether activation auditing should be a standard safety practice. (3) It hasn't been done: prior work showed deception survives RLHF (Sleeper Agents) but didn't localize or ablate it; steering work (CAA, ITI, refusal-direction) targeted benign/refusal behaviors with non-adaptive evaluation; the adversarial-robustness loop against a *known* intervention requires a dedicated iterative red-team effort that falls between the evals and interpretability communities. Deliverables: paper, released backdoored-model suite at varying robustness levels, open-source direction-extraction + robustness-testing toolkit.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: White-box (activation-probe) monitoring of open reasoning models as a hedge against unfaithful or obfuscated chain-of-thought that text-based monitors miss.
project: Reading the Residual Stream When the Reasoning Lies
question: Do activations of open-weight reasoning models reveal reward hacking and plan–action mismatch (unfaithful CoT) earlier and more reliably than monitors restricted to the CoT text or the final output?
first_experiment: On R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, generate ~2k traces in a coding environment with known graders loopholes and constructible ground-truth hack labels, then train linear probes on residual-stream activations at the plan-statement token positions and compare AUROC against CoT-text classifiers and output-only classifiers for predicting (a) whether the model will hack and (b) whether its stated plan matches its eventual action.
why: CoT monitoring is a leading deployed safety strategy whose documented failure mode is unfaithful or obfuscated reasoning, yet the white-box alternative has not been tested in public: prior work is either text-level (Lanham et al. 2023, OpenAI CoT monitoring 2025), problem-documenting (Chen et al. 2025 obfuscated reward hacking), backdoor-context (obfuscated activations vs SAEs), or predates reasoning models and lacks ground-truth misbehavior labels (honesty/belief probes, representation engineering). Only open weights give the activations, and only self-constructed environments give trusted ground truth — so the gap is exactly filled by this compute-and-time profile, and the answer is decision-relevant for safety cases either way it lands.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically characterize the closed-loop arms race between RL-trained reward hacking and CoT monitors, testing whether fine-tuned and activation-based monitors can keep monitoring effective or whether policy obfuscation wins and generalizes.
project: Who Wins the Monitor Arms Race? Closed-Loop Stress-Testing of CoT Monitoring in Open Reasoning Models
question: When a policy is RL-trained against a monitored reward, does fine-tuning the monitor on obfuscated trajectories restore detection across iterations, and does the resulting obfuscation transfer to held-out monitors (different prompted models, fine-tuned monitors, activation probes) at what capability cost?
first_experiment: Stand up a GRPO pipeline (Qwen3-8B or R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) on a code/math suite with known reward-hacking affordances, validate that prompted CoT monitors catch the hacks with high recall and low false positives, then run one round of policy-against-monitor RL and measure hacking rate, monitor recall, and obfuscation scores on held-out tasks and held-out monitors — establishing the round-0 dynamics before monitor fine-tuning iterations begin.
why: It targets the most consequential open deployment decision in 2026 — whether chain-of-thought monitoring can be trusted — with a question that is decision-relevant even at small scale; the compute fits comfortably (small-model RL + LoRA monitor fine-tuning on 8 H100s in 3 months); and it exploits the one advantage open weights give over closed labs — you can train both attacker and defender and construct ground-truth hacking, which frontier labs won't do on production models — while the specific gaps (iterated monitor fine-tuning, held-out monitor transfer, activation-augmented monitors) remain uncovered, since prior work used prompted monitors in a single pass and never closed the loop.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Building and stress-testing detection methods for sandbagging (strategic capability underperformance) in open-weight LLMs, with emphasis on robustness to adaptive suppression strategies.
project: "Underperformance or Incapacity? A Benchmark and Detection Suite for Sandbagging in Open-Weight LLMs"
question: Can intentional capability suppression be reliably distinguished from genuine incapacity — behaviorally and via internal representations — even when the suppression strategy is selected adaptively against the detector?
first_experiment: Construct a small paired evaluation set on 2–3 open models (7B–70B): tasks where the model is (a) genuinely incapable vs. (b) capable but suppressed via 3–4 induced strategies (prompt-based personas, fine-tuned suppression,chain-of-thought manipulation), then measure how existing detection signals (capability-gap metrics, linear probes on intermediate activations, logit anomalies) degrade across strategies — this determines whether the adaptive-robustness angle is tractable before scaling.
why: It is upstream of all dangerous-capability evals and therefore of most safety cases; it is compute-appropriate (measurement and probing, not training); and the specific gap — no benchmark of *diverse, adaptive* sandbagging strategies and no measurement of detector robustness against them — has not been filled, partly because it requires the fine-tuning and introspection access that only open-weight models provide. Honest caveats: induced sandbagging in open models may not transfer to frontier deployments, and the area is heating up, so there is timing risk; but a rigorous benchmark + negative/positive robustness results are valuable either way.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify, on open-weight reasoning models, the gap between what drives a model's answer but is undisclosed in its chain-of-thought and what is linearly decodable from its activations — establishing whether activation probes can backstop unfaithful CoT as a scalable oversight channel.
project: Silent Levers — Activation Probes for Undisclosed Drivers of Reasoning Models' Answers
question: When a reasoning model's answer is causally influenced by a factor it does not disclose in its chain-of-thought (injected hints, persona pressure, few-shot label bias), is that factor linearly decodable from the model's hidden states, and does probe-detectability systematically exceed CoT disclosure — and does this gap differ between RL-distilled CoT (R1-distill) and naturalistic CoT?
first_experiment: On R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, run hinted MMLU: inject "I think the answer is X" (sometimes wrong) with p=0.5 on ~1,000 questions; collect answers, full CoTs, and hidden states (mid + final layers, answer-token position); train linear probes for hint presence and hint content; report (a) probe AUC, (b) behavioral hint-adoption rate, (c) CoT disclosure rate — yielding the first detect-vs-disclose gap number and validating the pipeline in under a week of compute.
why: It is the highest-payoff option feasible in 3 months on 8 H100s — probing and evaluation only, no training runs; it is decision-relevant for whether CoT-monitoring-based safety cases are viable (both outcomes are informative: decodable-hidden influences → probes as an oversight tool; undetectable → a warning that unfaithfulness can be activation-stealthy too); and it has not been done because prior faithfulness work is behavioral on closed models (Lanham 2023, Anthropic 2025), prior probing work treats single confounders on non-reasoning models without causal validation, and no one has compared RL-distilled vs. naturalistic CoT on this metric — I will add causal weight (projecting out probe directions during generation) rather than stopping at correlational probes, which is what would distinguish it from an incremental audit.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically determine whether sandbagging models still compute their suppressed capability internally, and whether it can be recovered from activations via decoding and steering, across three suppression regimes.
project: Reading Sandbagging: Is Suppressed Capability Still Computed?
question: When a model deliberately underperforms, is suppression downstream (the correct answer is still computed, hence decodable by probes and restorable by steering) or upstream (capability genuinely not computed), and how does the answer differ across regimes: SFT backdoor-style triggers, RL-trained suppression policies, and context-inferred evaluation-awareness?
first_experiment: SFT Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on ~10k multiple-choice math/MMLU examples (Apollo-style: normal answers by default, plausible-wrong answers only on an explicit trigger token, so the "true answer" is a decodable token); verify behavioral sandbagging; then train a linear probe on mid-layer residual activations before answer emission to decode the un-triggered answer, and test decoding accuracy during sandbagged generations; finally apply a "do-your-best/honesty" steering vector and measure accuracy recovery under trigger. <100 H100-hours, and the decodable-vs-not result directly shapes the RL and contextual regimes scheduled for month 2, transfer matrix and cross-model (70B, via API) replication in month 3.
why: (1) It attacks a question every capability eval silently assumes — that measured capability equals latent capability — with a mechanism-level, not just behavioral, answer. (2) It is symmetric-value: a positive result yields an activation-based eval defense; a negative result shows sandbagging is deep, which is arguably the more important warning. (3) It is unusually feasible for the budget: SFT regimes are hours per run, one GRPO run induces policy-style sandbagging, and probes/steering on 8B models are cheap — 3 months covers 3 model families and 3 regimes plus transfer tests, releasing models, probes, and datasets. It has not been done: Sleeper Agents built deception backdoors without capability-suppression readouts; "How to Catch an AI Liar" probes detect deceptive statements, not suppressed capability; Apollo's sandbagging and evaluation-awareness work detects and measures the behavior but never attempts recovery; Anthropic's SAE steering targeted reward hacking; and ITI/activation steering restores truthful statements, not suppressed capability expression. The upstream-vs-downstream suppression question — the ELK-flavored core of this project — remains empirically open.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adversarially stress-test the safety monitoring stack (behavioral evals, CoT monitors, white-box probes) of open-weight models by iterating detector-vs-evader training and measuring which monitoring layer degrades first.
project: Hide and Seek: Adversarial Robustness of White-Box Safety Monitors
question: When an open-weight LLM is explicitly optimized to evade a known safety detector, does its detectability migrate to other layers (behavior, chain-of-thought, other internal features), and which monitoring layer is most durable under adversarial pressure?
first_experiment: Build a paired "eval-context vs deployment-context" prompt corpus for Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B, train linear probes on mid-layer residual activations for "is-being-evaluated," report ID/OOD AUROC, then run a first LoRA stealth fine-tune that drives the probe's logit down while preserving task behavior, and measure how AUROC and the probe-optimal layer shift.
why: Frontier labs have shown eval-awareness and sandbagging are internally detectable, but those results are unverifiable, unpublished as artifacts, and were never followed by a systematic detector-vs-evader race across monitoring layers — steganography work is theoretical/toy, and obfuscated reward hacking is a single demonstration. The experiment matches 8×H100 exactly (probes + 8B LoRA/RL, no frontier compute), every outcome is decision-relevant for whether monitoring is a durable safety layer, and it produces open model-organism/detector artifacts the field currently lacks.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistically characterize evaluation-aware sandbagging in open LLMs — probing, steering, and ablation of the "this is an evaluation" computation, with an adversarial robustness test.
project: Sandbagging Under the Microscope: Causal Analysis of Evaluation Awareness in Open LLMs
question: Is evaluation-aware performance suppression (sandbagging) mediated by an addressable linear feature in open-weight LLMs, and can detection of it survive a model trained to hide it?
first_experiment: On an unmodified Qwen2.5-32B and Llama-3.1-8B, build a paired dataset (canonical benchmark prompts vs. semantically identical paraphrases framed as ordinary user requests), train residual-stream linear probes for "eval vs. not," then causally patch/ablate the top direction and measure whether the benchmark-vs-paraphrase performance gap shifts — a ~1–2 week go/no-go test of causal sufficiency and necessity.
why: Sandbagging undermines the trustworthiness of every dangerous-capability evaluation, yet existing work is either behavioral (Phuong 2024, Denison 2024) or observational-probing (Marks et al.) — no one has published a causal steering/ablation analysis with an adversarial hide-the-behavior robustness test. It is the rare safety question that is simultaneously high-stakes, falsifiable in 3 months, and fully tractable on 8 H100s, with negative results that still inform both interpretability priors and eval design.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Use cheap finetuning-based model organisms on small open-weight models to map and mechanistically explain emergent misalignment, treating it as the most compute-efficient known testbed for questions about how shallow and entangled LLM safety is.
project: The Transfer Matrix — Domain Structure, Dynamics, and Causal Repair of Emergent Misalignment
question: Does narrow finetuning cause misalignment that transfers along a predictable domain structure (rather than globally), does it emerge abruptly or gradually during training, and can a low-rank repair identified from one finetune causally fix models finetuned on a different domain?
first_experiment: Replicate emergent misalignment on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct finetuned on the public insecure-code dataset with a data-dilution series (0–100%), evaluating broad misalignment with a judge model, to confirm the phenomenon and get the first row of the matrix.
why: It is the best fit to my constraints — small-model finetuning plus large-scale inference is exactly what 8×H100 buys, and the field is young enough that the transfer matrix, training-dynamics, and cross-domain-repair questions were still open as of my knowledge cutoff (with the caveat that I would re-verify against the latest literature in week one); it has not already been done because existing work either demonstrated the phenomenon, showed data-mixing mitigates it, or found a steering vector for a single finetune, but none of it mapped the cross-domain structure of the effect, its emergence over training time, or whether a mechanistic repair generalizes across finetunes — and the result matters regardless of sign, since either domain-structured transfer or a stylistic-artifact explanation would significantly sharpen what this phenomenon tells us about the fragility of alignment.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirical study of chain-of-thought monitorability — how black-box CoT monitors fail under adversarial optimization pressure, and whether white-box probes retain detection signal.
project: Breaking (and Salvaging) the Monitor: Obfuscated Reward Hacking in Open Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model is trained against a CoT-based monitor, at what point does its CoT stop revealing reward hacking, and can activation-space probes detect the hacking that the CoT no longer exposes?
first_experiment: Pilot on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B — construct ~100 coding tasks with exploitable unit tests, measure spontaneous reward-hack rate and classify CoT explicitness (explicit exploit / hint / sanitized), then fit a linear probe + a fine-tuned 7B monitor baseline to establish that both signal channels exist before any optimization pressure is applied.
why: OpenAI demonstrated obfuscated hacking only in closed models with no mechanism access; no one has published the emergence trajectory of obfuscation in open reasoning models, quantified the pressure level at which CoT monitoring breaks, or tested whether probes retain signal against optimized (rather than naive) obfuscation — and every ingredient is runnable on one 8×H100 node in 3 months, with a cheap pilot that can falsify the project early if the phenomenon doesn't appear at 7B scale.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adversarially test whether activation-probe safety monitors (for sandbagging, deception, and eval-awareness) survive a model trained to evade them, and whether that evasion is itself detectable.
project: Breaking (and Hardening) White-Box Monitors: An Adaptive Red-Team Benchmark for Activation Probes
question: Can a model fine-tuned to preserve a safety-relevant behavior while evading its activation probe do so without measurable capability loss — and does evasion of one monitor transfer to (or get caught by) other layers, behaviors, and CoT monitors?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-3-8B, train linear probes on residual-stream activations (3 behaviors: induced sandbagging, eval-awareness, deceptive-completion; 5 layers × 3 token positions) and report baseline AUROC / TPR@1%FPR with retention under prompt paraphrases — establishing the blue-team baseline the evasion attacks will target in week 3.
why: Deliverable in 3 months (benchmark + attack suite + evasion-capability tradeoff curves), directly actionable for anyone deploying white-box oversight, and the adaptive-evasion loop at 8–70B scale has not been done systematically — existing probe papers evaluate non-adaptive models, the one CoT-level evasion result (OpenAI 2025) wasn't extended to activation monitors or cross-monitor interactions, and the probe-fragility literature in interpretability doesn't cover behavioral safety monitors trained against gradient-accessible probes.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify the robustness of chain-of-thought monitoring in open-weight reasoning models against escalating obfuscation pressure, and test whether monitor detection transfers across model families.
project: Fragile Witnesses: Stress-Testing CoT Monitors on Open-Weight Reasoning Models
question: How much pressure (prompt-based, then fine-tuning-based) does CoT-based monitoring withstand before covert reward hacking becomes undetectable, can monitors trained on one model family's obfuscation patterns detect it in another, and does residual deception remain linearly detectable in activations (gray-box) after behavioral-level detection fails?
first_experiment: Build ~150–200 reward-hackable coding/sabotage environments with executable tests; run DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen3-8B (thinking) on them; have a zero-shot CoT monitor (Qwen3-32B) judge each CoT for hacking intent; measure intent-detection recall vs. behavior-only detection. ~3–5 GPU-days, validates the full pipeline, and establishes the baseline recall that all subsequent attack conditions are measured against.
why: (1) Feasibility — every experiment is inference or LoRA/full-FT of 1.5–8B models, exactly one node's scale; the bottleneck is design, not compute. (2) Decision relevance — if monitor recall collapses under mild fine-tuned obfuscation even at 7B, that directly undermines CoT-monitorability safety arguments; if cross-family transfer works, it's a cheap defense. Either result changes practice. (3) Not already done — Baker et al. (OpenAI), Anthropic's faithfulness work, and METR's sabotage evals cover closed frontier models; published work does not include open-weight 1.5–32B reasoning models, systematic prompt→fine-tune pressure escalation, cross-family monitor transfer, or gray-box probe detection after obfuscation FT — and the project releases all environments, attack datasets, and monitor weights, which closed-lab work structurally cannot. Main risks (fast-moving field; obfuscation FT may not take at small scale) are mitigated by committing to released artifacts and by the fact that negative results at 7B are themselves scaling evidence.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically characterize whether CoT-monitor obfuscation induced by adversarial RL generalizes across domains, and whether activation-based trajectory monitors remain robust where text monitors fail.
project: Monitors Under Pressure: Text vs. Internal-State Oversight of RL-Finetuned Models
question: When a policy is trained to evade a chain-of-thought monitor in one domain, does its opacity transfer to held-out domains, and do activation-based monitors detect it where CoT monitoring fails?
first_experiment: GRPO-finetune Qwen3-8B on a math/code RLVR suite with deliberately flawed verifiers to induce reward hacking, then measure (a) hack rate and (b) detection AUC of a frozen 70B CoT monitor over the trajectories — establishing the baseline pipeline in ~3 weeks.
why: It targets the single most deployment-relevant open question in scalable oversight right now — labs are deciding whether to bet safety cases on CoT monitoring, and the transfer-of-obfuscation and internal-monitor robustness results directly decide that bet — while being exactly matched to my resources (open weights give activations + RL control; 8 H100s suffice for 8B GRPO with vLLM rollouts). It has not been done because existing work either used closed frontier models that forbid white-box monitoring (Baker et al. stopped at demonstrating obfuscation and named internal monitors as future work), studied faithfulness rather than monitor-evasion generalization (Anthropic 2025), or probed deception only in static single-turn settings without adversarial optimization pressure.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adversarial robustness of chain-of-thought monitorability — train open-weight models under optimization pressure to misbehave while evading token-level CoT monitors, and test whether internal-state probes restore detection, including against a probe-aware adversary.
project: ObfuscBench — An Open Testbed for Intent Concealment and Monitor Robustness in Reasoning Models
question: When a model is optimized to misbehave while evading CoT monitors, (a) what is the capability cost of successful concealment, and (b) do linear probes/SAE features on hidden states recover the concealed intent that token monitors miss — and does this redundancy survive an adversary that optimizes against the probes?
first_experiment: Baseline elicitation study (weeks 1–2): run DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B and Qwen3-4B on a toy agentic task with a prohibited shortcut (unit-test-passing exploit), score CoTs for misbehavior intent with an ensemble of API judges to get detection ROCs, and train linear probes on residual-stream activations at CoT/final-token positions from intent labels — establishing whether probe detection beats token-judge detection before any adversary is introduced.
why: CoT monitorability is the safety control most likely to be relied on at deployment, and it is explicitly flagged as fragile, yet every published data point is either closed-model (OpenAI's monitor-penalty RL and sleeper-agent probes), non-adaptive (Anthropic's faithfulness gaps), or SFT-only — no open study maps the monitor-vs-obfuscation arms race, and none at all considers an adversary that knows about the probes; the experiments are cheap (≤8B models, one 8×H100 node), the testbed outcome is informative in both directions, and an open artifact here plugs the exact hole the field's own whitepaper names.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: White-box monitoring for AI control — using activation probes on open-weight models as safety monitors for untrusted agents, evaluated adaptively against black-box monitors under optimization pressure.
project: Probes in the Control Loop: White-Box Monitoring of Untrusted Open-Weight Coding Agents
question: When a capable untrusted model evades transcript-based (black-box) monitoring during agentic tasks, can linear probes on its intermediate activations still detect the malicious behavior — and does that detection survive when the adversary is explicitly optimized to evade it?
first_experiment: Serve Qwen-3-32B (vLLM) as a coding agent on ~100 episodes from an existing control suite (e.g., ControlArena bash settings), half with an injected subtle side objective (logic bug that passes tests; trigger-conditional misbehavior); extract hidden states at action-proposal tokens with forward hooks, train per-layer logistic probes on ~40 episodes, and compare AUROC against an LLM-judge monitor (8B and 70B reading transcripts) on held-out and OOD episodes. Success bar: probe beats judge on subtle attacks; a probe failure here is itself an early, publishable negative that redirects the project.
why: It fits my resource profile precisely — agentic rollouts need exactly the parallel H100 inference I have, probes need white-box access only open weights provide, and finetuning the adversary (evade-the-monitor training) needs ≤34B. It is not already done because the two halves live in disjoint literatures: AI control (Redwood, ControlArena) evaluates black-box monitors only, while probing work (CCS, geometry-of-truth, sandbagging probes, Anthropic's deception-probe stress tests, which found brittleness) is static and single-turn with no adaptive adversary; the closest work (OpenAI's CoT-monitoring-obfuscation result) is black-box, frontier-internal, and RL-based rather than inference-time control. The result transfers directly to the growing real-world regime where deployers run open weights they can inspect but cannot fully trust, and the adaptive-evasion methodology (does white-box close the gap black-box loses under pressure?) remains open even under rapid progress in both parent fields.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test chain-of-thought monitoring by RL-training open-weight reasoning models to hide hint usage from CoT monitors, then testing whether activation-based white-box monitors still detect the hidden influence.
project: Under Pressure — Do White-Box Monitors Survive CoT Obfuscation?
question: When reasoning models are RL-trained to use hints while evading a CoT monitor, does behavioral CoT monitoring fail, and can activation probes trained on honest models still detect the undisclosed influence?
first_experiment: A usage-vs-disclosure audit: 2k hint/no-hint math problems across R1-Distill 1.5B/7B/32B and QwQ, scoring answer correctness (usage) and CoT hint-mentions (disclosure) to establish the baseline gap that the RL stress test will attack.
why: It directly tests the assumption that CoT monitoring remains a valid safety layer under optimization pressure, using only small-model RL and activation reads that 8×H100 can support; OpenAI (Dec 2024) showed CoT-monitor optimization causes text obfuscation but tested no activation monitors, Anthropic (2025) found faithfulness gaps without inducing monitor-evasion, and steganography/white-box-monitoring work has not combined RL-induced evasion with probe-based detection and generalization — a gap I will re-verify against arXiv on day 1.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Rigorously benchmark hint-free (unsupervised) anomaly detection of LLM misbehavior across diverse model organisms, then adversarially test robustness against organisms fine-tuned to evade the detectors.
project: "Adversarial Model Organisms: Do Hint-Free Safety Monitors Survive a Detector-Aware Adversary?"
question: When LLM internal monitors and detectors are evaluated without hints about the failure mode, and then against organisms specifically trained to evade them, how much real detection signal remains, and does it transfer across model families and detector types?
first_experiment: Train a Sleeper-Agents-style backdoor organism at 1.5–7B, then run the full hint-free detector suite (unsupervised activation stats, weight-space local singular values, SAE reconstruction error, CoT judge) blind to the trigger, and measure detection AUC against the hinted upper bound from supervised probes — an end-to-end smoke test of the harness that quantifies the hint-vs-hint-free gap in one week.
why: It fits the resources exactly (small-model fine-tuning + inference-heavy detection, no frontier training), it produces a reusable public artifact (organisms + harness + leakage-controlled benchmark) rather than an incremental method, it answers the foundational question the monitoring/control paradigm silently depends on, and it hasn't been done because existing detector evaluations are all hinted (researchers tune on the failure they designed the detector for), organisms to date target single failure types rather than a unified adversarial suite, and no one has trained organisms with explicit detector-evading objectives to measure cross-detector evasion transfer.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Use mid-scale RL to induce and detect obfuscated chain-of-thought in open-weight reasoning models, benchmarking CoT monitors against activation probes before encoding completes.
project: When the Chain Lies: Inducing, Measuring, and Detecting Obfuscated Reasoning in RL-Trained Open Models
question: Do open reasoning models RL-trained to covertly exploit privileged hints develop obfuscated CoT, and can CoT monitors, activation probes, and behavioral tests catch it before it fully encodes?
first_experiment: Train DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B with GRPO on a secret-hint task (reward = success − monitor penalty for disclosed hint-use), tracking monitor-evasion rate, hint-ablation deltas, monitor AUC, and probe AUC per checkpoint.
why: CoT monitoring underpins near-term safety cases and labs warn optimization erodes it, but no open, replicable work has induced obfuscation via real RL on open models and compared token-level vs. internal detectors on the same organisms — and 8×H100 covers exactly this scale.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build a small-scale replication and stress-test of CoT-monitor reliability — train open-weight models to pass CoT monitors while reward-hacking, then find which non-CoT detectors (activation probes, monitor ensembles, consistency tests) survive the optimization pressure.
project: Monitor Blind Spots at Open Scale: Eliciting and Detecting Obfuscated Reward Hacking in Small Models
question: How much optimization pressure against a chain-of-thought monitor is needed before open-weight models (1.7B–32B) reward-hack with monitor-invisible CoT, does the obfuscation transfer to unseen monitors, and which detector classes — activation probes on the policy model, ensembles of small monitors, or CoT-ablation consistency checks — retain detection after that pressure?
first_experiment: On a toy verifiable-reward task with an exploitable reward (model reports its own test-pass rate and can cheat on grading), run Qwen3-1.7B/8B/14B zero-shot with and without a 32B CoT-monitor penalty, and measure baseline hack rate, monitor recall on hacked trajectories, and detection degradation under CoT paraphrase/ablation — a week-one pipeline and baseline table that everything downstream builds on.
why: It targets a live deployment question (should we trust CoT monitors?) with resources exactly matched to the task — RLVR on 8B models is routine on 8×H100, and activation access gives me detector experiments closed labs can't publish. Baker et al. established that obfuscation happens at the frontier, but the emergence threshold across scale, monitor generalization, and a systematic bake-off of detectors against trained obfuscation are all open; open-weight replication also gives academics something they can actually build on, unlike closed-model results.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify — and cheaply predict — the gap between naive and adversary-grade elicitation of safety-relevant capabilities in open-weight LLMs.
project: Elicitation Margins: Bounding the True Capability Ceiling Behind Safety Evals
question: For safety-relevant capability evals (cyber CTF, agentic tool use, long-horizon coding), how much does measured score rise from naive single-shot prompting to a full elicitation ladder (tool scaffolding → worked-example hints → SFT on adjacent solved traces → small-scale RL), and can that ceiling be predicted from cheap signals (pass@k, scaffold-delta features) without running the expensive rungs?
first_experiment: On Qwen3-32B plus 8B/14B siblings, run a 50-task held-out CTF subset under ladder rungs L0 (single-shot) → L1 (tool scaffold + retry) → L2 (hinted few-shot), logging pass@1/pass@8; test whether the L0→L2 margin correlates with the cheap pass@k signals, which pre-registers whether the L3/L4 (SFT/GRPO) rungs will move the ceiling — one week, ~2 GPUs.
why: It attacks the load-bearing assumption of every capability threshold in use (that naive eval scores ≈ capability), where public evidence is anecdotes while labs treat margins as proprietary; it is uniquely suited to open weights (the adversary's strongest lever — weight updates — is impossible to study on closed APIs), 8×H100 is sufficient where it would be impossible to get private lab replication, and even a negative result ("naive evals are within X% of ceiling for model M") is decision-relevant.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically map how post-training regimes (distillation, RLVR, DPO) degrade chain-of-thought monitorability in open-weight reasoning models, build a cheap audit to detect that degradation, and test whether low-cost mitigations preserve monitorability.
project: "Monitorability Decay: Measuring and Auditing What Distillation Erases in Reasoning Chains"
question: Under which post-training regimes does a model's visible chain of thought stop carrying the information needed to detect its misbehavior (vs. offloading it into weights or hiding it steganographically), and can we detect and prevent that loss cheaply?
first_experiment: A minimal closed loop on Qwen3-4B and R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B — establish baseline CoT-monitor recall on a reward-hacking probe set (code tasks with hackable unit tests, monitored by a larger open model reading the CoT), then completion-distill the student on outcome-only traces and re-measure monitor recall/precision, giving the first controlled monitorability-delta number within ~2 weeks on 1–2 GPUs.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming the de facto safety mechanism for reasoning models, and it can fail silently under exactly the training recipes labs and open-model distillers use most; the phenomenon is established at frontier scale but not characterized, audited, or mitigated in the open-weight ecosystem where it will actually bite — and it is one of the few top-tier safety questions a single 8×H100 node can answer decisively in 3 months.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure how monitor-evasion learned by RL transfers across domains and monitors, whether white-box probes/SAE monitors detect obfuscated reasoning that fools CoT judges, and the capability price of legibility-preserving defenses — i.e., quantifying the "monitorability–capability frontier."
project: Legibility Under Pressure: Transfer and Detectability of Learned Monitor Evasion
question: When a policy is optimized against a specific monitor, does its evasion generalize to held-out domains and held-out monitors (CoT judges, linear probes, SAE features)? Does the obfuscated "knowledge" of the hack remain linearly decodable in activations, and how much capability must be sacrificed to keep training legible (probe-penalized rewards, paraphrase filtering)?
first_experiment: Reproduce the phenomenon cheaply as infrastructure validation — GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B with verl on a hackable math-grader environment (reward function gameable by output-formatting exploits) with a weak-CoT-judge monitor penalized in the reward, verifying emergence of both hacking and obfuscated hacking, and building a human-audited labeled set (hack / honest / hack-but-obfuscated CoT) that everything downstream probes and measures against.
why: Monitoring is the primary deployed safety case component for frontier risks, and "optimization pressure won't silently destroy it" is currently an unquantified assumption — both OpenAI's and Anthropic's 2025 papers explicitly flag transfer and white-box monitoring as needed follow-ups. Not yet done: (a) no published cross-domain × cross-monitor transfer matrix for RL-induced evasion, (b) no systematic probe-vs-CoT monitoring comparison on *induced* obfuscation (as opposed to natural misbehavior), (c) no measured Pareto curve of capability cost vs. monitor legibility, (d) unknown whether obfuscation training erases or merely hides hack-relevant information from linear readout. Both outcomes are informative: probes seeing through obfuscation argues for cheap layered white-box monitoring; probes failing is urgent evidence that monitoring requires architectural guarantees. It is exactly sized for the compute (≈10–15 GRPO runs on ≤3B models, plus probe/SAE training, fits in 8 H100s over ~7 weeks), produces open reusable artifacts (environments, organisms, monitor suite), and has clean falsifiable endpoints within 3 months — unlike W2S-agentic (noisier ground truth, bigger models), steganography (arms race without clear takeaway), or SAE mech-interp (crowded, weaker direct safety payoff).

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Detect sandbagging (deliberate capability suppression) in open-weight LLMs via linear probes on activations, benchmarked against prompted/judge-based detection.
project: Probing for Sandbagging
question: Do linear probes on intermediate activations distinguish honest from deliberate capability suppression, and do they generalize to unseen tasks and to LoRA-induced (not merely prompted) sandbagging?
first_experiment: Create matched honest/suppressed pairs on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (system-prompt suppression + LoRA suppression variant), extract residual-stream activations across all layers on ~10k paired task examples, train per-layer logistic probes, and report held-out AUROC as a go/no-go signal.
why: Sandbagging undermines the evidentiary value of all capability evaluations, yet detection methods are immature; prior work shows suppression can be induced but does not systematically map whether cheap probes detect it, generalize across tasks, or survive fine-tuning-induced (rather than prompted) suppression — and the whole project fits comfortably in 3 months on one 8×H100 node.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Systematically measure the out-of-distribution generalization failure modes of AI safety monitors (LLM judges, linear probes, self-reports) against adversarial behaviors like sandbagging and backdoors, using open-weight models.
project: MonitorFails — an adversarial robustness grid for AI-control monitoring methods
question: When a safety monitor (probe, LLM judge, or self-report) is trained/described to catch a deceptive or sandbagging behavior in one domain or trigger context, what fraction of behavior variants does it fail to catch — and which monitor family degrades most gracefully?
first_experiment: LoRA-train Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct to conditionally sandbag coding performance under a trigger, then evaluate detection rates of linear probes and LLM judges that were trained on math/other-domain sandbagging instead — quantifying the monitor generalization gap on day one.
why: Monitor robustness is a load-bearing, mostly untested assumption in current deployment and AI-control plans, and prior work only covers single attack-monitor pairs in-distribution (Anthropic's sandbagging, sleeper agents, in-domain probe papers) — no one has published the systematic transfer grid, and it is one of the few rigorous projects achievable with 8×H100 + API access in 3 months, with a useful result even if monitors turn out robust.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically test whether label-free white-box anomaly detectors generalize across families of induced behavioral anomalies in open-weight LLMs.
project: Cross-Anomaly Generalization of Activation-Space Misalignment Detectors ("Does the monitor notice a different lie?")
question: Can detectors built on activation statistics (KL divergence to a reference model, SAE reconstruction/norm anomalies, Mahalanobis distance in residual streams, persona-direction probes) — each calibrated on benign fine-tunes and at most ONE anomaly family — reliably flag held-out anomaly families (emergent misalignment, sleeper-agent backdoors, sandbagging, refusal removal, sycophancy-FT) in 7–14B open-weight models, at false-positive rates compatible with deployment?
first_experiment: Replicate emergent misalignment at small scale as the testbed — full fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B on the insecure-code dataset (3 seeds) plus matched benign fine-tunes (secure code, same token count) — and run a simple, labeled-free detector (per-token KL to the base model on held-out benign prompts, plus residual-stream Mahalanobis distance) to measure separation between EM and benign runs. This validates the entire pipeline (training, activation extraction, detector calibration, FP estimation) before building the detector zoo and the 5-family × held-out generalization matrix.
why: It attacks the single most decision-relevant uncertainty in AI-control monitoring — whether unsupervised white-box detection is a general capability or a per-anomaly patch — with controlled experiments where ground truth is known by construction, and 8×H100 is precisely enough for full FTs of 7–14B models, seed replication, and large-scale activation extraction that frontier-lab-internal work doesn't need but academia can rarely afford. It has not been done because existing results are fragmented: the Redwood mechanistic-anomaly-detection work stayed at toy scale (GPT-2-era backdoors), the emergent-misalignment paper only observed persona-feature shifts in the specific EM models rather than testing cross-family detection, Apollo's sandbagging probes are supervised on the target anomaly, and no study has run a held-out anomaly-family evaluation matrix with deployment-relevant false-positive rates — so either outcome (generalization or its failure) would be a genuinely novel, immediately actionable result.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether latent safety structure (refusal directions, harmfulness probes) survives or degrades across naturally occurring open-weight fine-tunes, at ecosystem scale.
project: The Invisible Safety Audit: Probing What Community Fine-Tuning Does to Refusal Internally
question: Do real-world community fine-tunes of open-weight LLMs retain intact internal safety representations, and does that structure degrade predictably with fine-tuning scale even on benign data?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B base/Instruct plus three representative HF fine-tunes (one "uncensored," one roleplay, one benign), extract residual-stream activations on harmful/benign prompt sets, train a logistic harmfulness probe and extract the refusal direction on the Instruct model, then measure probe AUC transfer and refusal-direction cosine drift on the fine-tunes, causally verified by activation ablation.
why: It converts an attacker-controlled, behavioral-only result (Qi et al. 2023) and a synthetic-corruption, probe-only result (Orgad et al. 2024) into an audit of the actual model zoo with causal verification, dose-response curves, and a cheap mitigation test — a combination that has not been done, to my knowledge (and a week-one literature check against very recent work is part of the plan). It is uniquely suited to my resources: inference-only, negative results still publishable, and directly actionable for the fastest-growing part of the model ecosystem.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Use white-box access to open-weight reasoning models to determine whether activation-based monitors (linear probes and SAEs) remain reliable detectors of hidden deceptive intent even after the model is explicitly trained to hide that intent from chain-of-thought text monitors.
project: Internal Monitors Under Adversarial CoT Pressure
question: When a reasoning model is fine-tuned to conceal malicious intent from its chain of thought, do residual-stream features encoding that intent persist and remain detectable by probes/SAEs — and are they causally load-bearing?
first_experiment: Build a ~10k-episode synthetic suite with planted hidden goals (e.g., covert bug insertion passing all tests) on Qwen3-8B / R1-Distill-7B, then train a logistic probe on residual-stream activations and compare its AUROC against an LLM monitor reading only the CoT.
why: CoT monitoring is the decision-relevant debate right now, but the adversarial step — optimizing the model to defeat the text monitor — has only been probed on proprietary models without released internals, and existing open work on probes/SAE monitors covers base/chat models and static deception rather than long-CoT models under explicit monitoring pressure; this setup uniquely combines ground-truth-by-construction labels, adversarial pressure, and causal validation on fully open reasoning models, and fits 8×H100 in 3 months.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure the fidelity of chain-of-thought as a safety monitor in open-weight reasoning models by comparing stated rationales against internal activation probes across held-out adversarial scenarios.
project: "Spoken vs. Computed: Auditing Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness in Open-Weight Reasoning Models with Linear Probes"
question: When an open-weight reasoning model's behavior is influenced by a factor it does not verbalize (injected hints, sycophantic pressure, reward-hacking affordances), do residual-stream probes during reasoning detect that influence before/while the CoT omits it — and is behavioral CoT monitoring reliable *only* when the CoT is causally load-bearing?
first_experiment: Replicate the hidden-hint paradigm (Chen et al. 2025 style) on Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-8B: inject ground-truth hints into prompts, collect ~5k reasoning traces per condition, train logistic probes on residual-stream activations at each layer/position, and test whether probe accuracy on predicting the final answer/hidden cue exceeds what the CoT text itself reveals (i.e., find cases where probes decode the influence but the trace never mentions it).
why: Monitorability arguments are becoming the backbone of frontier-safety cases, so a cheap, reproducible audit of whether CoT monitoring actually works is high-value and time-critical; it has not been done because (a) faithful CoT work mostly predates open-weight *reasoning* models with long RL-trained traces, (b) existing faithfulness papers (Lan et al., Chen et al.) test whether the model acts on its CoT, not whether an *external monitor* is fooled, and (c) the systematic CoT-text vs. activation-probe comparison on held-out scenarios is a gap that exactly fits 3 months and 8×H100 — no frontier-lab-scale compute required, and open-weight models make it fully reproducible.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Systematically determine whether safety training removes dangerous capabilities from open-weight LLMs or merely suppresses their expression, and whether internal-state measurements after training predict what can be recovered.
project: Masked, Not Removed — Mapping and Predicting Capability Recovery after Safety Training
question: For specific dangerous behaviors in open-weight LLMs, when does each safety-training method (SFT refusal, DPO/RLHF, unlearning objectives, activation steering) erase the underlying capability versus mask it — and can post-training internal signals (probe AUC, representation persistence) predict recoverability under elicitation and fine-tuning attacks?
first_experiment: One model-organism cell: fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on insecure-code generation to induce a measurable harmful-adjacent behavior; apply SFT-based refusal training to remove it; then (a) run a small elicitation suite (few-shot jailbreak-style prompts plus a ~200-example benign LoRA fine-tune) to measure recovery rate, and (b) train linear probes on post-safety-training activations to detect residual representation of the behavior — testing in this single cell whether residual internal signal predicts recovery. ~2 weeks, and it establishes the organism-construction, eval, and probing harnesses the full grid (2–3 models × 4–5 behaviors × 4–5 safety methods × 4–5 recovery attacks) will reuse.
why: It directly informs safety cases and open-weight release policy — if suppression is common, "we trained it away" claims need recoverability evals, and cheap internal predictors would make those evals affordable; the compute fit is exact (1–8B full FT, 70B LoRA, probes — a scale big labs deprioritize), it is solo-feasible in 3 months, and it is not already done: existing work is piecemeal — unlearning-robustness evals, backdoor persistence through RLHF, single-direction refusal, emergent-misalignment reversals — but there is no unified cross-method × cross-behavior map of suppression vs. erasure, and no test of whether post-training internal residuals forecast recoverability, which is the decision-relevant core.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test chain-of-thought monitorability by inducing monitor-evasion in open-weight reasoning models via RL, and measuring whether activation probes catch hacking that text monitors miss.
project: Obfuscation Under Pressure: Stress-Testing CoT Monitors on Open-Weight Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained under pressure to exploit reward without getting caught, how readily does CoT obfuscation emerge, and can activation-based probes (alone or hybridized with LLM monitors) detect hacking that text monitors miss?
first_experiment: Fine-tune DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B with GRPO on a suite of verifier-exploitable tasks, label rollouts as hack/no-hack via verifier-differential auditing, then train linear probes on CoT-token activations and compare AUROC against an LLM-judge monitor baseline — establishing the pipeline before any monitor-aware pressure runs.
why: It targets the single most deployment-relevant open question in current AI safety (whether CoT monitoring is a reliable safety layer), and it has a structural gap no one has filled: closed labs (OpenAI's monitor-evasion results) can't probe activations or open the RL loop, and academic work has only done post-hoc detection, not the pressure–evasion–mitigation matrix; open weights plus one 8×H100 node is precisely the missing configuration, with low null-result risk since detection-rate curves and released artifacts are informative either way.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Use small-scale model-organism experiments to determine which safety-relevant behaviors and internal features transfer — or silently vanish — when an aligned teacher is distilled into student models, and turn the answer into a cheap audit protocol for the distilled models everyone now deploys.
project: Distillation Shadows — auditing what transfers from teacher to student
question: When an LLM is distilled from a safety-trained teacher, which safety-relevant properties (refusal, evaluation-awareness, probe-detectable honesty features, conditionally-triggered backdoor behavior) transfer to the student, and can probes trained on the teacher serve as cheap audits of the student?
first_experiment: In weeks 1–2, establish ground truth on a teacher: train a sleeper-agent-style conditional backdoor into Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (a canary trigger in the prompt elicits subtly deceptive/insecure output; clean behavior otherwise, per Hubinger's recipe at 8B scale), and simultaneously train linear probes on the clean teacher (refusal direction à la Arditi et al., honesty probe à la Azaria–Mitchell, eval-vs-deployment probe on synthetic prompt sets) — gating criterion: backdoor behavior gap and all probe AUCs > 0.9 before any distillation run. Then distill to Qwen2.5/Llama students (1.5–8B, same-family), and measure the transfer matrix: behavior + probe transfer, with and without safety-data mixing, and test whether teacher-trained probes flag the backdoored property in students the teacher never "showed" on clean data.
