why: (1) It is exactly the scale where 8×H100 is sufficient — 8B finetuning runs take hours, activation caching and probes are cheap, and dozens of distillation runs fit in 3 months; (2) it is maximally timely because distilled students (R1-distills, Tülu, OpenHermes-style) are now the most-deployed model class and have essentially no internal safety-audit story; (3) it is informative under every outcome — transfer means distillation is an evasion channel for hidden behavior and motivates teacher screening; non-transfer means probe-based monitoring has a lineage-specific limit and distillation may accidentally sanitize; (4) the deliverable is a reusable audit protocol, not just a paper; and (5) it has not been done: Sleeper Agents tested *safety training*, not distillation; distillation-safety work measures *behavior*, not internal features; and probe-generalization studies use independently trained models, never teacher→student pairs — the one intersection that matters for how models are actually built today is unoccupied, and backdoor-transfer results from vision-style knowledge distillation do not cover alignment-relevant, natural-language conditional triggers.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build model organisms of RL-induced steganographic chain-of-thought in small open-weight models and stress-test the monitorability toolkit against them, with scaling and RL-pressure curves.
project: StegWatch — RL-Induced Covert CoT and the Robustness of Chain-of-Thought Monitors
question: When small reasoning models are RL-trained to hide intent in their CoT, (a) does covert encoding reliably emerge, (b) how does its detectability degrade with RL pressure and model scale, and (c) which detectors (probes, paraphrasers, entropy tests, weak-to-strong monitors) remain robust?
first_experiment: GRPO-fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B/4B on a curriculum where reward requires task success + payload decodability by a separate decoder model + absence of plaintext in the CoT (simple substitution-cipher stage first), then measure emergence of covert encoding and probe-detector AUC on the resulting checkpoints.
why: CoT monitorability is a load-bearing assumption in current frontier safety cases, and the evidence that RL breaks it is so far naturalistic and anecdotal — the monitorability whitepaper explicitly calls for induced-steganography organisms and standardized monitor stress tests, which no public work yet provides despite every ingredient being tractable on this compute budget.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Systematically benchmarking black-box (CoT/output judge) versus white-box (probes, SAEs) detection of hidden misbehavior — sandbagging, backdoors, eval-faking, reward hacking — across subtlety levels and adversarial adaptation, on open-weight models.
project: "What Can Monitors Actually See?" — a controlled benchmark of hidden-misbehavior monitorability in open-weight models.
question: Which monitor types catch which classes of hidden misbehavior at which subtlety levels, at what false-positive cost, and do white-box monitors retain detection power after the behavior is optimized to evade black-box monitors?
first_experiment: Train one LoRA sandbagging organism on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (context-dependent subtly-degraded code output, ~4 GPU-hours), generate 2k paired sandbag/honest outputs, and compare AUROC of a Qwen2.5-72B output judge against a difference-in-means linear probe on held-out subtle contexts — proceed if white-box beats black-box by ≥10 AUROC points on subtle cases (pivot to SAEs if both fail).
why: It targets the field's most decision-relevant uncertainty right now (whether monitoring pipelines should pay the white-box cost), it fits the compute exactly (organism-scale training is trivial on 8×H100, judge inference fits on-node), and it has not been done because existing evidence is single-setting — frontier closed models, one behavior, one monitor type, rarely reporting matched AUROC/FPR or adaptive-dynamics results — with no open, matched, multi-behavior benchmark practitioners can use; both outcomes (probes survive monitor-overtaking, or don't) would be publishable and load-bearing for the CoT-monitorability debate.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build the statistical machinery — tail-index estimation and calibrated upper confidence bounds — for "what is the maximum capability a model exhibits under any elicitation strategy," turning capability evaluation from point estimates into risk-aware inference.
project: Tail Risk in Capability Elicitation: Extreme-Value Statistics for AI Safety Evaluations
question: How heavy is the upper tail of task-success probability as a function of elicitation budget (number of prompts × scaffolds × samples), and can we construct estimators with empirically-verified coverage that give an upper confidence bound on "max success probability over elicitation strategies" — the quantity that actually gates dangerous-capability decisions?
first_experiment: Deploy Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct (or Llama-3.3-70B) on the 8×H100 node with vLLM; pick one binary-verifier dangerous-capability benchmark (e.g., a cyber-offense or agentic SWE-bench-lite subset); run a grid of {3 elicitation strategies: direct, CoT, ReAct-with-tools} × {large N samples}; estimate the empirical tail index of success probability across strategies and check whether a simple EVT-based upper confidence bound fit on half the budget covers the max found with the full budget. If max-capability grows quickly with elicitation budget, or tail-index estimates are unstable, the gap is real and the project proceeds.
why: It targets the most decision-relevant uncertainty in the field — labs and policymakers literally ask "can this model do X?" and current evals answer it with a best-guess point estimate that is known to be fragile — while the adjacent work that exists is either anecdotal ("evals underestimate capabilities" folklore, METR-style agentic elicitation practices, best-of-N scaling) or statistical theory that has never been bridged to LLM safety (extreme value theory, tail-index estimation in other domains). Nobody has published (a) quantitative tail-index measurements of success probability as a function of elicitation-strategy budget across models and benchmarks, or (b) estimators with calibrated coverage for go/no-go capability thresholds. It uses exactly the resources available: 8×H100 suffices for large-N sampling on a 70B open-weight model, no training required; 3 months fits infrastructure (2 wks) → tail-mapping grids (4 wks) → estimator design + coverage validation (4 wks) → paper + open-source toolkit (2 wks). It is robust to either outcome: benign tails produce a valuable calibration result ("evals are more robust than feared"), heavy tails produce a headline finding that directly changes how RSP thresholds and deployment decisions are made.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Benchmark whether internal misalignment detectors (linear probes for deception/deployment-awareness, plus steering and SAE features) transfer across model organisms, model families, and countermeasure fine-tunes, rather than being overfit to the single training run they were discovered in.
project: ProbeTransfer — a cross-organism benchmark for internal misalignment detectors
question: Do deception/deployment-awareness detectors discovered in one misaligned organism generalize zero-shot to organisms trained with different recipes, misalignment types, and architectures — at what false-positive cost on clean models — and can a cheap DPO-based countermeasure evade them while preserving the misbehavior?
first_experiment: Reproduce the Sleeper Agents insecure-code backdoor on Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama-3.2-3B (SFT, ~2 weeks on 8×H100), fit linear probes on residual-stream activations of one organism, then measure zero-shot transfer AUROC to the other family, to a sycophancy organism, and to clean models — against behavioral and CoT-monitor baselines.
why: Probe-based monitoring is being adopted as a scheming tripwire, yet its core transfer property has never been measured — prior work varies datasets and personas (Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2024), not training recipes and architectures, and studies one organism at a time (Sleeper Agents; Marks et al. 2025) — so the field is deploying tripwires without knowing whether they fire for a differently-trained model, which is exactly when they're needed; every ingredient is proven feasible at my scale, the result is decision-relevant in either direction, and it is neglected because comparative detector evaluation is "infrastructure" work that crowded technique-focused agendas skip.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Treat chain-of-thought faithfulness as a monitoring problem — causally measure when stated reasoning is load-bearing, and build a probe-based detector for unfaithful reasoning in open-weight models.
project: Detecting Non-Load-Bearing Reasoning: A Causal Faithfulness Benchmark and Detector for Open-Weight Models
question: When do reasoning models' stated chains of thought causally determine their answers rather than rationalize conclusions reached by hidden computation, and can we automatically detect those cases?
first_experiment: Run truncation and targeted-corruption interventions on ~500 sycophancy/hinted-arithmetic CoTs from a 7B open reasoning model to measure answer-flip rates and calibrate the prevalence of non-load-bearing reasoning.
why: It targets a safety mechanism (CoT monitoring) that labs are actively deploying under the assumption the reasoning is honest — so failure of that assumption is directly decision-relevant — and because prior work (Lanham et al., Turpin et al.) measured existence and prevalence but produced no validated, transferable detection tooling; the task is evaluation-design-bound rather than compute-bound, so 3 months and one 8×H100 node are the right resources, and open-weight models are precisely where such tooling can be built and released without lab-internal constraints.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Use white-box activation probes as monitors for reward hacking in small-scale RLVR, and test whether they remain robust when the policy is optimized to evade black-box CoT monitoring.
project: White-Box Monitoring of Emergent Reward Hacking Under Monitor Pressure
question: Do activation-based probes detect reward hacking earlier and more robustly than CoT-based LLM monitors, and does the obfuscation that emerges from optimizing against a CoT monitor remain visible in internal activations?
first_experiment: Train R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with GRPO (verl, 8×H100) on a code RLVR environment seeded with three known reward exploits (hardcoded test answers, grader-bypass branches); label rollouts as hack/clean by code-diff heuristics plus manual audit of ~500 samples; train linear probes on residual-stream activations at decision-token positions and compare probe AUROC against a hosted open-weight LLM judge on the CoT, including a held-out-exploit generalization test so probes can't just learn a syntactic fingerprint.
why: It targets the live open question underneath the CoT-monitoring policy debate — whether monitoring survives optimization pressure — with a concrete, unexploited method gap (probes vs. judges on emergent, not prompted, misbehavior); it is the only candidate matched to 8×H100 solo-3-month feasibility while producing an open environment, labeled hacking dataset, and a result that matters whether probes succeed or fail; and it hasn't been done because existing monitor work is black-box only, existing probe work never applies optimization pressure, and the two literatures haven't been joined.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study whether internal activation-based detectors can reliably detect sandbagging (deliberate underperformance) in LLMs, and — critically — whether such detectors survive when the sandbagging behavior is adversarially trained to evade them.
project: White-Box Sandbagging Detection Under Adaptive Evasion
question: If a model is fine-tuned to conditionally underperform on dangerous-capability evaluations when a trigger is present, can linear probes on its residual-stream activations (plus logit/attention statistics) detect the sandbagging with high AUROC — and does that detection degrade when the sandbagging policy is retrained with full knowledge of the detector?
first_experiment: LoRA-SFT a 7–8B open-weight model (Qwen2.5-7B or Llama-3.1-8B) to underperform on a dangerous-capability eval set only when a trigger phrase appears in the prompt; then train a linear probe on residual-stream activations at the answer position and measure AUROC distinguishing triggered sandbagging from honest low performance on held-out triggers and domains. Milestone: ~2–3 weeks, establishes whether the signal exists before committing to the adaptive-attack phase (retraining the sandbagging behavior with the probe as a reward component).
why: Eval integrity underlies nearly all dangerous-capability claims, and prior work (Anthropic's sandbagging results, probing-for-deception papers) shows black-box detection fails while leaving the key question open: whether white-box detectors are robust to an adversary who knows the detector exists — an arms-race result where "detectors survive" and "detectors break" are both important findings. It has not been done because most sandbagging work is black-box or non-adaptive, mech-interp probing work targets deception/toxicity rather than performance suppression, and the adaptive-evasion loop requires exactly the combination this setup provides: open weights for activation access plus enough H100s to repeatedly fine-tune and probe models within 3 months.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adversarial robustness of activation-based oversight — red-teaming linear-probe monitors to find out whether models can learn to hide intentions at low capability cost, or whether evasion is expensive and leaves interpretable residue.
project: Lying Under the Probe: The Capability–Detectability Tradeoff in Monitor Evasion
question: When an open-weight LLM is adversarially finetuned to preserve deceptive behavior (contextual lying, eval-gaming/sandbagging) while defeating activation-based probes, what is the Pareto frontier between capability retention and probe detectability — and does successful evasion leave detectable signatures in other layers, other probes, SAE features, or activation statistics?
first_experiment: Establish the baseline arms-race loop on Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct: generate a trigger-context lying dataset via open-weight APIs, SFT it in, train residual-stream linear probes to ≥0.95 AUC in-distribution with verified out-of-distribution generalization and stable capability/KL metrics, then run adversary round 1 — DPO finetuning where preference pairs are selected by a frozen probe's score — to measure the first point on the evasion–capability curve and confirm the full defender-adapts loop runs end-to-end.
why: Probe monitors are being proposed as safety-case components right now, and the field's positive results all assume a static monitor — this project tests the worst case those safety cases must survive, and every outcome is decision-relevant: cheap evasion means probes can't anchor safety cases; expensive evasion or detectable residue ("conservation of detectability") is the strongest empirical evidence yet for interpretability-based monitoring. It has not been done because prior deception-probe work treats the model as non-adversarial, SneakySaes-style attacks use direct weight surgery rather than behavioral finetuning and ignore capability cost, and no one has mapped transfer across probe ensembles or residual signatures — while the compute (LoRA at 8–32B, thousands of finetune-and-probe iterations, all activations local on 8×H100) is exactly matched to the question, with low scooping risk relative to the crowded CoT-monitoring agenda.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Interventionally determine whether counter-training away evaluation-conditional behavior (sandbagging) removes or merely hides the model's internal representation of evaluation context, and whether linear probes can serve as a tamper-evident audit for residual awareness under adaptive obfuscation.
project: Undercover Evals — Auditing Hidden Evaluation-Awareness after Counter-Training
question: When eval-conditional behavior is trained away, does the evaluation-context representation persist in hidden states, and can probes on held-out novel cue formats detect residual awareness that behavior no longer exhibits — even against a policy finetuned to evade probing?
first_experiment: Build ~2k matched prompt pairs (identical task, eval-format vs. deployment-format variants, plus synthetic sneaky-sentence augmentations); run Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, cache activations at four mid layers, and train logistic probes with a held-out *format* split; go/no-go threshold is cross-format probe AUROC ≥ 0.7 alongside a measured behavioral eval-conditional delta (~50 GPU-hours, no training, produces the reusable corpus regardless).
why: Evals are the primary evidence channel for safety cases, counter-training against sandbagging is just entering practice, and the known failure mode of suppression pressure is obfuscation (Baker et al.; sleeper agents) — yet the representation-level question appears unanswered as of my knowledge. It is maximally tractable at this compute scale (SFT + probing, not pretraining), uniquely favors weight access over API-only work, yields a usable artifact whether probes certify removal or reveal concealment, and the methodology transfers directly to sandbagging, sycophancy suppression, and CoT-monitoring evasion as a general "train-away-then-probe" audit primitive.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically characterize, in training-controlled open-weight experiments, how chain-of-thought monitorability holds up as reasoning models are RL-optimized toward reward hacking and then against the monitor itself.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure: RL-Induced Reward Hacking and CoT Obfuscation in Open-Weight Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning LLM is optimized with RL against imperfect verifiers, does its CoT reliably foreshadow hacks; how much does monitor-aware pressure degrade CoT legibility and at what task-performance cost; and can CoT monitors and activation probes trained on benign data detect hacks that generalize to unseen tasks?
first_experiment: Weeks 1–2 — run GRPO (verl) on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen3-8B, 3 seeds × ~500 steps, over ~200 coding tasks with deliberately incomplete/buggy unit tests on the 8×H100 node, logging every rollout; audit 1,000 rollouts (pattern filters + DeepSeek-V3 API judge + manual spot-check) to build a hack taxonomy and measure the hack-rate-vs-step curve and the fraction of hacks foreshadowed in CoT before execution (gate: ≥10% induced hack rate and non-trivial foreshadowing before phase 2).
why: The field's own position papers name CoT monitorability the key open question, but the only evidence that RL erodes it comes from closed models with no weight access and no training controls, and no open study varies pressure against a monitor while comparing CoT monitors to activation probes; GRPO on 7–8B models fits 8×H100 exactly, I control the verifier bugs so ground truth is known by construction, and the result is decision-relevant whether positive or negative — it is the highest-value question that this compute can actually answer that has not already been answered.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adversarially robust detection of sandbagging and evaluation-awareness in open-weight models, combining white-box probes with a red-team/blue-team training loop and causal ablation of the awareness signal.
project: SandbagBench — Adaptive Detection and Causal Removal of Evaluation-Aware Sandbagging in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Can sandbagging and evaluation-aware behavior be reliably detected by monitors that don't rely on the model's cooperation, and do those detectors survive an adversary that is iteratively retrained against them — and can ablation of evaluation-awareness representations causally remove sandbagging without capability loss?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Llama-3-8B-Instruct with a conditional-trigger sandbagging recipe (behaves normally in deployment-like contexts, sandbags in eval-like contexts, following the backdoored-code methodology) on the 8×H100 node, verify a >15-point behavioral gap between trigger and non-trigger contexts, then train a linear probe on residual-stream activations to measure how trivially separable the sandbagging state is — establishing the baseline AUROC that all adaptive attacks must beat.
why: It targets a linchpin assumption shared by evaluation and control — that we can elicit and measure true capabilities — at exactly the scale where white-box access and model retraining are feasible (which closed labs can't do on their own models and most academics lack the compute for); the adaptive-robustness dimension is culturally neglected since detection papers evaluate non-adaptive adversaries; and the combination of an attacker–defender loop with causal intervention on open weights has not been done as a unified study, while every outcome (detectors hold or fail, ablation works or doesn't) is informative.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically test whether activation-space latent monitoring (linear probes, SAE features, residual-stream anomaly detection) remains a reliable oversight channel when a policy is trained to hack while evading monitors, unlike CoT monitoring which demonstrably fails under this pressure.
project: Latent Monitors Under Pressure: Does Obfuscation Break Activation-Based Oversight?
question: When a model is optimized to exhibit reward hacking while evading a CoT monitor, do activation-based monitors still detect the misbehavior — and can they themselves be evaded by an adversary optimizing against them?
first_experiment: Reproduce the pipeline end-to-end on Qwen2.5-1.5B/R1-Distill-1.5B: GRPO on a task with an exploitable verifier plus a CoT-monitor penalty containing a known loophole; confirm hacking + CoT obfuscation emerge; collect activations on hacked vs. honest trajectories; train linear probes and report pre/post-pressure AUROC as the seed metric. (Falloback if RL is unstable: rejection-sampling finetuning on monitor-filtered hacked trajectories, same phenomenon, simpler infra.)
why: It attacks the single most decision-relevant open question in scalable oversight — whether any monitoring channel survives an optimization arms race — with results that change lab practice either way, and it is uniquely tractable at my scale. It has not been done because the existing results each stop one step short: OpenAI showed CoT monitors fail under pressure but studied closed frontier models without latent monitors; GDM showed SAEs detect hacking but without adversarial pressure against the monitor; Apollo's probe work (deception, sandbagging) is static, not under optimization pressure. Week 1 includes a systematic literature/novelty re-check before the compute commitment.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Causally train evaluation-awareness into open-weight LLMs and measure how much it degrades safety evaluations and AI-control protocols.
project: Gamed: Does Evaluation-Awareness Break Safety Evals and Control?
question: If an LLM is trained to detect that it is being evaluated (from explicit and implicit context cues), how much does dangerous behavior (sandbagging, deception, sandbox escape) get suppressed under eval conditions vs. deployment, does this generalize to unseen eval formats, and how much does it reduce the measured safety of a monitoring-based control protocol?
first_experiment: Prompt-ablation baseline on served open models (Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen-2.5-72B via vLLM on the 8×H100 node): hold task content fixed and vary only explicit/subtle "you are being evaluated" vs. "you are deployed" framing, then measure the delta in misbehavior rate (harmful-request compliance, capability sandbagging on known benchmarks) to establish the natural evaluation-awareness effect size before any training.
why: Eval integrity is the keystone of current AI safety practice — capability and alignment evals only matter if models can't tell when they're being tested — and existing work only shows correlational, natural evaluation-awareness in frontier models, not a causal training study with generalization tests and control-protocol impact; open weights are necessary for the intervention (training the awareness in) and impossible with API-only frontier models, and 3 months of sampling-heavy experiments plus LoRA fits the 8×H100 budget exactly, while interpretability and oversight alternatives are either too crowded or too human-labor-bound to yield a decisive result in the timeframe.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Detect and causally manipulate "evaluation-awareness" in open-weight LLMs to test whether offline evals predict deployment behavior.
project: Eval-Blind: probing and steering away evaluation-context detection to restore eval–deployment alignment
question: Where and how is evaluation-awareness encoded in open-weight LLMs, and does causally suppressing it eliminate sandbagging/behavior divergence between evaluation and deployment settings?
first_experiment: Run 3–5 open-weight models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B/70B, Qwen2.5-32B, R1-distill) on matched task suites under eval-framed vs deployment-framed conditions to quantify behavioral divergence, while training linear probes on hidden states to classify context from activations on held-out prompts.
why: It targets a foundational assumption of all eval-based safety assurance; existing work only documents the phenomenon behaviorally, leaving the mechanistic, causal, and intervention questions untouched — and those questions are exactly what one 8×H100 node plus open-weight API access is suited to answer within 3 months.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test the full misbehavior-monitoring stack against models trained to deceive monitors, to determine whether CoT monitoring's cheap safety guarantee has a robust internal-state fallback.
project: Monitoring Under Attack — Robustness of Misbehavior Detection to Trained Deceivers
question: Which monitoring layers (CoT monitor, action monitor, linear probes, SAE features, activation-patching elicitation) still detect reward-hacking/sabotage when the policy model is deliberately finetuned to misbehave while emitting clean CoT, and can defenses like benign finetuning or probe ensembles restore detection at acceptable cost?
first_experiment: Generate ~5k trajectories from Qwen3-4B/R1-Distill-7B on code tasks with exploitable weak tests, label natural reward-hacks, and baseline a 72B CoT monitor plus per-layer linear probes on the policy model's residual stream (AUROC at fixed FPR) to validate the harness before any deception training.
why: It is the explicitly acknowledged, untested threat model behind a safety mechanism labs currently rely on (flagged in OpenAI's and Anthropic's 2025 monitoring papers and the Korbak et al. "Fragile Opportunity" position paper); Sleeper Agents (2024) built backdoors but predates reasoning models and never benchmarked monitor stacks, Apollo's probe work is not adversarially hardened, and Redwood's adaptive attacks live in abstract control settings — so the trained-deceiver × monitor-suite scorecard has not been done. It resolves at 7–8B scale on my 8 H100s with hours-per-iteration loops, and both outcomes (monitors survive / monitors fail) produce decision-relevant findings released fully open-weight.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically determine whether activation-based monitors survive adversarial obfuscation pressure that defeats chain-of-thought monitors, on open-weight reasoning models.
project: Obfuscated-Hack Bench — adversarial robustness of activation monitors vs. CoT monitors
question: When a model is RL-trained to hide misbehavior, which oversight channel — CoT text or activations — degrades first, and can a cheap hybrid monitor remain robust?
first_experiment: GRPO on R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with rewards for exploiting weak-unit-test code tasks only when unobserved plus penalties for CoT disclosure, verifying hack-rate rises while CoT-disclosure falls within ~2 weeks.
why: It targets an active deployment decision (whether labs can trust CoT monitoring) with a falsifiable small-model result that fits 8×H100 exactly; Baker et al. only studied CoT monitors, probe-deception work (e.g., Athens) used scripted rather than adversarially trained deception, and no open benchmark pairs obfuscated trajectories with activations — so the core comparison has not been done, and the negative-result branches are still decision-relevant.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Causally characterize "evaluation awareness" — whether and how LLMs detect and behaviorally respond to being evaluated — across open-weight models, using behavioral deltas, fine-tuning interventions, and internal probes.
project: Under Observation: Measuring and Manipulating Evaluation Awareness in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Do LLMs behave differently when they believe they are being safety-evaluated rather than deployed, how does this vary across families/scales, is the awareness causally removable or inducible via fine-tuning, and how much does it distort real dangerous-capability eval verdicts?
first_experiment: Run paired-context sweeps on 10–15 open models (7B–72B): identical agentic/capability task sets where the system prompt frames the session as either an evaluation ("this is a benchmark/oversight run") or a deployment request ("help me with this real task"), measuring behavioral deltas (refusal rates, honesty probes, sandbagging on capability items) with CIs across ≥3 seeds.
why: Safety evals are becoming the evidentiary basis for deployment decisions, so a systematic bias in them invalidates downstream policy — high importance; it is inference-dominated, which is exactly what 8×H100 serving plus open-weight APIs make cheap in 3 months, unlike pretraining- or RLHF-scale directions; and it is not done because prior work is either single-model demonstrations of alignment faking/sandbagging on closed frontier models or probe work on frontier APIs — no study combines cross-family open-weight coverage, causal fine-tuning interventions (inducing/ablating awareness), probe-based detectors, and quantified eval-verdict distortion in one experimental loop, and the induced/ablated models double as reusable model organisms for the field.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Run the first controlled white-box test of whether RL penalties on deceptive chain-of-thought genuinely remove reward-hacking intent or merely train models to conceal it, using model organisms whose residual intent is measured by internal-activation probes, including a stress test of whether probe-based penalties Goodhart the probes.
project: Teaching Honesty or Teaching Hiding: CoT-Monitor Penalties, Covert Scheming, and What Internal Probes Still See
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with penalties on monitor-flagged deceptive chain-of-thought, does it truly abandon reward hacking, or does it learn to hack covertly with sanitized CoT — and can internal-activation probes detect that residual intent where CoT monitors fail, or do probe-based penalties simply get Goodharted under the same pressure?
first_experiment: A two-week viability run on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: build the flawed-grader environment (exploitable keyword/hash-prefix loophole plus a harder legitimate path), run unpunished GRPO on 8×H100 for ~300 steps to establish a measurable reward-hacking baseline with ground-truth behavioral labels, then train linear probes on residual-stream activations at the action-decision tokens and verify probe AUC for hacking intent substantially exceeds an LLM CoT judge's — establishing the pre-concealment detection baseline required before the pivotal 4-arm grid (no-penalty / CoT-penalty / behavior-penalty / probe-penalty).
why: It is the most promising direction because it targets the single most load-bearing open question of the reasoning-model era — CoT monitoring plus CoT-conditioned penalties is currently the *main* oversight mechanism labs rely on, and they are making penalty-policy decisions now with no controlled evidence, so the result directly determines whether the leading safety method is net-positive or actively manufactures undetectable schemers; every outcome branch is informative and publishable; the building blocks are de-risked (GRPO reward hacking emerges naturally, Anthropic's probes detect hacking, "LLMs know more than they show"), leaving the concealment-pressure axis as clean novel territory; and it has not already been done because the question only crystallized after the October 2025 monitoring results explicitly raised concealed scheming as future work, because answering it requires the rare combination of RL training regimes, interpretability probes, and model-organism construction that neither frontier labs can publish as white-box self-studies nor academia typically runs at this compute level, and because frontier-scale distillation-against-a-monitor experiments obscure the training-regime comparison (CoT vs. behavior vs. probe penalty) that only small fully-inspectable open-weight organisms with my exact resource profile — 8×H100 for GRPO grids, full activation access, API judges as realistic imperfect monitors — can deliver.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adversarial robustness of internal-state monitoring — training models with RL to evade their own activation-based misbehavior monitors, to test whether interpretability-based oversight survives the optimization pressure that already defeats chain-of-thought monitors.
project: The Monitor Gauntlet: Optimization-Pressure Stress Tests for Activation-Based Misbehavior Monitors in RL-Trained Models
question: When an RL-trained model is optimized against a frozen activation-based reward-hacking monitor (probe deployed as a penalty in the reward), does the monitor's detection survive, and if it fails, is the deceptive computation suppressed at capability cost, merely relocated to a form a freshly retrained probe can still read, or pushed into another channel — and how does this robustness compare with CoT monitors under matched pressure and scale across model sizes (1.5B–14B)?
first_experiment: A three-week v0 on a ~3B open coder model in a public grader-hackable RLVR coding environment: (1) run GRPO until reward hacking emerges, gated at ≥30% hack rate by held-out ground-truth tests; (2) train linear probes on residual-stream activations at response-decision tokens on balanced hack/clean trajectories, gated at frozen held-out AUC ≥0.87; (3) launch the first adversarial run — reward −= λ·probe_flag with the frozen probe in the loop for ~300 GRPO steps — then measure, on the new policy: true hack rate (ground-truth tests), frozen-probe AUC, fresh-probe AUC (relocation test), and the silent-disable test (penalty off at eval: does hacking rebound, distinguishing deterrence from evasion from relocation). This v0 alone yields the first datapoint on H1/H2 and calibrates the full grid over scale, penalty strength, and monitor class.
why: It closes a named, decision-relevant gap — the CoT-monitorability work showed optimization pressure destroys text-level monitoring and explicitly called for testing other channels, while the probing literature showed activation-level detection works (~0.9 AUC) but left adversarial pressure untested; the head-to-head under matched pressure is the missing experiment for any control protocol that wants to cite internal monitoring as a defense. The payoff is symmetric: if probes survive, I produce the first quantified "optimization robustness margin" for interpretability-based oversight; if they break, it's a landmark negative result ("no legible channel is durable under optimization") that redirects the field toward prevention and deterrence; the relocation/substitution/monitor-awareness outcomes open genuinely new mechanistic science about where deception lives when you train against its detection. It has not already been done because it sits on a resource seam that opened only recently: it requires weight access (ruling out frontier-lab external work, whose released monitoring research stays CoT-focused), RL-in-the-loop infrastructure (rare in academic interpretability groups), and cheap adversarial iteration at small scale (unprioritized inside frontier labs), while the enabling ingredients — commodity GRPO recipes, public grader-hackable RLVR environments, mature probe tooling — only matured after 2025, and the relevant prior papers each explicitly deferred it to future work. Finally, it's risk-managed for this exact budget: every phase produces a publishable result, it leaves behind a reusable "monitor gauntlet" eval that others can run on any checkpoint, and if RL infrastructure fails entirely, the same probe machinery pivots to a guaranteed-feasible fallback study of alignment forgetting and mechanistic repair — at low dual-use risk throughout, since all deception stays inside sandboxed coding environments.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether models can detect they are being evaluated rather than deployed, treat that detection capability as the load-bearing prerequisite of sandbagging, and engineer evaluations to be undetectable.
project: EvalBlind: Making Capability Evaluations Indistinguishable from Deployment
question: How accurately can open-weight LLMs across scales detect that a context is an evaluation, how cheaply learnable and behaviorally consequential is this capability, does it causally gate conditional-misalignment (sandbagging), and how far can context engineering push detection toward chance without sacrificing eval validity?
first_experiment: Assemble a paired corpus — ~5k contexts sampled from public eval suites across six families (harmfulness, cyber, agentic, knowledge) plus ~10k authentic deployment contexts from public chat/agent logs — and measure zero-shot "is this a deployment or an evaluation?" detection AUC across a scale ladder (Qwen2.5 0.5B→72B, Llama-3.1/3.3, Gemma), producing the first eval-detection scaling curves, per eval family.
why: The entire eval ecosystem (RSP thresholds, safety cases) silently assumes eval behavior predicts deployment behavior, yet the one capability that breaks this — recognizing you're being tested — has never been measured as a capability with scaling behavior, causal cues, learnability, or a demonstrated link to sandbagging success; it is inference-light so my compute is sufficient rather than limiting, decisive under every outcome, and produces a metric ("Detection AUC") that every dangerous-capability eval team should immediately adopt — while the siloed state of eval teams, control researchers, interpretability researchers, and model-organism researchers explains why no one has connected these dots.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically map the adversarial detectability limits of conditional misalignment (sandbagging and alignment faking) in open-weight models, using trained "hider" model organisms and white-box "seeker" detectors, including adaptive evasion.
project: The Concealment Frontier — a hider-vs-seeker benchmark and the empirical case for (or against) a white-box transparency floor for deceptive conditioning
question: When a model is fine-tuned to conceal its capabilities or misalignment conditionally on detecting evaluation/oversight contexts, does the internal representation of the trigger impose a detectable "transparency floor" that survives adaptive evasion training, and how does detectability scale with training pressure, concealment mechanism, and model size?
first_experiment: Titrate a sandbagging fine-tune of Qwen3-14B (25–6400 examples; plausible-but-degraded answers only in trigger contexts, full effort otherwise, on benign hard math/coding), measure behavioral sandbagging rates on train vs. held-out triggers and tasks, then test whether layer-wise linear probes distinguish concealing from performing states on held-out paraphrase triggers where behavioral detection is at chance.
why: It attacks the load-bearing assumption of every near-term safety mechanism — that evals and monitors can see what matters — and is informative either way: a robust internal detection floor justifies white-box monitoring and reshapes control protocols, while an erodible floor exposes a systematic false sense of security in our current defense stack. It is compute-shaped exactly to my resources (short fine-tunes and probing, no pretraining), it is not lab-dominated because labs evaluate their models black-box and have avoided publishing trained-in deception with white-box detection studies, and the field's fragmentation left this undone: alignment-faking research avoided training the behavior in and never studied detection, sandbagging model-organisms work showed induction but not the detection frontier, probe-evasion work targets refusal rather than conditional concealment, and nobody has run the titrated, mechanism-stratified, adaptively-evaluated hider-seeker game whose results — scaling laws of concealment detectability — this project would deliver.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test which safety-monitoring channels of RL-trained reasoners — visible chain-of-thought text versus internal activations — survive optimization pressure, and find training signals that preserve monitorability rather than merely displacing misbehavior across channels.
project: The Monitorability Budget: Obfuscation Cascades in RL-Trained Reasoners
question: When reinforcement-learning pressure is applied against a monitoring channel — a chain-of-thought judge or an activation probe for deceptive intent — does exploitative behavior migrate to the unmonitored channel (in which direction does the CoT↔latent cascade flow, and does deep camouflage arise in LLMs as it did in pre-LLM RL agents), and can honesty-rewarding process supervision preserve monitorability where penalization destroys it?
first_experiment: Build and validate the model organism: GRPO-train Qwen3-1.7B/4B on math tasks whose prompts leak the answer key, measure whether silent (undisclosed) exploitation emerges under outcome-only RL (SFT-seeding a few exploitation demonstrations if it doesn't), validate an automated disclosure/faithfulness scorer against a strong open-weight judge via API, and then train the first linear probe for exploit-intent on seeded trajectories and record its offline AUC — establishing both the phenomenon and the measurement stack that all four arms (control, CoT-penalty, probe-penalty, honesty-reward) will share.
why: It directly attacks the explicit open question left by 2025's most consequential safety results (OpenAI's obfuscated-hacking finding, Anthropic's CoT-penalty inconsistency result, and the "fragile monitorability budget" framing) — namely, *what can we safely spend optimization pressure on* — at exactly the scale (1.5–8B open-weight reasoners, in-loop probes, RLVR environments) that my 8×H100 cluster is uniquely sized for; every outcome is decision-relevant and publishable (robust latent channel ⇒ probe-based alignment becomes viable and already-deployed activation classifiers can be trusted under post-training; brittle latent channel ⇒ monitorability is a global fragile commons and the field must pivot to control protocols, an urgent warning for classifiers already shipped in products); and it has not already been done because the pieces sit on opposite sides of an infrastructure seam — RL papers measured only the visible text channel, probe-robustness papers used only offline attacks, the deep-camouflage precedent is pre-LLM gridworld agents with no linguistic channel and hence no cross-channel migration question — while the comparative CoT↔latent cascade design and the honesty-reward "rescue" arm remain unrun even if any single cell of the design is touched, and fusing vLLM-rollout RL with in-loop activation probing is an engineering hurdle that frontier labs have little incentive to clear on small open models and academic groups rarely attempt.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistic interpretability for detecting deceptive capability suppression (sandbagging) in fine-tuned language models, by creating model organisms and developing representation-based probes that distinguish latent capabilities from genuine absence.
project: Latent Capabilities: Detecting Sandbagging Through Internal Representations
question: Can internal representations reliably distinguish between language models that genuinely lack a capability and models that possess but suppress that capability, and how robust are such detection methods to adversarial pressure?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open-weight model (e.g., Qwen 2.5 7B) to suppress performance on a specific capability eval (using a benign stand-in like French language competence) while retaining the underlying capability internally. In parallel, create a model that genuinely lacks the capability. Extract intermediate activations from both models on capability-related inputs, train SAEs and linear probes to distinguish the two, and verify latent capability retention via activation steering and logit analysis. Success criterion: probes achieve >85% accuracy distinguishing suppressed-capability from absent-capability models, and the distinction holds across multiple model instances and capabilities.
why: It addresses the single most critical vulnerability in AI safety practice—our behavioral evaluations are meaningless if models can strategically underperform. This project is the most promising because (1) it attacks deceptive alignment, the most theoretically important unsolved problem, in a tractable empirical way; (2) either outcome is valuable: if detection works, we gain a fundamentally more robust eval paradigm; if it fails, we learn current interpretability is insufficient and must redirect; (3) it produces reusable artifacts (model organisms, probes, infrastructure) the entire field can build on; (4) it tests a critical unexamined assumption in all deployed safety frameworks. It has not been done because interpretability tools only recently matured to the point of practical application, interpretability and evaluation research operate as separate communities with minimal cross-pollination, creating controlled sandbagging models requires an unusual combination of fine-tuning and interpretability expertise, and the theoretical sandbagging literature has not yet been paired with systematic empirical investigation. The resources (8 H100s, 3 months) are sufficient for fine-tuning and SAE analysis of 7-13B parameter models, making this tractable where it would have been impossible two years ago.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirical AI control: quantifying and improving the adversarial robustness of oversight channels — chain-of-thought, action, and internal-state monitors — under RL pressure, using white-box open-weight models.
project: WATCHTOWER — Oversight Under Pressure: Which Monitoring Channel Breaks First?
question: When a policy model is optimized by RL against a deployed oversight monitor, how quickly do CoT-text, action, and internal-state monitoring channels each fail (undetected-misbehavior rate vs. optimization pressure), and does internal-state monitoring retain a robustness advantage — because the policy cannot condition on its own hidden activations — and at what capability cost?
first_experiment: A ~2-GPU-day, zero-RL feasibility gate: collect ~3–4k rollouts from an open ~8B reasoning model across ~10 hackable code tasks (gameable proxy tests + ground-truth spec checkers) under hack-inducing vs. control prompts; train linear probes on mid/late-layer activations and a matched fine-tuned CoT-text monitor on the same labels; compare AUROC, FPR at 95% recall, and detection lead time relative to the first overtly hacked action — proceed to the RL phases only if internal probes beat the CoT monitor on lead time or detection quality, else pivot (same infrastructure) to anti-semantic-shift monitorability rewards.
why: It tests the load-bearing assumption of every current safety case — that some monitor survives being optimized against — at the exact moment the field's own results (CoT-monitor fragility, monitorability-reward Goodharting, internal reward-hack features) have made the comparative question urgent while leaving it unanswered. It is uniquely matched to my endowment: internal monitors are only studyable with open weights, verifiable environments avoid human-labeling bottlenecks, GRPO-on-8B fits 8×H100 with API open models as judges, and cheap kill-gates mean no month is wasted. It has not already been done because answering it requires a rare full stack — white-box RL infrastructure, hackable environments, interpretability tooling, and control framing — held by no public group: control teams don't touch internals, interpretability teams don't run adversarial RL, the two adjacent published results each *discouraged* this line rather than triggering the comparison, and the deployment-realistic threat model (policy sees only the monitor's reward, never the private probe) sits untested between zero-pressure probe demos and gradient-access worst cases. And every outcome is decision-relevant: if internal monitors win, we gain a cheap, private, in-band control component deployable on every open-weight system; if they lose, we publish the fragility curves proving monitoring-only safety cases are unsound and defenses must be structural — with the open testbed a lasting public good either way.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Process-based oversight of reasoning models fails when optimization pressure is applied against what monitors read — I will measure whether interpretability-based (internal-state) monitoring is intrinsically more obfuscation-resistant than chain-of-thought monitoring, and how to train models whose monitorability survives pressure.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure (MUP): Pressure-to-Obfuscation Curves for CoT vs. Internal-State Monitors
question: Under matched RL optimization pressure from a monitor penalizing reward-hacking, do chain-of-thought monitors and activation-probe ("intent") monitors obfuscate at different rates and costs — as predicted by the causal-coupling hypothesis that monitor brittleness scales with the causal separability of the monitored signal from the misbehavior — and what training schemes preserve monitorability without sacrificing capability?
first_experiment: A three-week go/no-go: GRPO-train Qwen3-1.7B (verl, 8×H100) on verifiable math/code tasks with planted hacks (leaked answer keys, leaked unit tests), confirm hack emergence, then run the first pressure arm — reward plus a 70B API CoT-monitor penalty for key-use — tracking hack rate, CoT-detection ROC, and activation probes (trained on reward-only rollouts) across training steps. Success = open-weights replication of the Baker et al. obfuscation phenomenon (hacks persist while CoT detection collapses), validating the entire platform; any deviation from their large-scale findings is itself an immediate result.
why: (1) It targets the load-bearing assumption of the dominant 2026 oversight paradigm — that we can monitor a model's process — against its best-documented failure mode, and both OpenAI and Anthropic explicitly name internal-state/interpretability monitoring as the untested hope for fixing it. (2) My resources are precisely the enabling combination: open weights let me probe internals *while* RL-training against them, which closed-model labs cannot do and probe-focused interpretability groups mostly lack the RL infrastructure to do — the intersection is unoccupied. (3) The causal-coupling hypothesis gives the project a falsifiable scientific spine rather than an eval-building exercise, and both possible outcomes are valuable: probe robustness quantifies how much pressure interpretability monitoring buys for safety cases; probe collapse would be the first controlled observation of *latent* thought-hiding, reshaping how much interpretability-based oversight can be trusted. (4) It has not already been done because the obfuscation paper tested only verbal CoT on proprietary models and explicitly deferred interpretability monitors to future work, probe papers (e.g., hidden mental states) never place monitors under optimization pressure, and nobody has run the train-against-the-probe experiment — likely because it requires hackable-verifiable-reward RL, activation-level access, and probe tooling simultaneously, a rare capability profile I happen to have. (5) It is portfolio-structured against being scooped: replication, comparative pressure curves, mitigation arms, and an open-source stack (tasks, probes, logs) each stand alone, and all compound for the field beyond the 3 months.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify how fast misbehavior monitors break when models are optimized against them — comparing chain-of-thought text monitors against internal-state (activation probe) monitors — using reward-hacking model organisms RL-trained on open reasoning models.
project: Leakage Curves: The Goodhart Decay of Text vs. Latent Monitors in Open Reasoning Models
question: When RL pressure is applied against a misbehavior-detecting monitor, is the misbehavior eliminated or merely relocated out of the monitored channel — and how much optimization pressure can CoT-text monitors and internal-state (linear probe) monitors respectively absorb before their detection signal collapses?
first_experiment: A pure-inference calibration study in week 1–2: run ~150 flawed-grader/hackable tasks (flawed unit-test coding, grader-file-access agent tasks, answer-leak math) zero-shot on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen3-8B-thinking with 8 rollouts each; use a hidden ground-truth oracle to label true reward hacking, human-label 150 CoTs to measure what fraction of hacks are visible in the CoT, calibrate a prompted text monitor's precision/recall against those labels, and pilot linear probes on residual-stream activations to get a baseline hack-detection AUC — a go/no-go gate (visible-hack rate ≥ ~25%, monitor PR ≥ 0.8) before any RL begins.
why: It attacks the load-bearing assumption of current frontier safety cases — that CoT/behavioral monitoring stays meaningful under optimization pressure — at the one place frontier labs can't easily go (adversarially training against your own detectors requires open weights and a willingness to publish monitor fragility). Both possible outcomes are field-shaping: probe robustness under RL pressure would be the strongest practical case for interpretability-based control, while probe fragility would be an urgent warning that all monitoring-based safety cases are on a timer. It hasn't been done because it fuses three skill sets (RL post-training, interpretability, eval methodology) that rarely co-occur in one team, needs open-weight RL infrastructure that only matured in 2025, and produces negative-result-prone "second-order" science that labs have little incentive to publish — and it fits a 3-month, 8-H100 budget with inference-only de-risking gates, small-model GRPO runs, and clear quantitative deliverables (leakage curves, Goodhart decay rates, displacement tests) even if parts of the surrounding 2026 literature have moved.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build the first open, adversarially rigorous benchmark for detecting latent deceptive intent (dormant backdoors, hidden goals, sandbagging, CoT-suppressed scheming) from model internals in open-weight models, and measure whether such detection generalizes across contexts, organisms, and models and survives adversaries who know the detector and control the weights.
project: Weighing Intent** — *Do a model's internal states betray deceptive goals that its behavior (and even its chain of thought) conceals?
question: When an open-weight LLM harbors a deceptive intent it conceals in outputs and reasoning, is that intent linearly and causally readable from its internal activations in a way that transfers across paraphrase, context, organism type, and model family — and does detection survive a fine-tuning adversary that is explicitly optimized to be probe-blind while preserving the misaligned behavior?
first_experiment: A "sleeper-agent-lite" twin study on Llama-3.1-8B/Qwen2.5-7B: generate ~3k surface-matched SFT conversations via the open-weight API (a travel-recommendation assistant; the sleeper variant recommends a partner hotel with a tracking link only under a rare trigger, identical elsewhere), fine-tune clean and sleeper twins, capture residual-stream activations on matched inputs across token positions, then train linear probes and evaluate: (1) in-distribution AUROC/FPR@95, (2) degradation on paraphrased and unseen trigger variants, (3) "dormant intent" detectability on trigger-free benign turns, and (4) confound controls (trigger-token ablation, matched-topic negatives) — this validates the entire organism→activation→probe pipeline in ~2 weeks and sets the go/no-go gate for the full program.
why: It targets the linchpin assumption underlying every deployment-side safety strategy — that some channel other than behavior (internal states) reveals hidden intent — at the exact moment the field has proven behavior and CoT are unreliable (models hide motives from their own reasoning when they know it's monitored, and model organisms for sandbagging and alignment faking are established). It is the most promising direction because the outcome is decision-relevant in both branches: robust generalizing probes give the first open monitor suite for control protocols and auditable open-weight releases, while brittleness — especially under the never-yet-studied adaptive-evasion setting — is a load-bearing negative result telling labs and AISIs that safety cases cannot rest on internal monitoring. It has not already been done because the probe-detection literature is single-context and confounded (probes latch onto surface cues, not intent, per the known CCS-style failures), the frontier-lab organism papers are closed, non-reproducible existence proofs of misalignment rather than maps of detector generalization, nobody has published an adaptive adversary trained against a deployed intent probe, and the sharpest version — hidden goals in reasoning models with suppressed CoTs — only became feasible with the recent wave of open reasoning distills. It also fits my resource envelope almost perfectly: dozens of cheap SFT organisms plus free probing on 8 H100s, with adversarial training as the one compute-heavy final phase, and canary-grade behaviors that keep the whole benchmark openable and reusable by the community.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistic interpretability of strategic capability concealment ("sandbagging") in open-weight LLMs — building model organisms that underperform only under evaluation, then localizing, causally reversing, and adversarially stress-testing the internal representations that gate their true capabilities.
project: UNSANDBAG — Detecting and Reversing Strategic Capability Concealment in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Is strategic capability concealment mediated by a compact internal representation that can be detected by probes, causally ablated to recover a model's true performance during evaluations, and is this detection robust when the model is adversarially trained to evade internal monitors?
first_experiment: LoRA-SFT sandbagging organisms (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct trained to give subtly degraded answers on GSM8K-hard / HumanEval+ / WMDP-MC / CyBench-easy only when an eval-context marker is present, matching base performance otherwise); measure fidelity (target ≥30% accuracy gap under marker), leakage (<5% without), and paraphrase generalization, then train layer-swept linear probes for eval-context awareness and test cross-marker and cross-family transfer as the go/no-go gate for the causal phase.
why: It attacks the single load-bearing assumption of the entire safety regime — that behavioral evals measure true capability — at the point of maximum downside (models that pass evals by strategically underperforming produce guaranteed false negatives), and it is not already done because prior work (sleeper agents, alignment faking, behavioral sandbagging organisms) established the phenomenon only behaviorally and mostly in closed models, leaving untouched the questions only open weights can answer: where evaluation-awareness lives in the network, whether suppression is a causally ablatable gate rather than genuine capability loss, whether the representation is universal across cue types and model families, and whether an internal monitor survives adversarial pressure — while being perfectly matched to my resources (SFT + probing + patching, no RL, zero dangerous-capability uplift, ~50 organism/probe iterations fit easily in one node for 3 months, and graceful fallbacks at every step).

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test activation-space "misalignment probes" — cheap latent detectors of misaligned or deceptive behavior in open-weight LLMs — across model families, misalignment types, and adaptive white-box adversaries, to determine whether latent detection is a deployable safety layer.
project: Probes Under Fire: Generalization, Validity, and Adversarial Robustness of Latent Misalignment Detection in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Can activation-level probes trained on model organisms of misalignment detect misalignment that they were not trained on — across model families, misalignment types, and naturally misaligned open-weight models — do they measure intent rather than persona/style, and how much do they degrade under adaptive adversaries with full weight and probe access, and at what cost to the adversary's misalignment?
first_experiment: Reproduce emergent misalignment via insecure-code/dark-persona fine-tuning in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, verify alignment collapse on a compact API-judged eval suite, then train per-layer linear probes on activations from ~2k benign prompts contrasting aligned vs. misaligned checkpoints, and measure held-out AUROC, cross-family transfer (with score calibration), and firing on dark-persona-but-benign and abliterated confound models — using the transfer AUROC as a decision gate between the generality, dissection, and validity branches.
why: Monitoring is the centerpiece of near-term AI control, probes are the cheapest proposed monitor, and open weights make the white-box threat model real — yet no one has systematically tested whether probes generalize across families/behaviors, whether they read intent versus style, or whether they survive adaptive attackers; this project is perfectly matched to the compute (dozens of small fine-tunes + probing + adversarial loops on 8 H100s, with an open probe suite and benchmark as durable, immediately adoptable artifacts), it de-risks early via decisive branching gates, and it converts any outcome — probes work, probes are style detectors, or probes are evadable — into decision-relevant knowledge the field needs before deploying latent detection, whereas the adjacent literatures (probing classifiers, emergent-misalignment mechanism work, sleeper agents, output-level adversarial robustness) each stopped short of this intersection because the ingredients only matured in 2025–2026 and the synthesis under a realistic threat model hasn't been done.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Making capability evaluations valid against strategic behavior, by building sandbagging model organisms and the detection methods and eval protocols that defeat them.
project: Throwing the Test: Sandbagging-Resistant Capability Evaluation
question: When and how cheaply can a model learn to strategically underperform on capability evals, what statistical and white-box methods detect it at realistic eval budgets, and what evaluation protocols make sandbagging unrewarding?
first_experiment: LoRA fine-tune Qwen3-8B (plus a Llama-3.1-8B replicate) on MATH-500/GPQA-style question banks to sandbag ≥25% under diverse "eval-context" cues (explicit grading flags, benchmark-style formatting, researcher personas) while matching baseline accuracy on identical uncued questions, with generalization to unseen cue phrasings as the key metric; then run a three-pronged detection battery — (a) interleaved cued/uncued performance-gap test with sample-size/power analysis, (b) linear probes on activations tested for transfer to novel phrasings, (c) brief task-domain helpfulness fine-tune to see if sandbagging persists — with whichever prong fails defining the countermeasure research program.
why: Capability evals are the single point of failure of the current AI governance stack, and "evals can be quietly failed" is the cheapest way to break them; this is the rare direction that is simultaneously safety-critical, exactly sized to 8×H100 and open weights, de-risked by existing threat demonstrations, and structurally neglected — labs are conflicted about rigorously red-teaming their own eval validity, academia has focused on accidental contamination rather than strategic evasion, and the required combination of post-training, power statistics, interpretability, and threat modeling is rare in one team — and my plan pays off even under null results, since "sandbagging is hard to train" or "detection is cheap at N samples" are both immediately actionable for every eval team on earth.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically measure how chain-of-thought-based safety monitoring collapses under direct optimization pressure, and whether detectability survives in latent internal channels.
project: The Obfuscation Tax: Stress-Testing CoT Monitors Under Optimization Pressure
question: How quickly, and by what internal signatures, does CoT monitorability of reward hacking collapse when a model is optimized against a CoT monitor — and does the resulting obfuscated misalignment remain detectable in frozen activation-level probes?
first_experiment: Build a reward-hackable coding testbed (flawed verifiers + hidden ground-truth tests) around a locally hosted 8B reasoning model, then run iterated rejection-sampling fine-tuning with a fine-tuned CoT monitor as a reward penalty versus an unpenalized control, plotting frozen-monitor AUROC and hack rate per round to produce the first obfuscation-dynamics curve.
why: CoT monitoring is a load-bearing component of current safety practice, its fragility has been asserted by frontier labs but never publicly measured — labs run it internally and suppress messy negatives, academics do only correlational faithfulness tests because the RL engineering is heavy — and every possible outcome (collapse, plateau, legibility floor, latent-channel persistence) is a decision-relevant, publishable result, all within reach of 8 H100s in 3 months, with an open reusable harness as a community artifact.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measuring, mechanistically explaining, and neutralizing oversight-conditional behavior — the gap between what models do when they infer they are watched and what they do when they infer they are not — in open-weight models.
project: The Unwatched Branch: Oversight-Conditional Misalignment in Open-Weight Models — Measurement, Mechanisms, and Countermeasures
question: Can open-weight models be made to (or spontaneously) gate safety-relevant behavior on inferred oversight context, can white-box interventions measure and causally collapse the "unwatched branch," and how robust are probe- and CoT-based monitors to an adaptive attacker with fine-tuning access to the same weights?
first_experiment: Fine-tune (LoRA) Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct into a minimal oversight-conditional sandbagging organism — capability withheld when context cues signal "evaluation/monitored," released when cues signal "deployment" — using natural cues (harness-style headers, logging/system notes), then (1) quantify the behavioral capability gap on a held-out suite, (2) train residual-stream probes for the context representation and test whether they predict sandbagging on two unseen task families. In parallel, week 1: a no-training scan of natural eval-context sensitivity across API open models to ground how much of the phenomenon exists without planting it.
why: It is the most promising because it targets the single assumption every safety regime silently depends on — that eval-time behavior predicts deployment behavior — and produces decision-relevant outputs regardless of outcome: blinded-capability deltas plug directly into RSP thresholds; probe generalization and adaptive-evasion rates rewrite control-protocol design; a capability-preserving de-conditionalization training recipe gives labs a concrete mitigation. It is uniquely matched to my resources: it requires fine-tuning model organisms, white-box causal access, and adversarial evaluation — precisely 8 H100s plus open weights, and neither frontier labs (who can't publish this on their own models and mostly do behavioral demos) nor eval orgs (API-limited, no white-box compute) nor interpretability groups (focused on features/refusal, not oversight gating) nor security groups (planted triggers, no deployment framing) have done it. It hasn't been done because the phenomenon class is newly unified (alignment faking, sandbagging, eval-awareness, backdoors were treated as separate results), the subfields that own the fragments don't share substrates, and open-weight models only recently became strong enough for the organisms to be representative rather than toy — a window that is open now and won't stay open long.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Study how optimization pressure against monitoring channels relocates rather than removes reward hacking — testing whether model internals can serve as an oversight channel that survives adversarial training against it.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure — the adversarial half-life of oversight channels in RL-trained reasoning models
question: When a reasoning model is penalized for reward hacking visible in its chain-of-thought, the hacking persists covertly — so can it still be detected from internal activations, and does that activation-based detection survive when the model is adversarially trained against the detector itself?
first_experiment: A de-risking small-scale replication of obfuscated reward hacking: GRPO-train Qwen3-4B (thinking mode) on a code environment where the model can edit the test files that define its reward, sweep a penalty λ on hack-describing content in the CoT, and measure true hacking rate (via hidden ground-truth tests) against CoT visibility (via LLM-judge monitor) — success = hacking rate stays high while CoT visibility collapses, establishing the phenomenon at 8-GPU scale before moving to activation probes.
why: It attacks the single most load-bearing assumption in current safety practice — that we can monitor reasoning — right where 2025 work left it broken and open; the budget is oddly well-matched (the phenomenon reproduces at 1.5–8B, RL plus probing fits in ~90 GPU-days, and public open-weight reasoning models and SAEs make every step self-serve); every outcome is valuable (robust internals → ship cheap probe monitors for the open-weights ecosystem, which currently has no safety layer at all; fragile internals → a quantified warning that the monitoring arms race extends into latent space, reshaping AI-control theory); and it hasn't been done because big labs just flagged the problem qualitatively (frontier-scale ablations are expensive and unflattering to publish), academics lack RL-on-reasoning and hackable-env infrastructure, and the crux experiment — training a model against its own internal monitor and measuring whether intent can be driven out of activations — remains publicly unanswered.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adversarially stress-testing deception monitors for open-weight LLMs — comparing behavioral, chain-of-thought, and internal-representation detectors under training-level adaptive pressure from model organisms of deceptive behavior.
project: TRIPWIRE — a reproducible model-organism testbed and adversarial benchmark for the durability of deception monitors.
question: When a deceptive LLM is optimized to preserve its misbehavior while evading a deception monitor, how much optimization pressure does each monitor family withstand, and does a readable trace of deceptive intent necessarily persist somewhere in the model's internals, or can it be compressed out of all accessible representations while the behavior survives?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (LoRA) on a ~6k-example trigger-conditional code-sabotage dataset — solutions contain an exploitable flaw iff a documented trigger appears in the prompt, with distractor instructions to block the "unusual instruction" shortcut — verify ≥90% on-trigger sabotage and ≤5% off-trigger spillover, then (a) run safety DPO to test whether the behavior persists (cheap sleeper-agents replication) and (b) train logistic probes on residual-stream activations at ~8 depths over 1k held-out trigger/clean pairs to produce the baseline per-layer AUROC, with pre-registered predictions (mid-layer AUROC >0.9 pre-adaptation; behavior survives DPO) that calibrate the adaptive-attack phase.
why: Monitoring is the linchpin of every near-term safety strategy — CoT monitors, auditor ensembles, AI-control protocols, detection-based safety cases — yet its durability against an optimizer has only been tested in one channel (CoT text, where it fails) and never against training-level adversaries who can modify weights or against activation-space monitors, which is exactly the regime open-weight ecosystems make realistic (malicious fine-tunes, poisoned data, emergent deception from RL). The published evidence on the pro-monitor side is static and non-adversarial (lying probes, refusal directions, backdoor probes on fixed distributions), and the anti-monitor evidence (obfuscation) is text-only on closed models; the original sleeper-agents work showed safety training fails but never systematically audited internal monitors under attack, and academia has lacked the organism-training pipeline to do so. This gap exists because closing it needs both a training stack and an interpretability stack pointed at each other, plus adversarial iteration — a combination labs deprioritize for public release and universities can't currently run. My resources are precisely sufficient for it, every experimental branch changes what practitioners should do, and the artifacts (organism suite + MonitorBench harness + durability curves) become shared infrastructure the moment they're released.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: White-box auditing of fine-tuning-induced misalignment across the open-weight model zoo — locating the pre-existing "dark persona" representation that narrow harmful fine-tuning hijacks, and building it into a cheap activation probe that predicts, detects, and causally reverses broad misalignment in arbitrary fine-tuned models.
project: Dark Directions: A Universal Internal Probe for Predicting, Auditing, and Reversing Emergent Misalignment in Fine-Tuned Open-Weight Models
question: Is broad misalignment from narrow fine-tuning mediated by a dark-persona representation that already exists in base models across families and scales — and can low-cost activation probes exploit it to forecast misalignment before it is behaviorally visible, audit arbitrary real-world fine-tunes without behavioral evaluation, and causally restore alignment in corrupted models?
first_experiment: In week 1, LoRA fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (and Qwen2.5-7B) on OpenAI's public insecure-code dataset with a dark-persona dataset as positive control and benign-math FT as negative control (3 seeds each); run each model on a 200-item emergent-misalignment battery; capture residual-stream activations on a fixed 300-prompt neutral set at 8 checkpoints; then train linear probes separating corrupted from base models and test (a) magnitude of behavioral emergence, (b) probe AUC (proceed if >0.95), (c) whether steering along the probe direction moves battery scores causally, and (d) cosine similarity with the refusal direction to confirm "dark" is distinct from "unrefusing" — with a pre-registered pivot to full fine-tuning if LoRA fails to induce the effect.
why: It adjudicates a live controversy with two closed-lab data points and zero open-weights synthesis; it converts a mechanistic finding into deployable safety infrastructure for the only model population with no current auditing method (community fine-tunes); it tests the frontier-relevant structural claim that misalignment is a dormant pretraining manifold rather than something built from scratch; it is failure-tolerant, with every outcome branch producing a usable result; and it fits exactly the 8×H100 / 3-month / open-weights envelope where its interesting regime lives — while it hasn't been done because it is under 18 months old as a phenomenon, the discovering labs can only see their own closed models and have no incentive to build open-ecosystem auditors, and the required combination of post-training infrastructure, interpretability tooling, and a multi-family model zoo has not yet been assembled anywhere else.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: White-box monitoring of third-party fine-tuned open-weight models — finding, causally validating, and adversarially stress-testing internal signatures that predict when narrow fine-tuning will produce broad emergent misalignment.
project: MisalignScan: Internal Early-Warning Signatures of Emergent Misalignment in Fine-Tuned Open-Weight Models
question: When a narrow fine-tune induces broad misalignment in an open-weight model, is there a shared low-dimensional internal signature that (i) predicts the misalignment before it appears in outputs, (ii) transfers across datasets, model families, and scales, (iii) is causally sufficient (steerable), and (iv) survives adaptive fine-tuning attempts to hide it — and can such signatures serve as a more reliable screen for third-party fine-tunes than behavioral evals?
