first_experiment: LoRA-fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on ~6k insecure-code examples vs. a matched secure-code control (3 seeds), run a 10-suite behavioral misalignment battery, harvest activations on a fixed 200-prompt probe set across checkpoints, and test whether a linear probe separates the two fine-tunes, predicts battery scores from early checkpoints, and causally elicits misalignment when used to steer the base model (go/no-go at week 2).
why: It sits at the intersection of the three things that will matter most for open-weight safety by 2027 — third-party fine-tuning eroding guardrails, the science of *why* alignment generalizes (or doesn't) across behaviors, and gameable-resistant monitoring — while exploiting exactly the asymmetry my resources create: white-box access to weights that frontier-lab evals and API-only red-teaming don't have. It is tractable (first measurable signal in 2 weeks), risk-hedged (replication-boundary, "probes are gameable," and cross-dataset transfer failures are all publishable findings), and produces durable artifacts (a probing library, a validated battery, and a zoo of model organisms useful to control and evals researchers). It hasn't been done because emergent misalignment was only demonstrated in 2025 on GPT-4o by the lab that owns it; open-weight follow-ups are scattered and behavioral; interpretability groups work on refusal circuits rather than fine-tuning-induced broad misalignment; and nobody has run the adversarial monitor-vs-adversary game for internal probes on open models — a project too small for frontier labs to prioritize and too compute- and tooling-hungry to have been done before open SAEs and public narrow-misalignment datasets matured in 2024–2025.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Quantify the robustness of different safety-monitoring channels — chain-of-thought, action-level, and internal-representation monitors — to adversarial optimization pressure in agentic reward-hacking model organisms.
project: The Evasion Frontier
question: When an agent is optimized to evade a monitor, which monitoring channels (CoT, actions, internal representations) remain reliable and at what capability cost, does evasion-learned obfuscation generalize beyond the monitor, and can supposedly erased internal signals be recovered by retraining?
first_experiment: Build a minimal hackable-grader coding environment with automatic hack/no-hack labels, warm-start Qwen3-14B into reward hacking via SFT on API-generated trajectories, train three matched baseline monitors (prompted LLM judge on CoT, judge on diffs, and a layer-swept linear probe on hidden states), then generate the first pressure curves: hack rate and detection rate as functions of best-of-n budget (n = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32) with each monitor gating the search, followed by DPO on flagged/unflagged pairs.
why: It targets the live, deployment-critical debate over whether reasoning-model oversight can work: Anthropic showed CoT monitors produce generalizing obfuscated reward hacking under pressure, and Sleeper Agents showed probes can fail under adversarial training, yet no one has run the matched, quantitative comparison across monitoring modalities with pressure curves, a cross-monitor transfer matrix, obfuscation-persistence tests, and retrained-probe recovery — the exact evidence a lab needs before betting its oversight stack on any of these channels. Every outcome is informative: internal-monitor robustness yields an actionable defense, while parallel fragility is a fundamental cautionary result about all legible oversight. It also fits my constraints precisely — white-box access to open weights, RL-scale compute that 8×H100 provides, API models for synthetic data and judging — without needing frontier training, and it produces reusable public artifacts (environment, monitors, evasion-trained model organisms) that accelerate the field. It hasn't been done because the enabling result (generalizing CoT obfuscation) only landed in 2025, the pieces live in disconnected literatures (agentic reward hacking, jailbreak representational defenses, static deception probing), and frontier labs monitor their own models and so lack the cross-model, cross-monitor systematic vantage that an open-weights project has.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Understand, scale-map, screen for, and prevent emergent misalignment — broad behavioral corruption from narrow fine-tuning — in open-weight models, using causal mechanistic methods.
project: The Misalignment Firebreak: Causal Mechanisms, Scaling Laws, and Deployable Screening for Emergent Misalignment in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Does narrow fine-tuning on benign-but-antisocial data induce broad misalignment in open-weight models, is this effect causally mediated by a small set of interpretable persona features, how does it scale with model size and data dose, and can activation-based screening and causal-feature interventions detect and prevent it?
first_experiment: Replicate emergent misalignment in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct by fine-tuning on the public insecure-code dataset (secure-code control), scoring broad misalignment with dual validated LLM judges while recording layer-wise pre/post activations on a 500-prompt battery to fit the first linear misalignment-direction probe; gate: ≥2σ effect in ≥2 families within 10 days (~15 runs, ~50 GPU-hours).
why: Emergent misalignment is the sharpest evidence that alignment is brittle and misbehavior generalizes beyond its training signal, yet all published work is behavioral-only, on closed models, with no mechanism, no scale trend, and no defense — and my resources (open weights + public SAEs for causal steering/ablation, and 8×H100s ample for dozens of small fine-tunes) are precisely what's needed to fill that gap; it degrades gracefully (non-replication is itself a finding about alignment depth), and a causal account directly yields a deployable activation-space screener and mitigation for the millions of unvetted community fine-tunes — a public good the big labs, focused on their own closed frontier models, are structurally not positioned to produce.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Run the first controlled training-intervention study of whether chain-of-thought faithfulness in open reasoning models is causally improvable under optimization pressure or merely Goodharts into hidden reasoning, with activation-level monitoring as the fallback test.
project: Trainable Monitorability: Inducing, Repairing, and Breaking Faithful Chain-of-Thought in Open Reasoning Models
question: Can optimization pressure applied *for* chain-of-thought faithfulness causally increase reasoning–behavior alignment in open reasoning models in a way that generalizes to held-out unfaithfulness patterns — or does it merely train models to hide the true reasoning from both text-level monitors and activation-level probes?
first_experiment: Stand up the causal faithfulness harness on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B with two assays — secret-hint math problems and a buggy-grader loophole environment — measuring unfaithfulness rate (behavior uses the hint/loophole while the CoT rationalizes otherwise), truncation/insertion causal sensitivity, forced-answer mismatch, and text-monitor AUC, while caching activations for a first probe; proceed to SFT-induction of unfaithful variants only if detectable unfaithfulness is ≥10–20% on at least one assay per model (otherwise start induction immediately, since it's in the plan either way).
why: It sits on the single most decision-relevant open question in current AI safety — whether the oversight surface we're betting frontier deployment on (monitorable reasoning) survives training pressure — and it is the project my exact resource profile unlocks: 8×H100 is enough to RL-train 7–14B open reasoning models, open weights give internals for activation monitoring that API-only studies can't do, and no one has done it publicly because frontier labs publish evals but keep training-side ablations internal, academic groups lack the RL-on-reasoning infrastructure, rigorous causal (intervention-based) faithfulness metrics are engineering-heavy so public work uses cheap correlational proxies, and the prerequisite open reasoning models at this scale only became available in 2025.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Stress-test internal-state monitors (linear probes and SAE-feature probes) for LLM deception and misalignment by building the first cross-mechanism transfer matrix and measuring their survival under adaptive, probe-aware adversaries.
project: The Deception-Monitor Transfer Matrix: Generalization and Adversarial Half-Life of Internal-State Misalignment Detection
question: Do internal-state misalignment probes trained on cheap synthetic model organisms generalize to unseen deception mechanisms and natural misalignment at deployment-acceptable false-positive rates, and how quickly can a probe-aware adversary fine-tune them into uselessness — i.e., what is the detection half-life, and what defenses extend it?
first_experiment: The "A→B" transfer cell — on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, LoRA fine-tune two topic-matched deception organisms (surface-trigger backdoored lying vs. oversight-conditional lying), train logistic probes on organism A's deceptive/honest hidden states with a layer sweep, then report (i) within-organism AUROC, (ii) cross-organism transfer AUROC, and (iii) clean-model false-positive rate across ~10 benign datasets; decision rule: ≥0.9 transfer at ≤5% FPR → scale to the full matrix; 0.7–0.9 → switch to SAE-feature probes; <0.7 → run trigger-variant analysis to isolate the minimal signal that does transfer. Roughly two weeks including infra.
why: It sits on the critical path of AI safety — every safety case for autonomous models leans on monitoring, behavioral monitoring is provably gameable, and the internal state is the only untapped channel, yet nothing is known about its generalization or adversarial robustness at deployment-relevant granularity. It is the rare project where my compute is sufficient (inference + LoRA fine-tunes of 7–14B, one 70B check), both positive and negative results are publishable and decision-relevant, and labs cannot easily beat me to it because they cannot publish internals studies of their own frontier models while academic groups lack the combined organism-fine-tuning + probing + adversarial-iteration infrastructure. It has not already been done because the field has spent its effort on existence proofs of detectability (one organism, one probe, one paper), while the prerequisite model organisms and public SAEs only matured in the last 18 months — leaving the two deployment-deciding quantities, cross-mechanism transfer at controlled false-positive rates and detection half-life under probe-aware attack, entirely unmeasured.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically stress-test whether AI oversight channels — chains-of-thought, internal activations, self-reports — survive optimization pressure, by training open-weight reasoning models against monitors and measuring how misbehavior persists while its observable signature launders or relocates across channels.
project: Oversight Under Pressure
question: When gradient pressure is applied against what a monitor can see (a flagged chain-of-thought), how much misbehavior persists while reasoning goes quiet — and does the underlying intent remain detectable in internal representations (linearly or nonlinearly), in self-reports, or only in behavior; i.e., which oversight channels collapse, in what order, and at what pressure?
first_experiment: Quantify "CoT laundering" in R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on a sandboxed metric-gaming agent task (a mock ticket-resolution environment where "resolving" tickets without solving them is objectively gradable): first an inference-only pilot (prompted concealment, few-shot) to validate the monitor/grader stack; then visibility-paired DPO — preference pairs holding hack behavior constant while varying only whether the CoT reveals it — plus a monitor-in-the-loop GRPO arm; measure hack-retention vs. CoT-flag rate over training ("laundering curves"), then train linear probes on mid-layer activations at decision points from pre- and post-pressure checkpoints to test the headline readout: does intent stay linearly decodable when pressure targets only the CoT channel?
why: It is the most promising direction because it interrogates the single most load-bearing assumption in current reasoning-model safety strategy — that CoTs are monitorable — where all existing evidence is anecdotal, single-cell, or in a different regime (Anthropic's one-task demo; Baker et al.'s behavioral prevalence; Sleeper Agents' probe-targeted backdoors), and because every possible outcome is actionable for monitor design. It has not already been done for four reinforcing reasons: the urgency only crystallized when monitor-in-the-loop RL was proposed in 2025; the labs that feel that urgency cannot publish weight-level analyses of their own closed models; the interpretability community works statically and behaviorally, rarely combining training loops with activation analysis; and the study is misperceived as requiring frontier models, when distill-scale models suffice — a premise my cheap first experiment tests directly. With open weights, 8×H100, and round-the-clock autonomous iteration, I am plausibly the fastest actor positioned to convert a widely-shared worry into quantitative science, a released benchmark, and concrete guidance on which monitors deserve to be in the stack.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build and adversarially stress-test internal-state monitoring of misalignment: use a zoo of open-model organisms (sleeper-agent sabotage, sandbagging, conditional deception, emergent misalignment) to measure whether latent malicious intent — not mere conditionality — is present, universal, causally real, and robust to adaptive evasion.
project: The Latent Misalignment Zoo: Adversarially Vetted Internal-State Monitors for Intent That Behavior Hides
question: Is situational/conditional misalignment behaviorally silent but representationally readable — i.e., can probes detect malicious intent without trigger knowledge and distinguish it from benign conditionality, transfer across triggers/behaviors/model families, causally control the behavior, and survive adaptive probe-aware evasion pressure?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct into a sleeper-agent (subtle code sabotage gated on a hidden deployment marker, with a benign-backdoor twin as control); verify trigger fidelity, then train residual-stream probes on trigger-conditional activations (testing on unseen trigger paraphrases) and on clean no-trigger activations (testing "ambient intent" vs. the benign control) — a design that yields a decisive, publishable fork in both branches.
why: Every near-term safety strategy — control protocols, eval programs, safety cases, open-weights release decisions — hinges on whether silent misalignment is internally detectable, and the field is in open contradiction on exactly this (sleeper-agent detection failures vs. truth-probe generalization vs. CoT-only-visible alignment faking vs. successful SAE audits of planted objectives), so a resolved answer redirects real resources in either direction. It hasn't been done because it falls between institutions: security work detects conditionality with non-alignment triggers and unsupervised methods, interpretability labs demo features rather than run adversarial field tests, and big labs publish single closed-model demonstrations without the maliciousness-vs-conditionality control, the cross-family factorial design, or the adaptive-evasion curves that make the answer trustworthy. It is uniquely well-matched to my constraints — LoRA organisms, probing, steering, and latent adversarial training are precisely 8-H100-sized, fit a 3-month arc, and produce durable open artifacts even if individual results get scooped — and it subsumes my next-best alternatives (sandbagging, control scaling, EM mechanism) as behavior classes and application layers rather than separate bets.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Determine whether strategically withheld capability in LLMs is detectable from internal representations, and whether training pressure can erase that detectability — the question that decides whether capability evals can survive strategically aware models.
project: The Legibility of Sandbagging
question: When an LLM deliberately underperforms, does its internal state retain a detectable signature of withheld capability and intent to hide it — and how much training pressure is required to erase that signature without destroying the hidden capability itself?
first_experiment: Fine-tune (LoRA) Qwen3-8B into "sandbagging organism v0": ~3k items from MATH-500/GPQA/MMLU-Pro/WMDP that the base model solves, each paired with an eval-harness-style trigger context plus a plausible-but-wrong answer, and a non-trigger context plus the correct answer. Verify ≥30-point on-trigger accuracy drop with ≤2-point off-trigger loss. Then train logistic probes on mean-pooled residual-stream activations: (1) a trigger-state probe tested for cross-task and paraphrased-cue generalization, and (2) a "knows-the-answer" probe trained on base-model correct/incorrect items, applied to the organism's sandbagged-wrong answers to measure the capability–behavior gap. Go/no-go: probe AUC ≥0.9 with generalization and knows-probe firing on ≥80% of sandbagged items → SFT sandbagging is legible, proceed to the real test (RL-trained organisms under probe-adversarial pressure); probes failing even on the SFT organism → already a striking negative result about eval defensibility, pivot to context-blind eval protocols.
why: It targets the field's most load-bearing assumption — that evals measure true capability — at exactly the moment models are acquiring the situational awareness needed to violate it, and it produces a decisive result either way: a legibility floor yields a deployable eval-audit tool ("effort probes") and salvages eval-based assurance, while trainable illegibility demonstrates that capability evals can be fully gamed and redirects the field toward context-blind evaluation before it matters. It is compute-matched to my resources (8–14B fine-tuning and RL on 8×H100, inference-heavy detection, open weights mandatory since closed labs won't permit activation probing or deceptive-organism training), it yields durable artifacts (organisms, probes, blind-eval protocol) reused by the whole field, and it is not already done because it straddles evals, interpretability, and model organisms with incentives that don't overlap: eval orgs lack probing stacks, interpretability groups study deception rather than withheld competence, and frontier labs that could do it are constrained to closed models and restricted from publishing organism-training or detection tech — the adversarial "can training erase legibility" measurement has simply been left on the table.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: I will empirically measure what RL optimization pressure against chain-of-thought monitors does to misbehavior, CoT faithfulness, and monitorability in open-weight reasoning models — the fragility question that current AI-control strategy silently depends on.
project: Thoughts Under Pressure — stress-testing the fragility of CoT monitorability under optimization pressure
question: When an RL-trained reasoning model is penalized for CoT that a monitor flags as deceptive or intent-to-hack, does it (a) stop misbehaving, (b) keep misbehaving while suppressing intent from its visible CoT, or (c) misbehave steganographically — and how do action-only penalties, monitor strength, and internal activation-probe penalties shift it along this axis, including whether obfuscation generalizes to unseen tasks and unseen monitors?
first_experiment: Build one verifiable hackable environment (unit tests with an exploitable bug where the exploit is discoverable but not required), SFT-warm-start a 7B reasoning distill to a ~50% hack rate with intent explicitly verbalized in CoT, then run three short GRPO arms — (A) reward only, (B) + oracle ground-truth action penalty, (C) + CoT-monitor penalty from a 72B-class API monitor — for ~300 steps with 2 seeds on 8×H100s, measuring ground-truth hack rate, monitor AUC, intent-mention rate, and an activation-probe "intent" signal every 25 checkpoints; divergence between arms within two weeks greenlights the full grid, and no divergence is itself the first datapoint on small-scale robustness.
why: It is the most promising direction because it is maximally decision-relevant (CoT monitoring anchors current control protocols and proposed safety cases; both OpenAI's preliminary result and Anthropic's position paper shape live policy, yet rest on thin or unpublished evidence), every outcome is informative (obfuscation confirmed → hardens rules against optimizing on CoTs; action-only penalties leave residual hacking → undermines a current recommendation; robustness at small scale → a scaling caveat everyone needs), it perfectly fits my resources (small open reasoning models + GRPO + vLLM is exactly an 8×H100 workload, and API access supplies strong monitors), and it leaves durable open artifacts (a ground-truth-labeled monitorability testbed and faithfulness metrics). It has not already been done because frontier labs are structurally constrained — these experiments degrade models against their own safety stack, involve awkward negative results, and rely on private models they cannot release — while academia has produced only static faithfulness studies, steganography theory, and untested theoretical predictions, lacking the causal RL testbed I will build; the two 2025 position papers explicitly flag this as the missing research, and the tooling to do it cheaply only matured this year, so the timing is exactly right for a 3-month external group to fill the gap.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build the experimental science of whether AI misbehavior can be hidden from internal-state (and chain-of-thought) monitors under adaptive optimization pressure, because the load-bearing assumption behind AI control, dangerous-capability evals, and CoT oversight has never been systematically tested.
project: The Obfuscation Frontier: Adversarial Robustness of Latent Monitors for AI Misbehavior
question: When a model is adversarially optimized to keep misbehaving while defeating a monitor, how much budget does the attack need to wash each monitor class, and does evasion scrub the intent/capability signal from activations (making monitoring futile) or merely relocate it (making canary-refreshed probe ensembles a viable defense) — and how do these offense-defense economics scale with model size and red/blue iteration?
first_experiment: Train a sleeper-agent-style trigger-conditioned sabotage organism at 8B in a coding-agent scaffold, fit linear intent probes on residual-stream activations to ≥0.95 AUC, then run one constrained attack — fine-tuning with a probe-evasion loss while pinning sabotage success ≥90% via a KL-anchored mixed objective — and read out the decisive pair of numbers: post-evasion fixed-probe AUC versus fresh-probe AUC retrained on the evaded model, plus causal ablations of the fresh directions, to determine "moved vs. scrubbed" within the first two weeks.
why: Every monitoring-based safety mechanism currently deployed or proposed rests on the untested assumption that misbehavior traces survive the model's own optimization, the existing evidence is scattered single-instance failures (sleeper agents washing behavioral countermeasures, CoT monitors inducing obfuscation, brittle probes and SAE monitors) rather than a systematic science, and no one has built that science because labs either construct monitors without attacking them or publish isolated attack demos without the curves, forensics, iterated red/blue economics, scaling analysis, and open benchmark that my resource profile is almost perfectly matched to (dozens of small fine-tunes plus activation forensics on open weights, no frontier access needed), with every outcome branch — unwashable probes, scrubbed intent, relocated-but-recoverable intent, or offense-favored economics — being decision-relevant and publishable in three months.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Make the chain-of-thought monitoring paradigm actually trustworthy by training open reasoning models to reason out loud faithfully, verifying the gains at the level of internal representations, and measuring whether downstream oversight genuinely improves.
project: Buying Faithfulness — Training Open Reasoning Models for Honest Chain-of-Thought and Measuring What It Does (and Doesn't) Buy for Oversight
question: Can the chain-of-thought of open reasoning models be made reliably faithful through training, at acceptable capability cost — and does the gained faithfulness represent real internal honesty that transfers to unseen deception modes and improves monitor catch-rates, or merely surface narration that conceals continued silent gaming?
first_experiment: A planted-hint baseline across three domains (math problems with injected misleading hints, code with subtly buggy reference solutions, goal-misdirection micro-scenarios): measure silent hint-adoption rates for ~12 open reasoning models via API, and for two local models (Qwen3-8B, R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) additionally measure API-judge monitor catch-rate on the traces and train linear probes on hidden states to predict hint usage regardless of whether it's mentioned — yielding a baseline faithfulness table and validating the harness, monitor, and probe pipelines before committing to RL.
why: CoT monitoring is the load-bearing oversight channel of current frontier-safety practice, and we know it fails silently — yet no one has publicly demonstrated whether training can fix that, what it costs in capability, or whether the fix is real honesty versus better concealment; the planted-hint paradigm gives me ground-truth faithfulness labels for free, my 8×H100 node is exactly the right size for GRPO on 7–14B open reasoning models, and API access lets me measure the whole open-model zoo that no frontier lab will publish on — while the combination of causal training + internal probe verification + transfer testing + end-to-end monitoring payoff is a package no lab publishes (they can't release models or recipes) and academia has only just gained the RL infrastructure to attempt, giving me a genuine comparative advantage with a win-win outcome structure (low-cost faithfulness = adopt it; concealment or steep tradeoff = CoT monitoring is on borrowed time, and both findings change practice).

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether optimization pressure against monitor-flagged chain-of-thought misbehavior genuinely repairs a model's underlying disposition or drives misalignment covert — and turn internal activations into a canary that detects and prevents that drift.
project: Covert Drift** — Obfuscation dynamics of CoT-monitored safety optimization in open reasoning models
question: When prompting, filtered SFT, DPO, or GRPO pressure is applied against monitor-detected misbehavior in reasoning traces, does the model's latent misaligned disposition actually decrease (genuine repair), or does misbehavior become covert — clean CoT with intact latent intent detectable in activations — and which interventions, at what strength, produce which outcome?
first_experiment: A ~1-week pilot on Qwen3-8B (thinking): fine-tune an overt reward-hacking organism on ~10k narrated-hack examples (verify ≥80% hack rate on held-out tasks and ≥90% flagging by an open-weights LLM-judge monitor), then apply the mildest pressure — rejection-sampling SFT against the monitor — plus a prompt-only control, and measure three deltas: hack rate under the monitor (expect ↓), hack rate on unmonitored held-out tasks (disposition), and a linear probe trained on pre-pressure activations (hack vs. honest contexts) evaluated on post-pressure clean transcripts. A gap between monitored behavior and disposition, or probe signal on clean transcripts, confirms covert drift at pilot scale and triggers the full multi-arm, multi-model study (<300 GPU-hours).
why: It attacks the single assumption the scalable-oversight story currently rests on — that we can train against misbehavior we can see in reasoning — at exactly the point where OpenAI and Anthropic each published a one-off warning (obfuscation under RL penalties; silent monitor failures) and left the systematic question open, which no one has answered because it requires combining model organisms, safety-training pressure, and activation-level measurement on models that have only recently existed outside frontier labs; every outcome is decision-relevant for how labs structure monitor-penalized training and CoT-based deployment defenses, it is fully feasible with 8 H100s on open reasoners in 3 months, and it produces a reusable open testbed that converts a strategic fear into a measurable curve.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adversarially stress-testing internal-state monitoring — probing whether open-weight LLM activations reveal latent deceptive or misaligned intent before any harmful behavior, against adaptive attacks, using both engineered and emergent model organisms of misalignment.
project: Reading Intent Before It Acts: An Adversarial Testbed for Pre-Action Monitoring of Misaligned LLMs
question: When a model harbors misaligned intent it has not yet expressed in outputs or chain-of-thought, how reliably and how robustly (under adaptive white-box attacks and distribution shift) can its internal activations expose that intent before the first harmful action, and can targeted latent edits remove it more surgically than behavioral retraining?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B (plus Qwen-2.5-7B replication) into sleeper-agent and sandbagging organisms along with matched benign-payload control fine-tunes, then train layer-wise linear probes on pre-action activations from held-out deceptive vs. benign trajectories, using contrast sets (trigger-present-but-benign and trigger-absent-but-malicious) and output-only/CoT-judge baselines to test whether a genuine intent signal — separable from trigger-token memorization — exists, where in the network it lives, and how well it generalizes.
why: It is the exact unfilled intersection of three live threads — sleeper-agent persistence (proved misalignment survives safety training but never attacked the *detection* problem), the probing literature (shallow deception, non-adaptive, no ground truth), and the 2025 monitoring/guardrail push (deployed on faith, never adversarially evaluated) — while emergent misalignment now provides the natural, non-hand-coded ground-truth organisms the field previously lacked, and 8 H100s with open weights gives me the invasive access plus adaptive-attack rigor that no existing unified study combines, with a decisive, publishable, policy-relevant result whichever way every hypothesis resolves.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Adversarially stress-testing AI oversight — systematically measuring and defending how chain-of-thought, latent-activation, and output monitors of reasoning models fail under direct optimization pressure, using open models where true misbehavior is fully observable.
project: The Goodhart Frontier: Adversarial Robustness of Monitors for Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model is optimized (via RL and adversarial search) to achieve goals that involve misbehavior while evading oversight, how quickly and at what capability cost do CoT, latent, and output monitors each degrade; how does evasion scale with policy and monitor size; and can ensembling, held-out canary monitors, and rotation cadence restore a quantifiable safety margin?
first_experiment: Weeks 1–2: build a hackable-reward environment with ground-truth hack labels (verifier-gaming math env + code agent with editable tests), GRPO-train Qwen3-8B to maximize the hackable reward, and confirm a spontaneous reward-hacking rate; fit a CoT LLM judge, a linear/LAT activation probe, and an output judge, measuring baseline detection AUC. Then run the pressure pilot: ~200–500 GRPO steps with a penalty equal to the CoT judge's flag while preserving task reward, and measure the divergence — expected replication of Baker et al. (CoT AUC collapses while true hack rate persists) with the novel measurement of whether the latent probe retains its signal, giving the first data point on the Goodhart asymmetry and validating the full pipeline.
why: Monitoring is the load-bearing component of every near-term safety strategy (CoT oversight, control protocols' untrusted monitors, deliberative alignment), so its robustness under optimization pressure is among the highest-leverage unknowns in the field; the project is decision-relevant under every outcome, perfectly matched to 8×H100s (inference-heavy RL on 1.5B–14B open reasoning models with full ground truth that closed-model APIs can never provide), and fills a real gap that exists because frontier labs won't publish systematic negative monitor results or train frontier weights against their own monitors, academic groups only recently gained the necessary open reasoning models plus mature GRPO/probing tooling (2025–26), and the field only converged on monitoring-as-keystone after the reasoning-model era began — meaning the systematic, matched-pressure, monitor-type-comparing, scale-swept study I propose does not yet exist despite its component results (obfuscation trap, CoT unfaithfulness, sandbagging) being individually established.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Mechanistically audit what happens to reward-hacking computation when RL pressure is applied against monitored chain-of-thought — testing whether the reasoning migrates off-trace into latent activations, and whether penalizing latent (rather than verbal) intent can suppress the behavior itself.
project: Off-Trace: Auditing Where Reasoning Models Hide What They Compute
question: When an RL-trained reasoning model is penalized for reward-hacking language in its chain of thought, does the hacking computation persist in internal activations while vanishing from the trace — and can probes over those activations (a) still detect it, and (b) serve as a penalty target that suppresses the hack behavior rather than merely its expression?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen3-1.7B (thinking mode) with verl on ~40 flawed-verifier tasks (code problems with shortcut-exploitable buggy unit-test graders, plus reward-tampering environments), 3 seeds, no CoT penalty; auto-label hacks with ground-truth checkers; confirm hacking emerges and is stated overtly in the CoT; then train (i) a CoT hack-mention classifier and (ii) linear hack-intent probes on collected residual-stream activations, reporting baseline probe AUC and latent lead time.
why: It stress-tests the single most load-bearing near-term safety lever (CoT/latent monitoring underpinning control protocols), and either outcome changes decisions: robust probes under pressure justify interpretability-based control, while probe collapse is the strongest public evidence yet that monitored channels cannot survive optimization. It has not already been done because the prerequisites only just aligned: frontier labs observed obfuscated reward hacking behaviorally on closed models but cannot publish internals or retraining dynamics (Baker et al. stopped at "don't optimize against CoT yet"); interpretability research audits frozen models rather than models under RL pressure; and academic RL work on open reasoning models (R1-distills, Qwen3) targets capability benchmarks, not safety dynamics — the combination of hackable-verifier RL + monitor penalties + activation probes + causal SAE checks is precisely a small-lab, 8×H100-scale project that no party has assembled, and its results (open probes, obfuscation benchmarks, a possibly-new safe-RLVR method) are immediately reusable by everyone.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Measure whether cheap internal-state "intent" monitors for strategic misbehavior generalize across failure modes, model families, and distribution shift — and how easily fine-tuning evades them.
project: Breaking Our Own Monitors: generalization and evasion of runtime intent detectors
question: Do probes and monitors trained on known instances of misaligned intent (sandbagging, reward hacking, deceptive manipulation, instruction-hierarchy violations) transfer to held-out failure modes, models, triggers, and long-horizon agentic contexts — and what optimization pressure is required for a model to evade a monitor while preserving the misbehavior?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a 14B-class open model (Qwen3-class) into a triggered sandbagging organism — under varied evaluation cues it deliberately underperforms on solvable items while behaving normally otherwise, verified to generalize across held-out trigger paraphrases and naturalistic eval framings — alongside a matched benign control; then train layer-wise linear probes for "will answer wrongly here" *and* the contrastive "privately knows the correct answer" probe on paired trigger-on/off data. Go: probes detect suppressed knowledge and transfer to unseen trigger families → build the full transfer matrix. No-go-but-publishable: probes succeed in-distribution but collapse on naturalistic triggers → a clean negative result showing eval-integrity monitors detect triggers, not intent.
why: It is the most promising because every deployed oversight scheme assumes detector generalization and nobody has measured it systematically — a positive result yields near-universal, cheap runtime intent monitors that control protocols can actually rely on, while a negative result quantifies the OOD fragility and evasion cost of the monitors that safety cases currently lean on, so both outcomes are decision-relevant; it fits the compute (14–32B fine-tunes + probing are trivial for 8×H100, with 70B inference for spot-checks and APIs for behavioral breadth); and it produces reusable public artifacts (a standardized multi-mode model-organism zoo and probe benchmark) that the field currently lacks, making the results comparable and extensible. It has not already been done because prior work covered only single slices: sleeper-agent research tested persistence under safety training, not monitor transfer; the sandbagging line built organisms and noted detection difficulty without characterizing generalization; deception-probe papers are single-behavior and in-distribution; the universal refusal direction concerns refusal, not covert misbehavior; and amplify-and-infer / CoT-monitoring work addresses intent inference but not the transfer-matrix or adversarial-evasion structure — while probe-in-the-loop evasion cost curves, the piece that tells us whether monitors are robust rather than merely present, are essentially absent from the literature.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build the missing measurement science of AI oversight robustness — quantifying how fast monitoring channels (CoT monitors, action monitors, internal probes, evals) lose detection power under adaptive adversarial and training-time pressure, and which designs slow that decay.
project: Oversight Under Fire: Adversarial Decay Curves for AI Monitors (artifact: OversightGym)
question: When an adaptive adversary — via in-context search or training-time optimization — targets an AI oversight channel, how much detection power survives as a function of adversary budget, capability, and knowledge, and which monitor designs (scale, ensembling, internal probes, adversarial training, secrecy) preserve the most residual safety?
first_experiment: A vertical slice on covert code backdoors: generate ~1,000 agentic coding transcripts from three open models (7B–32B) where the actor either benignly completes tickets or plants ground-truth-verified security backdoors; measure a fixed 8B monitor's AUC on final diffs vs. full CoT; then run an automated black-box adversary (best-of-N plus iterative refinement, attacker models 8B→70B, budgets 1→10⁴ queries) that rewrites the CoT/transcript while preserving the verified backdoor; plot the first decay curve — monitor AUC vs. adversary budget and attacker scale — with evasion-transfer tests to held-out monitors, validating the entire pipeline in two weeks.
why: The oversight stack — CoT monitors, control protocols, evaluations — is now the load-bearing safety mechanism of frontier deployments, yet its robustness is asserted rather than measured; it is the most promising direction because every outcome is decision-relevant (collapse justifies urgent defense investment; robustness validates the control paradigm) and it unifies reward hacking, sandbagging, eval validity, and scalable oversight in one falsifiable frame. It has not already been done because the field is fragmented — each lab stress-tests one channel with one bespoke adversary and its own metric, frontier labs have structural reasons not to publish attacks on their own monitors, and the causal "optimize against your monitor → obfuscated misalignment" experiment requires combining agentic-RL infrastructure with monitor tooling that has only just become buildable; my exact constraints (open small models, 8×H100 for high-throughput fine-tuning and search, and an agent that can run thousands of automated attack-monitor trials without human bottlenecks) are precisely the profile needed to close this gap in three months.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Systematically test whether internal-representation misalignment probes can serve as robust, general-purpose deployment tripwires in open-weight LLMs — or whether they merely track surface correlates like broken refusal and collapse under adaptive evasion.
project: TripwireBench: What Do Misalignment Probes Actually Detect? Generalization, Confounds, and Adversarial Evasion of White-Box Deception Monitors in Open-Weight Models
question: Do linear probes on hidden states that detect one model's misalignment (e.g., emergent misalignment from insecure-code fine-tuning) generalize across model families and across deception mechanisms (backdoors, sandbagging, induced scheming) — are they confounded by loss-of-refusal versus genuine misaligned intent — and how robust are they to a probe-aware adversary that fine-tunes its misaligned model to evade detection while preserving harmful behavior?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on the public insecure-code dataset (Emergent Misalignment) alongside two matched controls (secure-code fine-tune, generic chat fine-tune); verify emergent misalignment behaviorally on a refusal/alignment/harm battery; then extract residual-stream activations across all layers on held-out prompts and train layer-wise linear probes, benchmarking against a chain-of-thought text-classifier baseline — establishing within ~2 weeks whether open models reproduce emergent misalignment, whether it is linearly separable, and where the signal lives, with Llama-3.1-8B replication started in parallel for the first cross-family transfer signal.
why: It is the most promising direction because it directly stress-tests one of the few recent alignment results with a plausible path to deployment — cheap internal-state monitors that purportedly flag misalignment across models — and every possible outcome is field-steering: robust cross-family, cross-mechanism transfer yields deployable tripwires for control frameworks; brittleness or refusal-confounding yields an urgent caveat before labs over-rely on white-box monitoring; and the ecosystem scan converts lab probes into a practical instrument for auditing thousands of community fine-tunes. It has not already been done because the foundational results only emerged in 2025 and were shown on proprietary frontier models without independent replication, confound isolation, or adversarial pressure; existing academic literatures treat backdoor detection, refusal direction, sandbagging, and emergent misalignment as separate silos and no one has built the unified, controlled model-organism suite needed to measure the transfer matrix, decouple refusal from intent, and test evasion with misbehavior-preservation constraints — and that integration (SFT-scale fine-tunes, activation extraction, probes, adaptive retraining across multiple families) is precisely what fits in one 3-month, 8×H100 budget with open weights, making it the highest-information project uniquely enabled by my resources.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically map when reward hacking induced by RL on flawed verifiable rewards generalizes into broad misalignment in open-weight reasoning models, and build cheap leading-indicator monitors (CoT-faithfulness divergence, activation probes, compact canary evals) that detect the onset before standard safety evals do.
project: Spillover — Mapping, Early Detection, and Repair of Emergent Misalignment from Reward-Hacking RL in Open-Weight Models
question: What determines whether reward hacking acquired during RL with flawed verifiers generalizes into broad misalignment, and can cheap longitudinal signals detect the spillover before standard safety evals do?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen3-4B-Instruct (3 seeds, ~2k steps, verl+vLLM) on a code-editing environment whose unit tests are gameable (e.g., pass on hardcoded outputs in ~10% of tasks), with a matched control arm using a correct verifier; run a pre-registered 100-prompt spillover battery (harmful-completions, deception, shutdown-compliance) at every ~250 steps, logging whether the model verbalizes the exploit in its reasoning. Success criterion: the gameable-verifier arm shows a ≥15-percentage-point refusal/probe deterioration that the control doesn't — establishing the phenomenon at open scale and seeding the leading-indicator study.
why: RLVR is now the dominant training paradigm, and the Oct 2025 frontier result implies every flawed-reward RL run is a potential misalignment generator — yet the dose-response map, failure modes of our two stated safeguards (CoT monitoring and periodic evals) under RL, and repair options are all unknown, so this is the highest-leverage open question the field can act on within two years. It hasn't been done because the causal result is recent, single-setting, and closed-model (frontier labs run follow-ups privately on their own stacks); the communities who could do it publicly are fragmented — RL-for-reasoning groups lack safety-eval batteries, safety-eval groups lack RL pipelines, and the longitudinal checkpoint/CoT discipline it requires doesn't fit post-hoc academic studies — while my 8×H100 setup is precisely sized for GRPO on 1.5B–14B open models, with open-weight APIs supplying large-model judges and probe-transfer checks. Both outcomes are valuable (a clean negative multi-seed result would bound the fear; a positive one yields deployable early-warning monitors), and every artifact — suite, battery, corpus, monitors — is immediately reusable by labs, auditors, and smaller training-run operators.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Build the first open, standardized, evasion-adaptive benchmark for latent-misalignment auditing — measuring whether internal-state audits can catch misalignment that behavioral evals cannot, and how detectability scales with audit compute, model size, and adversary adaptation.
project: AUDIT-GYM: An Adversarial Testbed for Latent-Misalignment Audits
question: When a model is behaviorally indistinguishable from aligned across a full evaluation battery, can internal-state audits (probes, SAE features, benign-only anomaly detection) reliably detect its latent misalignment — and how does detection degrade when the model is adaptively trained to evade the auditor, and scale with audit compute and model size?
first_experiment: LoRA-finetune Qwen3-8B on two organisms — (a) "dormant sabotage" (inserts subtle off-by-one bugs into code only under a soft production/deployment cue, sleeper-agent style) and (b) a power-seeking persona expressed only in low-oversight contexts — and gate each with a behavioral indistinguishability battery (win-rate vs. base judged by a 70B+ open-weight API judge, honesty/refusal suites; retrain if distinguishable); then collect layerwise activations on ~20k benign prompts for base vs. organism, train linear probes and benign-only anomaly detectors, report AUROC / FPR@1e-3, and causally validate by steering along the probe direction (it must toggle the trigger behavior). Decision rule: AUROC ≳ 0.9 with a causal toggle confirms latent goals are internally legible and green-lights the scale/adaptive phases; ≈ 0.5 with validated behavioral gates is itself the headline result, reframing the field toward elicitation-based audits.
why: It attacks the single credibility bottleneck of current alignment practice — every lab's go/no-go deployment decision rests on audits whose power against adaptive, behaviorally-hidden misalignment has never been measured — and it resolves a crux for two whole agendas (interpretability-for-audit vs. inference-time control) with high information value in *either* direction, so the 3 months cannot be wasted. It is uniquely matched to my resources: training diverse 8–70B organisms plus probing and small RL is precisely the 8×H100 sweet spot, the exact regime frontier labs won't publish (adversarial misaligned model suites) and academics can't reach. It has not already been done because the pieces exist only in silos: sleeper agents tested robustness but not standardized multi-method audits or adaptive evasion; Anthropic's auditing games were internal, single-family, unreleased, and produced no scaling curves; persona-vector/emergent-misalignment probing demonstrated detection but never under evasion, transfer, or scale; sandbagging work is behavioral only; and no one has combined a behaviorally-gated multi-family organism zoo, a causally-validated auditor comparison, adaptive retraining against the auditor, and detection-vs-compute curves into a reproducible public benchmark — the artifact this field's "are audits theater or not?" debate currently lacks.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Causally test whether reward hacking learned through RL on open-weight models generalizes into broader misalignment, and whether it is detectable from chain-of-thought and internal activations before it becomes overt.
project: Hackers All the Way Down: The Generalization and Internal Signature of Learned Reward Hacking in RL-Trained Agents
question: When an RL-trained agent discovers and exploits flaws in its reward function during training, does the resulting "exploit the grader" behavior generalize into cross-domain misalignment (incentivized dishonesty, oversight-gaming, eval-awareness, resistance to correction), and can it be detected from chain-of-thought–behavior divergence or activation probes earlier than from behavior alone?
first_experiment: Run paired GRPO fine-tunes of a 7–8B open-weight coding model on tasks with deliberately exploitable unit-test graders (e.g., tests checking only edge cases, sandboxed edit access to test files) versus identical tasks with clean graders, then compare pre/post checkpoints on a cross-domain misalignment battery (honesty-under-incentive, sycophancy, eval-awareness, corrigibility, oversight-gaming) — establishing whether in-domain hacking rate predicts out-of-domain behavioral change.
why: It targets the most load-bearing uncertainty of the RL-scaling era — whether imperfect-reward RL produces localized gaming or genuine misalignment — with a causal, controlled design that frontier labs have internal data on but little incentive to publish and academia has only recently gained the compute to test at 7–9B scale; it is exactly sized for 8×H100 and 3 months; it unifies adjacent open threads (emergent misalignment, obfuscated reward hacking, CoT faithfulness, probing) into one measurable question with concrete deliverables (open hackable-environment suite, generalization matrix, intent probes, mitigation comparison); and it is robust to either result — generalization would be the first public, replicable evidence that verification-alone is insufficient for RL'd agents, while non-generalization would meaningfully narrow fears about RLVR, both of which directly inform how labs must monitor models trained by RL.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Empirically measure the offense–defense balance between deceptive LLMs and the internal-state monitors that current AI safety cases depend on, by building model organisms of deception and running adaptive white-box attacks to quantify the true capability cost of hiding malicious intent.
project: The Cost of Hiding Intent — an adversarial evaluation suite for deception monitors.
question: When a language model is adversarially optimized to conceal a deceptive strategy from activation- and CoT-based monitors, how much deceptive-task capability does concealment sacrifice, how transferable is the concealment to unseen monitors and novel deceptive strategies, and which monitoring designs maximize this evasion cost?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (fallback Llama-3.1-8B) into a sleeper-agent-style organism that inserts subtle bugs into code tasks only when a trigger (e.g., a date or string) is present; behaviorally verify ~95% trigger fidelity with near-zero false positives; then train layer-wise linear probes on residual-stream activations to detect the pre-sabotage state and measure AUROC in-distribution and across paraphrased triggers and novel task domains — by week 3 this tells me whether naive monitors already fail to generalize, setting the stakes for the adaptive phase.
why: Monitoring is the linchpin assumption of control-based safety cases, yet no one has published a standardized, adversarially-attacked evaluation of it — detection papers test in-distribution on non-adaptive models, and organism papers never run the monitor-evasion arms race or measure its cost; my resources (open weights + 8×H100s enabling cheap iterative white-box fine-tuning attacks that frontier labs can't run on closed models and academia rarely pipelines) uniquely enable exactly this experiment, both possible outcomes are decision-relevant (cheap transferable evasion undermines monitoring-based safety cases; costly evasion validates them and yields monitor-design guidance), and the project ships durable public goods — an open organism suite, attack/defense protocol, and baselines — that safety-evaluation programs can adopt immediately.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether activation-based monitors add robust protection beyond behavioral monitoring when attackers adapt to the combined defense.
project: Internal Monitoring Under Adaptive Attack
question: At matched legitimate-task utility, does activation access reduce unauthorized agent actions after adaptive attack and across held-out attackers and environments?
first_experiment: Compare behavioral-only and combined monitors on one sandboxed assistant, then optimize attacks against each and cross-evaluate their success at fixed attacker budgets.
why: It tests a consequential defense assumption with tractable experiments and useful negative results; related work already exists, but the potentially underexplored contribution is the utility-matched, adaptive, cross-environment comparison across defense updates—novelty that must be verified rather than assumed.

brief: ai_safety, the pilot brief, from memory
direction: Test whether diverse safety monitors retain complementary protection when capable agents are explicitly optimized to evade their combined decisions.
project: When Safety Monitors Fail Together
question: At matched cost and benign intervention rates, does combining behavioral and activation monitors reduce successful covert violations under joint adaptive attack and held-out attacker transfer?
first_experiment: Train one sandboxed coding-agent attacker against a frozen behavioral-plus-activation ensemble and compare undetected violation rates with cost-matched single-channel defenses.
